stories.Headline: HHS watchdog warns of cybersecurity and AI governance risks at HHS
stories.Summary:
The HHS Office of Inspector General issued an annual report on Tuesday, November 18, 2026, warning of persistent cyber weaknesses and AI oversight challenges at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. The report placed cybersecurity, AI and other tech-related issues among the top five categories of management and performance challenges facing HHS in 2026. The OIG said cyberattacks and related threats can jeopardize critical HHS operations and programs, potentially compromising the health and welfare of the individuals HHS serves. The watchdog said HHS has taken steps to modernize and strengthen its cybersecurity posture, but implementation varies across programs. The OIG said HHS's overall enterprise information security program has not yet reached the desired level of effectiveness.

The OIG said HHS must ensure consistent implementation of strong safeguards across operating divisions. The report warned that rapidly expanding adoption of AI technologies, dubbed "super intelligence" by the Trump administration, presents governance and security challenges when risks are not fully understood or tested before deployment. HHS in its 2025 inventory identified 446 AI use cases, including applications supporting core government functions, the OIG said. The OIG cited a 2025 cyber-related audit of the National Institutes of Health's All of Us research program and a 2024 security review of the HHS office of the secretary's cloud infrastructure unit. The OIG also cited 2026 findings involving weaknesses in cybersecurity protections of Medicare enrollee data at a large unnamed hospital in the southeastern U.S. and a 2025 settlement related to false claims allegations involving vulnerabilities in genomic sequencing systems from Illumina Inc.

The OIG wrote that responsible adoption requires clear governance, disciplined implementation and continuous oversight, so decisionmakers can weigh benefits and risks without compromising the people served by HHS or statutory obligations. The OIG wrote that rapid evolution and adoption create pressure to advance quickly, although some risks may not be fully understood or tested. The OIG wrote that HHS must ensure thoughtful adoption of technology that benefits HHS programs and their mission. The OIG stressed the importance of HHS establishing clear governance policies, providing appropriate training, maintaining human oversight and continuously monitoring technology-related risks. The OIG urged HHS to adapt its oversight and enforcement of HIPAA to better address evolving privacy and cybersecurity threats, working within existing HIPAA authorities.

Attorney Lee Kim, founder of consulting firm Keytera, said HHS should have a plan for reducing technical debt, including legacy IT and OT systems, and should implement compensating controls if certain systems cannot be modernized. Kim said HHS should regularly test redundancy, failover, incident response, business continuity and disaster recovery plans, and that regular vulnerability assessments and penetration testing are essential. Kim, former senior cyber and privacy adviser at the Healthcare Information and Systems Management Society, said HHS should establish technical standards for developing, evaluating and deploying AI systems, including standards for training and testing data and processes, model architecture, and model modifications and updates. Nitin Natarajan, founder of consulting firm NN Global LLC and former CISA deputy director during the Biden administration, said the technical debt most organizations face far exceeds available modernization budgets, and in some cases modernization isn't possible without significant operational impact. Natarajan said organizations need to fully understand the tools they implement, including cybersecurity, transparency, information security and privacy matters, and that AI vendors must be transparent about their tools and impacts.

The OIG wrote that effective cybersecurity must also extend to the thousands of HHS contractors, grantees and other external entities engaged by HHS programs. The report said healthcare organizations remain attractive targets for cybercriminals because of the sensitive information they maintain and their dependence on interconnected technologies. Limited financial resources, legacy technology and shortages of cybersecurity professionals further complicate efforts to defend against attacks that can compromise patient information and disrupt essential healthcare services, the OIG wrote. Natarajan said recent significant IT systems disruptions, including router issues allegedly at the center of last week's Federal Aviation Administration outage, underscore the risks involving legacy equipment. Natarajan said this is especially important in sectors such as healthcare, where there are significant third-party risks, substantial interconnectedness across the sector and high concentration risks in various elements of the healthcare ecosystem.

HHS did not immediately respond to ISMG's request for comment on the OIG's findings and how the department is addressing the watchdog agency's concerns. The OIG said the findings underscore the challenges facing HHS as it works to improve its own cybersecurity practices while overseeing security and privacy protections across the nation's healthcare sector. Natarajan said that without a focused effort to identify and invest in the modernization of legacy technology, impacts to the healthcare system across the nation will continue, ultimately affecting the delivery of safe and timely patient care. Natarajan said organizations across the public and private sectors need to do more to invest in short- and long-term plans to modernize legacy technology or face the risk of significant operational impacts in the near and long term. Kim said models should be tested for accuracy, bias, uncertainty, data leakage, adversarial vulnerabilities and other unintended behavior.

stories.Headline: South Korea surpasses 1 trillion dollars in annual exports driven by AI chip demand
stories.Summary:
South Korea reached a historic milestone on November 19, 2026, when its annual exports surpassed one trillion dollars for the first time. This massive growth was driven by a global artificial intelligence boom that increased demand for semiconductors and other information technology products. The country became only the fourth economy to reach this level, following the United States, China, and Germany. Semiconductor exports were the primary engine, reaching about 397 billion dollars between January and October of 2026. This surge represents a fundamental change in the national export structure as AI becomes a principal driver of growth.

The shift requires high-performance memory and storage, with ICT exports hitting 70.35 billion dollars in October, more than triple the previous year. ICT products made up 61 percent of total October exports, which reached 115.28 billion dollars, staying above 60 percent for three months. Semiconductor exports alone jumped 259.4 percent in October to 56.47 billion dollars, while September shipments exceeded 60 billion dollars for one month. Computer exports reached 5.99 billion dollars in October, and mobile phone exports rose 6.5 percent to 1.71 billion dollars that month. Shipments to China tripled to 27.2 billion dollars in October, while United States shipments increased sixfold to 15.56 billion dollars.

The Ministry of Science and ICT provided the October semiconductor figures, which showed a jump driven by high memory chip prices and demand. The government expects semiconductor exports to support overall shipments through the third quarter of 2027 due to AI data center investments. Officials from the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources identified nuclear reactors, defense products, and consumer goods as potential new growth industries. They believe the country must use semiconductor competitiveness to develop a broader ecosystem including robotics, biotechnology, and advanced manufacturing. The government also targets physical AI and data centers to attract more foreign investment into the national economy.

Foreign investors are responding, with third quarter direct investment notifications rising 10.8 percent to 22.9 billion dollars, while actual arrivals hit 14.87 billion. United States investment notifications specifically increased 35.1 percent to 6.69 billion dollars, with manufacturing facilities accounting for 80 percent of notified investment. This boom affects Korean manufacturers who now supply multiple layers of the AI chain, from memory chips to server solid state drives. However, the country is exposed to geopolitical risks, including technology restrictions between Washington and Beijing and changes in semiconductor export controls. The economy is also vulnerable to the cyclical nature of semiconductor prices and expanding production from Chinese semiconductor manufacturers.

The background shows that Korea exported just over 700 billion dollars in 2025 before the current AI investment cycle accelerated growth. During the first ten months of 2026, the cumulative trade surplus reached 294.9 billion dollars, tripling the 2017 record of 95.2 billion. IT manufacturing is now forecast to approach one third of the total gross domestic product for the coming year. Other sectors like pharmaceuticals, cosmetics, and shipbuilding for high value LNG carriers have also reached record export levels recently. These figures demonstrate how deeply the national export performance is now intertwined with global AI infrastructure investment cycles.

Next, the government will attempt to diversify the export base to avoid over dependence on the volatile memory chip market. The country aims to turn the current semiconductor boom into a sustainable long term growth cycle through new high value jobs. It remains to be seen if Korea can successfully expand its technology ecosystem beyond traditional semiconductor shipments to ensure stability. The articles leave open whether a correction in memory prices or a shift in AI architecture will rapidly change industry profitability. It is unclear if the current concentration of exports will amplify the impact of the next inevitable semiconductor downturn.

stories.Headline: Visa expands its Agentic Ready program in Asia Pacific to scale AI agent commerce
stories.Summary:
Visa announced the expansion of its Agentic Ready program across Asia Pacific on November 18, 2026, from its office in Singapore. This second phase of the program focuses on strengthening acceptance for transactions that are initiated by artificial intelligence agents. Visa is working with a diverse range of partners to prepare the region for these new types of AI commerce. The company aims to help scale trusted commerce by bringing together various technology partners and payment service providers. This expansion follows an initial phase that launched in April 2026 to focus on the readiness of issuers.

The program launches with over 50 participants, and Visa expects additional partners to join the initiative throughout the year 2027. Acceptance partners include Adyen, Stripe, Airwallex, 2C2P by Antom, Allinpay Merchant Services, ALTEKGLOBAL by VNPAY, ASB Bank, AsiaPay, and AXS. Other partners are Bank of China (Hong Kong), CAKE DIGITAL BANK, Checkout.com, Cherri Tech, Commonwealth Bank of Australia, and Credit Saison Co., Ltd. Participants also include Cuscal Limited, DBS Bank, DCS, dLocal, Eximbay, Fat Zebra, Fiserv, FOMO Pay, GMO Epsilon, Inc., and GMO Payment Gateway, Inc. Further partners are Hang Seng Bank, ICBC (Asia), Infcurion, Inc., Kasikorn Global Payment Co.,Ltd., KG Inicis, Maybank, and Mitsubishi UFJ NICOS Co., Ltd. The list continues with Mizuho Bank, Ltd., National Australia Bank, NETS, Nuvei, OCBC, OEN Tech, Pine Labs, Rakuten Card Co., Ltd., and Razorpay. Retail Payment Solutions as a Coles Group company, SB Payment Service Corp., Sumitomo Mitsui Card Company, Limited, Toss Payments, UOB, UQPay, Windcave, Wpay, Xendit, YeahPay, and YeePay are also involved.

T.R. Ramachandran, Head of Products and Solutions for Asia Pacific at Visa, stated that agentic commerce requires secure and reliable support. He noted that merchants and payment providers need a clear way to understand and strengthen their readiness for these transactions. Ramachandran believes the program helps merchants prepare for this next chapter while maintaining the trust and security consumers expect. AI assistants are moving beyond product recommendations to build shopping carts and make payments on behalf of consumers, affecting many merchants. Merchants must now determine how to recognize a trusted agent and support it through checkout, payment, and post-purchase service.

Visa is collaborating with Atlas Kitchen, CardInfoLink, Cleverbridge, Clink, Eats365 POS, FluxA, Juspay, [manif], Obenan, Pivota, Prava, and Reap Technologies Limited. They are also working with Set Sail AI, Shoplazza, and SHOPLINE to explore how agents discover products and connect to payment. These collaborations aim to test how agents can function in real-world commerce experiences across the Asia Pacific region. The first phase of the program saw over 100 issuers across 10 markets join in a controlled, production-grade environment. Agentic Ready builds on Visa Intelligent Commerce, which is a portfolio of initiatives enabling secure agentic commerce experiences at scale.

Visa uses its experience in digital payments, tokenisation, authentication, risk management, and network controls to support the broader ecosystem. The Visa Acceptance Platform provides capabilities for credential management, fraud protection, dispute resolution, and acceptance across various different channels. Additionally, Intelligence Commerce Connect enables agentic commerce experiences across networks, payment schemes, commerce platforms, and various AI agents. Acceptance partners will now work with Visa to assess existing systems, identify gaps, and test agent-initiated transactions in real-world environments.

Testing will examine how partners recognize trusted agents and support agent-led discovery, checkout, and post-purchase interactions using tokenised credentials. Organizations that are interested in joining Agentic Ready or collaborating on agentic commerce can contact their specific Visa representative. The articles leave open how many more partners will join in 2027 and the specific results of the system tests. They also do not state the specific names of the 10 markets that participated in the first phase.

stories.Headline: Marvell proposes a custom high bandwidth memory layout to increase compute area for AI accelerators
stories.Summary:
Marvell presented a custom high bandwidth memory layout at the OCP Global Summit in October. This new design moves the memory controller into a custom base die beneath each DRAM stack. The company aims to free up compute area and lower interface power for AI accelerators. This shift occurs as custom high bandwidth memory moves toward mass production for AI chips. The change moves memory control logic away from the edge of the compute die.

The layout replaces the wide XPU edge interface with a narrower die to die physical link. Marvell estimates this provides up to 25 percent more compute area and 33 percent more stacks. Interface power could drop by 70 percent, while adaptive power management cuts power by 42 to 75 percent. NVIDIA unveiled its NVHBM platform in August 2026 for AWS Trainium 4 and the Feynman GPU. These custom systems will use advanced logic processes, which increases the importance of TSMC.

Marvell stated that no single company can build custom high bandwidth memory alone in the current market. They argued that the base die, interface, and package thermals must be co-designed as one system. The company identified the die to die physical interface in the base die as a heat hotspot. Marvell suggested using silicon heat paths, copper to copper hybrid bonding, or etched coolant channels for cooling. They noted that package cooling must be designed alongside the memory stack to manage heat.

AI chip developers are evaluating custom memory because standard versions prioritize compatibility over optimization for individual accelerators. IBM Technology explained that some workloads are limited by memory bandwidth rather than by computing capacity. These bottlenecks are understood through the roofline model and the measurement of arithmetic intensity for data movement. Memory makers, foundries, OSATs, and XPU designers are all affected by this new division of labor. The design payoff depends on where memory logic sits and the specific AI workload needs.

HBM has traditionally been the home turf of memory makers like SK hynix, Samsung, and Micron. These companies previously controlled both the design and manufacturing of DRAM dies and the bottom base dies. Marvell estimates that HBM takes 30 percent of AI accelerator die area and half of XPU cost. A Samsung study showed internal thermal resistance is 57 percent of the HBM stack total resistance. This resistance is much higher than the 13 percent found in the adjacent ASIC total resistance.

Next generation memory running above 28 Gbps is expected to have heat flux exceeding 2.0 watts per millimeter. Projections indicate that internal temperatures in 16 high HBM stacks will exceed thermal budgets by the year 2028. TrendForce will provide more insights on foundry and DRAM breakthroughs at a Tokyo roadshow on December 8. The articles leave open how fast CPO will scale and how the US-China market reshapes servers. They do not state if these potential design gains will guarantee an increase in workload speed.

stories.Headline: South Korea inspects exam candidates glasses and blocks Wi-Fi to stop AI cheating
stories.Summary:
South Korea will inspect all glasses worn by students taking this week's national college entrance exam to prevent AI-assisted cheating. This action follows a confession on Sunday by a person who placed first in the 2026 tax accountant exam. The individual admitted to photographing questions with a microcamera and using an AI tool and smartphone to find answers. These events shook public confidence in the country's high-stakes testing system and caused panic before the college test. The government is now implementing strict security measures to protect the integrity of the upcoming national examinations.

The Education Ministry will inspect all glasses in every session of the College Scholastic Ability Test in Seoul and other centers. Smart devices were added to the banned items list in July, and public Wi-Fi will be blocked during the exams. Every exam room will have warning notices about criminal penalties, and each center will have one staff member monitoring devices. A hotline will link centers to local education offices and the ministry's control room to judge difficult cases on the spot. Prime Minister Han Seong-sook announced that emergency alerts will be sent before the exam to detect any hidden mobile phones.

Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin told a parliamentary hearing on November 16 that the ministry would inspect all eyewear worn by candidates. He stated that the ministry would work with parliament to lengthen the current one-year exam ban to three or ten years. Choi also noted that offenders may be reported to the police for obstructing official duties during the national testing process. Prime Minister Han Seong-sook said the government would form an emergency team to prepare measures to safeguard the college entrance exam. She urged officials to develop AI-based detection technology and called for strengthened penalties for those who cheat using technology.

Some people called for the university entrance exam to be postponed to ensure fairness, but the Education Ministry ruled out delays. The Suneung exam is seen as a ticket to well-paid jobs and better marriage prospects in a hyper-competitive society. Students are affected by these changes, as anyone caught using smart devices will have their results invalidated for the current year. They will also be barred from sitting the exam the following year under the current rules and potential new penalties. The national exam is so intense that much of South Korea will stand still on Thursday to minimize student distractions.

The scandal began when the top tax accountant candidate confessed on November 15 to using a microcamera and AI for cheating. Smart glasses are a global concern because they can record confidential material or people without their knowledge or any consent. Grepp, a company with a 90 percent market share in online proctoring, uses a service called Monito for recruitment exams. This technology is already used by major corporations like Samsung Electronics, LG Electronics, and SK hynix for their own hiring processes. Grepp recorded 13.5 billion won in revenue last year and is now expanding into physical test center AI solutions.

The ministry will consult specialists on radio-signal detectors and may introduce this technology for the 2027 test to stop AI cheating. Grepp CEO Lim Sung-soo is discussing a pilot deployment of Monito at Prometric test centers in the United States next year. The company plans to seek accreditation as a private operator of nationally recognized qualification assessments and pursue an IPO in 2028. Articles leave open whether thermal imaging cameras or radio-frequency detectors will be used, as they face legal and technical challenges. It remains unclear if the government will successfully implement these high-tech tools due to interference with nearby wireless communications.

stories.Headline: Microsoft unveils cheaper in-house AI models for coding and cybersecurity at Ignite
stories.Summary:
Microsoft introduced several in-house AI models for coding and cybersecurity at its Ignite conference in San Francisco. These announcements occurred on November 17, 2026, to target software development and digital security tasks. The company aims to reduce its reliance on external AI providers like OpenAI and Anthropic. These new tools provide comparable performance to rivals but at significantly lower costs for users. Microsoft also launched models for image editing, audio processing, and healthcare transcription during the event.

MAI Code 2 delivers 98 per cent of GPT-6.1 Sol performance at 40 per cent cost. It matches Claude Opus 5.5 at 96 per cent performance for only 5 per cent cost. MAI Code 2 Flash matches GPT-6 Luna performance at 65 per cent price and Claude Haiku 5.5 at 20 per cent. MAI Cyber 2 Flash outperforms GPT-6 Astra for less than 2 per cent of the cost per task. Other models include MAI Image 2.7, MAI Realtime 1, and MAI Transcribe 2 for various specialized business applications.

Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman said the system co-optimizes performance and price and is not a flash in the pan. He also stated that preventing AI from taking harmful actions remains a top priority for the company. CEO Satya Nadella posted on X that the goal is to turn technological advances into real outcomes. The company plans to integrate MAI Code 2 into GitHub Copilot for developers and Azure for enterprises. Customers can license model weights to fine-tune and customize these tools using their own private data.

Secure Code Warrior tested over 30 models and found that lower-cost systems can sometimes be safer than flagship models. Their research involved building 15,000 applications and 41.3 million lines of code across 11 different programming languages. The study found that curated security rule sets reduced measured risk in AI-generated code by as much as 70 per cent. GPT-6 Luna had a mean risk score of 19.4 at 0.10 dollars, while Claude Opus 5.5 scored 43.6 at 8.17 dollars. Software teams are affected as AI is expected to account for 65 per cent of committed code by 2027.

Secure Code Warrior CEO Pieter Danhieux said assumptions that newer or more expensive models are more secure do not always hold. He noted that models do not use secure coding by default and rely on the prompts and rules provided. Stanford University research found human-only commits introduced roughly 0.08 vulnerabilities per 1,000 lines of code. The AI benchmark showed a 15-fold gap between the best and worst performers, ranging from 0.24 to 3.66 vulnerabilities. This background suggests that procurement decisions based only on branding or price may not reflect actual security outcomes.

Microsoft is currently developing a general-purpose frontier AI model to compete with broader systems beyond task-specific tools. Access to the MAI Cyber 2 Flash model is initially limited to a small group of select customers. The company has not yet announced specific pricing or availability timelines for all of the new AI models. It remains open whether the pricing advantages are due to promotional discounts or actual operational cost reductions. The articles leave open how these specialized models will perform against general models in scientific research problems.

stories.Headline: Microsoft unveils Windows Server 2028 with hardened security and local AI inference
stories.Summary:
Microsoft announced Windows Server 2028, its next major server operating system release, at the Ignite 2026 conference on Tuesday, according to TechGig. Network World reported the announcement on November 18, 2026, calling it Microsoft's largest platform update since Windows Server 2025. TechGig published its report on November 19, 2026, at 05:34 AM IST. A second TechGig article on November 20, 2026, at 04:50 AM IST covered the public preview. The release is now in public preview, Network World said.

The release ships with a hardened Server Core configuration by default and a new security baseline, TechGig reported. The default security aligns with hardened DoD benchmarks including DISA STIG, according to the second TechGig article. Security settings include Kerberos over NTLM, LSASS protection, strong passwords, SMB signing and encryption, a firewall active in every profile, and legacy name resolution turned off. Cryptography is limited to modern TLS cipher suites with hybrid post-quantum ML-KEM key exchange, and the paging file is encrypted. Trusted Launch extends boot integrity protection to virtual machines, and Confidential VM support begins a journey toward integrity-protected runtimes on compatible CVM hardware.

Neil Hinnant, Director of Windows Server & I/O Fabrics PM, said the baseline lets administrators relax specific settings, reducing the effort to establish a secure environment from day one. Hinnant said the release "begins our long term investments extending Microsoft Foundry to bring AI inference to fleets of local token factories." He said this offers customers more choices to place intelligence with the right cost structure. In a blog post he wrote that different workloads have different needs shaped by cost, latency, IP protection, data residency, and regulatory requirements. Microsoft said the secure configuration is the starting state, not a project run after setup, which closes the window where a newly deployed server sits exposed.

John Annand, associate VP at Infotech, noted that because this is the public preview phase, a lot remains a promise on the roadmap. Annand said customers wanting local AI on existing hardware would need to add Nvidia or AMD accelerators and lots of ever more expensive RAM. He said 10GbE network cards will likely be a bottleneck until customers upgrade to 50 or 100GbE+. He called Server 2028 a viable midpoint upgrade for existing hardware and said later adopters may be the winners. Enterprises are affected, along with administrators who can register for the Windows Insider Program for Windows Server or apply to the Windows Server Technology Adoption Program for earlier access.

Windows Server 2025 will remain under extended support until 2034, Network World reported. Windows Server 2022 is covered until Oct 14, 2031, Windows Server 2019 until Jan. 9, 2029, and Windows Server 2016 sunsets on January 12, 2027, all through the Windows Long-Term Servicing Channel. AMD's Instinct MI350P card is to be in preview in the first half of 2027 for supported Windows Server systems including Server 2028. The hybrid intelligence capabilities are available to a limited number of customers through an early-access program that includes hardware requirements. NVMe and Intune management for servers are available for testing now.

Microsoft said Windows Server 2028 is a prerelease product, and some elements may be substantially modified before its official release. Microsoft advised enterprises to test apps and operational tooling against the locked-down security and memory defaults before deployment and to relax settings only when required. Microsoft said older protocols, legacy authentication, and some management tools and scripts may not work on Windows Server 2028 without configuration changes. The articles leave open when general availability will come and which features will change before release. The articles also leave open how many customers the early-access program includes.

stories.Headline: OpenAI expands ChatGPT Ads to 44 countries through exclusive reseller Aleph
stories.Summary:
OpenAI expanded the market presence of ChatGPT Ads into 44 countries on November 12, 2026. The company selected Aleph as the exclusive reseller to provide local support for brands and agencies. This partnership allows advertisers to contract and pay for ads through a local entity. The move aims to broaden access to AI tools for businesses in these regions. It provides an additional buying option alongside global technology partners and the self-service Ads Manager.

The deal covers 14 Latin American nations including Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Panama, Paraguay, Peru, Puerto Rico and Uruguay. Europe and Central Asia include 16 markets: Azerbaijan, Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Czechia, Estonia, Hungary, Kazakhstan, Latvia, Lithuania, Romania, Serbia, Slovakia, Slovenia, Ukraine and Uzbekistan. Middle East and Africa include 10: Egypt, Kenya, Kuwait, Morocco, Nigeria, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, South Africa, Turkey and the United Arab Emirates. Asia-Pacific includes 4: Bangladesh, Cambodia, Hong Kong for outbound ads and Sri Lanka. Aleph provides local invoicing in local currency, payment terms, onboarding, campaign support and training.

OpenAI stated that they have made significant progress in ten months but are still early in building the platform. They intend to focus on protecting user trust and helping businesses achieve their goals while developing new formats. Gastón Taratuta, the founder and CEO of Aleph, said AI gives businesses a new way to connect with people. He noted that Aleph turns global technology into local growth by speaking the local language. He emphasized that advertisers can now work with a local team that extends credit.

Jad Naamani from Seez said car buyers increasingly use AI conversations to research vehicles and compare different models. He believes dealers must be present when buyers ask AI assistants or they will not make the shortlist. Automotive retailers are affected as they use the Boost tool from Pinewood.AI to manage these new ads. This tool integrates ChatGPT Ads with Meta, Google, TikTok and Snapchat to reach potential car buyers. The system uses AI to shift budgets toward activities that deliver qualified leads and sales.

Over one hundred thousand marketers have already advertised on ChatGPT, which now has more than one billion weekly users. In 2026, Invoca research found 60 percent of UK car buyers used generative AI for research, up from 47 percent. Pinewood.AI, which was taken private by Ridgeview Partners in October 2026, acquired the AI company Seez in February 2025. Seez is headquartered in Dubai with an office in Copenhagen and operates in 25 different countries. Pinewood.AI serves a global user base in over 36 countries and partners with over 50 OEM brands.

OpenAI will continue to develop new optimization tools, measurement solutions, and advertising formats as the ecosystem evolves. Pinewood.AI and Seez plan to introduce additional advertising formats as soon as OpenAI makes them available. stories.Headline: House Democrats investigate Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over ties to Nvidia
stories.Summary:
House Democrats on the Judiciary and Foreign Affairs Committees launched an investigation on November 18, 2026, regarding Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. These lawmakers are examining if Lutnick's family ties to Nvidia influenced the government's response to alleged chip smuggling into Beijing. This probe follows claims that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. That individual allegedly used the firm Megaspeed to funnel advanced technology into China.

The investigation focuses on why Lutnick omitted Megaspeed from a list of companies considered national security risks. Representatives Jamie Raskin and Gregory Meeks intend to use their new majority in January to expand these inquiries. They are specifically looking into the fact that Lutnick previously held over $1.3 billion in Nvidia stock. This wealth was managed through Cantor Fitzgerald, a firm he ran until transferring ownership to his children during his 2025 confirmation.

Representatives Raskin, Meeks, and Sydney Kamlager-Dove signed a letter questioning the relationship between Lutnick and Huang. They expressed concern that the Commerce Secretary appeared too close to the executive and failed to crack down on sales to China. The lawmakers want to determine if financial interests compromised the administration's ability to handle the Nvidia scandal. They are also scrutinizing the operations of the investment firm Cantor Fitzgerald as part of this broader oversight effort.

stories.Headline: Paul Meinshausen says a personal AI agent grades marketing messages more ruthlessly than he would
stories.Summary:
Paul Meinshausen, Head of Agentic Decisioning at MoEngage and Co-Founder of Aampe, asked Meta's Muse to check his notifications from marketing brands while listening to a conference talk in New York. He loaded up the personal AI agent because he was curious whether brands were responding to customers who now have software reading on their behalf. The verdict was harsher than he expected, and he said it gave a rundown on them that was sort of even more ruthless than he would have. He shared the experiment in a conversation with CX Today, published on 20 November 2026. For marketers, that small experiment points to a bigger problem, because if a customer's agent is reviewing every message, relevance stops being a nice-to-have.

Meinshausen said executives have long had human assistants who watch over their affairs even more obsessively than they do themselves, and agents are now making that available to everyone. He said most people are not just a professional in their job, they are also a parent or a partner or family member and a friend, and they give each task a small amount of focus, whereas an agent can spend far longer on a single decision. He said the expectation for detail, for relevance, and for personalization is just a lot higher, and that it is a good thing, but it just means that the rate of work has increased as well for everybody involved. He called messaging across every channel the previous wave of automation, where the aim was just to make machines do things. He defined intelligent activity as the ability to take an action, observe a result, and then update the action.

Meinshausen said activity should be intelligent activity, and that for marketers this means giving agents a way to read the response, not only the authority to send. He pointed to a much wider set of signals before and after a purchase, including how customers read material, how they click around, and direct feedback such as whether something was relevant. He compared it to everyday use of tools like ChatGPT, where people learn to prompt and then correct the system, and said businesses need their agents to be correctable in the same way, sometimes directly and explicitly and sometimes indirectly and kind of implicitly. He said one form of response can be a negative form, saying I don't like this, unsubscribing, or not responding when you kind of were expected to respond, and those are really important to learn from. He said the agent that over-messages is the one that ignores those signals.

CX Today has previously explored how suppression and next-best actions can reduce personalization fatigue, and the principle is similar. Meinshausen sees AI decisioning arriving quickly in lifecycle and CRM marketing, and spreading into orchestration and content production. He admitted there is too much to do, so teams will need to prioritize and calibrate which adoption decisions they make first. He was clear on one point, that there is definitely no time to do nothing. He suggested marketers consider how a customer's agent would grade their last week of messages and what it would say.

Genesys launched Standalone AI Agents and Genesys Arena on 18 November 2026 for organisations that want to deploy agentic AI in customer service without replacing their existing systems. Standalone AI Agents lets organisations deploy the Genesys Cloud Agentic Virtual Agent within existing customer service environments in a few days, without first migrating more widely to Genesys Cloud. The software can operate within defined business rules and hand an interaction to a human employee, along with the conversation context, if a request needs further expertise. Genesys Arena is built around prebuilt Agent Kits covering more than 50 industry-specific scenarios, and teams can create a functional AI agent in as little as 10 minutes before customising it with natural language and deploying it into Genesys Cloud. The announcement includes a new pricing structure that groups interactions into simple, moderate or complex tasks and measures usage in Experience Units, the new name for what Genesys previously called AI Tokens.

Tony Bates, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer at Genesys, said enterprises want to move faster with AI but need the flexibility to do it on their own terms without compromising trust and governance. Bates said that with Standalone AI Agents, Genesys Arena and a new effort-based pricing model, the company is giving organisations more choice in how they put agentic AI to work today and scale it as their needs evolve. Youssef Nokta, Senior Vice President of AI Forward Deployed Engineering at Genesys, said AI is advancing quickly and enterprises shouldn't have to start from zero every time they want to put a new idea to work. Nokta said Genesys Arena gives teams a practical head start so they can spend less time on the foundational work and more time shaping AI around their customers, business and the results they want to achieve. Each Agent Kit includes a working model with prebuilt knowledge, integrations, skills and guardrails for a given use case, according to Genesys.

Voice customisation tools are due to be added to Arena and the Genesys Cloud platform, letting organisations choose and adapt how AI agents sound by adjusting personality, tone and delivery using natural language prompts. Genesys cited Charles Sturt University as an existing user of its agentic virtual agent technology, and Michael Buttsworth, Associate Director, Student Experience Service Centre at the university, said using Genesys Agentic Virtual Agent has shown them how AI can improve the customer experience and drive efficiency by resolving more interactions autonomously. Buttsworth said getting that value into production depends on how quickly teams can move from an idea to an experience that works in the real world, and that Genesys Arena and Agent Kits will make that path easier. Mila D'Antonio, Principal Analyst, Customer Engagement at Omdia, said enterprises are under pressure to move agentic AI from experimentation into production quickly, but they aren't all starting from the same place, with some operating in the cloud while others navigate complex hybrid or on-premises environments. D'Antonio said Genesys Arena and Genesys Standalone AI Agents give organisations different paths to deploy agentic AI based on their existing environment and requirements, and the introduction of effort-based pricing highlights how commercial models are evolving.

Genesys said Standalone AI Agents are generally available now, while Agent Kits through Genesys Arena are due to become generally available later this month. Insight launched an online Agent Store for business customers, now generally available in 14 countries, offering a catalogue of AI agents, platforms and related services designed to automate routine work across business functions. Customers can deploy the tools in days or weeks rather than months, either as standalone products or alongside consulting, implementation and managed services. The launch adds six new agentic products to Insight's AI portfolio, bringing the total in its library to 15, and nine products were introduced earlier this year. Products listed in the store include Insight AI Flight Academy, focused on training and change management, and TokenScope, which tracks token usage and AI consumption costs for finance teams.

Insight said the offerings were first developed for clients or used internally in areas including security, finance and legal. New products available at launch include Quote Advisor, which assesses pricing, inventory, freight and contract requirements to produce sourced quotes, NDA Review Agent, designed to review non-disclosure agreements against a company's legal policies, and Parts Order Assist, which helps warehouse, maintenance and field staff search catalogues and place parts orders. Jack Azagury, Chief Executive Officer of Insight, said organisations are feeling the pressure to move AI from isolated pilots into production, and that as Client Zero, Insight has built a repeatable approach proven first across its own organisation. Azagury said that having driven over 90% internal AI adoption, Insight knows firsthand what it takes to deploy and scale agentic AI rapidly and responsibly, and that combining the solutions offered in Agent Store with its consulting and managed services expertise empowers clients to move from hype to how with AI. Culligan International is the first external customer to implement Flight Academy, according to Insight, and the water services company is using a mix of AI tools including Microsoft Copilot, Cowork, Copilot Studio, Azure and Microsoft Fabric while putting governance in place around cost and responsible use.

Laura Walsh, Global Chief Information Officer of Culligan International, said at Culligan they believe technology doesn't transform a company, people do, and that generative AI adoption is far ahead of the learning curve, so it is their responsibility to arm teams with the best tools to lead now into the future. Walsh said that with partners at Insight, Culligan has prioritised AI education so teams can confidently leverage AI productively and responsibly, and that they are leveraging Insight's best practice and have established a functional champ. The deployment centres on workforce education and internal adoption rather than a single operational use case, and Insight said the training-led approach is intended to help organisations build confidence in AI tools across teams and geographies. Insight is positioning the store as a way for businesses to move AI projects beyond the pilot stage and into wider use, and said it applied the approach within its own operations before making the products available more broadly. The articles leave open how a customer's agent would grade any particular brand's messages, and what it would say.

stories.Headline: China's LineShine supercomputer remains the fastest system in the world
stories.Summary:
China's LineShine supercomputer retained its status as the world's fastest system during rankings released in Chicago on Monday. This machine is installed at the National Supercomputing Center in Shenzhen and first claimed the top spot in June. It outperformed the United States based El Capitan system in both the TOP500 and the HPCG Benchmark results. The system achieved 2.198 exaflops on the High Performance Linpack benchmark, which is about 21 percent ahead of El Capitan. LineShine also led the HPCG tests with 22 petaflops, while the American El Capitan system achieved 17.41 petaflops.

The system is the first in TOP500 history to exceed 2 exaflops of sustained double-precision performance using only domestic CPUs. On Monday, the US Commerce Department released an interim final rule titled Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors for chip exports. This rule requires licenses for advanced chips sent to Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, and Brazil to prevent them reaching China. The new rule imposes stricter restrictions on foreign companies while it retains specific exemptions for eligible companies based in the US. Washington is also mulling bans on Chinese optical transceivers used in data centers to prevent data theft or malware installation.

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said the US is overstretching the concept of national security to target China's high-tech industry. He argued that Washington views normal artificial intelligence competition as a zero-sum game and abuses export control measures to interfere in trade. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for a constructive relationship based on balance and reciprocity during a talk in New York. Bessent stated that a new bilateral dialogue aims to guard against shared risks and prevent misunderstandings between the two different systems. He noted that both countries expect to exchange best practices for testing advanced models before they are released to the public.

Microsoft and other trade groups urged the US administration to reconsider plans to ban imports of crucial AI data center components. These companies argue that such a ban could undermine the US competitive edge by delaying the rollout of new data centers. Developing economies are affected by a fragmented AI landscape, while Chinese open-source models currently dominate the popularity rankings on OpenRouter. These open-source models are used by developers across the developing world and by various companies located within the United States. The articles state that US economic coercion and long-arm jurisdiction disrupt global supply chains and harm the rights of Chinese firms.

The articles explain that LineShine's success follows years of investment in homegrown supercomputing despite US efforts to cut off advanced GPU accelerators. The US is accused of coercing other countries to join exclusive closed-source ecosystems while China promotes inclusivity and open source sharing. Both nations agreed in September to establish a dedicated communication channel for addressing unexpected AI incidents and exchanging model testing practices. The two countries share a responsibility to keep AI under human control and uphold a people-centered approach for the common good. This cooperation is seen as a way to ensure that artificial intelligence advances human progress and avoids becoming a bloc confrontation.

The APEC meetings in Shenzhen this month offer an opportunity to turn the consensus on strengthening AI communication into actual practice. Participants at the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting could build consensus on AI governance and create practical plans for risk management. The two sides aim to use a direct channel for alerting each other of serious incidents involving advanced artificial intelligence systems. The articles leave open whether Washington will move beyond zero-sum thinking and heed the voices of the business sector regarding supply chains. It remains unclear if the US will stop using national security as a pretext to maintain its own technological dominance.

stories.Headline: Woman sues Los Angeles police for investigating her stillbirth under California privacy law
stories.Summary:
A woman is suing the city of Los Angeles and detectives within the Los Angeles Police Department over an allegedly unlawful interrogation and investigation following a stillbirth she had in 2024. The suit comes two years after California authorized patients to sue for being investigated because of their pregnancy outcomes. It is the first known lawsuit under the state's Reproductive Privacy Act. The plaintiff was granted anonymity Thursday and is referred to in the complaint as Jane Doe. The complaint was filed late last week.

The Reproductive Privacy Act was amended in 2022 to prohibit the state from taking punitive action based on pregnancy decisions and outcomes. The plaintiff alleges that in November 2024 she was unhoused and living in a city shelter. She alleges she was menstruating irregularly due to her epilepsy medication. An emergency visit for stomach pains revealed she was pregnant, but the fetus did not have a heartbeat. According to the complaint, Doe was initially told she was in the first trimester and could miscarry at home, then learned she was around 29 weeks pregnant.

The complaint says Doe passed significant blood clots in the shelter toilet and left without flushing. She was taken by ambulance to the hospital and treated for significant blood loss. The complaint notes Doe did not realize she had passed the stillbirth. According to the complaint, police came to the hospital, shackled her to a bed and interrogated her for hours. She was told a fetus had been found outside the shelter.

The complaint says that was the first time Doe learned she had passed into the toilet. It was also the first time she heard someone had reportedly moved the fetus from the toilet to an alley outside the shelter. The complaint alleges police pursued a homicide investigation for about a year despite a medical examiner telling them fetal demise had occurred in utero. The Los Angeles Police Department declined to comment, citing the pending litigation. Sara Ainsworth, chief legal and policy director at If/When/How, said all the things done to Doe violate the Reproductive Privacy Act.

Ainsworth said it is very important to show state actors in California that they must abide by the law, which prohibits criminalizing somebody. If/When/How helped California pass the right-to-sue law and filed the complaint alongside law firm BraunHagey & Borden LLP. At least 13 states and the District of Columbia have in recent years enacted measures protecting pregnancy decisions and outcomes. They include California, Colorado, Hawaii, Illinois, Michigan, Missouri, Montana, New Mexico, Ohio, Oregon, Vermont, Virginia and Washington. Ainsworth said that among the few other places explicitly allowing damages suits, including D.C., Colorado and Illinois, California is the only state to eliminate common legal immunities for law enforcement.

Brittany Watts in Ohio last year sued the city of Warren, city policy officers and a hospital after she was arrested and charged with abuse of a corpse following a miscarriage in her home. Ainsworth said that in other states it can be harder to determine who is accountable. She said it is typically hard to hold government officials accountable for wrongful criminalization because of legal barriers. In the first three years after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, more than 900 women faced criminal charges for conduct related to their pregnancies. Most of the charges were for child abuse, neglect or endangerment, mostly related to substance use during pregnancy, but some involved allegations about failing to obtain prenatal care or other actions during pregnancy or after pregnancy loss.

Doe alleges she had to leave the shelter after police told reporters they suspected a homicide and headlines circulated about a newborn baby dropped from a fourth-floor window. In February 2025 she contacted a legal helpline run by If/When/How and began working with litigation counsel Shantal McNeil. McNeil helped Doe navigate the investigation and petitioned the city attorney not to bring charges. McNeil said reputational damage and other harms often outlast these types of arrests and investigations, even when charges are dropped or never filed. She said police often investigate vulnerable women like the California plaintiff, who according to her attorneys is a young woman.

stories.Headline: TSMC restricts Chinese chip designers following new US export control rules
stories.Summary:
Taiwan's TSMC tightened restrictions on Chinese chip designers around November 19, 2026, by suspending some previously permitted advanced manufacturing orders for those customers. The world's largest contract chipmaker limited affected clients to older technology after new US Commerce Department rules took effect on Thursday. These measures close a remaining route for Chinese firms to produce powerful AI processors, which complicates Beijing's domestic chip development efforts. The company halted orders using manufacturing processes of 16 nanometres and below unless the customers could obtain US export licences. This action follows reports that TSMC and South Korea's Samsung Electronics suspended some chip shipments to Chinese customers on Thursday.

Affected Chinese designers are generally limited to 28-nanometre and 40-nanometre processes, provided they avoid advanced packaging and high-bandwidth memory. The new US rules remove a compliance route that previously allowed some Chinese companies to access advanced manufacturing without individual licences. TSMC can no longer use its verification process to check if certain Chinese chip designs fall outside of US export controls. Advanced chips are now presumed to be covered by US controls, requiring export licences unless a specific exception or exemption applies. These rules reach beyond AI processors and apply to various advanced manufacturing services provided to mainland Chinese firms and designers.

TSMC stated that it will comply with the new US export rules that strip Chinese chip designers of a key exemption. The company instructed that advanced orders be halted and issued guidance requiring closer scrutiny of customers' operating locations and parent companies. TSMC will now check major shareholders, packaging providers, and shipping routes to ensure full compliance with the updated US government regulations. These checks extend to orders placed through intermediaries or overseas subsidiaries located in Taiwan, the United States, Europe, Japan, and Southeast Asia. The company is implementing these strict verification steps to align with the new requirements set by the US Commerce Department.

Chinese technology giants and independent chip designers developing alternatives to Nvidia processors are particularly affected by these new manufacturing restrictions. Most leading AI chips require 7-nanometre processes or smaller for energy efficiency, while high-bandwidth memory handles the vast data volumes. Advanced packaging is also critical because it integrates chips and memory to boost computing power for complex artificial intelligence applications. A US government list of approved chip designers includes Apple, AMD, Nvidia, and Taiwanese firms MediaTek and Realtek, excluding Chinese firms. Some Chinese AI chip designers had access to 7-nanometre technology before Thursday, though Reuters could not independently verify those specific arrangements.

The background involves China's ambition to develop domestic alternatives to AI chips designed by Nvidia and manufactured by the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company. Previously, TSMC could verify the technical characteristics and computing power of certain designs to determine if they fell outside US controls. This verification process served as a loophole that allowed some Chinese designers to access advanced services without needing individual export licences. The US government maintains a list of approved designers to control who can access the most advanced semiconductor manufacturing technology. These geopolitical tensions have led to increasing restrictions on the export of high-end computing hardware to mainland Chinese technology companies.

TSMC will continue to monitor the operating locations and shipping routes of its customers to prevent the evasion of US rules. The company will maintain the suspension of advanced manufacturing orders for Chinese clients who lack the necessary US government export licences. The articles leave open whether Chinese firms will find other ways to produce chips or if other foundries will follow. It remains unclear how many Chinese designers were using the 7-nanometre process before the new rules took effect on Thursday. The reports do not specify if the US government will grant any new exceptions to the affected mainland Chinese firms.

stories.Headline: MP High Court pulls up state government for using AI to cite non-existent Supreme Court judgment
stories.Summary:
The Madhya Pradesh High Court cautioned the state government on Tuesday for using artificial intelligence to cite a non-existent Supreme Court judgment. The court found that the state blindly resorted to AI tools to draft a reply in a specific legal matter. This incident occurred during a hearing regarding a petition filed by a police sub-inspector who was dismissed from service. The court criticized the state for its callous and irresponsible drafting of the legal documents submitted to the bench. Justice Vivek Kumar Singh presided over the case and quashed the dismissal of the police officer in question.

The state cited a fake case called State of Andhra Pradesh vs S.S. Mohammad Nisar, reported as (2008) 5 SCC 230. This fabricated citation was actually from the Sidhartha Vashisht alias Manu Sharma vs State (NCT of Delhi) case regarding criminal appeals. The government used this fake ruling to argue that reappreciation of evidence is impermissible under Article 226 of the Constitution. The court held that the state could not bypass a departmental inquiry under Article 311(2)(b) in this specific case. The ruling requires the government to reinstate the sub-inspector forthwith while allowing for a fresh inquiry under the law.

Justice Vivek Kumar Singh stated that the respondents had blindly used AI tools, resulting in a fabricated name and unrelated citation. The judge noted that pleadings filed before a constitutional court are solemn documents and must be handled with professional care. He observed that inserting fictitious case law without verifying citations wastes precious judicial time and borders on actively misleading the court. The bench strictly cautioned the state machinery against such reckless practices in the future to maintain legal integrity. The court further ordered that the office of the Advocate General must meticulously verify all legal propositions and citations.

The police sub-inspector was affected by this case after being dismissed within twenty four hours of a sexual harassment complaint. Government advocate Swati Aseem George and Advocate General Prashant Singh both declined to comment on the court's stern observations. The court expressed no opinion on the merits of the allegations made against the officer regarding his alleged behavior. The bench emphasized that the state's justification for invoking Article 311(2)(b) was unsustainable in law for this particular dismissal. The officer had been accused of indecent behavior toward a woman cleaner at the state situation room in Bhopal.

The background involves a sexual harassment complaint lodged against the sub-inspector on May 26, 2024, in the city of Bhopal. He was suspended on that same day and then dismissed from his service on May 27, 2024, without inquiry. The state had invoked provisions that allow departmental inquiries to be dispensed with only in very exceptional and rare circumstances. This led the officer to file a petition challenging the dismissal process as a violation of constitutional due process. The court found that the state had bypassed necessary legal steps before removing the officer from his professional position.

The state government must now reinstate the police sub-inspector immediately as per the directions issued by the High Court. The government retains the liberty to conduct a regular departmental inquiry in accordance with the law regarding the original allegations. The office of the Advocate General is now responsible for ensuring that all future citations are verified before being recorded. The articles leave open whether the state will pursue the fresh inquiry into the officer's behavior toward the cleaner. It remains unclear if any disciplinary action will be taken against the officials who used AI to draft the pleadings.

stories.Headline: Mikhail Lukin leads a $12 million Harvard project to link quantum computing with AI
stories.Summary:
A $12 million federal grant will fund a Harvard-led collaboration aiming to link quantum computing with artificial intelligence. The project is called Application-Aware Error Correction Codesign for Scientific Quantum Computing, or ASQC. It is part of the Department of Energy's Genesis Mission. Mikhail Lukin, Harvard's Joshua and Beth Friedman University Professor and co-founder of QuEra Computing, will lead the effort. The collaboration unites researchers from MIT, Cornell University and three national labs alongside tech partners NVIDIA and Anthropic.

The project is one of 12 Phase II awards announced Oct. 9 under the Genesis Mission. The grant is administered by the Advanced Scientific Computing Research division of the Department of Energy. Lukin is the project's principal investigator and co-director of the Harvard Quantum Initiative. He will work with Harvard physicists Markus Greiner and Susanne Yelin and researchers at MIT, Cornell University, Los Alamos National Laboratory, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Sandia National Laboratories, QuEra Computing, NVIDIA and Anthropic. The team will train AI models to learn which errors matter for problems in quantum simulation, materials science, chemistry and nuclear science, use AI to design codes and decoders tailored to them, and test the results on hardware at Harvard, MIT and QuEra.

University President Alan M. Garber said Mikhail is a visionary leader who will do an excellent job driving progress and strengthening partnerships to ensure America's competitiveness in this area of vital importance. Lukin said this kind of collaborative approach is really needed in this case, and that the team wants to make something no one else has been able to make. He said the team will take all help. He said this is really an attempt to establish scientific foundations for useful fault-tolerant quantum computers and to really accelerate this progress using AI. He said that as we build larger and better quantum computers, we will really start making more and more scientific discoveries.

Garber said some of the most thrilling questions in science have long seemed out of reach, but the barriers to discovery are falling rapidly as quantum computing and artificial intelligence expand the realm of the possible. Lukin said you can really explore corners of the universe where you have never been, like a new kind of telescope. The team stated that we can really see these dreams the community has had for the last 40 years, for the first time, in the direct line of sight. Co-investigators on the program include Vladan Vuletić, Soonwon Choi and Hengyun "Harry" Zhou of MIT, Eun-Ah Kim of Cornell, Andrew Sornborger, Lukasz Cincio and Michael McKerns of Los Alamos, Wibe de Jong and Costin Iancu of Lawrence Berkeley, Andrew Landahl, Riley Chien and Kevin Thompson of Sandia, Nathan Gemelke and Michael Gullans of QuEra, Krysta Svore of NVIDIA and Alek Kemeny of Anthropic. The project will build on research Lukin and his collaborators published last year, which addressed a key challenge in quantum computing related to environmental noise and the inherently unstable quantum bits, or qubits, that make up quantum computers.

Through quantum error correction, the group suppressed errors to the point that adding qubits would reduce errors rather than add them, paving the way for larger, more complex calculations. Recent advances in quantum error correction have enabled the suppression of errors to the point where adding qubits now reduces, rather than increases, computational errors, a critical step toward building larger, more complex quantum computers. In an April preprint, Lukin, Yelin and colleagues described a neural-network decoder, software that identifies errors during computation, that cut error rates up to 17 times below existing versions and ran thousands of times faster. In another recent work, in collaboration with QuEra and Anthropic, the team used large language models to discover state-of-the-art quantum circuits for tasks spanning numerical computation, chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation and number theory. The Department of Energy grant specifically encourages partnerships between universities and national laboratories, an approach Lukin explained is unusual in quantum computing research, where institutions often operate more independently, and is essential to achieving goals previously considered unattainable.

The ASQC project will develop an AI-driven, fault-tolerant QEC system that can adapt to scientific problems relevant to the Energy Department. The Genesis Mission aims to integrate the world's best supercomputers, experimental facilities and AI systems to advance American research and innovation. Lukin and Greiner are co-founders of QuEra Computing, where Lukin is a chief scientist. Lukin views the resulting quantum computer not merely as a faster calculator, but as a novel scientific instrument capable of exploring previously inaccessible realms of knowledge. The articles do not say when the hardware tests will begin or how the $12 million will be divided among the partners.

stories.Headline: MIT-led team uses large language models to review code sharing in nearly 4,000 medical studies
stories.Summary:
An international team led by researchers at MIT and Dana-Farber Cancer Institute used large language models to examine nearly 4,000 medical studies and hundreds of code repositories, as reported by MIT News on November 19, 2026. The team identified statements about shared code in papers and then followed those statements to assess the associated repositories. The review revealed two key gaps: code sharing remains uncommon, and making code public does not consistently mean providing the documentation and supporting information needed for reuse. The open-access findings were recently published in Nature Medicine. The work examined how code is currently shared in clinical prediction studies, which develop or evaluate models to estimate patient outcomes such as disease risk.

The review included almost 4,000 studies that developed, updated, or validated prediction models and whose full texts were available through PubMed Central's open-access collection. The team identified studies citing either TRIPOD or TRIPOD+AI, checklists that help researchers report how clinical prediction models were developed and evaluated. Only about 1 in 8 studies reported sharing code. Among journals, the proportion of studies sharing code ranged from zero to more than 70 percent. Two researchers independently checked 500 papers and a separate sample of repositories, resolving disagreements before comparing their assessments with the automated results.

Tom Pollard, a research scientist at MIT's Laboratory for Computational Physiology and Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, said studies involve many choices about preparing data, developing models, and evaluating performance. Pollard, a senior author of the study, said the choices researchers make affect the results and a methods section in a paper can only capture so much detail. He said the real benefit of LLMs is their ability to process unstructured information such as text, helping the team work with information scattered across papers and software repositories. Pollard said this allowed the team to examine how code was being shared in much more detail across a large collection of studies. He said the team wants to give researchers practical guidance on how to share code and give journals clearer expectations to communicate to authors.

Thomas Sounack, the study's first author, said the challenge was that the information was highly inconsistent and the team first had to identify whether or not a paper shared code. Sounack said authors discuss and link to code from a paper in many different ways. He said some repositories were extremely well-organized and documented, while others gave almost no guidance at all. Sounack said good code sharing means giving enough information to understand what the code does and be able to run it to reproduce the results reported in the paper. The authors emphasize the overall patterns rather than treating every count as exact because classification errors remain possible.

TRIPOD-Code builds on TRIPOD and TRIPOD+AI, checklists that help researchers report how clinical prediction models were developed and evaluated. The workflow went beyond checking whether a link existed, assessing repositories against characteristics such as completeness of documentation, software requirements, and terms of reuse. Agreement between human reviewers and the automated results was stronger for concrete characteristics, such as whether a license file was present, than for judgments about the adequacy of documentation. Some journals with low sharing rates nevertheless had written code-sharing policies, suggesting that policies alone may not be enough to motivate code sharing. The review also helped to identify examples of effective practice, such as researchers providing synthetic datasets to assist with code reuse where original patient records could not be shared publicly.

The open-access findings are informing TRIPOD-Code, a reporting guideline being developed to clarify what researchers should share. Through an expert review process, the team is developing guidance on which elements of shared analytical code should be considered essential. Clinical prediction research brings together people from medicine, statistics, and computer science, whose expectations for documenting and sharing code may differ, and TRIPOD-Code aims to establish a consensus. Pollard said the review gives the team evidence to inform those discussions. The articles leave open which specific elements of shared analytical code will be deemed essential under TRIPOD-Code.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang steps down as Nvidia becomes AI financing hub
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA’s longtime chief executive Jensen Huang has stepped down, and the company he led is now described by industry insiders as the “central bank” of the AI circular financing economy, a role that has drawn close attention from Wall Street and Silicon Valley. Under Huang, NVIDIA built the GPU chips that serve as the underlying foundation of the global AI wave and assembled what the article calls a huge capital ammunition depot. Regulatory filings show that as of September 30 the market value of NVIDIA’s shares in eight publicly listed companies exceeded 48 billion US dollars, with holdings concentrated in partners that buy its GPUs. Interim CEO Colette Kress said on Tuesday’s earnings call that NVIDIA is proud of the role it has played in supporting the industry and will keep evaluating future transactions with a rigorous attitude, adding that the company still has a lot of work to do to judge whether these are the right investments to make.

The article reports that NVIDIA’s total investment portfolio exceeds 1000 billion US dollars, covering equity stakes in cutting-edge labs and bets on power producers and cloud computing companies, and that its shareholding in cloud computing unicorn CoreWeave has reached 10 percent. Its capital has also extended to cloud platform Nebius Group, semiconductor firm Intel and xAI before it was merged into SpaceX, and during Huang’s tenure it placed large bets on Anthropic and OpenAI, which lack investment-grade ratings. As part of Anthropic’s initial public offering on Thursday, NVIDIA committed to buying 10 billion US dollars of Anthropic shares, and Anthropic has reportedly signed a 350 billion US dollar agreement with Lambda, another NVIDIA-backed company, to lease data center computing power run on NVIDIA chips. According to PitchBook, as of November 13 NVIDIA had taken part in 129 venture capital and startup accelerator transactions this year, with the total venture capital it joined other investors in reaching 2200 billion US dollars, or 27 percent of the global total of that kind, and at least 293 investment and acquisition deals since the AI boom heated up in 2023.

NVIDIA reported on Tuesday that its commitments in areas such as long-term supply agreements and data center leases total 5180 billion US dollars, up sharply from about 850 billion a year ago. One guarantee is that NVIDIA will provide up to 1050 billion US dollars in backing for SB Energy, a SoftBank subsidiary, for its planned Ohio data center to help it issue bonds for construction costs, along with a 1.5 billion US dollar equity investment, and OpenAI has agreed to lease the computing capacity once the center is complete, with NVIDIA holding exclusive chip supply rights for the first half of the project. In August, Huang led efforts to obtain commitments from Apollo, Blackstone, BlackRock, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR to raise 5000 billion US dollars, with NVIDIA providing fallback arrangements and guarantees, to help startup customers finance chip purchases, but people familiar with the matter say no funds have actually been invested so far. The article notes real doubt about whether many of these commitments and guarantees can be fulfilled, and says that since NVIDIA’s stock hit an all-time peak on October 6, the combined market value of the eight listed companies it holds has fallen by 820 billion US dollars, with SpaceX and Intel accounting for most of the decline, while rising borrowing costs are straining many AI enterprises.

stories.Headline: Police find Lee Jin-woo dead at Seoul motel as AI cheating probe continues
stories.Summary:
Lee Jin-woo was found dead on Thursday, November 19, 2026, at a motel in eastern Seoul after police began searching for him. The man was a dental student at Seoul National University who had achieved a perfect score on the Legal Education Eligibility Test. He had gone missing since Wednesday night after he told reporters he would dispel cheating allegations through a public live stream. Emergency authorities discovered his body on the roof of a motel located in Cheonho-dong, Gangdong District, at around 1:12 p.m. that day.

He was found in cardiac arrest after failing to appear for a planned test of his abilities at 8:40 a.m. Thursday. The planned demonstration required Lee to solve questions from the Korean language section of the 2027 College Scholastic Ability Test in real time. He had previously visited a lodging facility in Gwangjin District before taking a taxi toward Songpa District between 8 and 9 a.m. The investigation involves the Legal Education Eligibility Test, the 2024 and 2026 college entrance exams, and the national tax accountant certification exam.

Lee was admitted to Korea University's Department of Political Science and International Relations in 2024 and Seoul National University's School of Dentistry in 2026. He had previously scored in the sixth to eighth tiers on past college entrance exams using a nine-tier grading system. The Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency assigned a criminal complaint against Lee to its Provincial Special Detective Corps on Wednesday, November 18, 2026. The charges included fraud, obstruction of official duties, and obstruction of business, though police will likely close the case without prosecution. A note found at the scene reportedly stated that Lee was physically and mentally exhausted, but it contained no admission of cheating.

The note also offered no apology or explanation regarding the allegations that he used artificial intelligence to achieve his perfect scores. Police began their search for Lee after receiving a report expressing concern for his safety at around 8:42 a.m. Thursday. Some people raised allegations that Lee cheated on the LEET and the college entrance exams for the 2024 and 2026 academic years. These suspicions grew after a separate case of alleged AI-assisted cheating on the national tax accountant certification exam recently surfaced in Korea.

Over 550,000 students sat for the college entrance exam under tighter anti-cheating measures, and 98 test-takers were caught cheating in 2026. The government tightened national exam rules, including expanded CCTV and random phone calls, after concerns about AI and smart-device cheating grew. Lee had previously claimed he gained a new understanding of reading comprehension and studying to improve his low previous scores. Lee had previously posed for a photo during an interview at the JoongAng Ilbo headquarters in Mapo District on September 8. He was the first person to ever achieve a perfect score on the Legal Education Eligibility Test while attending Seoul National University.

The articles mention that both Korea University and Seoul National University are regarded as prestigious schools within the country of South Korea. The case emerged during a broader storm of AI fraud allegations affecting various national qualification exams and college entrance tests in Korea. Authorities are now examining the motel scene to determine the exact circumstances surrounding the death of the controversial test-taker. Police said they will continue their probe into the AI-assisted cheating allegations even though Lee Jin-woo is now dead.

The investigation into the law school entrance exam cheating case faces an uphill battle because the primary suspect cannot be prosecuted. Authorities plan to further examine the scene at the motel near Cheonho station to gather more information about the event. The articles leave open whether other individuals were involved in the alleged fraud or if more cheating cases will surface. It remains unclear if the police will find evidence that confirms Lee used artificial intelligence to ace his various exams.
