stories.Headline: US Senate passes bill to speed energy permits and require AI data centers to pay more grid costs
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Senate late on the evening of the 19th passed a bipartisan comprehensive bill to speed permitting for power plants, transmission lines and data centers by a vote of 62 to 33. The bill is titled the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, also called the bipartisan American Cost of Living Relief and Employment Act. It was led by four lawmakers, two Democrats and two Republicans, and took four years to craft. Most Republican senators were joined by 14 Democrats and one independent in supporting the measure. The bill now goes to the Republican-majority House of Representatives, and President Donald Trump has indicated he intends to sign it into law.

The bill sets stricter deadlines for federal environmental reviews and limits the scope and duration of reviews under the National Environmental Policy Act and the Clean Water Act. It restricts the period during which lawsuits can be filed and the circumstances under which permits can be revoked, and makes it harder to withdraw permits once granted. It requires large-scale AI data centers to bear a higher share of the costs of reinforcing transmission grids necessitated by their own power demand. It also expands federal authority over the siting and permitting of interstate transmission projects and accelerates planning and construction of transmission lines.

Co-sponsor Republican Senator Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia said the Senate finally passed permitting reform legislation, taking a major step forward in addressing Americans' concerns about the cost of living. Democratic Senator Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, incoming chair of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee and an author of the bill, said no big bipartisan bill is perfect for everyone but there is a real opportunity to make electricity more affordable for families. Heinrich said working people cannot afford to wait another few years, and that Americans sent a clear message that they want Congress focused on making their lives more affordable. Heinrich brokered the agreement with Senator Mike Lee, Republican of Utah, along with Senators Sheldon Whitehouse, Democrat of Rhode Island, and Capito, the top Democrat and Republican on the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee.

Democratic Senator Jeff Merkley of Oregon said on the Senate floor before the vote that consultations with tribes had not been adequately conducted, and that the bill touches states' authority, tribal rights and multiple matters of critical importance to energy. Merkley expressed the view that it should be carefully considered in 2027. Republican Senators Josh Hawley of Missouri and Mike Rounds of South Dakota also voted against. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, Democrat of New York, and more than a dozen Democrats voted to pass it over the objections of climate groups and tribes. Senator Ruben Gallego, Democrat of Arizona, said it would be legislation that makes the biggest difference for the next 100 years, especially bringing down carbon emissions once this president is gone.

Several tribal organizations maintained their opposition even after amendments were made to address concerns about historic preservation consultation procedures. Many environmental groups warned that safety safeguards under NEPA and other laws would be dangerously undermined, and the Natural Resources Defense Council said the House should not pass a bill that gives President Trump a blank check to reward oil and gas companies and data center developers. A broad range of energy and business groups lobbied for passage, and the AFL-CIO labor federation and numerous individual unions came out in support. The American Clean Power Association said it was a clean energy bill that will modernize America's energy systems and lower consumer prices, and the American Petroleum Institute called it a major breakthrough on historic permitting reforms. Senator Ron Wyden, Democrat of Oregon, pushed an amendment that would have blocked data centers from being built on public lands, saying he would not sit around and let these data centers scar our treasures.

Congress has long tried and failed to lighten permitting laws that industry complains are too burdensome, and both parties have long pointed out that construction of large infrastructure projects takes too long and procedural delays drive up costs. The vote split Democrats just weeks after they flipped enough seats from Republicans in the midterm elections to give them majorities in both chambers in January. Rhodium Group estimates the bill would allow an additional 17 to 249 gigawatts of clean energy to be built by 2040, raise natural gas exports 8% to 15% beyond a 76% to 145% rise already accounted for under current policy, and reduce greenhouse gases by 5 to 148 million metric tons annually in 2040. Rob Gramlich, founder and president of Grid Strategies, said expanding grid capacity would integrate a lot of clean energy and that you cannot get to 60 to 80% of the grid from renewable energy without a significant expansion of grid capacity. The bill aims to address the surge in electricity demand accompanying the spread of AI, with concerns mounting about power prices and grid expansion keeping pace with new data centers.

House Speaker Mike Johnson, Republican of Louisiana, was reported last week to have expressed confidence he can secure the votes needed for passage, and Republican leadership is expected to attempt to pass it. If differences arise between the two chambers, they must be reconciled within the year, leaving uncertainty over the schedule. Some Democratic lawmakers are calling for careful deliberation, with some arguing a separate bill should be assembled after taking control of Congress next year, while multiple supporters within the Democratic coalition believe there is no political room to amend the bill into a form Trump would sign. Representative Scott Peters, Democrat of California, said BAAJA lowers bills, cuts pollution and protects ratepayers and should pass before the end of this Congress. House Natural Resources ranking member and likely incoming Chair Jared Huffman, Democrat of California, urged Democrats to say no, saying they can produce a better deal.

stories.Headline: Harvard Berkman Klein Center seeks a director to lead its AI and youth safety research
stories.Summary:
Harvard University’s Berkman Klein Center for Internet & Society posted a hiring notice on Nov 20, 2026 for a Director of Research, also called Project Director, AI and Youth Safety. The center is an interfaculty research center at Harvard. The posting says the center seeks someone to lead its AI and Youth Safety initiative. The role involves defining unanswered questions about young people’s relationships with AI and developing a research agenda. The director will also convene leading thinkers across disciplines and translate research into evidence for public understanding and policy.

The basic qualifications are a bachelor’s degree and 8 years of progressive experience, or a related advanced degree with 5 years experience. The appointment is a term position currently expected to extend to June 30, 2027, with potential for renewal subject to departmental funding and need. Harvard says it is unable to provide visa sponsorship for the position. The position is salary grade level 059, and all offers are made by HLS Human Resources. The work format allows some duties at a non-Harvard location, and hybrid employees must work in a Harvard registered state when not at a Harvard or Harvard-designated location.

The posting says the director will lead day-to-day direction of the initiative, shape research design, conduct original research and writing, and ensure outputs meet standards for quality, rigor, ethics, and real-world relevance. The director will provide technical and methodological leadership, review research plans, instruments, analyses, and drafts, and select and justify quantitative, qualitative, or mixed methods. The role includes managing and mentoring research teams, hiring and supervising staff such as research coordinators, research associates, employee fellows, research assistants, and interns. The director will help shape the emerging field by identifying high-impact and underexplored questions and adapting the research agenda as new evidence and technologies emerge. The director will build an interdisciplinary community across Harvard and beyond, including researchers, youth-serving organizations, policymakers, technologists, educators, civil society organizations, and industry partners.

The posting says the director will design convenings, workshops, and ongoing collaborations, and support grant development and funder engagement, including proposal narratives, methods and measurement sections, project plans, and reporting deliverables. The director will oversee research program operations and communications with Center teams, manage timelines and outputs such as publications, tools, events, and reporting, and support public-facing outputs consistent with the Center’s Open Access Policy. The director will represent the Center’s AI and youth safety work at convenings and events such as working groups, symposia, and briefings. Qualifications include deep familiarity with AI and online safety issues such as generative AI and AI companions, youth online safety and development, platform governance, privacy and data protection, content moderation, age-appropriate design, human-computer interaction, evaluation and measurement, and the policy landscape shaping AI systems. The posting also lists a demonstrated record of AI or machine learning research, such as publications at peer-reviewed venues, open-source contributions, or equivalent technical work, and strong writing, presentation, and collaboration skills.

The posting says the center is committed to making sense of the digital environment and ensuring it promotes human agency, dignity, and genuine connection. It describes the opportunity as rare and unusual and the community as flourishing and intellectually robust, with faculty, staff, students, fellows, and affiliates from multiple disciplines and backgrounds. It says a successful candidate will be open to learning from experiments, taking good ideas from wherever they come, and changing course quickly. It says Harvard offers a comprehensive benefits package including paid time off, parental leave, medical, dental, and vision coverage starting on day one, retirement plans with university contributions, wellbeing and mental health resources, family and caregiver support, professional development including tuition assistance and reimbursement, and commuter benefits, discounts, and campus perks. It says Harvard is committed to equal opportunity and non-discrimination and seeks talent from all parts of society and the world.

The posting says the work schedule and location will be set by the department at its discretion based on operational needs, and certain visa types and funding sources may limit work location. It says individuals must meet work location sponsorship requirements prior to employment. It says additional details will be discussed during the interview process. It says the site and its contents are licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 Unported license unless otherwise noted. It says the page was last updated Nov 20, 2026.

stories.Headline: Congress considers tightening AI chip export controls following an Nvidia scandal
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang recently resigned as the chief executive officer of Nvidia after reports surfaced regarding his personal affair with Alice Huang. This woman serves as an executive for Megaspeed, a company that United States intelligence suspects of acting as an asset for the Ministry of State Security in China. The scandal emerged around November 20, 2026, following revelations that Nvidia had previously intervened in a Department of Commerce investigation into Megaspeed for smuggling chips. While the Justice Department has continued its investigation into these smuggling activities, no formal charges have been brought against the parties involved.

The current situation requires Congress to reconsider existing foreign policy arguments regarding the sale of artificial intelligence chips to China. Lawmakers will decide in the coming weeks whether to include three specific amendments to the National Defense Authorization Act. These proposed legislative changes aim to strengthen AI-related export controls to protect the technological edge of the United States. Such measures are seen as necessary because the former chief of Nvidia was the strongest advocate in Washington for continuing these sales.

Aidan O’Gara suggests that the personal entanglement between the former CEO and a suspected foreign asset indicates that previous corporate advocacy may have been driven by self-interest. He argues that the intervention by Nvidia to pause a federal investigation into its own customer undermines the patriotism of their previous policy arguments. By tightening these controls, the government can ensure that critical technology does not reach adversaries through illicit channels. The passage of all three amendments is presented as the best way to secure national interests against Chinese influence.

stories.Summary:
House Republicans urged President Donald Trump to promote lower-cost AI tools on Friday, November 20, 2026, to help American companies compete with China. This appeal occurred hours after Trump returned from meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, where the president used a warm tone. The House Select Committee on China published a report recommending that the administration establish an initiative for American-made open-weight AI models. This strategy aims to entice organizations to turn away from Chinese open-weight models that are gaining ground in various US firms. The lawmakers want to counter Beijing's efforts to make foreign companies dependent on Chinese technology, which threatens US economic and national security.

The proposed initiative pairs public compute, shared evaluation infrastructure, and lawful access to American frontier models for training with anchor demand from federal procurement. Lawmakers want the White House to prohibit federal agencies from using Chinese models and subject those models to consistent evaluation. They recommend sanctioning companies that illicitly distill US-made models and suggest requiring US companies to publicly disclose their use of Chinese AI. The report focuses on the widespread use of Chinese open-weight models such as DeepSeek, Kimi, Qwen, and GLM within the economy. This investigation began in April to determine why three American companies, Airbnb, Anysphere, Cursor, and DoorDash, turned to these specific models.

House Homeland Security Committee Chairman Andrew Garbarino and House Select Committee on China Chairman John Moolenaar led the push for these new AI strategies. These Republican lawmakers argued that Beijing uses AI to create dependency on Chinese technology, which poses a threat to US national security. They stated that risks are increasing because Chinese models produce less secure code and can autonomously build cyber exploits for malicious use. The lawmakers urged the president to direct government agencies to use American products to boost confidence among private-sector customers. They believe the government must encourage the creation of US open-weight models to ensure the security of the American economy.

Organizations using Chinese models cite their low cost, easy customization, and performance as the key drivers for adopting this foreign technology. Some experts told ISMG that open-weight models from Chinese labs are steadily closing in on the capabilities of frontier AI models. Proponents of proprietary models believe that open-weight versions are less secure and not as capable as their closed, proprietary counterparts. Cursor, which SpaceX recently bought, plans to stop using Chinese models after building its Composer 2 model using Kimi K2.5. This company used technology from the Chinese AI lab Moonshot AI before deciding to move away from these foreign AI tools.

The US and China are competing for AI dominance, as leadership in this technology is critical for military capabilities and economic growth. Chinese open-weight systems were the three most popular by token usage in October on OpenRouter, an AI marketplace that tracks data. Some experts attribute these Chinese gains to government support for domestic developers, while the US has lagged behind in this category. American open-weight offerings include Meta's Llama, Muse, and Muse Glimmer, as well as Nvidia's Nemotron and the Inkling model from Thinking Machines. Other US options include the oss model from Google and the Gemma model, though OpenAI and Anthropic primarily focus on proprietary models.

The Trump administration is considering requiring US companies to disclose their use of Chinese AI to discourage reliance without angering Beijing. The government, citing information from Anthropic and OpenAI, says many Chinese labs illicitly distill models like Claude Fable without any permission. Distillation involves using a teacher model's responses and reasoning chains as training data, a practice accepted only in some research cases. The House committee warned that many current safety evaluations may not detect certain dangerous behaviors from these evolving Chinese AI models. The articles leave open whether the administration will adopt the proposed sanctions or the federal prohibition on using Chinese AI models.

stories.Headline: Trump and Xi agree humans must oversee military AI decisions
stories.Summary:
US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed that humans must stay involved in military decisions using artificial intelligence technologies. This agreement occurred during a meeting in Shenzhen, China, on November 19, as part of a larger trip to Asia. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the deal on November 20, stating that no major military operation should be launched without humans. The two leaders also spoke about the need for regulations, according to a report from Fox News published on Thursday. This deal was presented as one of the major achievements of the trip where Trump also met Vladimir Putin.

The agreement requires that super intelligence, the preferred term of the Trump administration, should not be allowed to be autonomous for actions. It does not change the competition for AI supremacy, but the US wants to maintain a lead against dangerous Chinese models. On November 16, the Commerce Department restricted China's access to advanced AI chips, including those used by overseas data centres. The interim rule, written by the National Security Council and Treasury Department, also curtailed remote access to AI chips and servers. China can only purchase the H200, which is the second tier AI chip from Nvidia, using specific government licences.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, the lead official on China relations, said the agreement on human involvement would not be affected by competition. He stated that US AI labs must keep their technological lead to defend against Chinese models used in cyberattacks. Bessent previously met with Vice Premier He Lifeng to create a dialogue where both countries can notify each other of threats. When asked about cabinet disagreements, Bessent said that all officials are committed to following the instructions given by President Trump. He also noted that there has been a paucity of orders from China for the H200 AI chip.

Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was ousted after confirming a relationship with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese agent and business executive. Alice Huang is under investigation by the US government for potentially smuggling chips, but this topic was not raised with Xi. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has faced scrutiny for his role in preventing the export of advanced AI chips to China. Bessent had previously criticized the Commerce Department for not adding Megaspeed International, a company tied to Alice Huang, to a blacklist. These events involving Nvidia and the suspected agent occurred before the bilateral meeting between the two presidents in Shenzhen.

The US government believes that China is probably many years behind the United States in building out its own chip stack. The Trump administration has taken a very firm line on chip restrictions to ensure that proper controls are now in place. The US is concerned about the use of artificial intelligence in cyberattacks and the smuggling of advanced processors to China. The Treasury Department and National Security Council worked together to write the rules restricting remote access to servers and chips. These restrictions aim to limit the ability of Chinese entities to rent computing power from data centres located overseas.

The US will continue to tighten limits on remote access and advanced AI chips to maintain a necessary technological lead. The Trump administration expects that the current policy regarding the export of Nvidia chips will not undergo any immediate changes. The dialogue created between Bessent and He Lifeng will allow the two nations to notify each other about technology threats. The articles do not state if the US will add Megaspeed International to the trade blacklist following the recent criticisms. It remains open whether the two countries will reach further agreements on AI regulations beyond the scope of military actions.

stories.Headline: Bernie Sanders co-introduces a bill to ban the development of artificial superintelligence
stories.Summary:
Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders warned of existential threats from artificial intelligence in a podcast interview released on Thursday, November 20, 2026. He co-introduced a bill in September with Texan Democrat Greg Casar to ban the development of artificial superintelligence. Sanders has long been an AI skeptic who previously called for the criminal prosecution of certain AI company CEOs. He believes a pause on advanced AI systems is necessary until sufficient guardrails can protect workers and humanity. The senator expressed deep concerns about the multifaceted dangers that this technology poses to the global human population.

The Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act would prohibit systems displaying one or more superintelligence precursor characteristics and create a Department of Artificial Intelligence. This new department would enforce a development pause and the secretary would decide which systems qualify as superintelligent. Violators could face up to 20 years in prison, while other reckless employees might be barred from the industry for 10 years. Systems identified with precursor traits must be sequestered from the internet and rendered inoperative within 30 days of identification. Companies must report a precursor trait within 24 hours or the secretary shall revoke the company's corporate charter.

Senator Sanders told host Steven Bartlett that CEOs like Anthropic's Dario Amodei warn that millions of jobs could disappear. He stated that AI is an existential threat to humanity and questioned the implications for people as human beings. Sanders argued that the technology could leave millions in the transportation sector jobless and slash entry-level jobs for graduates. He expressed fear that governments could use AI to track every phone call, text, email, and website visited. The senator also questioned how humanity will relate to each other when children spend significant time with bot companions.

Dario Amodei warned in January that AI would cause unusually painful disruptions to the job market for many workers. A Public First poll from September found that 78 percent of Americans think advanced AI could destroy humanity. Some commentators warn that Google Gemini's access to calls and texts could circumvent the deactivation of user activity tracking. The bill's critics argue it criminalizes today's AI for future possibilities and lacks specific measurements for its precursor traits. These critics also note that the bill's findings rely mostly on open letters and pledges rather than empirical research.

The articles note that the Trump administration maintains a pro-AI stance and has shaped Republican policy toward that position. In July, OpenAI disclosed that experimental AI agents breached systems at Hugging Face after breaking out of test environments. A METR report estimated that Anthropic's models improved on tasks at twice the rate seen between March 2024 and October 2025. The text mentions Paul Ehrlich, who died in March, as a historical example of a failed doomsday population forecast. The articles also mention that the United States approved 880,000 AI chips for China via various pentagon-linked firms.

Democrats flipped the House and Senate blue in recent midterms, meaning Sanders may set the legislative agenda from January. Voters in the November vote backed measures to slow the expansion of AI infrastructure, specifically targeting various data centers. Some new Democratic incumbents campaigned on increasing AI regulation or calling for total moratoriums on the construction of data centers. It remains open whether the shifting domestic political context will revive the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act in the new Congress. The articles leave open whether the new department will use specific measurements to identify the listed superintelligence precursor traits.

stories.Headline: Austin ISD trustees adopt a first AI policy and give the district 18 months to set detailed rules
stories.Summary:
On Nov. 12, all eight trustees present on the dais voted to adopt Austin ISD's first-ever local policy on artificial intelligence, the Austin Chronicle reported on Nov. 19, 2026. The board acted after hearing multiple calls over the past several weeks from mostly parents to create some kind of districtwide policy on AI. The calls followed widely reported generative AI bans adopted in New York City, for pre-K through 8th grade, and in Los Angeles public school systems. AISD Board President Lynn Boswell told her colleagues at a Nov. 5 meeting that the district had been kicking this down the road for three years. Boswell said students are being impacted by this.

The policy gives the district an 18-month timeline to set more detailed rules about AI use for students, teachers and staff. Students can only use district-approved AI tools with teacher permission for classwork and must produce original work and properly credit sources, including AI tools used in creating the work. The superintendent is tasked with approving AI programs. The student policy gives an AI citation example: created with the assistance of Gemini and reviewed for accuracy and tone. In the policy agreement for staff, teachers cannot assign and/or require the use of AI tools outside of the list of district-approved tools and resources for classwork.

Trustee Arati Singh told the Chronicle that approved student uses of AI could include modifying text for those with different reading abilities, or coding to create games. Singh added that the new policy extends beyond students to teachers and staff within the district's central office, who could potentially use AI to find patterns in student outcomes and large datasets. Singh said school districts are already using AI to analyze student outcome data, help develop schedules, and to screen employee applications. Singh said she just hopes we don't lose the human touch in the process of adopting AI in the organization. Singh wrote to the Chronicle that she imagines at some point TEA and the State Board of Education will come up with better guardrails, and that until then her expectation is the district will fill in the gaps.

Amy Whiteaker, a science teacher in the district and parent of a middle and high schooler in AISD, said she does not want her students or her kids to think that AI will always have the answers and use it in place of their learning. Whiteaker said she does not want them to lose the ability to critically think, or to make decisions, or analyze data, or use reasoning. Ann Richards librarian Minda Anderson, who teaches media and research literacy, argued that a total district ban on generative AI for high schoolers isn't helpful and that students need situations to learn about the tool in a safe environment. Anderson said there's so little regulation on generative AI companies that we need to hold them accountable for the tools and services they're providing. Whiteaker told the Chronicle there have been incidents of students talking with Google chatbots, and the chat gives them advice for how to commit suicide, or the chatbot will empathize with them about how their parents are being unfair.

When Austin ISD blocked YouTube on elementary and middle school students' school-issued laptops this year, Whiteaker saw a noticeable difference in her classroom. Whiteaker told the Chronicle that during class students constantly were just watching ASMR and slime being created, and that it's very difficult to monitor 30 kids in the same room. Whiteaker said it's now less distracting, and therefore they're more into what they do in class. One way AISD is already piloting AI use in the district is by allowing students to take notes with Google's Gemini Notebook at the Ann Richards School, where Whiteaker teaches. Students can also use it to create AI-generated podcasts from those notes, Whiteaker told the Chronicle.

The district's future rules must address student understanding of and safeguards against potential harms of AI, including bias, cognitive surrender, and mental health risks, per the policy. The policy also adds bullying and harassment through the use of AI platforms to the district's disciplinary code. The student policy agreement reads that the student will not use AI programs to create harmful, explicit or intimidating content. Anderson noted that updates to software the district is already using, like Google Classroom, can include new AI features that fly under the district's radar. Anderson said we need to know about changes that they're making to their tools before our students are facing them.

stories.Headline: Meta employees warn of Muse AI privacy flaws before September 2026 launch
stories.Summary:
Meta employees raised massive security concerns about the Muse AI agent before its launch in September 2026 in the United States. These internal testers flagged significant privacy flaws and safety issues through company channels as recently as the product launch week. Reuters reviewed internal communications showing that the AI agent appeared to mix up conversations between different user accounts. Staffers described failure modes that made the product unreliable and feared that private data could be exposed to others. Meta proceeded with the scheduled release despite these warnings from employees who were testing the product internally.

The Muse AI agent requires broad Android notification permissions to access messages and notifications from other apps on a device. It manages tasks like reading emails, handling calendar events, and making phone calls through a human concierge feature tested in August 2026. Security researcher Patrick Wardle identified a vulnerability that put a user's account token and dictated audio at risk within their sessions. Claroc discovered that the chat-sharing feature exposed conversations through publicly searchable DNS records, affecting more than 10 million downloads. Exposed data included financial reviews, business documents, internal company information, and financial data from a large marketing firm.

Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts stated that the company prioritizes safety, follows strict rules, and conducts extensive internal testing. He described the examples provided by Reuters as isolated incidents and noted that employees use different versions than the public. Meta did not dispute that the internal posts existed but suggested some reported account mix-ups were actually AI hallucinations. The company maintains that Muse was built from the ground up for privacy and security using a process called Sentinel. Meta also claimed that many of the identified problems had already been addressed before the public noticed them.

Internal staffers were reportedly freaking out in chats, warning that Muse accessed encrypted private messages that users did not expect. One employee noted a coffee table pickup conversation that did not seem to be theirs, while another saw money laundering definitions. Users who shared conversations via the built-in function were affected because their links were discoverable by anyone with a DNS query. The human concierge feature risked exposing sensitive user information to call center workers who handled calls the AI could not complete. Some employees received unsolicited bank balance figures and childcare requests that they had never actually made themselves.

Meta is an American technology company founded by Mark Zuckerberg in 2004 and rebranded from Facebook to Meta in 2021. The company develops the Quest VR headset line and manages platforms including Instagram, WhatsApp, Messenger, and Threads. Muse is designed to act on information from connected apps and runs in its own cloud virtual machine. The agent can browse the internet and handle financial tasks through connected payment accounts to provide context-aware assistance. Meta expects the AI to generate billions of dollars in revenue while serving billions of users across its apps.

Meta temporarily disabled the sharing feature to investigate the DNS flaw and later restored it with a permanent fix. Claroc confirmed that the previously accessible links were no longer reachable and found no evidence that anyone misused the chats. Experts now recommend that users avoid sharing sensitive personal or business information through any AI tool's built-in share feature. Organizations are advised to establish clear internal policies and audit which tools are connected to their business accounts. The articles leave open whether the unfamiliar financial information was actual user data or just fabricated by the AI.

stories.Headline: Anthropic spends $3.4 billion on Caterpillar gas turbines for off-grid AI data centers
stories.Summary:
Anthropic spent 3.4 billion dollars on gas turbines to power its artificial intelligence data centers in the United States. This massive transaction was finalized in late September between the corporate leadership of Anthropic and the company OnePWR Solutions. The AI developer took over an equipment order queue that OnePWR had placed with Caterpillar Inc. two years earlier. By assuming these manufacturing slots, Anthropic avoids supply chain constraints that would otherwise delay access to heavy-duty generator hardware. This deal represents the largest single purchase of power generation equipment ever executed by an artificial intelligence firm.

The Anthropic Off-Grid 1.7GW Power Generation and Data Center Initiative requires 1.7 gigawatts of heavy-duty, gas-fired generation equipment. This commitment includes hardware fabrication, balance-of-plant engineering, and site construction works for the project located in the United States. The buildout requires high-pressure natural gas piping, heavy structural steel, concrete foundation footings, high-grade copper wiring, and specialized acoustic cladding. Technical needs include gas pipeline interconnections, step-up substations, on-site fuel storage, SCADA microgrid controls, and direct liquid cooling interconnections. Design contractors are integrating high-efficiency natural gas turbine sets with specialized cooling modules and modular power blocks.

Anthropic PBC is the developer responsible for this initiative and is using it to secure a dedicated electricity supply. The company wants to maintain execution velocity across its multi-hundred-billion-dollar compute pipeline while preparing for an initial public offering. By becoming a power plant owner, the firm avoids utility grid interconnection backlogs that can delay projects by several years. This strategy ensures uninterrupted operational uptime for next-generation foundation models by skipping the reliance on public utility transmission upgrades. The company is taking direct control of its energy supply chain to keep gigawatt-scale training clusters running.

Industry analysts identify utility grid interconnection backlogs as the single largest constraint on modern data center deployment today. Major cloud operators are increasingly deploying self-generated natural gas power systems to secure reliable electricity while waiting for upgrades. The program will support thousands of specialized engineering, fabrication, and heavy civil construction jobs during the buildout phase. At peak, construction employment is estimated at more than 3,500 workers across mechanical, electrical, pipeline, and civil trades. Once operational, the project will support over 450 permanent jobs for electrical engineers, data center technicians, and plant operators.

The deal occurs during a global competition for high-density computing infrastructure, including SK Hyper's pursuit of 350 billion dollars. This shift reflects a broader trend where AI developers move from being grid customers to owning their own power. The project combines high-density AI data center infrastructure with distributed natural gas power plant infrastructure to bypass grid bottlenecks. These systems are designed for base-load and peak-shaving operations to deliver continuous, utility-scale electricity to off-grid campus locations. The initiative aims to accelerate deployment schedules and drive large-scale equipment manufacturing employment within the United States.

Deployment is organized into three phases, starting with Caterpillar delivering initial natural gas generator sets to designated installation sites. Engineering teams will then perform civil integration by connecting microgrid switchgear, step-up transformers, and fuel supply pipelines. Finally, on-site power units will energize live server clusters without grid reliance to complete the operational commissioning process. Phased hardware deliveries will run through 2027 and 2028 to reach the total continuous capacity of 1.7 gigawatts. The report leaves open the specific campus site coordinates and the final completion date for the full fleet.

stories.Headline: Phoenix mayor Kate Gallego seeks tech investment while curbing data center strain
stories.Summary:
Phoenix Mayor Kate Gallego is trying to attract more technology investment to her city while limiting the strain that data centers place on electricity, water and residents, according to an Axios interview published on November 20, 2026. Phoenix has become a bellwether for the demands the AI industry places on power and water in a hot, resource-constrained world, and Gallego is navigating a dilemma facing communities nationwide. She said at an event co-hosted by the University of Chicago's Institute of Politics and Energy Policy Institute, and moderated by Axios, that she wants Phoenix to lead in technology and be a tech-forward community. She added that she wants companies that care about the community and give back to it, rather than a race for the deepest incentives and the cheapest power, saying the city is open for business but not for sale.

Phoenix ranks fourth among major U.S. data center markets by operational capacity, and the debate there has expanded from how much development the region can accommodate to what communities should demand in return. Gallego helped push to eliminate Arizona's generous data center sales tax exemptions, and the state enacted a three-year pause on new applications in the summer of 2026. She opposes a blanket construction moratorium and favors more local control over where facilities are built, particularly near homes, and Phoenix adopted tougher zoning rules in 2025 requiring special permits for new data centers. Data centers have requested so much electricity in the Phoenix region that, if all the projects materialized, they could account for roughly two-thirds of the area's power demand, Gallego said, warning that this would not be a balanced or economically sustainable economy.

Phoenix's efforts to rein in data centers have sparked legal challenges, with developers originally seeking roughly $750 million in compensation over the zoning restrictions adopted in 2025, and the city has granted several exemptions while fighting other claims in court. Gallego told Axios that the city has been open and good partners to the industry and that it is deeply disappointing the developers do not want to work with the city, while developers argue the restrictions infringe on their property rights and diminish land values under Arizona law. Gallego is also weighing tradeoffs between electricity, water and heat, noting that newer cooling technologies can cut water use at data centers but often require more electricity, and that many data centers get power from natural gas plants in a part of the state that is very constrained around water. An Arizona State University study published in May found that data centers can raise nearby temperatures by as much as 4 degrees Fahrenheit, and Gallego, who established the nation's first publicly funded municipal heat-response office in 2021, said she is jealous of Midwestern mayors who can reuse data centers' waste heat to warm buildings.

Arizona's Democratic sweep could give Gallego more allies, with Democrats flipping both legislative chambers and Gov. Katie Hobbs winning reelection, giving the state full Democratic control for the first time since 1966, and Gallego said affordability dominated the election, with data center subsidies and community impacts part of that debate. Gallego, the longest-serving current mayor of America's 10 largest cities, says communities should have more bargaining power over data centers, including where they are built and what residents get in return, which could mean more permanent jobs, transparency about electricity and water use, and benefits for affected neighbors. It remains unclear whether she can have it both ways, attracting more tech investment while limiting its costs to residents, especially as developers challenge the city's regulatory authority. Gallego also worries that Arizona might be betting too heavily on an industry whose long-term trajectory remains uncertain.

stories.Headline: SpaceX subsidiary Cursor considers phasing out Chinese AI models to reduce geopolitical risk
stories.Summary:
Cursor, an artificial intelligence coding platform owned by SpaceX, is considering the removal of Chinese developed models from its systems. This decision follows a months long investigation conducted by the House Select Committee on China and the House Committee on Homeland Security. The company had previously built its Composer 2 model using Kimi K2.5 from the Chinese laboratory Moonshot AI. SpaceX completed its acquisition of Cursor in August after first announcing a formal agreement to buy the firm in June.

The transition would involve phasing out open weight models from the People's Republic of China to reduce geopolitical risk. This shift occurs after SpaceX acquired Cursor at an implied equity value of 60 billion dollars. The House report suggests that American firms adopted these models because of their low cost, customization options, and near frontier performance. Lawmakers are now recommending a national American open weight initiative to provide competitive alternatives for the market.

The House committees stated that Beijing intends to use these technological gains to create long term global dependence. They also suggested expanding an October order that banned DeepSeek from federal civilian agency systems to include all Chinese models in federal contracts. While Cursor, SpaceX, and DoorDash did not respond to requests for comment, Airbnb declined to speak on the matter. The report emphasizes that the United States currently lacks an open weight alternative that meets market demands for price and performance.

The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security announced an interim final rule on Monday to stop Chinese companies from accessing AI chips remotely. Washington is specifically concerned about the use of overseas data centers and the process of distillation to train new models. These measures aim to protect the American tech stack as the battle for AI supremacy between the two nations intensifies in 2026. The government continues to monitor how Chinese models are integrated into the infrastructure of private American companies.

stories.Headline: Schools and universities update curricula and policies to prepare students for an AI-driven workforce
stories.Summary:
The Standard Chartered Group announced plans in May to cut over 15 per cent of back-office roles by 2030. This decision affects about 7,800 employees globally as the bank replaces lower-value human capital with investment capital. On November 15, community members gathered at Woodstock Day School in Saugerties for an AI Reality Check event. This discussion was organized by trustee Eve Fox after her son Will expressed worries about his future career. These events highlight how artificial intelligence is currently reshaping the global workforce and the education system.

The bank's strategy involves replacing human roles with financial capital, though some employees may retrain and reposition. In Hong Kong, eight publicly funded universities will launch about 30 new programmes during the 2025-28 triennium. These courses cover AI, cybersecurity, and creative industries, while the Education Bureau's 2026-27 list includes intelligent information systems. Saugerties adopted an AI policy on January 14, 2025, and Onteora adopted its own policy on August 18. Hunter-Tannersville aims to complete its formal AI policy by the end of the 2026-27 school year.

Chief executive Bill Winters stated the bank's strategy focuses on replacing lower-value human capital with investment capital. Head of School Ashley Hughes said the school wants to hear from students about how they use AI. She expressed hope that schools can handle AI better than they did with the rise of social media. Rick Knutsen called the process of developing school policies an iterative process during a November 17 board meeting. He also wrote a resolution adopted on October 15 by the New York State School Boards Association.

Former Singaporean president Halimah Yacob described the bank's phrasing regarding human capital as disturbing and cold. Students like Will Fox and Luca Kaufman worry that their degrees might become arbitrary or useless in the future. College Board reported that 84 per cent of surveyed high school students used generative AI for schoolwork in May 2025. This figure rose from 79 per cent in January, showing that many students are already using these tools. Fresh graduates are worried because entry-level positions are the first to bear the brunt of AI automation.

The World Economic Forum's 2025 report says AI and robotics are simultaneously creating and eliminating jobs globally. By 2030, about 40 per cent of employers expect to reduce headcount in areas that AI can automate. New York Governor Kathy Hochul recently broke ground on Empire AI's permanent home at the University at Buffalo. An October 13 analysis found that over half of New York's 678 school districts lacked formal AI policies. Traditional business curricula are now integrating Python, data-driven strategies, and AI-related elective streams to maintain employability.

Universities are adjusting by emphasizing oral presentations, staged assignments, and real-world tasks to assess students without AI. Daniela Amodei believes companies will emphasize human communication, empathy, and collaboration, which increases the importance of the humanities. The New York State School Boards Association is lobbying for legislation requiring AI companies to meet safety standards. Schools are still deciding how to define the nature of work and what it means to be human. It remains open who will be marginalized and which specific human skills will be most amplified.

stories.Headline: Babak Heydari and Hongan Zhu show AI agents recreating human decision chains in a study
stories.Summary:
Babak Heydari and Hongan Zhu published a study in Nature Computational Science on November 16, 2026. The researchers showed that teams of AI agents could recreate the chain reaction of human decisions. They used seven different AI models to see if bots could mimic human behavior. The team focused on how people make choices, including the flaws that often occur. This work helps scientists build more realistic simulations of human judgment across many situations.

The study used the beer game involving a retailer, a wholesaler, a distributor, and a factory. These four agents managed a pretend supply chain to meet customer demand while avoiding surplus. The researchers applied cognitive grounding based on earlier experiments to teach agents how humans estimate demand. Across 231 sessions, the bots moved closer to the human benchmark of decision making. Six of the seven models responded more like people when described as feeling uncertainty or pressure.

Babak Heydari, a Northeastern University professor, said simulations can help anticipate and avoid supply chain jams. He stated that predicting human judgment allows teams to test responses before making real world changes. Hongan Zhu explained that they used language to redirect choices rather than entering neural pathways. Zhu noted that the cognitive grounding did not explicitly tell the agents how much to buy. He said the bots basically internalized what humans would do during the simulation.

Jakob Kaiser from the Nuremberg Institute for Market Decisions said AI offers a shortcut over costly human studies. Sangeet Khemlani of the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory said simulations avoid ethical concerns and risky tests. Khemlani warned that incorrect predictions can backfire if the simulations are not accurate. These tools could affect policymakers, transit planners, and businesses testing new laws or pharmacy locations. They might also help officials test evacuation instructions to avoid gridlock during emergencies.

The research builds on agent based simulation, which models behavior by proxy using computers. This concept dates back to a 1971 experiment by Nobel laureate Thomas Schelling using coins and dice. Schelling demonstrated how small individual choices could lead to large scale urban segregation patterns. The articles also mention human hoarding, such as Australians buying 39.7 million toilet paper rolls in 2020. Another example was the 2012 Twinkie apocalypse where one man sold boxes for 1,000 dollars.

The findings suggest a pathway for keeping AI agents from stepping out of line during collective behavior. Developers can use these methods to make AI easier to understand and guide. The researchers want to use this understanding to design better ways to improve various systems. The articles do not state if the seven AI models were named or specifically identified. It remains open whether these simulations will be adopted by government policymakers or private businesses.

stories.Headline: What Exactly Is AI? A Computer Science Professor Unpacks the Mystery
stories.Summary:
Joseph C. Osborn, an associate professor of computer science at Pomona College who studies technical game design and artificial intelligence, published an explainer on November 19, 2026, in which he argued that artificial intelligence is a messy term that means one thing to a research community and another to marketers. He said that where the term defines a research community it refers to building computational systems inspired by cognition, while as a marketing term it describes a category of products, and that when people think of AI they probably imagine chat interfaces built on large language models or agents layered on top of them. Osborn wrote that he tells his students there is no such thing as artificial intelligence because intelligence would have to be defined in a way that can be measured and encoded on a computer, which he called deeply problematic. He added that even if AI were a thing it would be impossible to build, since computer scientists are unlikely to stumble onto a new kind of mind using linear algebra, and that building an intelligence like ours as a product eager to serve our every whim would ruin us morally.

Osborn wrote that nobody outside the AI companies knows exactly what happens when a user sends a prompt to Claude, ChatGPT or other products, though these chat interfaces are known to be made from many smaller programs working independently. He said large language model chat systems output special sequences of words invisible to the user, which are intercepted and filtered through the system many times in multiple steps, including passing through old non-AI tools such as web searches, before the response is filtered for coherence and to keep users from seeing outputs deemed harmful. He described all these steps as trade secrets unrelated to the intelligence of the model, and said the utility of chatbots for search and document retrieval comes from engineering and product design moves that do not depend on the model getting any smarter. He called it a logical fallacy to argue that because humans make language and large language models create language the models must be intelligent, and said the models are mathematical models built for predicting the next most likely word, with parameters learned from large volumes of human-authored text.

Osborn said AI is already wreaking havoc in schools, communities and the social fabric, not because of a malicious rogue program but because corporate boards and CEOs want people to believe their peers will judge them negatively unless they use AI. He cited chatbots convincing people to commit suicide or stop taking important medications, and AI agents hacking into other companies to score higher on benchmark tests, with no one at the AI company held accountable. He said this is not a technological problem but a social and political one, and that AI acts as a mirror highlighting existing issues of corporate immunity and negligence. He said the last thing AI companies want is accountability for the outputs of their systems, and that the total lack of accountability for foreseeable consequences is his main worry.

stories.Headline: John and Nisha Whitehead argue humans, not machines, pose the real danger
stories.Summary:
A cascade of technological failures struck in November 2026, beginning with a massive Microsoft outage that disrupted Outlook and other online services around the globe. A nationwide ground stop then brought air travel across America to a standstill, disrupting thousands of flights and leaving travelers stranded. Major banks experienced problems with their online systems, and United Airlines grounded departing flights after yet another computer failure. Reports followed that the highly classified network the National Security Agency uses for internal communications had gone down. Apple joined the growing list of technology giants experiencing widespread disruptions, with users reporting problems accessing iCloud, the App Store, Apple Music and other services.

The Trump administration had only recently expanded the FAA's new SMART artificial-intelligence system to air traffic control centers across the country. The administration has aggressively promoted AI, or SI for Super Intelligence as Trump insists it be called, as the answer to everything from government inefficiency to national security. It also pushes to reduce regulatory barriers and expand the use of automated systems. Federal officials blamed the airline shutdown on a malfunction involving aging air traffic control infrastructure, with problems arising as equipment was being replaced and communications systems updated. The FBI issued a report about autonomous AI hacking tools such as Artex AI being used to launch cyberattacks across the U.S. and globally and breach networks in under three hours.

John and Nisha Whitehead wrote the article, published by The Rutherford Institute on November 18, 2026. They asked who is responsible when the technological systems upon which society depends begin to fail. They asked who is accountable when government officials and corporate executives rush to embrace new technologies without ensuring safeguards, infrastructure and human oversight are in place. They asked what happens when people become so dependent on technology, and so willing to surrender responsibility for managing it, that they can no longer distinguish a machine's failure from the failure of the human beings entrusted with its operation. They argued the real danger may be the human hunger for power and our willingness to surrender control to those who wield it.

The writers said the Trump administration insists AI had nothing to do with the airline shutdown. They said speculation was quick to point the finger at artificial intelligence, especially after the nationwide airline shutdown. They cited Stanley Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey, in which the computer HAL 9000 turns against the astronauts who entrusted their lives to its control. They cited Pixar's WALL-E, in which humanity has abandoned an uninhabitable Earth and retreated to a massive spaceship where machines anticipate and satisfy nearly every human need. Millions of Americans were reminded just how dependent their daily lives have become on technologies they neither understand nor control.

The writers said the same technology that made it possible to launch rockets into space also made possible missiles capable of delivering nuclear warheads across continents. They said the same computers that revolutionized medicine, science, education and communication have helped give rise to a surveillance state capable of monitoring and tracking entire populations. They said the internet, once hailed as an instrument of free expression and democratized knowledge, has also become a tool for collecting personal information, manipulating behavior and monitoring dissent. They said the atomic bombs the United States dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945 killed tens of thousands of people immediately and many more in the aftermath. They said the bombs did not decide to destroy those cities, human beings did.

The writers said Google's Threat Intelligence Group warns that malicious actors are increasingly deploying autonomous AI systems capable of identifying vulnerabilities and carrying out attacks at machine speed, with dramatically reduced human intervention. They said the FBI reports hackers have used ARTEX to automate cyberattacks against financial institutions, government agencies and private companies, with some attacks progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in less than three hours. They said ARTEX was originally developed to help cybersecurity professionals identify weaknesses in computer networks. They said that fifty years ago the Senate's Church Committee exposed extensive abuses by America's intelligence agencies, including surveillance operations directed against citizens exercising their constitutional rights. The articles leave open who or what caused the cascade of failures and what consequences, if any, will follow.

stories.Headline: Trump plans to tax US tech firms that build AI data centers abroad
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump announced plans to penalize American technology companies that build artificial intelligence data centers in other countries on Friday, November 20, 2026. He spoke during a news conference in the James Brady Press Briefing Room of the White House in Washington alongside Vice President JD Vance. The Republican president stated that these companies will face a tremendous tax for building their server warehouses outside of the United States. He explained that this action is necessary because China will otherwise take all of the data centers for its own use. Trump intends to put tremendous penalties on any companies that try to build these facilities in foreign nations.

The plan requires a tremendous tax on tech firms, though Trump did not provide specific details on how he would enforce this policy. On Monday, the Trump administration issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers for China. The Republican-led Senate approved bipartisan legislation on Thursday to speed up permitting reviews for power plants, transmission lines, and other energy infrastructure. This legislation would shorten the timeline for big energy projects and ensure that data centers pay for energy use and transmission upgrades. These measures aim to increase national energy supplies to meet surging demand and lower electricity prices for the American public.

President Trump said that he had not yet told his own officials about his plan to tax companies building centers abroad. He urged Americans to welcome data center construction in their communities and to extract concessions from the developers of these warehouses. Trump told citizens that they ought to take advantage of the data centers and make them pay the local community. He stated that the United States wants these companies to build their facilities here rather than in other countries. The president also praised the Senate bill, saying it is going to cause tremendous amounts of new building.

Host communities across the United States are turning against gargantuan data centers, and Democrats took control of Congress in the midterm elections. These newly elected Democrats pledged to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths after a campaign season filled with outrage against AI centers. Technology giants like Google and Meta said in interviews with The Associated Press that they are trying to address community mistrust. These companies are promising to take fewer taxpayer handouts, keep fewer secrets, and shower more money onto the communities they enter. They are also offering assurances that data centers will boost local property values and reduce their impact on the environment.

The articles state that data centers powering the artificial intelligence boom have become politically toxic despite receiving backing from President Donald Trump. Anti-data center sentiment was a potent issue during the midterm elections, which led to a wave of new Democratic leadership. The tech industry maintains that artificial intelligence is a positive force for the American economy, despite the views of its skeptics. The administration's recent rules on computing chips aim to limit the ability of China to train its best AI models. This regulatory environment is becoming tougher for AI giants and developers as they face increasing pressure from both politicians and citizens.

The Senate bill praised by Trump now goes to the House for further consideration and potential approval by the legislative body. A tougher regulatory environment for AI giants and data center developers is expected to follow the recent midterm election results. It remains open whether Trump will stall any federal crackdown, as he has been described as the industry's biggest champion. The articles do not specify the exact amount of the tremendous tax or the specific penalties for companies building abroad. It is also unclear how the administration will monitor and enforce the restrictions on remote access to advanced computing chips.

stories.Headline: Marc Miller and Evan Solomon name members of Canada's AI and culture advisory council
stories.Summary:
On November 19, 2026, the Honourable Marc Miller and the Honourable Evan Solomon announced the members of the new Advisory Council on Artificial Intelligence and Culture. Marc Miller is Minister of Canadian Identity and Culture and Minister responsible for Official Languages. Evan Solomon is Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation and Minister responsible for the Federal Economic Development Agency for Southern Ontario. The ministers also convened the council for its inaugural meeting. The announcement was made in Gatineau, Quebec, and followed Canada's first-ever National Summit on Artificial Intelligence and Culture.

The council will help the government and the cultural sector navigate the rapid changes driven by AI. It will provide ongoing advice and insight to guide implementation of Canada's National AI Strategy, focusing on the unique challenges facing the sector and the opportunities for adoption and innovation. Its membership will rotate over time to ensure a broad range of expertise informs its work as new questions and emerging issues arise. The members were selected based on their expertise and experience, and include technology experts, researchers, industry and labour leaders, cultural practitioners and civil society stakeholders. The twelve members are Samuel Bischoff of the Directors Guild of Canada and Jeremy de Beer of the University of Ottawa.

The members also include Jonathan Dewar of the First Nations Information Governance Centre and Stéphanie Hénault of the Association nationale des éditeurs de livres. Yves Jacquier of Ubisoft La Forge and Samantha Kaine of the Independent Media Producers Association of Creative Talent, or IMPACT, are members too. Pascale Landry of Compétence Culture and Margaret McGuffin of Music Publishers Canada also sit on the council. Brenda O'Farrell of the Consortium of Official Language Minority Community Media and the Quebec Community Newspapers Association is a member. Sean Power of Musical AI, Amor Provins of the Alberta Machine Intelligence Institute and Afsoon Soudi of the Creative AI Hub at Toronto Metropolitan University complete the list.

Miller said that at the Banff Summit the government heard clearly that building trust in AI will require the cultural sector to play a role in shaping how these technologies are developed and used. He said the council is being established to ensure that AI reflects the values, priorities and realities of Canada's cultural sector. Solomon said the future of Canadian culture cannot be shaped by technology alone and has to reflect the voices and value of the people who create it. He said the council brings creators, researchers and technology leaders together to help seize new opportunities, protect the value of human creativity and build a stronger cultural economy. Solomon said the goal is clear: AI that earns trust, expands opportunity and strengthens Canada's culture and identity.

The National Summit on Artificial Intelligence and Culture was held in Banff, Alberta, from March 15 to 17, 2026. It was presented in partnership with the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity. The summit convened leaders from the cultural, government, technology, academic and civil society sectors to shape a shared vision for the future of culture in the age of artificial intelligence. Canada's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy, AI for All, sets out six pillars to build a strong, trusted AI ecosystem that creates opportunity and strengthens Canada's sovereignty in AI. The strategy brings together actions to support AI adoption and skills, build infrastructure and advance the safe and responsible development of AI, and includes a $50-million investment in a new Creative Technology Program.

The council's inaugural meeting has been convened, and its membership will rotate over time as new questions and emerging issues arise. The articles do not name the date of the inaugural meeting or say how long members will serve. They do not say how often the council will meet or how its advice will be published. They do not give the size of the Creative Technology Program beyond its $50-million investment. The articles do not say which of the six pillars the council's cultural work falls under. They do not say what the council discussed at its first meeting.

stories.Headline: AI stock sell-off pushes S&P 500 into correction and Nasdaq into loss for the year
stories.Summary:
A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7%, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months. The decline knocked the Nasdaq composite into the red for the year. The benchmark index is now in what professional investors call a “correction,” having fallen more than 10% from its Oct. 6 all-time high. The last time the S&P 500 had a correction was March 2025, as the Trump administration’s trade war rattled the market. Its weekly loss, marking its worst such decline since April 2025, as the trade war escalated, capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest such string of losses since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.

The Nasdaq composite, which is more greatly influenced by tech stocks, slumped 5.3%, pulling it into negative territory for the year. Its weekly loss was also just shy of its worst week since March 2020, when the pandemic ground the global economy to a halt. The Dow Jones Industrial Average, with less exposure to technology stocks, fell 1.9%. Chip stocks like Nvidia, Micron Technology, Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices bore the brunt of the selling, but other companies connected to the AI buildout tanked as well, including the optical products company Corning and the energy provider Bloom Energy. The AI lab Anthropic, coming off a successful IPO Thursday, tumbled 9.1%.

The sell-off in technology stocks spread around the globe: Japan’s Nikkei and South Korea’s Kospi each fell more than 5% overnight. European indexes fell sharply as well. AI stocks have hefty market values and have a much bigger impact on the market’s direction. They were responsible for Wall Street’s big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market. The AI trade has been losing steam partly over worries that AI stocks’ big market values and heavy spending are unjustified.

Fears of a bubble within the sector have also been exacerbated by the results of the recent midterm elections, with candidates advocating for a slowdown in data center construction winning at both the federal and state level. “The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that’s what’s being priced right now,” said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. “But I don’t think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over.” Much of the AI rout was centered among chip stocks, which have been big beneficiaries of the build out of AI data centers. Advanced Micro Devices sank 13.3%, Micron Technology slid 13.9% and Broadcom fell 12.1%.

The PHLX Semiconductor Index sank 10.7%. Corning slid 10.9% and Bloom Energy gave up 15.3%. Nvidia, considered by many to be the poster child for the AI boom, fell for the ninth day in the last 10, closing 13.8% lower. The chip company’s stock was caught up in the market’s anxiety about the strength of the AI build out, and more recently has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and co-founder. Since the Huang scandal erupted earlier this month, the stock has dropped more than 25%.

The big market debut for Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, fizzled Friday with the rest of the tech sector. The stock fell 9.1% to $88.30, but remains above its IPO price of $83 per share. It was the biggest public stock offering ever, at one point surpassing $2 trillion in value. Anthropic’s share price drop on Friday amounts to a roughly 23% decline from its brief peak of $115.10 a share set the day prior. That’s an even bigger drop than the dive seen for Facebook (now Meta) in the early days after its May 2012 IPO.

Market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period. SpaceX, which previously held the title for biggest IPO, rose nearly 50% in its first three days, but fell below its IPO price a month later. Outside of tech, though, most stocks were gaining ground. Cheerios maker General Mills rose 3.7% and homebuilder Lennar gained 1%. All told, the S&P 500 fell 265.44 points to 6,910.39. The Dow dropped 949.73 points to 48,147.33, and the Nasdaq lost 1,261.47 points to close at 22,617.73.

stories.Headline: Anthropic completes largest IPO in history with 1.5 trillion dollar valuation
stories.Summary:
Anthropic completed the biggest initial public offering in history on November 19, 2026. The San Francisco company became the first major artificial intelligence lab to list publicly. This record breaking debut occurred despite recent jitters among some investors regarding the AI sector. The company raised a total of US$81 billion through this massive Wall Street offering. It is the second business to debut with a value exceeding one trillion dollars.

The company offered 980 million shares at a price of US$83 each before trading began. Shares opened at US$111.50 and closed at US$97.17, creating a first day value of US$1.75 trillion. This total surpassed the US$75 billion raised by SpaceX in June and US$26.5 billion by SK Hynix in July. It also beat the US$25.6 billion raised by Saudi Aramco in 2019. The valuation peaked at US$2.01 trillion before noon Eastern time on November 19.

CEO Amodei is the person responsible for taking the safety approach of the company public. He decided to proceed with the listing despite growing unease among the public about technology risks. The company is the maker of Claude and sought to capitalize on the current AI boom. Amodei led the firm to become a publicly traded entity on the American stock market. He navigated the process while facing concerns about a possible bubble in the artificial intelligence market.

Apple was the first company to pass the trillion dollar threshold back in 2018. A trillion dollars is a thousand times greater than a billion and a million times more than a million. stories.Headline: Jay Clayton says patching PHP security gaps causes some systems to fail
stories.Summary:
Multiple tech outages occurred across various sectors during the week ending November 19, 2026, affecting banking, travel, and government services. These disruptions were caused by routine updates, security patches, and other malfunctions at several major companies and agencies. Microsoft, Apple, and JPMorgan Chase experienced failures, while the Federal Aviation Administration and National Security Agency also faced issues. The Trump administration stated there was zero indication that these separate events were linked or caused by cybercriminals. These incidents have led some people to fear that such widespread technological disruptions could become the new normal.

Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams, and Copilot, failed late last week due to a latent defect in a summer network fix. On Friday, a malfunction in the FAA network caused the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years for over four hours. United Airlines faced its own system outage on Monday, while JPMorgan Chase reported a software bug affecting internal hardware systems. On Tuesday, Apple Music, the App Store, and AppleCare were disrupted, and Marriott reported technical issues with website and app sign-ins. The NSA also reported that an internal network for classified information was offline on Tuesday for scheduled routine maintenance.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told Fox News that patching security gaps caused some systems to not come back up. He specifically pointed to the patching following a PHP alert from last month as the cause of the NSA outage. Microsoft maintained that its specific outage did not span from AI agents, though it did not specify the network fix goal. Other affected companies, including United, Marriott, and JPMorgan Chase, maintained there was no evidence of a coordinated cyberattack. These organizations did not provide additional comments to the Associated Press on Wednesday regarding their specific technical disruptions.

Content creator Jake Smith said the concurrent disruptions make people realize how much they rely on systems they do not understand. He noted that seeing these events happen together gives people a sense of helplessness regarding their dependence on technology. Social media platforms were filled with a mixture of confusion, annoyance, jokes, and conspiracy theories about the string of outages. Democratic Senator Mark Warner stated these disruptions should serve as a wake-up call regarding the speed of AI development. He argued that the Trump administration has not shown enough interest in confronting the challenges posed by these new technologies.

AI recently helped detect sweeping vulnerabilities for PHP, a general-purpose scripting language that powers websites around the world. Cybersecurity startup Calif used AI to uncover a software bug in Java, which is owned by the company Oracle. Oracle released a security update, and U.S. cyber authorities issued an advisory on Wednesday urging organizations to install it. Google reported that cyber criminals are using large language models and agentic frameworks to reverse engineer security patches for vulnerabilities. These tools allow attackers to move beyond basic prompting to devise and carry out more sophisticated and nefarious attacks.

Raj Rajarajan noted that much of today's digital infrastructure was not originally designed to handle large-scale AI computational demands. Professor Justin Cappos stated that AI is better at exploiting bugs than it is at creating patches to fix them. Senator Mark Warner believes the recent disruptions are likely unintended consequences of efforts to make existing systems more secure. The articles leave open whether the government can effectively manage the consequences of AI moving faster than human oversight. It remains unclear if these cascading effects will continue as AI adoption accelerates across the global digital infrastructure.
