stories.Headline: Michelle Hinchey introduces bill making fake AI citations judicial misconduct
stories.Summary:
State Sen. Michelle Hinchey introduced the Judicial AI Accountability and Integrity Act on Thursday, November 19, 2026, according to Wisevoter. The bill would classify a judge's knowing or reckless use of fabricated legal authority in judicial writings as misconduct in office. Using AI alone would not constitute misconduct under the bill. The legislation follows rulings in Mississippi, New Jersey and Oklahoma in which judges acknowledged that their decisions contained AI-generated fictitious citations.

The bill provides that misconduct occurs when a judge relies on a citation containing fabricated legal authority or one that is materially false. It would authorize the New York State Commission on Judicial Conduct to refer misconduct determinations to the Assembly for impeachment. Judges would avoid misconduct by verifying all information against reliable, legitimate sources before including it in judicial writing. A 2026 survey found that over 60% of federal judges report using AI tools, with at least 20% using them weekly, and legal AI tools have produced factually incorrect information 17% to 33% of the time. The survey does not address New York judges specifically.

The New York State Commission on Judicial Conduct, the state body that investigates complaints against judges, is reviewing the bill. Hinchey, who represents the Hudson Valley region, plans to advocate for the bill's passage in the 2027 legislative session, when its prospects will become clearer. The bill seeks to ensure that rulings rest on real case law and facts, because judicial decisions directly affect people's freedom and rights. If enacted, it would give New York a formal mechanism to address the misuse of AI in judicial writing that the Mississippi, New Jersey and Oklahoma cases exposed.

stories.Headline: Beyer releases AI safety outline as Warner introduces AI finance disclosure bill
stories.Summary:
Representative Don Beyer and Senator Mark Warner each moved forward with separate artificial intelligence measures in Washington on Thursday, November 19, 2026, approaching the technology from opposite ends of the Capitol. Beyer, a Democrat representing Virginia's 8th District, released an outline for bipartisan legislation that would require the companies building the most powerful AI systems to adopt safety frameworks, report incidents and submit to outside review. Warner, a Democrat from Virginia, introduced a bill that would force publicly traded companies to disclose more about how they finance and oversee AI. Beyer's proposal is a blueprint only, and the legislative text has not yet been written, while Warner's bill has been formally introduced.

Beyer's outline would apply to the companies building the most powerful artificial intelligence systems, requiring them to adopt safety frameworks, report incidents and submit to outside review. Warner's bill would require publicly traded companies to disclose more about how they finance and oversee artificial intelligence. The two measures were pushed on the same day, Thursday, November 19, 2026, according to The Alexandria Brief. Beyer's plan remains a blueprint, meaning the legislative text has not been written, while Warner's bill was introduced. The articles do not give further numbers, dates or names beyond these.

Beyer is a Democrat representing the 8th District, and Warner is a Democrat from Virginia, and each is responsible for his own measure. The articles do not quote either lawmaker directly, so what they said is not available beyond the descriptions of their proposals. Beyer released an outline for bipartisan legislation, and Warner introduced a bill, according to the report. No further statements from either office are included in the articles.

The context is that the two Virginia lawmakers pushed separate artificial intelligence measures in Washington on the same Thursday, approaching the technology from opposite ends of the Capitol. Beyer's effort is at the blueprint stage, with the legislative text still unwritten, and Warner's bill has been introduced. The articles do not say what happens next beyond those stages. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Scott Carr urges accounting firms to adopt AI tools for HR operations
stories.Summary:
Scott Carr, owner of Farmhouse Networking in Grants Pass, Oregon, published an article on CPA Practice Advisor on November 19, 2026, arguing that accounting firms should adopt practical AI tools in their human resources operations. He wrote that AI tools built for HR can screen candidates, draft onboarding materials and answer staff policy questions, freeing partner and office manager time for higher-value work. He noted that most firms do not have a dedicated HR department, so recruiting, onboarding and staff support typically fall to a partner, office manager or whoever has the bandwidth that week. That bandwidth disappears fastest heading into busy season, which he said is exactly why AI-assisted HR tools are gaining traction in the profession.

Carr listed action steps for firm leadership and IT, including mapping which HR tasks consume the most staff time during peak season and evaluating AI tools for applicant screening and interview scheduling that operate independently of the firm's client financial data environment. He recommended deploying an AI-assisted internal knowledge base so staff can get quick answers about firm policies without pulling a partner away from client work, and confirming data segregation with IT before rollout so HR tools never have access to or storage overlap with client financial records. He also advised using AI-generated summaries of staff engagement or exit interview feedback to catch retention issues before busy season, establishing a written policy on what staff can and cannot input into AI tools, and scheduling a security review of any HR software before firm-wide rollout. In a question-and-answer section, he said AI tools can speed up initial screening but hiring decisions should still involve a partner or manager review, and that a properly configured HR chatbot should be kept fully separate from client data systems, with that separation verified before deployment rather than assumed.

Carr wrote that accounting firms treating HR as an afterthought tend to lose good staff to burnout and administrative friction, particularly during the compressed timelines of tax season. He said AI-assisted HR processes offer a practical way to reduce that friction, but only when implemented with the same rigor firms already apply to client data security. He added that any tool touching employee records deserves the same scrutiny as one touching client financials, since a poorly vetted HR platform can just as easily become a point of exposure. Firms considering this shift should treat it as a technology decision, not just an HR decision, one that belongs on the same checklist as any other system with access to sensitive data.

stories.Headline: IRS advisory council urges IRS to expand AI guidance for tax practitioners
stories.Summary:
The IRS Advisory Council recommended in its annual report, released Wednesday, November 19, 2026, that the IRS revisit and expand recent guidance on tax practitioners' use of artificial intelligence, saying existing standards for preparer conduct and taxpayer information were not developed with modern AI-assisted tools and workflows in mind. The 37-member council said in the report that AI is increasingly used in ways affecting how practitioners receive, process, analyze, transmit, and store taxpayer information, yet there appears to be little or no direct guidance addressing these uses. The council recommended that the IRS seek comments on guidance issued this year by the Office of Professional Responsibility, reissue that guidance after reviewing the comments, and expand AI guidance to all preparer tax identification number holders rather than limiting it to practitioners subject to Treasury Circular 230. The recommendation arrives as tax practitioners and regulators debate how existing professional standards apply to rapidly evolving AI technology, and the AI proposals were among 33 in the annual report. IRSAC also pointed to uncertainty about how AI vendors handle taxpayer information, saying the taxpayer and preparer may not fully understand how an AI provider receives, stores, uses, or retains information submitted to the system.

The council said increasing AI use creates a gap in the IRS's model security guidance concerning vendor selection, data handling, access controls, retention, and other risks specific to AI-enabled systems. The report repeatedly emphasized the need for technology-based solutions as the agency operates with a substantially smaller workforce, saying digital tools, analytics, and automation can improve productivity and direct scarce personnel to higher-value work but do not eliminate the need for experienced employees to resolve complex cases, protect taxpayer rights, and administer a changing tax code. IRSAC also recommended that the IRS create a business version of its Identity Protection PIN program to help combat employer identification number theft, urging the agency to pilot an EIN Protection PIN or similar filing authorization tool and expand alerts in Business Tax Account. The council said businesses lack a protection comparable to the IP PIN available to individual taxpayers, calling business identity theft a persistent tax-administration risk in which a stolen or misused EIN can support an unauthorized return, refund or credit claim, information return, or account change. IRSAC urged the IRS to create a public-facing tracker for tax-related identity theft cases, since victims now can obtain updates only by phone or correspondence, and it proposed a tool modeled on the IRS's Where's My Application for Tax-Exempt Status system.

Average resolution times for identity theft cases exceed 15 months, IRSAC said, noting an inventory of roughly 387,000 unresolved cases. The council also urged the IRS to increase efforts to combat ghost preparers, improve processing of penalty and interest abatement requests, simplify Form W-4, enhance worker-classification determinations, expand small business tax literacy efforts, and study elective withholding by partnerships on behalf of domestic partners. The AICPA has raised concerns about portions of the OPR guidance regarding practitioner fees, and OPR director Thomas Curtin said at last week's AICPA National Tax Conference that additional guidance is forthcoming. The article does not say when the IRS will respond to the council's recommendations or whether it will adopt them.

stories.Headline: TSMC suspends advanced chip orders for Chinese design firms amid tighter export controls
stories.Summary:
On November 19, Reuters reported that TSMC tightened restrictions on certain Chinese semiconductor design companies. The company suspended manufacturing orders using 16nm technology or more advanced nodes. These actions occurred as export controls evolved toward manufacturing capacity and advanced packaging. The restrictions target the entire AI supply chain rather than individual chips. This shift happened during a period of extraordinary demand for AI infrastructure.

Affected Chinese customers are generally limited to older 28nm and 40nm manufacturing processes. This limitation applies provided their products do not require advanced packaging or incorporate HBM. TSMC can no longer use the previous technical verification process for these specific designers. Advanced chip orders are now presumed to fall under export controls unless authorizations exist. These rules apply to companies operating across Taiwan, China, Southeast Asia, Europe, and the United States.

The U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security introduced an interim final rule on November 16. This regulation targets overseas data centers providing substantial computing capacity to restricted foreign entities. Regulators stated that restricting physical exports may be insufficient if users obtain remote access. They are concerned with who ultimately accesses the computing capacity that advanced chips provide. Compliance now involves monitoring beneficial ownership and cross-border computing arrangements for cloud providers.

Chinese semiconductor designers are the primary entities affected by these new manufacturing restrictions. They face challenges in rebuilding an entire ecosystem including domestic foundries and memory technologies. Using older nodes increases electrical power consumption, silicon area, and system integration complexity. NVIDIA, AMD, and smartphone manufacturers may absorb the capacity left by canceled Chinese orders. These high performance computing customers represent a shift in TSMC's potential customer mix.

TSMC reported October 2026 consolidated revenue of approximately NT$586.9 billion, a 59.7 percent increase. Revenue for the first ten months of 2026 increased 43.3 percent over 2025. NVIDIA announced expanded manufacturing commitments on November 17 with Foxconn, Samsung Electro-Mechanics, Kinsus, Amkor, SPIL, and TSMC. The Vera Rubin NVL72 platform and Vera CPUs began volume shipments during the third quarter. These products leverage CoWoS technologies and TSMC's 3nm and 5nm nodes.

NVIDIA provided multibillion-dollar funding to SPIL for expanded advanced packaging operations in Taiwan. The company also made substantial prepayments to Amkor for expansion in South Korea and the United States. OSAT providers and equipment suppliers must now demonstrate the traceability of their delivery networks. The articles leave open whether these restrictions will produce temporary or permanent shifts. Future developments over the next twelve months will determine the final impact.

stories.Headline: Indian AI startups raise $1.6 billion as US AI firms raise $329.2 billion
stories.Summary:
US AI-native companies raised $329.2 billion across 981 equity funding rounds between January 1 and November 3, 2026, according to Tracxn data. Indian AI-native companies raised $1.6 billion across 90 rounds during the same period. The artificial intelligence boom has put India's startup ecosystem in a strange fix, the article states. India is pitching itself as an attractive technology investment destination while global venture capital concentrates around American AI companies. For Indian AI startups, the challenge is convincing investors their businesses can deliver growth, commercial returns and technological differentiation.

India's startup equity funding was $11.7 billion across 1,362 equity rounds between January 1 and November 3, 2026. That compares with $11.2 billion across 2,180 rounds during the corresponding period in 2025. Early-stage funding covering Series A and B rounds increased from $3.7 billion to $5.1 billion. Seed funding declined from $1.3 billion to $873 million, while late-stage funding remained broadly stable at $5.7 billion against $5.8 billion. Tracxn data shows Indian startup funding touched $39 billion in 2021 across over 2,000 rounds.

Siddharth Pai, Founding Partner at 3one4 Capital, says caution around AI has been in the market for a while because the business case for AI has lagged the industry's growth. He says three AI companies, SpaceX, OpenAI and Anthropic, will raise more capital in their IPOs than the US markets have in the past 15 years. He says Anthropic cut its valuation expectations from $2 trillion to $1.4 trillion. Pai traces the difficult funding environment to 2022, following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, and says India is yet to reach the high watermark of 2021's fundraising. He says India has the capital for its AI ambitions but lacks the policies to channel this capital.

Supratik Shankar, Co-founder of AI-native data intelligence platform Dview, says confidence in the technology and confidence in a particular valuation are two different things. He cites US Federal Reserve figures showing productivity grew about 1.5% a year from 1973 to 1995 and about 3.3% a year from 1995 to 2003. Bhaskar Majumdar, Founder and Managing Partner of Unicorn India Ventures, says US AI startups reach $10 million ARR within six months of launching. He says the rush for capital in US AI is having a knock-on effect on follow-on investments in India. Pai says early-stage AI businesses need strong customer traction and repeat business, and cautions they risk having their offerings absorbed into larger platforms.

Pai points to pension funds, provident funds, insurance companies and banks facing unfavourable regulations when investing in alternative investment funds that finance startups. He calls for reforms to pricing for foreign investors, tax-free share swaps, a shift to residence-based taxation and better taxation of employee stock ownership plans. Shankar says a company can build valuable intellectual property in its data architecture, domain logic, evaluations, integrations and workflow execution. He says investors will examine compute costs, implementation time and effort, dependencies, renewals and margins after deployment. Pai expects it to take another two to four quarters for this to register with investors and for more capital to flow back into the system.

The article was published on November 19, 2026, and updated the same day. It was written by Ridhika Basnet, a journalist covering the real-world impact of artificial intelligence. The article carries the headline that America is flooding AI with billions while Indian startups fight for survival. It states the disparity in funding amounts between US and Indian AI companies raises concerns for emerging markets. It states market caution persists due to the lagging business case for AI compared to its rapid growth.

Articles.Title: America is Flooding AI With Billions. Indian Startups are Fighting for Survival - Analytics India Magazine

stories.Headline: Wisconsin lawmakers Severson and Stroud agree AI firms should be liable for harmful errors
stories.Summary:
In the national Democratic wave of the Nov. 3 election, Wisconsin Democrats won a trifecta by taking the governor's office and both houses of the Legislature, but Republican Sen.-elect Erik Severson and re-elected Democratic Assembly member Angela Stroud still found common ground on regulating artificial intelligence companies. The two lawmakers, who gave nearly identical answers on AI during their pre-election candidate interviews on Wisconsin Public Radio, appeared together on "Morning Edition" with host Robin Washington to discuss where they agree and disagree. Severson previously served two terms in the Assembly and was elected to the 25th Senate District, while Stroud was re-elected in the 73rd Assembly District. Both said AI companies should be held liable when their products cause harm by giving users patently wrong information, such as citing court cases that do not exist.

On the question of whether AI firms should be accountable for harmful errors, both lawmakers answered "100 percent" during the campaign, and each said they could work together on the issue. Severson said that if both are at 100 percent he does not see how they could fail to cooperate, arguing that companies teaching their machines to lie and cause harm should be held accountable, and that this is what is best for the people of his district. Stroud called it a clear moral question and tied it to the Democratic principle of holding corporations accountable for polluting the environment, harming children and taking financial advantage of people. Washington noted that the National Conference of State Legislatures has models of bills from around the country and said he would search to see whether anyone is addressing the issue.

Stroud said her top goal is to represent the people of the 73rd District and to get as much done as quickly as possible so people see improvements in their lives, adding that there are many pent-up Democratic ideas that have not had a chance to see the light of day. She said her main advice to anyone serving is to stop focusing on partisanship, arguing that parties focus only on winning elections when the point of winning is to get things done. She said that under Republican control last year 3.8 percent of Democratic bills got a hearing, while the last time Democrats held a trifecta 16 years ago, 38 percent of Republican bills were heard in committee, and she intends to hear Republican bills. Severson said he will do exactly what he said during the campaign, which is to make it less expensive to live and more affordable for people, and that if Democrats want to lower taxes he will work with them any time.

Severson said there will be many areas where the parties can work together and probably more things they agree on than disagree on. When asked for advice on serving in the minority, he said Stroud won her election by telling people what she stood for and does not need his advice. Stroud said she was reluctant to advise someone with more legislative experience than she has but appreciated his service. The interview was originally published by Wisconsin Public Radio.

Articles.Title: Northern Wisconsin Lawmakers Find Common Ground On AI Rules

stories.headline_source: Northern Wisconsin Lawmakers Find Common Ground On AI Rules

stories.Headline: Researchers argue that security generalization error is U-shaped and minimized at a finite optimal model size
stories.Summary:
Qi Tan, Tianyu Cui, Qi Li and Ke Xu posted a paper titled Condensing Law of Security Information on arXiv on 20 November 2026, arguing that the common belief that larger language models always perform better does not hold for security work. They say security decisions depend on unusual inputs such as zero-day attacks, which are long-tailed and poorly served by likelihood fitting, so scale does not help in the way it does elsewhere. They add that the capability that comes with scale, such as inferring an intended whole from a corrupted part, can lead a model to silently repair an anomaly before any downstream security head sees it. The authors formalize this as a tradeoff between the cognitive capability a model holds about the world distribution and the security-information retention that survives in its intermediate representation.

The paper derives three information-theoretic bounds that connect these two quantities, including an upper bound on restoration accuracy in terms of cognitive capability and an upper bound on retention in terms of restoration error. It also gives a Fano lower bound on security-task error in terms of retention, and the authors say these theorems approximately imply that usable security information is a product of how much security information survives and how well it can be extracted. They state the condensing law of security information, which says usable security information is unimodal in model size, so security generalization error is U-shaped and is minimized at a finite optimal size rather than decreasing without bound. Experiments on various real-world language models validate the law, and the authors conclude that there is an optimal model size for solving security issues.

The work is listed under Cryptography and Security, with Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning as additional categories, and the full paper is available as a PDF, as experimental HTML and as TeX source. The posting appears on arXiv, which describes arXivLabs as a framework that lets collaborators develop and share features directly on the site and states that partners in it have embraced its values of openness, community, excellence and user data privacy. arXiv says it is committed to working only with partners who adhere to those values and invites ideas for projects that would add value to its community. The articles give no further details on the experiments, the specific models tested or any planned follow-up work.

stories.Headline: Carlson LLC sues Anthropic and Meta for using self-help books to train AI models
stories.Summary:
Carlson LLC filed a federal lawsuit on November 19, 2026, against the artificial intelligence companies Anthropic PBC and Meta Platforms, Inc. The plaintiff claims that these two tech giants illegally used more than two dozen self-improvement books to train their AI models. These literary works were written by the husband and wife team of R. and K. Carlson, including the famous Don't Sweat the Small Stuff series. The legal action was brought in the Northern District of California under case number 3:26-cv-14248.

The complaint alleges that the defendants harvested training materials from pirate libraries such as Anna's Archive and Books3. It further asserts that the companies scanned physical books without permission to feed their respective systems, Claude and Meta AI. Carlson LLC specifically opted out of the Bartz class action settlement with Anthropic to pursue this separate claim. The company argues that these bestsellers are more valuable than other works and have suffered direct harm from competition with large language models.

Brian Matthew Grossman of Tesser Grossman LLP is representing Carlson LLC in this copyright infringement matter. The plaintiff maintains that the books in question possess a long and successful history that distinguishes them from other literary works. While the lawsuit joins both Anthropic and Meta in one complaint, it does not identify a coordinated copying operation between the two. The defendants have not yet challenged this joinder, and the court has not yet addressed the issue.

This case follows other attempts to sue multiple AI companies together, which judges Pitts and Chhabria previously rejected in other lawsuits. Those judges ruled that alleging multiple defendants infringed the same copyright does not satisfy the legal requirements for joining parties. It remains to be seen if the court will allow Carlson LLC to distinguish its case from those prior rulings. The legal process will determine if the AI companies are liable for using the copyrighted self-help materials.

Articles.Title: COPYRIGHT NEWS—Anthropic and Meta self-helped themselves to AI training materials, new lawsuit asserts

stories.Headline: Solidigm reports $8.7 billion net profit in first nine months of 2026
stories.Summary:
SK Hynix's enterprise NAND subsidiary Solidigm and its controlling entity reported KRW 11.56 trillion, or about $8.7 billion, in net profit during the first nine months of 2026, according to The Herald Business. That figure was roughly 42 times the KRW 277.4 billion the same business reported a year earlier. The subsidiary's revenue reached KRW 21.96 trillion, about $16.5 billion, over the nine-month period, nearly quadrupling from KRW 5.61 trillion, or about $4.2 billion, a year earlier. Its net assets climbed to KRW 12.61 trillion, roughly $9.5 billion, and the $8.7 billion represents reported net profit rather than the subsidiary's valuation.

Solidigm specializes in enterprise solid-state drives built using NAND flash memory, which provides the persistent storage needed to retain large volumes of information. SK Hynix had been reviewing a U.S. listing of Solidigm with an anticipated fundraising target of approximately $10 billion, but the company suspended its IPO review on Oct. 23. Solidigm's controlling entity, formerly SK Hynix NAND Product Solutions, was renamed HYAICO on Oct. 30 and restructured as a holding company. The Herald report said the two entities' operations and financial results are nearly identical, and it estimated that HYAICO's full-year net profit could exceed KRW 17 trillion if the current pace continued, an extrapolation rather than company guidance.

CEO Kwak Noh-Jung explained in the company's third-quarter results announcement that the listing was originally intended to raise external capital for Solidigm's production expansion and reduce SK Hynix's investment burden. After reviewing market conditions, management concluded that proceeding would not deliver the originally anticipated outcome. Investors should watch whether enterprise SSD demand and profitability remain strong as AI data-center capacity expands, and how SK Hynix funds Solidigm's next production investments without an IPO. The question is how durable the NAND business's contribution will be if memory supply catches up with demand.

Articles.Title: SK Hynix Has an $8.7 Billion Profit Engine Hiding Outside Its HBM Business - Benzinga

stories.Headline: SEBI Explores India-Made AI Model for Stock Market Regulation, Says Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey
stories.Summary:
The Securities and Exchange Board of India is exploring the development of an India-made artificial intelligence model for the securities market, Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey said on Friday, November 20, 2026. Speaking at the CII DFS Financing Summit in Mumbai, Pandey said a committee was examining whether a domestically governed SEBI AI model could be developed jointly with market participants. The proposed system is intended to make AI-based regulatory tools more affordable, secure and accessible, particularly for smaller regulated entities. The regulator is considering whether the model could be developed as part of India's Digital Public Infrastructure.

The committee is assessing the costs, opportunities and risks involved, along with the safeguards required before such a system can be introduced, and Pandey said the proposal remains at an initial stage with consultations underway. No development or implementation timeline has been announced, and SEBI has not specified how such a system would be operated or which entities would be involved. The committee is also looking at the risks associated with AI, including the possibility of systems producing incorrect or misleading information, often referred to as AI hallucinations. SEBI has not announced whether the proposed model would be used for surveillance, compliance reporting, risk assessment or other specific regulatory functions, as these details would depend on the outcome of the feasibility assessment.

Pandey said appropriate safeguards would be necessary while examining the opportunities offered by the technology. The discussions come as SEBI expands the use of technology in market supervision and compliance monitoring, and the regulator has already introduced AI-based tools to monitor advertisements issued by market intermediaries and examine compliance reports. The latest comments follow an earlier announcement in October, when Pandey said the regulator was considering a domestically governed AI model for the securities market and outlined plans to strengthen AI risk management through international regulatory cooperation. SEBI is working on implementing the International Organization of Securities Commissions' supervisory toolkit for artificial intelligence, which focuses on improving oversight of AI systems and managing the risks arising from their use in financial markets.

SEBI has separately been examining the responsible use of AI and machine learning by regulated entities, and its June 2025 consultation paper proposed principles covering accountability, governance and oversight of AI applications in the securities market. The proposed domestic model would be a separate initiative and remains under consideration. For now, the committee's assessment will determine whether the model can be developed collaboratively and what safeguards would be needed. SEBI has not announced a formal rollout plan or a date for completing the exercise.

Articles.Title: SEBI Explores India-Made AI Model for Stock Market Regulation, Says Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey

stories.Headline: Ukrainian citizens sue Texas Instruments, Intel and AMD over chips in Russian weapons
stories.Summary:
Five Ukrainian citizens sued Texas Instruments, Intel, AMD and Mouser Electronics in December 2025 in Dallas County state court. They claim the companies' components wound up guiding Russian weapons used against Ukrainian civilians. The case has already been dismissed once, revived once, and fought over twice in federal court. Plaintiffs seek more than $1 million each in damages. Lawyers on both sides include some of the biggest names in American trial law.

The complaints cite five missile and drone strikes between 2023 and 2025 that killed or wounded dozens of people in Ukrainian cities. The original filing date was December 11, 2025, in Dallas County District Court. The case moved to the US District Court for the Northern District of Texas. The lead case is Liudmyla Dmytrivina v. Texas Instruments. The filings state that the war makes it impossible to bring the cases before Ukrainian courts.

The plaintiffs are five named Ukrainian citizens representing dozens of civilians hurt or killed in specific attacks. Lead counsel are Mikal Watts and Charla Aldous, with supporting firm BakerHostetler, including attorneys Robert Julian, Dustin Dow and Lauren Attard. Watts said the plaintiffs no longer opposed the case being handled in federal court. Watts called the US companies "merchants of death" making a "farce" of US sanctions law. Mouser, based in Mansfield, Texas, was acquired by Berkshire in 2007 when it bought Mouser's parent company TTI Inc.

Texas Instruments is represented by attorney Tom Melsheimer in dismissal hearings. Melsheimer argued that Texans made a deal with the Ukrainian people that if they gave up their nuclear weapons, the US would protect them. TI has denied wrongdoing throughout the litigation and argues the claims rest on speculation rather than direct proof. Intel's leadership, including CEO Lip-Bu Tan, has publicly denied knowledge of misuse, while AMD echoes commitments to ethical supply chains. Both companies argue liability should fall on illegal resellers, not manufacturers.

The lawsuits detail a network of third-party resellers and shell companies that facilitated the transfer of restricted chips to Russian entities. One attack allegedly involved Iranian-made drones with components associated with Intel and AMD. Others involved Russian-made KH-101 cruise missiles and Iskander ballistic missiles. The companies counter that thousands of resellers worldwide handle their products, making it nearly impossible to track every final buyer. Plaintiffs' lawyers claimed they learned that TI, Intel and AMD were told by the federal government that their practices did not follow US rules.

Defendants filed removal motions within hours of being sued in December 2025. At a hearing in February 2026, lawyers for the plaintiffs told the judge they would not oppose having the case tried in his federal courtroom. US District Judge Sidney Fitzwater is overseeing the entire litigation, and his rulings on dismissal motions have shaped the case. The judge gave plaintiffs a chance to fix the problems in their complaint rather than ending the case.

Articles.Title: AI Lawsuit Ukraine 2026: What the Chip Case Means for You

stories.Headline: Datavault AI (DVLT) Stock Looks Undervalued On Founder Lawsuit Turmoil
stories.Summary:
Datavault AI's share price has fallen 99.9% over the past five years, and the stock now trades at a price to sales ratio of about 0.4x, according to Simply Wall St. The article, published on 20 November 2026, ties part of that low multiple to a boardroom dispute involving founder Nathaniel Bradley. Bradley has sued over his removal as CEO and over the alleged concealment of a proposed funding package worth between US$90m and US$100m. The piece weighs whether the remaining market value is justified by the sales the company currently generates. The 0.4x ratio sits far below the wider semiconductor group at roughly 5.3x and below similar peers at about 0.9x, the article states. It says the gap suggests the market attaches a modest value to each dollar of Datavault AI's sales compared with both the sector and closer comparables.

On the publication's preferred valuation model, which blends growth, profitability, scale and risk into a tailored fair multiple, the shares screen as undervalued on this metric. The article adds that part of the low multiple may reflect governance and funding concerns rather than only the revenue base. The article attributes the lawsuit to Bradley, the founder, and says it concerns his removal as CEO and the alleged concealment of the funding offer. It reports that a community narrative on Simply Wall St, written by an investor posting as DrFountain, argues the current market value overlooks key pieces of the company's commercial progress. That narrative says a clear disconnect emerges when Datavault AI is compared with other publicly traded AI and data infrastructure companies, many of which trade at significantly higher market capitalizations.

The article presents this as one of the top community narratives, which puts the company at 100% undervalued. The article notes that Datavault AI is still loss making on free cash flow, which is why it says revenue is the clearest anchor for the share price. It also points readers to a separate lens comparing the current price with where professional models think the business could be in a few years. Beyond that, the piece does not say what happens next in the lawsuit or the funding dispute.

stories.Headline: Leaders call for institutional capacity and rights-based AI governance to support sustainable development in Asia
stories.Summary:
Eco-Business and the United Nations Development Programme organized the inaugural Unlocking AI for Sustainability forum on 20 November 2026. Over 100 senior delegates gathered at the Shangri-La Singapore to discuss how artificial intelligence can support sustainable development. These leaders explored ways to manage technology risks while optimizing trade, power grids, and operational efficiency across the region. They focused on the intersection of technological deployment, infrastructure investment, governance, and climate strategies. The event aimed to address whether AI would lead to a great divergence or a great convergence.

Investment must shift toward rights-based approaches, institutional capacity, and clean-energy infrastructure to avoid widening the digital divide between economies. AI could add US$15 trillion to global GDP by 2030, including US$1 trillion for Asean economies, if governed properly. The ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement, signed on 14 November, aims to help the regional digital economy grow to US$2 trillion by 2030. Singapore is taking over as Asean chair to turn diverse AI provisions into practice across all 11 member states. The European AI Office is developing the AI for Public Good initiative, while a Copernicus mirror site was established in the Philippines.

Edward Vrkić of the UNDP said governance must account for stakeholders who lack the economic clout to manage technology risks. He noted that women are twice as exposed to job losses from AI automation, which risks creating poverty within poverty. Jessica Cheam of Eco-Business stated that Asean has a rare chance to rewrite digital economy rules by centering people. Benoît Sauveroche of the European Union Delegation said AI must be anchored in trusted infrastructure, sound governance, and fundamental rights. Hwee Ping Sim of Gurīn Energy said clean, renewable energy is central to capturing economic opportunities and national decarbonisation goals.

The forum highlighted that data centers and computing infrastructure place mounting pressure on electricity grids, land, and water systems. Without deliberate policy choices, AI could deepen existing technological and digital divides within urban, peri-urban, and rural areas. The Principles for Responsible Investment explored how varying speeds of AI integration could shape Asia's landscape by 2030 and beyond. Gurīn Energy and other stakeholders discussed balancing economic opportunity with power-system constraints, environmental safeguards, and community needs. The discussions emphasized that the most valuable innovation is innovation that people can trust.

Eco-Business was established in 2009 as a business intelligence platform dedicated to advancing sustainable development across the Asia Pacific. The organization is headquartered in Singapore and maintains a presence in Manila, Kuala Lumpur, Jakarta, Bangkok, Hong Kong, Beijing, and London. Its work aligns with the 17 United Nations Sustainable Development Goals and utilizes a 15-year archive of research and news. The UNDP is a United Nations organization that works in 170 countries to fight poverty, inequality, and climate change. The forum specifically addressed AI's dual role as both a climate risk and a climate solution.

Future efforts will focus on making AI trustworthy, interoperable, and climate responsible across the diverse member states of the Asean region. The European AI Office will continue leveraging models and algorithms to improve healthcare management, optimize energy use, and mitigate climate impacts. Local capacity in the Philippines will be built through data-driven environmental and disaster monitoring via the EU Copernicus programme. Stakeholders will continue to explore safety and governance frameworks required to keep innovation accountable and human-centered. The articles leave open how specific national policies will be implemented to prevent the predicted digital divide.

stories.Headline: Fed governor Lisa Cook says AI is disrupting parts of the US labor market unevenly
stories.Summary:
Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook said in an address at Oakland Tech Week on September 28, 2026, that artificial intelligence is already disrupting parts of the United States labor market. She described the disruption as uneven, concentrated in specific corners of the workforce rather than spread across the whole economy. Cook began with the big picture, noting that the overall unemployment rate sits at 4.3 percent and that layoffs have stayed low and stable over the past two years even as companies adopted AI tools at a growing pace. She acknowledged targeted disruptions in particular sectors, singling out reduced demand for software coding roles and fewer entry-level openings for recent graduates.

Cook expressed hope that job creation could keep pace with displacement, while warning that skill mismatches could push unemployment higher on a temporary basis. She framed the skill mismatch as a supply-side issue that could limit the Federal Reserve's ability to respond effectively. Cook also flagged a split timeline for inflation, saying heavy investment in AI might add to inflationary pressures in the short term while medium-term productivity gains could be modest. Analysis from the San Francisco Fed backs up her comments, pointing to a 0.2 percentage point increase in the natural rate of unemployment since large language models emerged.

Fellow Fed Governor Michael Barr has struck a similar tone, emphasizing the potential for significant short-term disruptions as AI spreads through the workforce and highlighting the risk of widening inequality. The most immediate takeaway is that the headline unemployment rate may understate what is happening in AI-exposed fields, since a 4.3 percent national figure can coexist with a much tougher market for new graduates and software developers. The figures worth watching include hiring rates for recent graduates, demand for software roles and any further revisions to estimates of the natural rate of unemployment. Layoff data will matter too, because layoffs have so far stayed low and stable despite rising AI adoption, and a change in that trend would signal the disruption is spreading beyond the pockets Cook described.

Articles.Title: Fed Governor Lisa Cook says AI is reshaping parts of the US labor market

stories.Headline: Socialist MEP González Casares criticizes EU data center assessment plan as insufficient
stories.Summary:
Members of the European Parliament have on their desks the draft of the future Cloud and Artificial Intelligence Development Act, known as CADA, the Demócrata article of 19 November 2026 reports. The rapporteurs have presented their proposed report, opening the phase in which political groups will try to incorporate their positions into the initiative. The Socialist group intends that the rule coming out of its processing in the European Parliament, before negotiations begin with the member states, guarantees a “people”-centered approach. The European Commission presented the proposal on 3 June 2026 as COM(2026) 502, and it is processed through the ordinary legislative procedure. The file number is 2026/0138(COD), and as of 19 November 2026 the text is in the committee work phase of the first reading.

The text sets out four different levels of assurance at EU scale to regulate security, operational autonomy, and the location of data in computing services. The initiative aims to consolidate the continent’s technological sovereignty and reduce its dependencies on third countries. The draft links the expansion of data center capacity to compatibility with the European climate targets for 2050 and proposes that these infrastructures actively contribute to decarbonisation. Before declaring an area as an acceleration area for data centers, member states must carry out an impact assessment verifying that projected electricity demand is compatible with their Integrated National Energy and Climate Plans and with households’ supply needs. The draft adds that these areas must endeavor to cover practically 100% of their energy demand through local, zero-emission renewable sources.

The Socialist MEP and member of the Committee on Industry, Research and Energy, Nicolás González Casares, said this week during a closed-door meeting that “each law is an opportunity.” He argued that the continent “needs rules to also recover citizens’ trust” in technological development that works “not only for the digital world, but also for people.” He explained that crossing Germany, Finland, Denmark or Portugal would reveal different approaches, and argued for common requirements at the European scale with room to adapt them to each territory. He added that geographical realities must be taken into account because not all member states have the same energy mix or the same climate. He said of the proposed classification system “it is not enough,” and that “we have a very nice label, but we do not know the reality.”

González Casares is critical of some approaches being developed by the Community Executive, especially the assessment scheme for these infrastructures. He considers that the proposed classification system does not provide sufficient information to know the real impact of data centers. He regrets that the assessment includes no specific data on absolute electricity consumption in megawatt-hours or kilowatt-hours, the total volume of water used, or the amount of renewable energy consumed over the year. He pointed out that when labels are added without knowing the total energy consumption of these data centers, “we probably do not have a complete picture.” The draft also analyzes the feasibility of interconnecting smaller or geographically distributed data centers so they can train artificial intelligence models in parallel.

The European Commission’s initiative seeks to harmonize the efforts of the member states and establish a common framework for a sector considered strategically important for the Union. Regulatory fragmentation and differences in national criteria can hinder the expansion of infrastructures and Europe’s capacity to compete in a market shaped by computing and artificial intelligence model development. The legislation will have to address the impact of data centers on electricity consumption, the availability of water resources, and the needs of national networks. The draft proposes that, when direct and continuous supply is not technically feasible, the rest of the needs may be met through grid electricity, storage systems, or flexible demand management mechanisms. Interconnection could reduce electricity consumption during periods of peak demand on the grid by distributing computing tasks across different facilities.

Political groups now begin to shape their priorities and the modifications they intend to introduce in the report. The committees have not yet approved the draft report and the Plenary has not set its position, so it is not an approved regulation nor is it in force. Parliament and Council must agree on the text through the ordinary legislative procedure. The socialists see in this phase an opportunity to strengthen demands for transparency, sustainability, and control of consumption. The articles leave open how the negotiations between Parliament and the Council will conclude and what the final text will contain.

stories.Headline: HaystackID hosts a webinar where in-house counsel discuss 2026 AI case law
stories.Summary:
HaystackID is presenting a webinar titled “AI on Trial: An In-House Counsel Roundtable on 2026 Case Law and the Road to 2027” on December 2nd, 2026, from 11:00 am to 12:00 pm CST. The webinar was announced on JDSupra on November 19, 2026. During 2026, courts issued several decisions affecting AI-related issues in connection with litigation and the discovery process. Enterprises have experienced challenges over the past few years as they grapple with technological developments in artificial intelligence. In-house counsel from various organizations will discuss their views about recent AI case law developments at the program.

The webcast topics include the nature and extent of requirements courts may have imposed on parties using AI-assisted document review workflows. Topics also include protective order practices regarding AI-restrictive provisions and whether courts will actually enforce those provisions. The program covers the application of the attorney-client privilege and work product doctrine to AI-generated materials. Panelists will explore governance strategies for managing the retention of AI-related information, including how organizations can build defensible policies as case law continues to evolve. They will also address growing concerns about deepfakes and other AI-generated media and what enterprises can do to prepare.

Stacey Blaustein is Counsel and e-Discovery Lead in the Corporate Litigation Department of the IBM Corporation in Armonk, NY. She litigates IBM commercial and employment discrimination matters and handles third-party commercial, employment, antitrust, contract subpoenas as well as government and regulatory CIDs, requests and subpoenas. She works with IBM’s Legal Operations Department in modernizing many of IBM’s Litigation and e-Discovery processes and practices and is involved daily with AI and the practice of law. She is a subject matter expert on Cross-border discovery, e-Discovery, AI and Legal Ethics, Retention and Preservation. She manages many aspects of E-Discovery for Corporate Litigation and departments across IBM, from global and domestic litigation cases to antitrust 2nd reviews, tax audit matters, DOJ and other governmental non-target investigations.

Stacey is an active member of the Sedona Conference and a member of Working Group 1 and Working Group 6 on Cross-Border Discovery. She is a 15 year Faculty Member of Electronic Discovery Institute (EDI). Stacey has been with IBM for 18 years, and her previous experience includes 18 years in private practice as a securities litigation attorney and two years as a general litigator. Stacey is a graduate of Barnard College of Columbia University and the Emory University School of Law. Stacey can be reached at blaustei@us.ibm.com.

Philip Favro is the founder and president of Favro Law PLLC, where he counsels clients on ESI, AI, and discovery issues and serves as a special master, mediator, and expert witness. Phil is nationally recognized for his expertise on ESI, discovery, and information governance, with courts acknowledging his credentials, as in Oakley v. MSG Networks, Inc., No. 17-CV-6903 (RJS), 2025 WL 2061665 (S.D.N.Y. July 23, 2025). As a special master, Phil is acclaimed for his collaborative approach, working with parties to find stipulated solutions to complex issues. For disputes that require adjudication, he is renowned for the clarity and vigor of his written dispositions.

Philip Favro is the moderator. Andy Hansell is Director Counsel at Target Corporation, bringing more than 25 years of experience in legal practice, legal operations, eDiscovery, and technology-driven legal solutions. Throughout his career, Andrew has held leadership and advisory roles in corporate legal departments, prominent law firms, and legal services organizations, developing deep expertise in litigation support, information governance, legal technology, and operational efficiency. Prior to his current role at Target, he served as Lead eDiscovery Program Manager and held positions with Taft Stettinius & Hollister, Faegre Drinker, CPA Global, and Northwest Airlines. Brian Morrison is Senior Lead Counsel, eDiscovery, for CrowdStrike, a global cybersecurity company.

He advises on discovery strategy across a complex litigation and regulatory docket and collaborates with product and IT teams on retention and preservation policies. Brian actively integrates AI tools and agents into eDiscovery workflows and contributes to developing bespoke tools used by other legal teams. Prior to this role, Brian was Discovery Counsel at Google. He also practiced for over a decade at nationally recognized law firms, focusing on class actions and mass tort litigation, including major antitrust and consumer protection matters, multidistrict automotive defect litigation, generic pharmaceutical pricing antitrust cases and large financial fraud disputes. Leah Aaronson Powell is Vice President, Legal & Business Affairs, Litigation at Madison Square Garden Entertainment Corp., a role she has held since December 2023.

In this capacity, she focuses on litigation, dispute resolution, and dispute prevention across the MSG family of companies. The MSG family of companies encompasses Madison Square Garden Entertainment Corp. (NYSE: MSGE), which owns and operates Madison Square Garden, Radio City Music Hall, and the Beacon Theatre; Sphere Entertainment Co. (NYSE: SPHR), home to Sphere in Las Vegas and MSG Networks; MSG Knickerbockers Corp. (NYSE: MSGK), home to the New York Knicks; and MSG Rangers Corp. (NYSE: MSGR), home to the New York Rangers. Prior to joining MSG, Leah practiced complex commercial litigation at King & Spalding, focusing on disputes in federal court and Delaware and New York state courts. She is a graduate of the University of Miami School of Law and a member of the Florida and New York Bars. As the law attempts to keep pace with the rapid pace of AI technological advances, enterprises must also try to stay current with case law developments on AI that may impact their operations.

The program is presented by HaystackID. Registration is available now. The webcast is covered under topics including Artificial Intelligence, Attorney-Client Privilege, Data Collection, Data Retention, Deep Fake, Discovery, Document Review, e-Discovery Professionals, Electronically Stored Information, Information Governance, Legal Technology, Protective Orders, Technology-Assisted Review, Webinars, Work-Product Doctrine, Civil Procedure, Electronic Discovery, Professional Practice, and Science, Computers & Technology. stories.Headline: Google buys unfinished Wyoming data center from Crusoe after $17 billion investment
stories.Summary:
Google bought an unfinished data center project in southeastern Wyoming from Crusoe on Friday. This sale followed a Google announcement on Thursday regarding a 17 billion dollar investment. The Denver based AI infrastructure developer Crusoe confirmed the transaction to the press. Google previously declined to sign on as a customer for this specific site. The purchase gives Google direct control over the unfinished Wyoming facility.

The project requires construction with Tallgrass Energy, Black Hills Energy, American Electric Power, and Related Digital. Crusoe originally planned to scale the campus to 10 gigawatts of power capacity last year. The power strategy mixes fuel cells, grid power, and natural gas turbines for energy. Tallgrass will use a regional CO2 sequestration hub to capture carbon over the long term. Neither company disclosed the final price Google paid for the Wyoming site.

Crusoe CEO and co-founder Chase Lochmiller said his company handled origination, entitlement, and de-risking. He stated these efforts set the project up for construction and eventual operation. Lochmiller added that Crusoe now has over 40 GW in its pipeline. He also noted that the company has more than 6 GW of contracted capacity. Crusoe believes its pre-development role on the project is now complete.

Google reportedly raised concerns about the construction timeline and the project cost under Crusoe. Reports of a potential sale first surfaced in June before the final deal. Independent developers are affected by equipment shortages, power access, and local opposition to projects. Google now assumes the risk of the clock and cost for the site. The company previously rejected the site before deciding to buy it outright.

Crusoe started eight years ago as a crypto-mining business using burned off natural gas. The company raised 3.9 billion dollars in September and reached a 30.9 billion dollar valuation. It currently develops a Google campus in Armstrong County, Texas, near two 265.5 MW wind farms. Crusoe also builds campuses in Abilene, Texas, for Oracle, OpenAI, and Microsoft. Meta is a customer, and Jane Street reportedly signed a 13 billion dollar deal.

Google will now manage the construction of the southeastern Wyoming data center campus. A separate Microsoft campus in Texas should bring its first building online in mid-2027. Crusoe continues to develop AI infrastructure for Google, OpenAI, and Microsoft in Texas. The articles do not state when the Wyoming facility will be finished. They also leave the specific purchase price of the data center undisclosed.

stories.Headline: NTT Data's Sandip Ghosh urges multi-factor authentication and proactive cybersecurity as AI speeds up attacks
stories.Summary:
In the past week and change, Microsoft Outlook went down for an extended period, and the Federal Aviation Administration blamed its first nationwide ground stop since 9/11 on a telecom outage, according to CNN. The U.S. National Security Communications network used by the NSA also went down, and several other tech outages were reported at United Airlines, Apple, JPMorgan Chase and more. Initial reports indicate these outages have been unrelated, with no evidence bad actors are to blame. A real, large-scale cyberattack also affected customers of the website designer Optimizely, including Zoom and Equifax. The FBI issued an ominous warning about hackers and scammers using an AI-powered tool called ARTEX.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters Tuesday that patching, the term for small code updates to fix bugs and close security vulnerabilities, is creating short-term disruption in the way the system works. This month, Microsoft has implemented more than 1,200 patches, according to data firm Qualys' monthly update, nearly 20 times more than reported in the November 2025 update. According to NTT Data's research, less than half of organizations have formal plans to manage AI- and cloud-related security risks. Japanese tech giant NTT Data recently opened a cyber defense center in Plano. Sandip Ghosh is managing director for cybersecurity of NTT Data.

Ghosh said, "Please, please, please enable multi-factor authentication," calling it part of what he called cyber hygiene, or cybersecurity basics that every person and company should be practicing. He said, "We are using AI to beat AI," with agents used at various places to detect what is going on and start taking the right kind of corrective action so that the attack does not go through. He said cyberattacks have also increased thanks to AI, necessitating more patches, but what he is seeing is more often an increase in the pace and scale of relatively normal attacks, and less an increase in the sophistication of attacks. He said, "Let's not think of cybersecurity as an afterthought after an incident. Let's go and do cybersecurity proactively.

Put a program in place, and run that program effectively." He said that if somebody is urgently asking for a money transfer or urgently asking you to give your code away immediately, that is a strict no-no and should be a red flag. Ghosh said basic cybersecurity practices can still be very effective for businesses and consumers. He said many attacks NTT Data sees on smaller organizations are due to basic cybersecurity neglect like default passwords being used or patches that are very old, simple fixes that go a long way. For small- to medium-sized businesses that can't afford their own chief information security officer, he said to bring in an outside service provider to be a fractional or virtual CISO and look at how you can allocate your budget to establish a dedicated cybersecurity plan.

He said multi-factor authentication is a must for consumers because it gives you an additional layer of protection. He said AI is driving things like deepfake scams, so beware of calls asking for voice authentication, especially unsolicited, and verify requests for money or private information through multiple channels. The article says no one likes taking out their phone to log in to their computer. It says cyberspace these days feels more like "Twin Peaks" than Tomorrowland.

It says there is a growing consensus that efforts to stop hackers, and not hackers themselves, are behind many of the recent outages. It says AI, including autonomous AI coding agents, is allowing companies to patch software much faster, and that the rapid increase in the pace of software updates could be behind the software outages. It says sheriffs' offices, toll authorities and more regularly put out notices that say, "We will never ask for money over the phone." More to follow.

stories.Headline: Cyprus chamber and communications office hold AI and cyber summit in Limassol
stories.Summary:
The Cyprus Chamber of Commerce and Industry and the Office of the Commissioner of Communications will hold a Communications, Cyber and AI Summit in Limassol on December 9 and 10, the Cyprus Mail reported on November 19, 2026. The event will take place at the City of Dreams Mediterranean under the auspices of the President of the Republic of Cyprus. It will bring together public authorities, businesses and technology experts to discuss developments shaping the digital future of Cyprus and Europe. The summit aims to provide a platform for dialogue between representatives of European and national institutions, regulatory authorities, public organisations, businesses and technology specialists.

The agenda will centre on electronic communications, cybersecurity and artificial intelligence, with discussions on emerging European and national policies, regulatory requirements, digital infrastructure, business resilience and security, and the responsible use of AI. Among the legislative and regulatory developments expected to feature are the NIS2 Directive, the AI Act, the Cyber Resilience Act and the Cybersecurity Act. Other subjects will include next-generation networks, critical digital infrastructure, cyber threat management, regulatory compliance and the use of artificial intelligence in cybersecurity. The organisers said the event would give businesses an opportunity to keep up with the latest European and national legislative and regulatory developments and to gain practical insights into compliance, risk management and digital resilience.

The summit is aimed particularly at chief executives, managing directors and board members, as well as chief information officers, chief technology officers, chief information security officers, data protection officers and professionals in cybersecurity, technology, risk management and compliance. It is also relevant to businesses and organisations affected by changing digital security requirements and the transformation associated with artificial intelligence. Participation is free of charge, although advance registration is required, and the official language will be Greek with simultaneous interpretation into English. The full two-day programme, including details of speakers, thematic sessions and registration, is available on the summit's official website. The organisers encouraged businesses and their executives to attend, describing the event as an opportunity to stay informed about developments affecting their operations and competitiveness while building connections with relevant institutions, specialists and business leaders.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia head amid scandals and federal investigations
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as the head of Nvidia last Thursday after admitting to an extramarital affair with Alice Huang. This Singapore based executive is believed to be a spy for China, which created a major scandal for the company. A New York Times report also stated that the chief executive had a second affair with a subordinate at Nvidia. These revelations led to federal investigations and a sell off of the company stock by many worried investors.

The scandal involves the easing of export controls on AI chips that were originally established under the administration of Joe Biden. Jensen Huang lobbied President Donald Trump to allow more chip sales to China, which he argued would maintain a United States advantage. The Commerce Department reportedly stopped an investigation into whether Alice Huang smuggled chips into China after an Nvidia lawyer contacted them. Trump was warned about the relationship with the suspected Chinese asset last year and again in May before a Beijing trip.

President Donald Trump said on Monday that he hoped there was no problem regarding the situation with the former chief executive. He has continued to describe Jensen Huang as an honorable, amazing, and high quality guy who will end up in good shape. Stephen Witt told the New Yorker that it is generally regarded as bad if a chief executive is sleeping with spies. The president previously decided that AI companies should self police after meeting with Huang and other executives in the tech industry.

The AI company Anthropic is preparing an initial public offering estimated at 1.4 trillion dollars and has received investment from Nvidia. Anthropic has warned its potential investors that artificial intelligence technology poses existential or catastrophic risks to the future of all humanity. The current board of Nvidia is populated by longtime associates and early investors who had no succession plan for the company. This lack of planning means that the company was left without a clear replacement when the chief executive finally resigned.

Nvidia was the most powerful and valuable AI company in the world and Huang served as the closest adviser to the president. The company is now being led by chief financial officer Colette Kress while the search for a permanent replacement begins. The current administration has followed a laissez faire approach to AI regulation that was pushed by the former chief executive. This approach is now being questioned as the technology is seen as dangerous and ill understood by many outside observers.

The new Congress includes members who were elected on promises to rein in data centers and other aspects of AI technology. These members may find it challenging to change current policies as long as Donald Trump remains in power in Washington. The articles leave open whether the federal investigations will lead to criminal charges for the former chief executive or others. It remains unclear if the United States will reinstate the stricter chip export controls that were previously eased by the president.

stories.Headline: Law Society issues practice note tying solicitors' AI use to existing duties and insurance checks
stories.Summary:
The Law Society published a new practice note on 21 October 2026 that brings together existing professional obligations and practical guidance on using AI in legal practice. It follows the SRA's strongly worded warning notice in August, which Hogan Lovells Cadwalader examined at the time. The note distinguishes AI used in the "practice of law", such as legal research, drafting and analysis, from AI used in the "business of law", such as billing and marketing. It states that there is no AI-specific regulator for the legal sector, so solicitors' use of AI sits within existing professional, data protection and cybersecurity frameworks, including the SRA Standards and Regulations. The note also addresses insurance, highlighting the potential implications of firms' use of AI for both professional indemnity and cyber insurance.

The note says the SRA has not certified AI products and that responsibility for work produced using AI remains with the solicitor and cannot be transferred to the technology provider. It states that AI cannot reliably verify its own output, so lawyers should check AI-generated material against authoritative sources rather than asking the same, or another, AI system to confirm it. It cites Ayinde v London Borough of Haringey and Al-Haroun v Qatar National Bank [2025] EWHC 1383 (Admin), in which the High Court addressed the use of false authorities and emphasised lawyers' responsibility for material put before the court. It cites SRA v Kumar, in which a Registered Foreign Lawyer was removed from the Register of Foreign Lawyers after repeatedly relying on false or unsupported AI-generated authorities, including following an express warning. It cites R v FGD [2026] EWCA Crim 918, in which the Court of Appeal warned that using AI to prepare a witness for cross-examination may amount to coaching and, in an extreme case, create sufficient unfairness for the court to consider excluding evidence.

The note states that although there is currently no general obligation to disclose the use of AI, transparency may be appropriate where AI has been used materially in preparing documents. It states that a witness statement must remain the witness's own evidence and accurately reflect their recollection. It cites the Civil Justice Council's final recommendations on AI use in court documents, published on 29 October 2026, which propose that factual witnesses should declare that AI has not generated or influenced the substantive content of their statements, with a different disclosure requirement for expert evidence. It cites R (Munir) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2026] UKUT 81 (IAC), in which the tribunal highlighted the potential confidentiality and privilege consequences of uploading client material to a publicly available AI tool. It states that using an "enterprise" or specialist "legal AI" product does not remove these risks, and that information described as anonymised will only fall outside data protection law where individuals are genuinely no longer identifiable.

The note states that AI may create new categories of potentially relevant material, including prompts, draft outputs and audit logs, whose treatment under existing privilege principles remains largely untested. It states that a business user may ask AI for legal advice and create unprivileged material, even if it is later sent to the legal team. It states that professional competence increasingly includes understanding the systems lawyers use and their limitations, and that one particular concern is automation bias, where users place undue confidence in an output simply because it has been produced by technology. It states that professional liability could eventually arise from failing to use AI where a reasonably competent lawyer would have done so, and that there is currently no positive professional duty to use AI, but the applicable standard of care may evolve as increasingly reliable tools become embedded in legal practice. It states that the risks become more significant with AI agents and agentic AI, which can take actions and carry out multi-step processes across systems with reduced human intervention.

The note states that firms should limit systems' permissions to what is genuinely necessary and build in appropriate human review and approval points as autonomy increases. It states that firms need effective AI governance even if they have not formally adopted AI, because staff may independently use publicly available tools, creating the risk of "shadow AI". It states that appropriate controls may include an AI-use policy, approved-tools list, restrictions on the information that may be entered into AI systems, staff training and clear processes for escalating errors or data breaches. It states that clients should receive appropriate information about how AI may be used on their matters, which firms can address upfront through engagement letters or terms of business. It states that where work is billed by time, firms should not charge for the hours the task would have taken without AI, and that any separate AI or technology charge should be transparent, agreed appropriately and should not duplicate other fees.

The note states that AI risks extend beyond hallucination and confidentiality, and include bias and discrimination, cybersecurity, operational resilience and concentration risk arising from dependence on particular technology providers. On professional indemnity insurance, it recommends that firms consider whether their use of AI changes their professional indemnity risk profile or falls outside the considerations upon which their insurance was arranged. It recommends that firms check whether their existing professional indemnity policy, proposal form or renewal documentation asks about matters such as the use of AI, automation and legal technology. It recommends that firms consider their disclosure obligations including in respect of risks that the firm ought to be aware of, in addition to those which the firm is aware of. It recommends that firms maintain clear supervisory documentation and evidence of risk management, as insurers may be interested in the firm's AI governance processes and may ask about the extent of human oversight of AI-assisted work.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Rep. Vince Fong introduces bipartisan bill to place private AI experts inside CISA
stories.Summary:
Representative Vince Fong introduced a bipartisan bill on November 20, 2026, to strengthen cybersecurity in the United States. This legislation follows several widespread technical outages that have recently impacted various systems across the entire country. The Bridging Resources for Innovative Defense and Government Expertise in Artificial Intelligence Act would authorize the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to collaborate with private professionals. This bill calls for a pilot project involving about 100 private sector workers to serve within the CISA. It also requires a semi-annual report on the status of the program and ways the agency could improve it.

Republican Representative Vince Fong of Bakersfield stated that communities and critical industries are struggling to keep up with a surge in AI-related cyberattacks. He noted that attacks in the Central Valley have targeted water systems, hospitals, and schools to steal sensitive data. Fong argued that bringing in private sector specialists ensures that national experts have the tools needed to modernize systems. Democratic Representative Josh Gottheimer of New Jersey co-authored the bill and said that adversaries are using AI to attack American networks.

He claimed that the agency on the front lines of defense does not have enough capacity to keep pace. Gottheimer stated that the act is a common sense fix to help the agency hunt intruders and patch vulnerabilities. The bill follows a nationwide plane ground stop and outages impacting the National Security Agency and Microsoft Outlook. Other affected entities include Apple, United Airlines, and multiple banks that experienced technical failures.

These events highlight the vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure that the new legislation aims to address through private sector expertise. The bill must be approved before the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency can begin collaborating with the private sector AI professionals. The legislation aims to stress-test AI tools before they are exploited by adversaries to protect national security. The articles do not state when the bill will be debated or if it has passed.
