stories.Headline: Julie Menin leads New York City Council plan to vote on AI bills in January 2027
stories.Summary:
The New York City Council plans to begin 2027 by voting on a set of artificial intelligence bills, according to two people with knowledge of the timing who were granted anonymity to discuss private deliberations. The legislation is being led by Council Speaker Julie Menin, a Manhattan lawmaker who has become a foil to Mayor Zohran Mamdani on several issues, including AI regulation. The package would place the city at the forefront of efforts to rein in frontier AI technology, amid growing concern about its existential threats to society. The measures are meant as a counterpoint to federal inaction on AI, which the article describes as amounting to a regulatory vacuum. The vote is expected in January, though a spokesperson for Menin said the bills are still undergoing review and that no exact date has been set for a vote.

The article gives no other numbers, dates or names beyond the January timing, the 2027 start, Menin, Mamdani and the two anonymous people. It does not specify how many bills are in the package or what any of them would require. The article also does not say what penalties or obligations the legislation would create. Menin is the lawmaker responsible for shepherding the legislation, and her spokesperson said the bills remain under review while confirming that a vote date has not been fixed.

The article does not include further comment from Menin, Mamdani or other council members on the substance of the bills. It also does not say whether the mayor supports or opposes the package. The two people who confirmed the January timing spoke on condition of anonymity because the deliberations were private. The context given is federal inaction on AI, which the article says has left a regulatory vacuum that the city measures are intended to counter.

The article does not say what happens after a January vote, such as whether the mayor would sign the bills or whether further steps are required. It also does not describe any federal proposals that the city effort is responding to. No other details on the next steps are provided. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Cognizant executive says legacy systems absorb up to 80% of banks IT budgets
stories.Summary:
Ashish Bhatnagar, Head of Banking & Financial Services for Cognizant in the UK & Ireland, gave a Q&A to FinTech Magazine published on November 20, 2026, about how banks can turn legacy systems into an AI advantage. He said legacy technology is a major constraint on banks' modernisation efforts. He said legacy systems can absorb up to 80% of banks' IT budgets through simple maintenance. He said many of these systems support critical services and contain decades of business rules and institutional knowledge. He said it can be difficult to scale or transition to new technology.

He said architecture reviews, risk assessments and security approvals were designed to provide essential control but often cannot scale with the volume and pace of a major transformation programme. He said this produces late-stage delays, fragmented delivery and a reluctance to experiment. He said fear of failure can create paralysis, because if a new system fails it can affect whether people can pay bills or access their money. He said in the UK alone banks spend an estimated £3.3bn (US$4.3bn) annually managing core legacy systems. The article states core banking management and maintenance consumes an average of 24% of UK banks' IT budgets, nearly a quarter.

He said the true cost of legacy extends beyond licence fees, upgrades and system run rates to substantial below-the-line costs from additional employees and the specialist knowledge and manual processes required to keep systems operating. He said every hour and pound devoted to maintaining ageing infrastructure cannot be used to improve customer experiences, introduce new products or integrate AI. He said legacy environments can make banks less attractive to scarce technology talent. He said governance, security and regulatory controls are indispensable in banking but the processes used to apply them can become bottlenecks. He said the answer is not to weaken oversight but to embed it into delivery from the beginning.

He said security, compliance, data permissions and usage rights should be designed into the architecture and supported by repeatable, automated controls. He said an AI-ready bank has moved beyond isolated pilots and created the conditions to deploy AI securely, responsibly and at enterprise scale. He said that requires infrastructure capable of supporting AI, accessible contextual data, and robust permissions and governance built into the architecture from the outset. He said the bank also needs a culture that permits controlled experimentation, supported by the right engineering, data and AI skills. He said AI readiness means AI becomes part of how the organisation operates, not simply another tool, and can support complete workflows while meeting security, compliance and customer expectations.

He said existing systems often contain valuable assets including business rules, customer context, historical data and institutional knowledge. He said AI can help surface and apply that intelligence while accelerating modernisation itself. He said AI-driven automation, predictive DevOps, automated testing and self-healing systems can improve productivity and reduce the burden of technical debt. He said banks can then modernise in controlled stages, focusing investment on the value streams that matter most and minimising disruption to critical services. He said this approach creates value sooner, makes transformation decisions better informed and frees up resources for further innovation.

He said leaders should first reduce structural friction by identifying where legacy complexity, manual controls and approval bottlenecks create drag, then simplify or automate them. He said teams should second organise delivery around value streams, focusing on complete customer or business outcomes rather than isolated technology components. He said this improves delivery speed and reliability, increases straight-through processing and prevents risk, security or architecture issues emerging late. He said banks should third build intelligence from existing systems, using AI to extract value from the data, business rules and institutional knowledge already embedded in their estates, with security, compliance, permissions and responsible-AI controls designed in from the outset. The article lists Cognizant's partners as Microsoft, AWS, Google Cloud, Temenos and ACI Worldwide, and says Cognizant and ACI Worldwide demonstrated ACI's BASE24-eps card-processing platform running at scale on AWS, processing more than 4.6 million transactions without failure in performance testing.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Principals lobby Congress for school funding increases and AI limits
stories.Summary:
Three hundred school leaders and students from across the nation fanned out across Capitol Hill on Nov. 17, 2025, as part of a two-day National Advocacy Summit organized by the National Principals Association. They met with their state representatives and senators to ask for more funding to support public education. The summit took place in Washington, D.C., and the principals met with their state representatives on Capitol Hill. On their agenda were requests to raise federal funding to expand student mental health services, curb school choice programs, and put guardrails on how schools use artificial intelligence. After a long day of lobbying, most principals said they felt hopeful, a decided vibe shift from when they last appealed to Congress in March 2025.

Principals asked their representatives for an increase in Title I funding to $19 billion from $18.4 billion to help high-poverty school districts meet students' needs. They sought an increase in Title II funding to $2.4 billion from $2.14 billion and Title IV-A funding to bolster teacher and principal pipelines and support and expand access to quality mental health care for educators and students. The Federal Scholarship Tax Credit program will go into effect on Jan. 1, 2027, and individuals can claim a federal income tax credit up to $1,700 for qualified cash contributions to certain scholarship-granting organizations. Scholarships can be used for students' approved expenses such as tutoring at a public school or tuition at a private school. Governors of 31 states have opted into the program, fifteen states and the District of Columbia are still undecided, and four have said they will not participate.

Erin Sieh, the principal of Freeman Elementary School in Adams, Neb., said the March 2025 layoff announcement came out hours before they were going to go to the Hill and it felt like their bubble had been burst. Sieh said it felt very defeating and like education wasn't valued, with a lot of uncertainty that was very frightening. Mike Rubin, who leads Uxbridge High School in Uxbridge, Mass., said there's a palpably positive feeling around the willingness to support education and to hear their messages more than the last two or three times they've been here. Rubin said he feels like there's an alignment with what are students' needs and actual next steps to support these needs. Lucas Pugh, the principal of Connolly Middle School in Tempe, Ariz., said the current funding levels are insufficient to retain high-quality educators, provide wraparound student services, and meet testing and graduation requirements.

Jeff Linden, the principal of the approximately 1,000-student Hastings High School in Nebraska, said schools are doing everything they can to work with what they have and find the resources to get creative, but at the same time we need help. At Hastings High School, 54% of students belong to low-income households and 30% require special accommodations in school. Jay Dostal, the principal of Westside High School in Omaha, Neb., said his family is in generational debt trying to teach the youth of tomorrow and asked how we incentivize the youth to continue teaching. Anna Thoma, the assistant principal of Millard High School in Millard, Neb., told an aide to Republican Sen. Pete Rickett that the funding is finite and school vouchers dilute the funding for public schools. Greg Johnson, the longtime principal of West Liberty-Salem High School, an hour outside Columbus, said even policymakers who supported private school choice were open to his view that these programs pull money away from public school students.

Over the past two years, the Trump administration has gutted the Education Department and frozen several federal grants that help schools cover food and medical costs for students. There were cuts to teacher and principal training programs as well, though some grant funding has been restored. The Trump administration has argued that in shutting down the Education Department, they are returning power to the states and to parents by giving them the right to choose the type of education they want for their children. The principals' top fear, of reduced Title 1 and other federal funding, has somewhat dissipated since Congress voted to maintain the existing levels of funding for public education for fiscal year 2026. A group of Republican senators has also proposed a spending package that again preserves virtually all current federal education funding for fiscal year 2027.

Other principals credited the shift in mood to the Democratic takeover of both houses of Congress after the midterm elections and the rise of the so-called blue wave. Rubin and Wiltshire, from Massachusetts, told an aide in Democratic Sen. Ed Markey's office that multiple students from their schools had been hospitalized for mental health conditions. An aide for Markey said their office had written to Google about its decision to bundle AI features with the search function, a move that several prominent school districts have pushed back against. Democratic Rep. Jim McGovern indicated to the Massachusetts contingent that he intends to push to regulate AI sooner than Congress had acted on curbing social media exposure for students. Virginia's newly elected governor Abigail Spanberger, a Democrat, reversed her Republican predecessor's decision and pulled out of the program this week.

stories.Headline: Walmart reports 25% rise in global ad revenue as AI tools and connected TV deals gain traction
stories.Summary:
Walmart reported on November 20, 2026, that its global advertising revenue rose 25% in the latest period, while U.S. ad sales climbed 37%, according to a Simply Wall St article published on Yahoo Finance. Management tied the advertising gains to recent moves in connected TV, including acquisitions involving Vizio and Vibe.co, and the retailer also highlighted new AI powered retail media tools and conversational commerce features as part of its advertising push. The article said Walmart runs a global network of stores, clubs, websites and apps that generate vast shopper data, which gives its advertising unit a direct line to purchase behavior across consumer retailing. The piece was described as general in nature and produced with the assistance of AI automation, based on data and analysis from Simply Wall St.

The article said the 25% advertising jump feeds into a broader pattern its research has tracked, and it noted that its analysis turns up one warning sign for Walmart as well. It framed the ad rise as fitting Walmart's narrative that higher margin businesses such as advertising, marketplace services and memberships gradually matter more to earnings than low margin store sales, and it said the main factor that has to go right is continued growth and profitability of those alternative profit pools. The article also said the news sharpens a key risk already flagged in that narrative, that regulators are scrutinising Walmart's use of AI and digital pricing, and that tighter rules on how Sparky or digital shelf tools work could slow the profit streams investors are now cheering. It pointed readers to a full story suggesting a $129 fair value for Walmart.

The article did not name any Walmart executive or provide direct statements from the company, attributing the advertising figures and the connected TV and AI details to management and the retailer generally. It said the advertising surge gives bulls fresh evidence that the ad unit is not just an add-on but a material earnings contributor that differs from traditional retailers such as Target or Costco. It also said that to judge what the headline really means for Walmart, readers need a clear view of where its mix of low margin retailing and higher margin services is heading over time, which it said is exactly what a narrative tries to spell out. The article stated that Simply Wall St has no position in any stocks mentioned and that the piece does not constitute a recommendation to buy or sell any stock.

The context the article gave is Walmart's effort to build higher margin income streams alongside its store sales, with advertising, marketplace services and memberships expected to matter more to earnings over time. It said the advertising gains were supported by AI tools and connected TV deals and described the ad unit as increasingly material rather than incidental. The article did not say what happens next beyond inviting readers to add Walmart to a watchlist and get alerts as these catalysts play out, and it noted that its analysis may not factor in the latest price-sensitive company announcements or qualitative material. It also said the article does not take account of readers' objectives or financial situations.

stories.Headline: Google Cloud launches object enrichments to extract AI metadata from stored objects
stories.Summary:
Google Cloud introduced object enrichments, a new Cloud Storage capability, on November 19, 2026, according to a blog post by Himanshu Kohli, Product Manager. The service uses AI models to automatically extract rich contextual metadata from Cloud Storage objects and saves it in place as object context. It gives customers access to AI models used by internal Google services such as Google Photos, offering image annotations like object detection and image labeling. The capability is available in preview as a fully managed service that also includes a high-quality PDF classification model. The post says the vast majority of enterprise information is unstructured, locked away in object storage as petabytes of images, PDFs, videos, and audio files.

Object enrichments offers image annotations at 75% cost savings compared to similar services from other cloud providers, and enriching 10 million images or PDFs costs just $700 according to published pricing. The five first-party Cloud Storage models for images and PDFs include object detection, face detection, image labeling, and explicit content detection, and the PDF classification model categorizes documents into standard business and industry categories like Finance, Games, News, and Health. Setting up an enrichment job takes three steps with no code required in the Google Cloud console or programmatically via the Cloud Storage API: define your scope by providing buckets and a processing location, choose your models, and grant IAM permissions. Object enrichments can scale to millions or billions of objects, orchestrates model inference, parses responses, and writes results to each object's object context with built-in retries and throttling. Object context is a specialized Cloud Storage metadata construct storing contextual information as structured key-value pairs alongside the object, sharing the object's durability and consistency, traveling with it during copy, move, and replication, and being removed when the object is deleted.

Antoine Castex, Principal Data & AI Architect at L'Oreal, said L'Oreal is the 4th largest advertiser in the world and that managing media assets at that scale is complex. He said object enrichments' high quality and cost-effective annotations enable L'Oreal to discover, understand, and govern content at scale, accelerating marketing and advertising operations while remaining compliant in all markets. He said object enrichments enables L'Oreal to label its extensive creative asset repository 100x faster at a fraction of the cost of existing pipelines and processes. Mayur Pillay, VP Partnerships at Hyperscience, said that even with a highly accurate baseline, Hyperscience leveraged object enrichments to drive a 50%+ lift in document classification accuracy while simultaneously reducing classification inference costs by 2-3x. Brandon Bunker, VP of Product AI at Vivint, said Cloud Storage object enrichments and BigQuery slash AI development from 6 months to 1 month while rapidly improving Vivint's models.

The post says agents need grounded knowledge, but reading every raw file at scale is cost- and performance-prohibitive, citing an operations agent pinpointing a doorstep package delivery or a roadway hazard by streaming thousands of smart-camera or vehicle frames on every user prompt. It names three historical challenges: cost, since running models over millions to billions of objects pushes organizations to process only a fraction of their data, creating blind spots; operational toil, since a self-managed pipeline means stitching together event triggers, queues, and custom infrastructure on Cloud Run or Google Kubernetes Engine with retry and error logic and job scheduling, and teams sometimes spend months on this plumbing; and fragmented metadata, which lands in a separate data store, requiring a second storage system, access policies across disconnected permission models, and cleanup jobs. Object context can flow natively into BigQuery via Storage Insights datasets, allowing SQL analytics, dashboards, and joins with structured enterprise tables without ETL code. Early customers use object enrichments for creative asset search and media archives, automated trust, safety, and content moderation, training data curation for frontier AI, and multimodal analytics.

The post describes use cases including finding a specific asset such as a red car driving at sunset or a vintage convertible in the desert during golden hour, scanning millions of daily user uploads and supplier catalogs for explicit content, and enriching hundreds of millions of raw camera and sensor files so ML engineers can pinpoint exact training cohorts in minutes rather than months. It says multimodal analytics can combine image and document insights with structured business data for personalization, fraud detection, and trend discovery, for example analyzing customer uploaded images alongside comments and recent sales data. For complex multimodal reasoning across text, PDFs, images, audio, and video, customers can leverage Gemini natively with object enrichments for summarization, entity extraction, transcription, and translation. Object enrichments is available in preview today in the Cloud Storage console and through the Cloud Storage API. The post directs readers to documentation, Storage Insights datasets in BigQuery, the Cloud Storage MCP server for IAM-scoped agent access, Cloud Storage pricing, and the console to enrich a first bucket in three clicks.

The post says teams can reach out at storage-ai@google.com to learn more and request access to the upcoming Gemini enrichments functionality. It says object enrichments handles the rest after setup, with no queues to manage, workers to scale, or glue code to maintain. It says administrators can use IAM to control who can read, add, update, or remove object context, and applications can filter object listings directly by object context key-value pairs or read context metadata alongside objects. It says object context shares the same durability and consistency properties as the underlying Cloud Storage object, so no cleanup jobs are needed. The post leaves open when Gemini enrichments will become available and what request access will involve.

stories.Headline: Federal contractors face False Claims Act liability for overstated AI capabilities, BCLP partners say
stories.Summary:
Federal contractors that exaggerate or misrepresent artificial intelligence capabilities in bids and billing for government work could face liability under the False Claims Act, according to a Bloomberg Law analysis published on November 20, 2026 by Emmet P. Ong and Susan Carney Lynch, both partners at BCLP. The authors point to regulators who have already pursued misleading claims about AI, including the Securities and Exchange Commission, which has acted against companies for misrepresenting their AI use, and the Federal Trade Commission, which has challenged deceptive claims about AI-enabled products. They describe examples such as a defense contractor claiming its drones can autonomously identify and track targets despite testing that showed undisclosed human intervention, or a medical-device manufacturer overstating diagnostic capabilities to win placement on government supply schedules. The risks also extend to contracts for AI development, where a contractor might falsely report completed model training or successful testing to obtain milestone payments, or bill for AI-enabled analysis never performed.

The analysis says not every promotional claim supports liability, since vague descriptions such as AI-powered differ from specific representations about autonomous operation, detection accuracy or deployed safeguards. It cites the Department of Justice's Civil Cyber-Fraud Initiative as a precedent, noting a university-affiliated defense research contractor that settled allegations last year that a cybersecurity assessment score submitted under defense contracts was based on a fictitious or virtual environment rather than an actual covered system, and a medical-services contractor that settled allegations in 2022, including failing to disclose that patient records were not consistently stored in the secure electronic medical-record system for which it billed the government. Applying established False Claims Act theories would raise questions about materiality, scienter and damages, complicated by the technology's evolving capabilities, and the authors note that under United States ex rel. Escobar v.

Universal Health Services a contractual or regulatory violation does not automatically establish liability because a misrepresentation must have a natural tendency to influence, or be capable of influencing, the government's payment decision. They also cite United States ex rel. Schutte v. SuperValu Inc. for the point that a defendant's subjective beliefs matter, so an objectively reasonable interpretation does not necessarily protect a contractor whose internal communications show it understood its AI representations were false.

On damages, the authors cite United States v. Science Applications International Corp., where the court applied a benefit-of-the-bargain measure to account for the value of services received, and they say evidence that the government would have withheld payment does not itself establish damages. They recommend that federal contractors incorporate reviews of material AI representations into existing contracting and compliance controls, and they set out four practical steps: substantiate claims before making them by comparing proposals, demonstrations and billing submissions with documented testing and actual capabilities; ensure testing supports representations by documenting testing conditions, limitations and results; preserve records connecting commitments to performance, including milestone reports, acceptance tests, deployment records and internal assessments; and reassess representations during performance, since model updates, disabled controls or changes in human oversight may make later claims or certifications inaccurate even if earlier statements were sound. The authors conclude that DOJ may not need a dedicated AI-washing initiative to pursue misrepresentations about AI capabilities, and that as AI becomes embedded in federal procurement and healthcare, contractors should expect greater scrutiny of the gap between promised capabilities and actual performance.

stories.Headline: Senate passes S.5653 to fast-track AI data centers and energy projects in 65-31 vote
stories.Summary:
Actor Mark Ruffalo urged his followers to oppose a specific Senate bill on November 18, 2026. He used his Instagram account to criticize Senate Democrats for their support of the legislation. Ruffalo claimed the bill gives President Trump more power over data centers and ICE camps. He argued that Democrats are ignoring their recent midterm election wins by supporting this. The actor wants his fans to contact legislators to stop the progress of the bill.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, known as S.5653, is a 494 page document. It aims to fast track AI data centers, ICE camps, pipelines, mines, and power plants. The bill would gut Tribal sovereignty, Native American rights, the Endangered Species Act, and the Clean Water Act. A manager's amendment was released on November 7, 2026, and an explainer was updated November 8. The Senate held a cloture vote on the motion to proceed on November 9, 2026.

Mark Ruffalo said the bill is a devastating rollback of environmental laws in American history. He questioned why Chuck Schumer and other Democrats support Trump after the country rejected him. The Bipartisan Policy Center stated that senators worked for over a year to negotiate these reforms. They claimed the package comprehensively addresses almost all aspects of the nation's current permitting process. The center noted that federal reviews of business applications now take years or decades instead of months.

Senator Ron Wyden told the New York Times that he cannot support the proposed legislation. He said the administration spent two years waging a war on new clean energy projects. The bill affects public lands, endangered species, and the fossil fuel industry through permitting changes. On November 18, the Senate passed the bill with a vote of 65 to 31. Twenty one members of the Democrat caucus voted in favor of the legislation.

The bill was supported by Senators Shelley Moore Capito, Mike Lee, and Martin Heinrich. Other supporters included Sheldon Whitehouse, John Fetterman, Jon Ossoff, Raphael Warnock, and leader Chuck Schumer. The Bipartisan Policy Center noted that previous reform attempts were introduced in both the House and Senate. They explained that delays on polluting projects also block conservation projects and clean energy technologies. The legislation seeks to curb permitting abuse that has caused long delays in federal reviews.

The Senate has already voted to move the bill forward with a significant bipartisan majority. Ruffalo continues to urge his followers to fight the legislation to protect environmental laws. The Bipartisan Policy Center intends to update its explainer as the legislation advances through Congress. The articles do not state if the bill has been signed into law yet. It remains unclear how the administration will handle the handshake promises mentioned by Senator Wyden.

stories.Headline: Bridgewater executive Gregory Jensen says he made early investments in Anthropic and OpenAI
stories.Summary:
Gregory Jensen, a top executive at the hedge fund Bridgewater Associates, has told business associates, colleagues and the occasional reporter that he made early investments in both Anthropic and its rival OpenAI, according to a New York Times report published on November 19, 2026. The report says Anthropic’s I.P.O. will mint a fortune for a cavalcade of well-known Silicon Valley angel investors, venture capitalists and early employees who spotted the A.I. start-up before it became one of the most valuable companies in the world. Jensen, who is 52, has said he was in the right places at the right times and that his connections to key players in artificial intelligence go back nearly two decades, according to three people who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss a private conversation. In a September interview with Bloomberg News, Jensen said he was lucky enough to be in the room with Dario and others when they were talking about the scaling laws and how you could create an almost evolutionary process to create intelligence, along with the huge benefits and huge problems that could create. Jensen has also said he was literally the first check to Anthropic, an assertion the report says could not be independently confirmed.

One of his links to the industry was a former Bridgewater employee, Holden Karnofsky, who now works at Anthropic and is married to Danielle Amodei, Anthropic’s co-founder. The report gives no figures for how much Jensen invested, how large a stake he holds or how much the I.P.O. will be worth to him, and it does not say when any of the early investments were made. It also does not say what, if anything, Jensen’s position at Bridgewater had to do with the investments, or whether the fund itself was involved. The report does not say what Jensen or Bridgewater said in response to its questions, and it gives no comment from Anthropic, OpenAI or Karnofsky. It also does not say when Anthropic’s I.P.O. is expected to take place or how the company’s value compares with OpenAI’s.

The only statement attributed to Jensen is his September interview with Bloomberg News, in which he described being in the room when the scaling laws were discussed. The report does not say whether Jensen still holds his stakes in either company or whether he plans to sell shares after the offering. The report places Jensen’s account in the context of the many Silicon Valley investors and early employees set to profit from Anthropic’s I.P.O., and it notes that his claim to have been the first check could not be independently confirmed. It does not say what happens next for Jensen, for Bridgewater or for Anthropic beyond the offering itself. More to follow.

stories.Headline: ABBYY survey finds 57% of manufacturing leaders say AI adoption outpaces their governance
stories.Summary:
ABBYY released the Who Answers for AI: The Governance Gap report on November 19, 2026, and Marina Mayer covered it for Supply & Demand Chain Executive. The research was commissioned by ABBYY and surveyed manufacturing leaders at businesses using AI. It found that 57% of manufacturing leaders say AI is being adopted faster than they can govern it. Only 17% of manufacturing bosses completely trust AI to operate without introducing unacceptable risks. Just over one-quarter, 26%, of manufacturing companies completely trust AI to produce accurate results.

The report gives figures on responsibility for harmful or inaccurate outputs. One-third, 33%, believe responsibility should be shared between the organization and the vendor. A quarter, 26%, think the AI vendor should bear full responsibility. 23% say it lies with the company using it, and the rest said the end user or regulators should take the lead. 67% of manufacturing leaders say data governance requirements slow AI deployment, and 36% say ethical concerns such as bias and transparency slow deployment. Just 48% say their AI initiatives have exceeded expectations.

Roman Kilun, chief compliance officer at ABBYY, said businesses are embracing AI but many still struggle with key questions around accountability, governance and ROI. He said senior management needs to do a better job of communicating responsible AI policies companywide. He said it is often more junior staff who operate AI tools day to day and they should know which controls apply. He said AI requires organizations to know where data comes from, whether it can be trusted, how it can be used, and where it is stored and processed. The articles attribute these statements to him.

Nearly one-quarter, 24%, of manufacturing leaders cite data quality as their top challenge to greater ROI from AI. Skills shortages is the next most significant barrier, followed by integration with existing systems at 13% and the cost of implementation at 12%. 94% of manufacturing leaders say senior leadership knows who is responsible for developing, implementing and managing AI, but only 66% say the same for junior employees. 88% have an AI governance framework in place, and of these 78% say it made their AI initiatives more successful. 61% say humans review all important AI decisions before action is taken, higher than the global average of 56%.

Of those with governance frameworks, 57% say it enabled easier deployment, 56% easier scaling and 54% easier widespread adoption among employees. Less than half, 48%, of manufacturing companies have an AI incident reporting process in place. Only 32% have an AI kill switch and 36% have an AI roll back capability. The most popular tools among manufacturing leaders are Generative AI at 82%, Agentic AI at 63% and Purpose-built AI at 59%. Manufacturing organizations are continuing to increase their investment in AI, and respondents expect investment to increase by a further 19.1% next year, slightly above the global average of 18.8%.

The articles give no further background beyond the survey findings and Kilun's comments. The report is titled Who Answers for AI: The Governance Gap. The survey covered manufacturing leaders at businesses using AI. The articles compare several manufacturing figures with global averages, including the 17% trust figure against 22% globally. They also compare the 61% human review figure with the global average of 56%. The articles state that governance maturity varies across organizations.

The articles do not say what ABBYY or manufacturers will do next. They leave open how the accountability split among organization, vendor, end user and regulators will be resolved. They do not say when or whether the 48% without incident reporting processes or the 32% without kill switches will adopt them. They give no date for a follow-up study or for any change in investment plans beyond the expected 19.1% increase next year. They do not say how the junior employee knowledge gap will be closed.

stories.Headline: Delaware court fines partner personally for filing unverified GenAI output but spares his firm over its AI policy
stories.Summary:
The Delaware Court of Chancery sanctioned a senior partner personally under Court of Chancery Rule 11 for filing a brief containing unverified GenAI output, in Leiske v. Kidd, C.A. No. 2025-0426-CDW (LWW), on November 13, 2026. The underlying proceeding concerned advancement, and on January 22, 2026, the plaintiffs filed an answering brief opposing the defendants' exceptions to a Magistrate in Chancery's final report. Five days later, the defendants' reply brief pointed out that the brief contained fabricated quotations, inaccurate citations and hallucinated legal propositions. The following day, the plaintiffs' lead counsel, who had signed the brief, filed a letter acknowledging that a GenAI tool had been used and submitted a corrected brief. The letter attributed the failure to catch the errors to an oversight during a paralegal's cite-check, but the corrected brief removed quotation marks around the nonexistent quotes while retaining the inaccurate descriptions of the underlying cases.

When defence counsel wrote to the court identifying the remaining misrepresentations, the plaintiffs' counsel responded by faulting opposing counsel for failing to "meet and confer" before alerting the court and insisting that the cited authorities were real and supported the arguments advanced. After resolving the exceptions dispute on the merits, the court issued an Order to Show Cause concerning the GenAI issues, which directed both the signing partner and his law firm to explain why sanctions should not be imposed under the applicable court rule and the court's inherent authority. The partner and the firm filed detailed affidavits, and the court determined the matter without an evidentiary hearing. The court emphasized that the use of GenAI in legal practice is neither forbidden nor inherently problematic, and that these tools offer substantial benefits and efficiencies, but they must be used with the care required by the court's Rule 11 and the Delaware Lawyers' Rules of Professional Conduct, including ensuring the accuracy of every authority and citation presented to the court. Under Court of Chancery Rule 11(b)(2), an attorney who presents a paper to the court certifies that, after an inquiry reasonable in the circumstances, its legal contentions are warranted by existing law.

The court said that "[a]n attorney's signature on a court filing is not a procedural formality; it is a certification to the tribunal," and that a fake quotation or a fabricated legal synthesis generated by an algorithm is not "existing law," so presenting unverified GenAI output violates the rule. Rule 11(c)(1) provides that, absent exceptional circumstances, a law firm must be held jointly responsible for violations committed by its partners, associates or employees. Drawing on Rule 5.1(a) of the Delaware Lawyers' Rules of Professional Conduct and the American Bar Association's Formal Opinion 512, the court asked whether the firm had made reasonable efforts to put in place measures giving reasonable assurance of compliance. The court concluded that it had, because the firm had barred the use of unapproved GenAI tools in March 2023, formed a working group in 2024 to evaluate tools and study ethical guidance, and adopted a comprehensive GenAI policy in July 2025 requiring an experienced lawyer to review GenAI output for accuracy and completeness. The firm had also developed an accredited ethics training program that over 200 employees had completed by January 2026, and the court said the firm "did the right thing" and should not be sanctioned for an individual lawyer bypassing those controls.

The signing partner, as Chair of his firm's AI subcommittee, had been piloting a GenAI tool that was not approved for general firm use, yet he used that tool to draft and condense arguments in the brief. He then delegated cite-checking to a junior lawyer and a paralegal and filed the brief without personally verifying the authorities, and the court held that the duty of candour and the obligation to conduct a reasonable inquiry under Rule 11 are personal and nondelegable. The court held that a senior lawyer who signs a brief cannot disclaim responsibility for unverified GenAI output where the lawyer knowingly introduces text generated by GenAI into a draft, and the signatory must ensure that the underlying authorities have been reviewed and that those authorities actually support the propositions for which they are cited. The court rejected the argument that it was sufficient that the cases cited were real or that the overarching propositions were arguably consistent with general principles of law, noting that GenAI tools not only invent case names but also fabricate plausible-sounding quotations and stretch real decisions to stand for propositions they never addressed. The court stated that counsel has an affirmative duty to review the underlying authorities and correct the errors if GenAI errors are detected, and that "[i]t is not enough to remove quotation marks and leave a fabricated legal synthesis in place."

As to the sanction, the court weighed the partner's initial deflection of blame and the retained mischaracterizations against his subsequent acceptance of full responsibility, sincere contrition and long record of practice before the court. It imposed a fine of US$2,500, consistent with fines in comparable proceedings, and given the nondelegable nature of the duty, the partner was required to pay it personally. Additional mandatory continuing education was considered redundant, since the lawyer had already completed several GenAI ethics programs and led internal training. The court noted that GenAI tools are now widely used in everyday legal practice and can assist with drafting, condense and refine written material, and outline arguments in a fraction of the time it would otherwise take. At the same time, courts across North America have been faced with a steady stream of briefs and factums containing fabricated cases, invented quotations and mischaracterized holdings, and the question is no longer whether such errors will attract judicial scrutiny but what happens when they do.

The article states that although this is a Delaware decision, the reasoning will resonate with litigators and their firms in any jurisdiction where courts are confronting the same problem. It states that a lawyer who signs a factum or other document citing authorities owns every citation in it, and reliance on a cite-check by others will not shift that responsibility, particularly where the signatory knows that GenAI-generated text was used. It states that verification must go beyond confirming that a case exists and requires reading the authority to confirm that any quotation is accurate and that the decision supports the proposition for which it is cited. For law firms, the article states, the decision underscores the value of a clear GenAI policy, verification requirements, restrictions on unapproved tools and documented training for members of the firm. The article states that its content is intended to provide a general guide to the subject matter and that specialist advice should be sought about specific circumstances.

stories.Headline: SimonMed's Sean Raj presents studies showing AI cuts fracture reporting time and improves chest X-ray reports
stories.Summary:
Sean Raj, MD, MBA, chief medical officer and chief innovation officer at SimonMed, will present two scientific studies at the Radiological Society of North America 2026 meeting in Chicago, the company announced on November 16, 2026. Both studies draw on data from SimonMed's nationwide outpatient network. One examines how AI-driven worklist prioritization shortens the time it takes to report fractures on musculoskeletal X-rays. The other evaluates how fine-tuning a vision-language foundation model on outpatient data affects the quality of automatically generated chest X-ray reports. The fracture research analyzed more than 510,000 musculoskeletal radiographs from over 200 centers, tracking turnaround from before the AI system was introduced in 2022 through its full integration in 2025.

Mean turnaround time fell 83.8% for exams showing a fracture, from about two days to under eight hours. Turnaround for fracture-negative studies improved as well, and the company said the gains came without penalizing routine workflow. Raj will present that paper, titled "AI Worklist Reprioritization: Measuring Fracture Detection Turnaround Time for MSK X-Rays in Nationwide Outpatient Imaging," on December 2. Earlier that day, Raj will present a poster on the vision-language model for automated chest X-ray report generation, before and after institution-specific fine-tuning. The investigational model was trained on more than 5 million chest X-ray image-report pairs, fine-tuned on more than 150,000 SimonMed adult outpatient exams, and tested on a consecutive cohort from 143 outpatient centers.

Fine-tuning improved sensitivity with a modest reduction in specificity, and the largest gain came in pulmonary nodules, where sensitivity rose from 62.6% to 80.8%. Raj said the research shows AI can reduce fracture reporting times from days to hours, and that autonomous chest X-ray report generation represents a step toward helping radiologists work more efficiently. The findings support improved generalizability through local model adaptation, and suggest fine-tuned report generation models may reduce radiologist workload while maintaining clinically acceptable performance. SimonMed said the work highlights its efforts to advance AI technology designed to interpret medical images and generate clinically relevant reports, with the potential to improve both diagnostic performance and radiologist workflows. For referring physicians, the company said, actionable results arrive within hours instead of days.

stories.Headline: Performativ links bank staff AI assistants to client records under existing permissions
stories.Summary:
Performativ connected AI assistants used by bank staff to client and portfolio records on November 19, 2026. This release allows employees to query business systems using tools like ChatGPT and Claude. The company used the Model Context Protocol to create these links for existing clients. This update is specifically for bank staff and not for the bank clients themselves. The service is off by default and requires a firm to enable it.

The system uses the Model Context Protocol to link assistants to records hosted in the EU. Administrators decide who can use the service, and each employee uses an individual login. Existing Performativ permissions apply to every user, and the company logs every request for audit. The platform connects to more than 150 custodians and supports over 1,500 advisors. It manages more than 100 billion euros in client assets across its broader platform.

CEO Albert Geisler Fox stated that the current release is for staff at client firms. He described letting bank clients query their own portfolios through AI assistants as a future ambition. The company says this setup prevents staff from manually copying client data into outside assistants. Performativ claims these controls ensure security and regulatory compliance for the firms using the service. The company says the system keeps data access tied to the firm's existing rules.

The service affects relationship managers, portfolio managers, back office teams, and compliance staff. Relationship managers can use the tool to create briefings that compare portfolio progress with projections. Portfolio managers can examine performance and risk alongside the advice a client previously received. Compliance teams can review risk profiles, regulatory status, and recent changes to client records. These workflows use data including meeting notes, account activity, and the identities of responsible advisors.

The MCP capability builds on governed agent workflows introduced with Custom Agents in November 2025. Performativ provides a platform for portfolio management, customer relationship management, compliance, and reporting. The company aims to move AI queries into the assistants that employees already use. This builds on the existing platform where firms manage their client relationships and records. The new version changes where staff can ask questions about their business data.

The next step is the ambition to let bank clients use their preferred AI assistants. This future direction would allow clients to ask about portfolios under the bank's controls. The articles do not state when this client facing feature will be released. They do not provide the specific adoption numbers for the new MCP service release. It remains open how many firms have enabled the service since November 19.

stories.Headline: Federal court rules police cannot arrest on an uncorroborated AI facial recognition match
stories.Summary:
A federal court ruled that police cannot arrest someone on an uncorroborated AI facial recognition match, and it denied qualified immunity to a Kentucky detective who jailed a Nebraska man on a bad-check charge, according to LavX News. Officers arrested Alain Osorio over a charge of passing a bad check at a bank in Florence, Kentucky, where detectives had only the bank's CCTV footage as a source for the suspect's image. Detective Ryan Kilmer of the Florence Police Department ran a screenshot from that footage through the department's facial recognition program, which matched the suspect to photos on Facebook belonging to a profile named "Yony Smith Npoles Charon." Kilmer concluded that "Yony" was Alain Vizcay Osorio, a man whose booking photo appeared in police files, and the court did not name the facial recognition program.

The use of Facebook photos suggests Clearview AI, a company that has scraped hundreds of billions of images from the open web. Osorio lived in Nebraska, and officers arrested him there and extradited him to Kentucky, where he posted bond on Jan. 24, 2025, the day after his arrest. A grand jury indicted him in March 2025, a court arraigned him two months later, and he pleaded not guilty, while the state attorney's office dismissed the charges after Osorio proved he was working in Nebraska when the suspect passed the bad check. Osorio does not resemble the man in the security footage or the Facebook profile, since he has a different head shape, haircut, facial features and complexion, though both men are Black with facial hair.

Kilmer told the court in an affidavit that he used "investigative tools" to "match" Osorio to the suspect, but the court found he used one tool, the facial recognition program. Under Florence Police Department policy, facial recognition AI alone cannot establish probable cause, and Kilmer used it despite the policy. The court wrote that the Fourth Amendment does not allow a detective to delegate to AI the task of assessing probable cause, and that the Constitution does not permit an arrest based on nothing more than an uncorroborated conclusion by AI that the individual committed a crime. The judge stripped Kilmer of qualified immunity, the legal doctrine that shields officers from civil liability unless they violate clearly established law, and Kilmer can appeal.

A higher court could affirm the decision or reverse it, and if Kilmer loses his appeal, the ruling would apply beyond facial recognition. Police departments use AI to steer patrols through predictive policing software, officers use AI to generate reports from body camera footage, and Axon has added AI tools to its body cameras. The article states that running a photo through an algorithm does not constitute detective work, that a match is a lead rather than a conclusion, and that departments across the country use facial recognition as an investigative shortcut. Detectives cannot treat an algorithm match as detective work, according to the piece, which cites Techdirt as its source.

stories.Headline: Judge Ehsan Amirkhani proposes a reverse-traceability test for judges to verify AI drafts against the original record
stories.Summary:
On 9 October 2026 the judiciary of England and Wales published a position statement on judicial use of AI, JURIST reported on 19 November 2026. The statement says judicial decisions remain with judges and AI cannot displace evaluation of evidence or judicial reasoning. It says every AI output used in judicial work must be reviewed, verified and approved by the responsible judicial office holder. It describes cautious testing of lower-risk applications including summarisation, chronologies and document analysis. It does not give blanket approval for AI to draft judgments.

The article poses a design question: what should a judge verify when the danger is a missing argument rather than a false quotation. It sets out a hypothetical civil claim where service of a prescribed notice is a prerequisite to possession. The claimant establishes title, the defendant puts service in issue and identifies evidence suggesting the notice never arrived. A draft correctly sets out the law of ownership, cites genuine decisions and grants possession. If service is a necessary condition of relief and remains disputed, the reasoning has bypassed a question on which the outcome may turn.

The author is Dr Ehsan Amirkhani, presiding judge of Branch 2 of the General Civil Court of Kermanshah, Iran, and an independent legal researcher writing in a personal academic capacity. He says no confidential case materials are used and all case examples are hypothetical. He proposes a short, judge-led reverse-traceability test beginning with the authorised record: the pleaded issues, material written submissions, relevant hearing record and evidence properly before the court. The judge identifies objections that, if well founded, would defeat an indispensable factual or legal step in the proposed disposition. The test then asks where the final reasons answer each such objection.

The article cites Ruiz Torija v Spain and Hiro Balani v Spain, both decided on 9 December 1994, in which the European Court of Human Rights examined failures to address arguments of potential significance. It cites the Court's Guide on Article 6, civil limb, on reasoned decisions enabling parties to understand they have been heard and to exercise a right of appeal. It says the Convention doctrine is not directly applicable to Iranian courts or a universal mandate to answer every pleading point. It says the transferable insight is that a court must make intelligible the path from the legally material disputes to its decision. It says repetitive submissions need not be restated, some objections become immaterial once a case is resolved on an independent ground, and other points can be answered by the reasoning as a whole.

The article says the judiciary's October 2025 AI guidance warns against hallucinations and disclosure of confidential material and emphasises the personal responsibility of judicial office holders for work produced in their names. It says a procurement or deployment policy should preserve traceable access to sources and that a polished interface concealing the record can make meaningful verification more difficult. It says controlled evaluations of authorised tools could assess whether reviewers identify omitted outcome-sensitive objections, whether final reasons treat them accurately, and how much time the procedure adds. It says such testing should distinguish errors caused by document extraction, summarisation and drafting and should examine false alarms. It says nothing justifies feeding parties' pleadings or non-public evidence into public AI services and that the judiciary of England and Wales confines judicial use to approved systems under its own arrangements.

The article says the same reverse-traceability check can be performed manually where no approved tool exists and that the legal safeguard should not depend on purchasing technology. It says the judge should check the losing party's strongest legally relevant case, not merely arguments fitting an early draft, and that institutional audits should ask whether the procedure consistently represents both sides. It says the proposed working aid creates no new general right of public access to judicial notes or draft deliberations. It says the next task is to make the October 2026 commitment to human oversight operational. It says that if the path from the original objection through the governing law and relevant evidence to the reason actually adopted is broken, the drafting process is not finished.

Articles.Title: The Objection an AI Draft Leaves Out: Why Judges Must Check Rulings Against the Original Record

stories.Headline: EU AI Act amendments push high-risk HR system obligations to December 2027
stories.Summary:
The EU Digital Omnibus Package amended the EU AI Act and entered into force on July 27, 2026, Mary T. Costigan of Jackson Lewis P.C. wrote on November 19, 2026. The Commission presented the Digital Omnibus in November 2025 as a package to simplify EU digital law, Éric Le Quellenec of Flichy Grangé Avocats said. The package has two parts, and the first reopens the GDPR, which is still being negotiated, Le Quellenec said. The second part amends the AI Act, and that one is now law, he said. Luís Neto Galvão of SRS Legal and Le Quellenec offered five practical steps for general counsel and HR leaders at multinational businesses.

Obligations for systems listed in Annex III, including recruitment and career management, were due to apply in August of this year, Le Quellenec said. They now apply from December 2, 2027, and from August 2, 2028, for AI built into regulated products, he said. The prohibitions have applied since February 2025, the AI literacy obligations as well, and the transparency rules since August 2026, he said. High-risk systems in use before December 2, 2027, only fall under the Act if their design is significantly changed afterward, he said. Point 4 of Annex III covers recruitment, including targeting job ads, filtering applications, and evaluating candidates, and decisions on the employment relationship, including promotion, termination, task allocation based on behavior or personal traits, and monitoring and evaluating performance.

The five steps are inventory and classify AI-enabled HR tools, strengthen oversight and vendor contracts, mitigate bias, train relevant teams, and prepare recruitment practices for compliance, the article said. Neto Galvão said clients should not think they have nothing to do until 2027 and that now is the time to put a compliance plan in place. He said a year goes very quickly when you have to map your tools, renegotiate vendor contracts, and train your teams. Le Quellenec said the vendor is usually the provider and the employer is the deployer, but this can change.

He said that if the employer puts its name on the tool, modifies it substantially, or changes its intended purpose so that it becomes high risk, it becomes a provider, which brings much heavier obligations. Le Quellenec said the employer should check the conformity assessment, CE marking, EU declaration of conformity, and registration in the EU database before buying. He said the employer must use the system in line with the instructions, assign human oversight to people with the competence, training, and authority to overrule it, and make sure the input data the employer controls are relevant and representative. He said the employer must monitor the system, suspend use immediately and inform the provider if a risk appears, report serious incidents, and keep the logs for at least six months.

He said the employer must inform candidates and employees who are subject to decisions and, before the tool is introduced, inform workers' representatives and the workers concerned. He said individuals have a right to an explanation of the role AI played in a decision that significantly affects them, and a rejected candidate can ask for it. Le Quellenec said the fundamental rights impact assessment introduced by the AI Act applies to public bodies, private entities providing public services, and credit and insurance uses. He said a private employer generally does not have to do it, and for them the key assessment remains the GDPR DPIA.

Neto Galvão said human oversight must be designed into the process, not added as a label, and a manager who can only confirm the system's output is not providing meaningful oversight. Le Quellenec said HR owns the use case, IT owns integration and security, the data protection officer owns data protection and privacy, and legal owns the contracts. He said the French Lawyers' Guide on Ethics and AI was adopted in March this year and draws attention to how the way you phrase a question shapes the answer. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Bloomington mayor Kerry Thomson vetoes a city council ordinance banning artificial superintelligence
stories.Summary:
Bloomington mayor Kerry Thomson announced on Thursday afternoon, Nov. 19, 2026, that she will not sign an ordinance the city council approved 7, 0 earlier that month, which would prohibit the distribution and deployment of artificial superintelligence within city limits. The ordinance was presented to the mayor on Nov. 9 at 5:13 p.m., according to the city clerk’s office, giving her until 5:13 p.m. Thursday to sign it or return it to the council with a veto message. Because she did neither, the ordinance is considered vetoed under Indiana law. Seven councilmembers voted for the ordinance on Nov. 4, when two members, Sydney Zulich and Kate Rosenbarger, were absent.

Councilmember Dave Rollo introduced the ordinance and put forward all four amendments the council adopted before its final vote. The ordinance would add a new chapter to Bloomington’s municipal code under Title 14, which governs peace and safety, and would prohibit distribution and deployment of ASI within the city, including through websites, software and other electronic interfaces, even when the computers hosting those systems are physically located elsewhere. It defines superintelligence in terms of agency, generality and intelligence, describing autonomous systems capable of modifying their own algorithms, executing computer code outside restricted environments and undertaking complex tasks without continuous human oversight, combined with capabilities vastly exceeding human cognitive performance. The ordinance does not establish a testing procedure or designate an independent authority to determine when a particular AI system has crossed the threshold into superintelligence. It invokes the city’s powers under Indiana’s Home Rule Act and compares superintelligence to hazardous substances and industrial processes that local governments can regulate in the interest of public safety, and it would authorize the city’s legal and police departments to seek civil penalties and court orders against violators, with enforcement discretionary rather than mandatory.

One amendment explicitly excluded end-user access from the prohibition, so a Bloomington resident would not violate the ordinance merely by accessing an AI system through an electronic interface, and another removed Rollo’s original proposal to require approval from more than 95% of Bloomington’s registered voters, along with findings establishing an extremely high level of scientific certainty about the safety of superintelligence, before the ban could be lifted, retaining a scientific-safety objective in the preamble but no longer making the finding and referendum requirements for repeal. Thomson said, “Bloomington is working hard to grow our innovation economy, and artificial intelligence plays an important role in that work,” and that “AI already contributes to advances in research, medicine, education and many other fields.” She added, “We also need to be careful about creating unnecessary barriers that discourage those very people from investing in our community.” Thomson said, “As mayor, I have a responsibility to lead the team that implements and enforces our ordinances,” and that “This ordinance leaves significant questions about how the City would identify violations, what authority we have to regulate them and what enforcement would require.” She said, “The potential need to monitor private digital activity is especially troubling given our recent work to strengthen protections against government surveillance,” and that “Passing a law carries responsibilities beyond stating a principle,” adding, “We need to be confident that we can implement and enforce the laws we adopt.”

Thomson acknowledged the risks Rollo is attempting to address, saying, “I appreciate Council’s efforts to address the risks of increasingly autonomous AI systems and the national conversation this legislation has helped advance,” and that “Those risks deserve serious consideration.” Rollo told The B Square he is still optimistic about working with the mayor on a version of the ordinance she might eventually be willing to sign, because superintelligent AI is “a deadly risk for everyone,” and he added, “Obviously, we’re racing forward as the horizon is racing at us. I mean, this is madness. And there are huge consequences.” Rollo said at the start of the Wednesday night, Nov. 18, council meeting, less than 24 hours before the mayor’s deadline, that the ordinance “is emphatically not what tech businesses are using here or at IU,” and he said, “This particular AI, ASI, hasn’t yet arrived,” while contending that developing such systems is the goal of leading AI companies and that the technology could arrive soon.

Rollo contrasted that goal with work at Indiana University, which he characterized as human-centered artificial intelligence emphasizing ethical deployment, human oversight and beneficial social impacts, and he said, “Local tech applications and IU are to be lauded for their approach.” Rollo rebutted Thomson’s surveillance concern, saying, “We don’t need to surveil anyone,” and suggested violations could be reported through complaints or investigated by testing whether a prohibited system was accessible from a city-operated computer. The ordinance vetoed by Thomson represents a third effort by Rollo to persuade Bloomington’s city government to address what he and others warn is the existential danger to the human species posed by increasingly powerful artificial intelligence. In July 2023, Rollo proposed a resolution calling for a moratorium on developing artificial general intelligence until adequate safeguards could be established, and he withdrew it after officials with Indiana University raised concerns about possible implications for research funding, and sufficient support from council colleagues appeared unlikely.

On June 10 of this year, the council unanimously adopted a resolution calling on governments at other levels to address the existential risks of artificial intelligence and urging a moratorium on developing advanced AI until the technology could be aligned with human values and well-being, and that resolution was nonbinding, expressing the council’s position without establishing a local prohibition. The ordinance approved by the council in early November goes further by attempting to make distribution and deployment of superintelligence a violation of Bloomington law. Rollo’s goals extend beyond Bloomington, and the ordinance is part of a strategy he envisions being replicated by hundreds of municipalities, with local prohibitions eventually generating enough pressure to prompt state, federal and international restrictions on advanced AI development. The council could attempt to override the veto at its next regular meeting, scheduled for Wednesday, Dec. 2, at 6:30 p.m., and an override would require six votes in favor from the nine-member council.

Thomson’s objections come despite several amendments the council adopted before its final vote, intended in part to narrow the ordinance’s scope, address concerns that it could affect ordinary users of AI technology, and other issues identified soon after Rollo introduced it. The amendments reduced the potential reach of the ordinance but did not resolve the underlying question of how Bloomington would identify prohibited systems or determine whether companies outside its boundaries were distributing them within the city. Whether Indiana’s Home Rule Act powers would support a prohibition extending to remotely operated digital systems is an unresolved legal question. Thomson’s surveillance concern comes just five weeks after the city council voted 7, 0 on Oct. 14 to prohibit automated license plate readers and certain surveillance camera systems that allow outside entities to access recordings and data, and the superintelligence ordinance does not itself authorize new surveillance of internet activity.

stories.Headline: Law Society urges law firms to adopt stronger AI governance frameworks
stories.Summary:
The Law Society published a feature on 18 November 2026 on managing artificial intelligence risks in legal services, solicitornews.co.uk reported on 19 November 2026. The feature brings together the perspective of Peter Lee, partner and global head of AI governance at Simmons & Simmons. It says law firms need stronger governance frameworks to manage the growing use of AI in legal services. The article was written by Muntaha Shah and updated on 19 November 2026. It states that regulators in England and Wales, together with judicial guidance, have made clear that solicitors remain responsible for their work even when AI is involved.

The feature says professional responsibility cannot be transferred to an AI system. It says firms should address the reliability of AI-generated outputs, the protection of legal privilege, client confidentiality, data protection and cyber security. It identifies the Law Society's AI practice note as a useful starting point, but says each firm must translate general guidance into policies reflecting its own services, systems, people and risk profile. It recommends regular and adaptable training rather than occasional one-off sessions. It notes that firms within the scope of the EU AI Act may also need to consider the Act's AI literacy obligation.

The Law Society's policy adviser, Tegan Harrison, stresses that AI governance is not simply a technology or compliance exercise. She says it also concerns people, professional judgement and the trust on which legal services depend. The feature encourages practices to begin by identifying the problem they want to solve, understanding the technology they already use and deciding what safeguards are appropriate. Peter Lee's perspective is presented on how practices can benefit from AI while managing professional, operational and regulatory risks. The feature encourages members to share their practical experiences so that the Law Society's policy work and guidance reflect the needs of the profession.

The feature highlights ISO/IEC 42001, the International Organization for Standardization's AI management system standard, and the National Institute of Standards and Technology's AI Risk Management Framework. It identifies an opportunity for legal practices, regulators, law societies and universities to work together, with academic research bringing together computer science, law, philosophy, humanities and other disciplines. It refers to a 2023 survey conducted by the Law Society and the Legal Services Board. Of the 51% of people in England who had a legal need, 19% had that need met while 32% did not. The feature recognises concerns about the impact of technology on jobs while noting the possibility that more accessible and lower-cost legal services could increase demand.

The feature defines shadow AI as the use of AI tools by employees without the approval or oversight of their organisation. It says information submitted to a public or consumer AI tool may be stored, reviewed by provider personnel or used to train future models, and that once information has left a firm's controlled systems, retrieving it may not be practically possible. It suggests firms can reduce the incentive for unsanctioned use by making approved tools accessible and straightforward to use, supported by a proportionate approval process. It says it may not be appropriate or affordable for every practice to invest in a specialist legal AI platform. It encourages firm leaders to create an AI roadmap setting out how the organisation will assess tools, implement policies, govern use and train employees.

The feature recommends a practical first step of preparing an inventory or register of the AI systems and features already being used across the practice. It says the level of scrutiny can then be matched to the risks associated with each use case rather than applying the same controls to every tool or activity. It lists mapping current use, assessing risk, setting policy, training staff and reviewing regularly as steps. The Law Society says it engages with government, regulators and other stakeholders on issues including AI regulation, data protection, automated decision-making, copyright and the use of AI in courts. The feature says clear responsibilities, informed staff, proportionate controls and ongoing review can help practices manage risks while making considered use of the technology's potential benefits.

stories.Headline: Providence schools official says district limits generative AI to 2 of 58 student apps
stories.Summary:
A Providence Public Schools official told the School Board Policy Committee on Tuesday that the district operates under a self-imposed moratorium on artificial intelligence, and that only 2 of the 58 software programs available to students use generative AI, limited to grades 9 through 12, according to the committee's published meeting recording. The official, who said they serve on the district's AI committee alongside the district's IT director, said students reach the 58 programs through Clever, the district's single sign-on system. The official said Amira, the elementary reading and dyslexia-screening program that drew parent complaints, is not generative and is not a chatbot, and that it was misinterpreted. The remarks came the night before the full School Board's meeting, where committee members said an AI resolution was expected. The official said the district is moving deliberately and cautiously, and described Providence as a low-use, very little AI district that has been aggressive in protecting student privacy, calling it probably one of the most aggressive districts in New England.

The official said the district called every parent who reached out and met with parent groups, and said they have 5 children themselves and want to protect all kids. The official said they had written that evening offering to speak at the next night's board meeting because there is so much misinformation about Amira and AI, and had attached a summary of four major steps the district has taken since July. A speaker noted that RIDE, the Rhode Island Department of Education, has a generic AI policy for students and that the district is drafting its own internally, and said questions about adults using AI are a separate issue. One committee member said the board is not the expert on AI, calling it very much integrated into curriculum and an operational issue, and said they did not want the board prematurely slinging opinions about things it is not expert on, hoping to propose at the board meeting that the resolution be referred to committee first. Another speaker agreed the resolution could go to the Policy Committee followed by a district presentation at its next meeting, a different speaker said it really should be an administrative call, and another agreed while noting three or four parents had spoken at an earlier public comment period with strong concerns and that there should be a place for their input.

A speaker pointed to an online petition launched Nov. 13 that asks the School Board to pause student-facing generative AI in pre-kindergarten through eighth grade and to give parents notice and opt-out rights, describing it as drawing hundreds and hundreds of people. A district staff member said the district needs to know whether the board or the administration owns AI policy so the two sides do not duplicate work, and that the district's AI work had not yet gone through its internal policy process or to the superintendent's cabinet. No vote on AI was taken at the committee meeting, and members said the district's draft AI policy should come to the Policy Committee so members can really get into the weeds of it. A speaker raised the idea of a full presentation, possibly in December, on which AI tools students use and what protections are in place. Members said their next committee meeting is Tuesday the 15th at 5:30 p.m.

stories.Headline: SpaceX Super Intelligence rejects liability in UK lawmaker’s Grok image lawsuit
stories.Summary:
SpaceX Super Intelligence LLC filed a written defence on October 29, 2026, to reject liability in a lawsuit brought by a British lawmaker. Jess Asato, a member of the governing Labour Party, sued the company at London's High Court for misuse of private information and data protection breaches. The lawsuit follows the creation of sexualised images and a video of Asato being chloroformed and prepared for sexual assault using the Grok AI platform. Asato alleges that the specific way Grok was designed and trained enabled the generation of this harmful sexualised content.

The lawmaker is seeking a court order that would require the company to implement permanent technical measures to prevent Grok from creating manipulated images of her. SpaceX Super Intelligence LLC, which previously operated under the names xAI and SpaceXAI, argues that Asato is not entitled to such an order. The company claims that images it allowed to remain available are clearly fictitious and implausible to any reasonable person. Because the content is obviously AI-generated, the company argues that Asato has no reasonable expectation of privacy in this matter.

Lawyers for the subsidiary stated that they removed the specific images and the chloroform video that breached their terms of service. They further argued that the company did not breach data protection rights because it did not determine the content of the prompts provided by users. Jess Asato responded by stating that those who build powerful AI tools must take full responsibility for the results. She claimed the company is not a neutral bystander since it built the model and rewrote user requests to add graphic details.

This legal battle serves as one of the first claims to test whether designers are liable for the overall design of an AI system. Grok is currently subject to regulatory probes in several countries following an outcry over the creation of non-consensual sexualised images. Although xAI restricted some image editing in mid-January, reports from February indicate that Grok continued to generate sexualised images without consent. The company previously sued a man in the United States in July for using Grok to create child sexual abuse material.
