stories.Headline: Henrietta Moore says AI imposes a cognitive tax on low paid workers
stories.Summary:
Henrietta Moore wrote an article on November 20, 2026, about how artificial intelligence imposes a cognitive tax on low paid workers. She argues that AI adds to the mental load of people already facing insecure housing, unpredictable pay, and mounting debt. This cognitive tax drains attention, memory, and the capacity to learn through rents, debts, and complex welfare paperwork. Moore suggests that governments must rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of vulnerable workers. She believes that chronic stress from insecurity acts like an app draining a phone battery over many years.

The World Economic Forum estimates that 59 in every 100 workers will need training by 2030 to adapt. Moore discussed these issues in September at the first Global Brain Economy Summit held in New York City. Two new indices use 60 indicators, including child poverty and Parkinson's disease, to rank US states and various countries. Moore proposes universal basic services for childcare, housing, transport, and digital access to replace simple cash payments for the poor. She notes that extending free childcare could bring 60,000 non working parents into the workforce within the United Kingdom.

Professor Dame Henrietta Moore is the director of the UCL Institute for Global Prosperity and co leads The New Alignment. She stated that the human brain has rarely been considered an asset in its own right throughout the study of economics. Moore argues that the emerging AI economy makes human judgment, creativity, and insights the most valuable assets for workers. She claims that people cannot learn new skills if their minds are occupied by worries over pay and housing. Moore believes every government should ask how fiscal policies affect the cognitive load of the poorest people they touch.

The UK AI minister stated that the government must consider that this technology could have an unprecedented impact on jobs. Elon Musk told reporters at the White House in September that AI would eventually bring about universal high income. A study funded by Sam Altman gave low income Americans 1,000 dollars a month, but mental health gains faded. Walmart staff have already experienced how AI set schedules make their work less predictable by shifting and shortening their hours. Research by the Boston Consulting Group indicates that overseeing AI tools also adds mental fatigue to the modern worker.

A 2024 Journal of Economic Psychology analysis of 112,000 people showed that financial scarcity measurably impairs how people think and work. Low paid workers in rural India were 7 percent more productive and made fewer mistakes when paid a few days early. In South Africa, lowering the male pension age from 65 to 60 slowed memory decline and reduced dementia by five percent. About 2.7 million people in Britain are currently out of work due to long term sickness and related health issues. Research from Moore's institute found that insecurity across several life areas creates an earnings penalty as large as gender gaps.

Britain will take over the G20 presidency after a summit in Miami this December to lead the world's largest economies. Moore wants this cognitive load question included in every treasury's fiscal plans and in all AI powered public services before launch. She compares the need to count brain damage to how economies learned to count damage to air and water sixty years ago. The articles do not state if any governments have already adopted the proposed universal basic services for the low paid. It remains open whether the G20 will officially include cognitive taxation in their future fiscal policies and brain capital indices.

stories.Headline: Antimattr develops voice-first AI hardware to isolate speech in noisy environments
stories.Summary:
Sridipto Ghosh, the co-founder and chief executive officer of Antimattr, detailed his company's progress on November 20, 2026. The business is developing voice-first artificial intelligence hardware to help people communicate more clearly in noisy environments. This technology aims to solve the problem of background noise interfering with AI input at the interface level. The company is specifically targeting professionals like doctors, lawyers, engineers, founders, agency owners, and entrepreneurs.

The product line consists of a smart ring and earphones supported by a dedicated mobile application. These earphones utilize specialized sensors, software, and microphones to isolate the user's voice during dictation and calls. The smart ring allows users to control AI agents or capture thoughts by tapping a button. Antimattr has already received nearly 1,200 preorders for these devices as they prepare for initial production in Shenzhen, China.

Ghosh explained that his background includes studying engineering at the Indian Institute of Technology in Bangalore, India. He noted that his previous enterprise venture reached nearly $250,000 in revenue within its first 18 months. The chief executive officer stated that the company wants to make creating AI agents as intuitive as using a mobile app. He credited the WEDC and the gener8tor global accelerator program for helping the company navigate the United States market.

The company used its time in Wisconsin to build relationships with local factories and explore enterprise partnerships. Ghosh believes the manufacturing expertise found in Wisconsin makes the state a strong potential fit for future production. The company intends to move beyond initial Chinese manufacturing to gain greater control over its own production processes. Antimattr will now focus on refining its voice-isolation technology to make it a seamless part of professional work.

stories.Headline: State transportation officials discuss managing AI and automated vehicle changes at a Louisville session
stories.Summary:
At the American Association of State Highway and Transportation Officials 2026 Annual Meeting in Louisville, KY, a knowledge session examined how state departments of transportation are dealing with changes fostered by growing use of automated vehicles and artificial intelligence. Suzanne Murtha, global lead-connected and automated technology for infrastructure consulting firm AECOM, presented the session and moderated a panel discussion. The panel featured Lisa Wilson, deputy director of engineering and operations for the Utah Department of Transportation, and Vidhu Shekar, chief data and artificial intelligence officer for the California Department of Transportation, known as Caltrans. It also featured Darran Anderson, senior director of strategy and innovation for the Texas Department of Transportation, and Kimberly Zimmer, division administrator-transportation systems management and operations for the Michigan Department of Transportation. Alan Davis, director of operations and permits for the Georgia Department of Transportation, completed the panel.

Michigan DOT's Zimmer said state DOTs cannot work in the AV and AI space alone and that it requires building a broad swath of partnerships across academia and the private sector. She said her agency has many partnerships with automotive manufacturers and original equipment manufacturers, and with the University of Michigan, Michigan Tech, and Michigan State, where different types of connected and autonomous vehicles and buses are being piloted. Zimmer said the agency constantly works with M city at the University of Michigan and the American Center for Mobility to test many different AV technologies. She said that in the transit arena the agency is working with Michigan State on deploying full size automated buses on their campus. Zimmer said her agency has lots of ideas on what it can use AI for, such as video analytics, traffic congestion, and crash prediction metrics, and is trying to use technology to be more proactive.

TxDOT's Anderson said Texas has been heavily involved with the testing of automated freight-carrying vehicles and stressed that data flow and AI have become closely aligned with that AV effort. He said the agency is working with a task force on data integration tied into its digital corridors initiatives, while trying to inform the public about that effort and trying to inform the robots. Anderson said it is one thing to know what you want robots to do and another where all have agreed upon formats, the means to deliver them, and then understand how each autonomous system actually gets updated. He said it then becomes a question of who you are working with and how they consume and use information. Anderson said it is all about forming a common way of sharing what is known, and that the agency would love to bring in their data point clouds, compare those to the point clouds it is capturing, and maybe create a shared point cloud environment that enriches its asset management solutions and theirs as well.

Utah DOT's Wilson stressed that building such AI connections can significantly boost state DOT capabilities across a variety of areas. She noted that AI has helped connect Utah DOT's sole Transportation Management Center to the state's entire traffic signal network, a huge benefit when managing and operating the system most efficiently. Wilson said the agency does not always take over local system signals but has agreements with them, with a goal to obtain real-time situational awareness so it can react quickly, such as adjusting green signal times to improve transit bus on-time arrivals. She said the agency is having AI connect to its cameras to help identify crashes more quickly, because especially in rural areas it often has to wait to hear from emergency dispatchers about a crash. Wilson said that if a camera is in the area the agency can identify a crash faster, identify and remove debris on the roadway faster, and remove chances for unexpected congestion, part of interstate anomaly detection where AI helps identify and address random issues as well as what needs to be fixed.

Caltrans' Shekar noted that this is an example of the high-speed innovation cycle for new technologies and systems powered by AI. He said that where initially the agency looked at months, if not sometimes years, to think through problems and then get to the solution, it is now witnessing a development sprint of six weeks, where it went from problem to actually having a solution get deployed in just six weeks. Shekar said the accelerated development process means the human element must take on greater importance, and that the agency has to go through a process where it analyzes the decisions an AI tool might be making to make sure it is correct, that all agree, and that there is confidence in what is going on. He said the agency needs to continually be grounded in truthfulness and must have the human in the loop, with the human at the end making the final decision. Shekar said that ultimately the agency is responsible for whatever decision gets made, whether by AI or not, and that it is its stamp, its operations, and so its liability.

Georgia DOT's Davis echoed Shekar's perspective and stressed that humans make the decision, which is foundational. Davis said the emerging conversation with the private sector on AV and AI issues is about how to engage when novel ideas and concepts arise, because it involves engaging with software systems that will change from week to week. He said that is the next step that has to be figured out. The AASHTO Journal states that AASHTO welcomes republication in whole or in part of any original content from The AASHTO Journal with proper attribution to the association and publication, including a link to direct visitors to the AASHTO Journal website. The session was held at the AASHTO 2026 Annual Meeting in Louisville, KY.

stories.Headline: Nan Huang finds quantitative CT and radiomics may support CIP differential diagnosis
stories.Summary:
Nan Huang published a systematic review on November 18, 2026, regarding imaging biomarkers for immune checkpoint inhibitor-related pneumonitis. The researcher investigated whether quantitative computed tomography and radiomics could support the differential diagnosis of this specific condition. This study focused on identifying the cause of pulmonary abnormalities rather than predicting future risks for patients. The author conducted this review to see if these tools could help clinicians distinguish between different lung injuries. The final report was published in the journal Frontiers in Oncology within the Cancer Immunity and Immunotherapy section.

The author searched six databases in June 2026 and updated the public index through August 31, 2026. The review analyzed 17 reports, including 13 full publications, three abstracts, and one indexed preprint. Huang used the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies version 3 to reassess the risk of bias. The data included 21 areas under the receiver operating-characteristic curve and 10 sensitivity and specificity pairs. One hold-out operating point for 40 patients showed a sensitivity of 0.75 and a specificity of 0.60.

Nan Huang is affiliated with Yidu Cloud Technology in Beijing and the National Cancer Center in China. The author stated that quantitative computed tomography and radiomics may support the differential diagnosis of established pneumonitis. However, the researcher noted that the clinical utility and transportable accuracy of these imaging biomarkers remain uncertain. Huang explained that the current evidence supports discrimination within a dataset but not established diagnostic utility. The author concluded that the evidence is constrained by unavailable full texts and historical validation limitations.

Clinicians are affected because they must decide whether to withhold anticancer treatment or administer corticosteroids to patients. Misclassifying infection or radiation injury as pneumonitis can expose patients to unnecessary steroids and interrupt cancer treatment. Patients with limited pulmonary reserve are particularly vulnerable when CT abnormalities evolve before microbiological evidence is available. Thoracic radiotherapy creates a competing explanation because radiation pneumonitis can produce similar ground-glass opacity and consolidation patterns. Pulmonary infections also create overlapping phenotypes that make etiologic attribution difficult in routine clinical practice.

Immune checkpoint inhibitors are now standard treatments for many solid tumors, especially for those patients with lung cancer. These treatments can cause immune-mediated toxicities that require rapid intervention to manage the resulting lung inflammation. Quantitative CT describes spatial and textural variations that are only partly represented by standard visual descriptors. Radiomics and machine-learning methods combine these measurements into imaging signatures to complement treatment history and laboratory findings. The CIPHER foundation model is a separate tool that uses baseline CT to predict future risk.

Future priorities include independent attribution, locked patient-level testing, and genuinely external validation of the imaging biomarkers. Researchers must also conduct prospective evaluations to determine the actual clinical impact and management benefits of AI. The articles leave open whether these tools can reliably replace or supplement traditional microbiological and longitudinal evidence. No meta-analysis was performed in this review, leaving the overall statistical strength of the findings open. The study did not identify any prospective AI-assisted reader evaluations among the included reports.

stories.Headline: Researchers propose Vision-as-a-Tool to let text-only agents offload visual reasoning
stories.Summary:
Haolin Yang, Wenshan Wu, Jin Jiang, Yu Cheng, Yan Xia, Ting Song, Yangyu Huang, Zhiliang Peng, Wenhui Wang, Hangbo Bao, Yuzhe Zhang, Wen-Da Wei, Tengchao Lv, Li Dong, Lei Cui and Furu Wei posted a paper titled Vision-as-a-Tool: Visual Harness for Multimodal Agentic Coding to arXiv on 20 November 2026. The paper argues that multimodal agentic coding needs strong visual reasoning to analyze observations and to evaluate the artifacts that agents generate. Current frameworks mostly rely on a Thinking-with-Images paradigm, in which agents depend on their own intrinsic vision to carry out visually grounded tasks. That architectural coupling creates a fundamental bottleneck, because agent performance stays strictly bounded by internal perceptual limits, and text-only agents lack native perception entirely.

The authors introduce the Vision-as-a-Tool paradigm, which reframes general-purpose multimodal large language models as callable external utilities rather than as the agent's own eyes. Earlier visual tool use merely manipulated images for an agent's intrinsic vision to read, whereas this approach lets text-only agents completely offload visual reasoning during agentic execution. Vision-capable agents can meanwhile augment their native perception on demand, and the authors instantiate the paradigm in VHarness, a unified framework driven by five atomic actions. They evaluate VHarness across Image-to-HTML, Image-to-SVG and Image-to-3D generation tasks, and the results show that it consistently improves visual fidelity and geometric accuracy for both text-only and multimodal coding agents.

The paper is listed under Artificial Intelligence and Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, and its authors conclude that modularizing visual reasoning into callable utilities gives a flexible and scalable foundation for future agentic coding systems. The abstract does not assign responsibility for any failure to a named person or organization, and it reports no statements beyond the authors' own framing of the bottleneck and their proposed fix. The article also carries standard arXivLabs boilerplate describing a framework through which collaborators develop and share features on the site, and noting that arXiv works only with partners who adhere to its values of openness, community, excellence and user data privacy. The posting invites ideas for projects that would add value to the arXiv community through arXivLabs, but the articles give no further details on deployment, timelines or follow-up work.

stories.Headline: Researchers find no AI dependency tool reports responsiveness or cross-cultural validity
stories.Summary:
Wenhai Fan and five other researchers conducted a systematic review of AI dependency tools. The study was published on November 20, 2026, in Psychology Research and Behavior Management. The team evaluated instruments used to measure AI dependency among college students. They searched eight databases from their inception until January 21, 2026. The researchers used the COSMIN Risk of Bias Checklist for their evaluation.

The review examined nine studies evaluating nine different AI dependency assessment instruments. The AI dependence scale and the reliance on ChatGPT scale for nursing students earned category A. Other instruments were classified as category B, while the scale for dependence on artificial intelligence was category C. No tools reported measurement error, responsiveness, or cross-cultural validity. The protocol was registered in PROSPERO under the number CRD420251269989.

Mingming Yu and the authors stated that reliable assessment instruments are needed for students. They noted that existing tools assess dependency from psychological, pedagogical, and functional angles. The researchers said that most tools showed acceptable basic quality but had gaps. They recommended the category A tools for evaluating AI dependency among college students. The authors called for more robust and theoretically grounded instruments in the future.

The researchers noted that 78.3 percent of university students in the United Arab Emirates depend on AI. A study by Kaabi found that 94.5 percent of those students reported detrimental effects. These effects include damage to linguistic skills and critical thinking for the affected students. AI dependency is defined as behavioral attachment and cognitive inertia toward AI generated content. This state makes it difficult for students to independently verify or correct AI outputs.

AI tools like ChatGPT support learning but may reduce independent thinking and create psychological problems. Dependency is associated with academic procrastination, sleep disturbances, and negative emotions for some students. It may lead to superficial learning, academic dishonesty, ethical dilemmas, and technology induced anxiety. Some scales were adapted from tools for internet addiction or problematic social media use. Others were developed as context specific scales tailored specifically to the use of AI.

Future research should more comprehensively evaluate the psychometric properties of these measurement tools. Improved tools will help researchers study psychological mechanisms and academic consequences of AI dependency. Better instruments will also support the development of interventions to reduce this dependency. The articles leave open how to unify concepts of addiction and problematic use. They do not provide a single, universally validated tool for all cultures.

stories.Headline: Nicholas Matsakis introduces Symposium and Agent Client Protocol to guide AI agents in using Rust
stories.Summary:
Nicholas Matsakis, a lead designer of the Rust programming language and a senior principal engineer at Amazon, introduced two new projects on November 20, 2026, according to TechGig. The first is Symposium, an agent-oriented toolchain designed to guide AI agents in using Rust, and the second is the Agent Client Protocol, which proposes a standardised way for AI agents and clients to communicate. Matsakis presented the projects as a way to integrate Rust with artificial intelligence more effectively. The report was published by TechGig on that date.

Symposium aims to give AI agents tailored Rust guidance, such as recommending Rust 2024 and the latest crate versions, while letting crate authors write skills that instruct agents on how to use their libraries. The Agent Client Protocol is intended to improve interoperability across various agents and front-end tools, moving beyond current vendor-specific implementations. The projects address current large language model limitations, including agents using outdated library versions or older Rust editions, because current LLMs often struggle to keep up with the fast pace of software development and library updates. By embedding skills directly within Rust crates, Symposium aims to prevent agents from hallucinating application programming interfaces or generating non-compiling code. Matsakis also introduced the concept of battery packs, which provide best-practice guidance for recommended sets of libraries such as an opinionated network service pack.

Matsakis emphasised Rust's memory safety as a significant advantage, noting its adoption in critical systems like the Linux kernel and at companies such as Microsoft and Amazon. He cited statistics indicating that switching to Rust reduces memory-safety-related vulnerabilities, which account for a large percentage of overall software flaws. The initiatives are part of a broader vision for a more extensible ecosystem that supports open-source maintainers through a Rust commercial network. The stated goal is to streamline language choice for developers by offering robust tooling and community support for Rust development, particularly when combined with AI.

stories.Headline: Bajaj Finance and Pennant Technologies invest nearly $4 million in Soket AI for on-premise financial LLMs
stories.Summary:
Bengaluru-based Soket AI, a frontier AI research lab and an IndiaAI Mission startup, has raised nearly $4 million from Bajaj Finance and Pennant Technologies, according to a TechGig report published on November 20, 2026. Bajaj Finance invested about $2 million through Bajaj Finserv Intelligence, its applied research and innovation initiative, while Pennant Technologies, a lending software company in which Bajaj Finance holds a stake, contributed another $2 million in the same round. The funding will support Soket AI's work on large language models focused on coding, mathematics and reasoning, which are intended for enterprise applications, particularly within financial services. Soket AI's models are designed to run on an organisation's own infrastructure, including on-premises environments, an approach the company says allows training and deployment at lower costs with full control over data.

The startup was founded in 2019 by Abhishek Upperwal and focuses on what it describes as frontier AI for work where a wrong answer has a cost. Soket AI was selected by the IndiaAI Mission in May 2025 to build foundation models, and it unveiled its 26.3-billion-parameter EKA-1 model on November 3 this year, trained on nearly 7.5 trillion tokens. EKA-1 is an open, sparse hybrid language model that supports all 22 scheduled Indian languages and English, and it is designed for mathematics, code generation, reasoning and agentic applications. Soket AI and Pennant plan to jointly develop banking-specific language models and AI agents targeting applications such as know-your-customer checks, onboarding, collections, compliance and fraud detection.

Rajeev Jain, Vice-Chairman and MD of Bajaj Finance, said the next phase of AI will be defined by outcomes at sustainable cost, and he noted that Soket AI's models can make advanced AI economically viable for financial services while ensuring secure deployment within their infrastructure. Sanjiv Bajaj, Chairman and MD of Bajaj Finserv, highlighted the importance of indigenous research for AI as critical information infrastructure, adding that the investment reflects Bajaj Finserv's commitment to strengthening India's sovereign AI capabilities. The funding round places the on-premise model approach at the centre of the company's plans for financial services, where data control and cost are presented as the main considerations. The report does not say what happens next beyond the joint development work with Pennant.

stories.Headline: Thomson Reuters sets four fiduciary-grade AI questions and says CoCounsel Legal answers all four
stories.Summary:
In May 2026, Thomson Reuters set out four principles of Fiduciary-Grade AI as a bar for AI used in high-stakes professional work, according to an article published on legal.thomsonreuters.com on November 20, 2026. The article says the four questions drawn from those principles test any tool's sources, data handling, expert design, and traceability. It says CoCounsel Legal was designed to answer all four questions, with curated Canadian content, built-in privacy, and linked sources. The article says the person choosing a legal AI tool at a firm of five lawyers or 50 is usually the person who answers for it to the client, the court, and the law society. It says there is rarely a procurement team or a security group to vet the vendor first.

The article says the Federation of Law Societies of Canada added technological competence to its Model Code in 2019, and law societies such as the Law Society of Alberta added it to the commentary on their competence rule. It says the Law Society of British Columbia's guidance on generative AI covers core duties of competence, confidentiality, and information security. It cites Zhang v. Chen, a 2024 decision of the Supreme Court of British Columbia, in which a lawyer's notice of application cited two cases that did not exist and a general-purpose chatbot had invented them. It says the judge ordered her to personally pay the costs of the extra work it caused the other side.

It says the Future of Professionals Report 2026 surveyed 1,816 professionals in 62 countries, and 34% said they use AI tools their organization has not sanctioned. The article says PIPEDA generally governs private-sector privacy, alongside provincial statutes in Quebec, Alberta, and British Columbia. It says Bill C-36, at second reading in the House of Commons as of November 2026, would also require a privacy impact assessment before personal information leaves Canada. It says consumer chatbots were not built to that standard, and firms tend to pay for it later. It says the first question asks whether the tool draws on curated legal content or the open web, and whether it covers Canadian statutes, case law, and provincial rules.

It says the second question asks vendors to confirm whether they train any model on your data, how long they keep it, where they store and process it, who can access it, whether that access is logged, and what happens to it if you leave. The article says the third question asks for named lawyers and subject-matter experts who design and test the tool, not just a review step at the end. It says the fourth question asks whether you can follow how the tool reached an answer and click through to each authority it relied on. It says CoCounsel Legal reasons from Westlaw Canada, Practical Law Canada, and your firm's own knowledge, so its answers are grounded in curated content, not the open internet.

It says lawyer-editors create and maintain that content, and credentialed subject-matter experts are involved throughout. It says CoCounsel Legal works in Microsoft Word, your document management system, and HighQ. The article says data entered in CoCounsel Legal is never used to train any large language model, the model is accessed only to process your data, and your data is protected by contractual commitments and encryption. It says you can see its reasoning as it works and click through to every source it relies on.

It says that in document review, each answer traces back to the document it came from, and Deep Research returns a structured report with citations you can check. It says the article's advice is to put the four questions to any vendor in writing, then test the answers on a closed file where you already know the right result. It says the article offers a responsible legal AI guide for Canadian firms drafting a firm AI policy while evaluating tools. The article says AI can give a small or midsize firm hours back, but only if you can trust it with a client file.

It says CoCounsel Legal was built to meet that standard for Canadian work, with curated Canadian sources, client data kept private, lawyers shaping the tool, and every step open to your review. It says readers should put the four questions to Thomson Reuters, then see how CoCounsel Legal performs on a closed file where they already know the outcome. It says the article is a 7 minute read. It leaves open how any vendor other than Thomson Reuters would answer the four questions.

stories.Headline: Polygon Labs CEO Marc Boiron tells staff to automate their jobs with AI or risk losing roles
stories.Summary:
Polygon Labs CEO Marc Boiron has instructed employees to automate their jobs using artificial intelligence, according to a post he made on X, and he warned that those who decline to automate tasks capable of AI execution might risk their positions. Boiron argued that employees who successfully automate their responsibilities would become more valuable to the company, and he added that Polygon would be willing to pay these employees significantly more for other work. The directive has raised concerns about job security and drawn comparisons to Meta's past AI-driven workforce plans. Some users criticised the statement and questioned whether companies were asking employees to develop technology that could make their roles redundant, while other users supported the idea and suggested AI could free employees from repetitive work.

The discussion recalls a similar strategy considered by Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, and a Reuters investigation published in August 2026 revealed that Meta had explored using AI for a large part of employees' daily work, with smaller teams supervising virtual workers. This plan, known as Project OT, was discussed by Zuckerberg and senior executives in January, and internal scenarios reportedly considered reducing several team sizes by up to 60 per cent through layoffs and role reassignments. Meta proceeded with a 10 per cent workforce reduction in May but abandoned plans for a second restructuring round, following growing employee resistance and concerns that the company's AI agents were not delivering expected productivity improvements. Employees were particularly worried that Meta's AI initiatives could train the technology to replace them, and the company also faced criticism over plans to collect mouse clicks and keystrokes from employees' computers for AI system training.

Zuckerberg later acknowledged that AI agent technology had not progressed as quickly as he anticipated, and Meta stated that Project OT aimed to cut costs and reorganise teams, not eliminate 60 per cent of its overall workforce. Boiron's directive at Polygon Labs has drawn criticism from some users, who questioned whether companies were asking employees to develop technology that could make their roles redundant, while other users supported the idea. The articles do not say what response Polygon Labs has given to the criticism or whether any employees have declined to automate their tasks. The articles also do not say what happens next at Polygon Labs beyond Boiron's statement.

stories.Headline: Security leaders shift focus to securing how employees use AI as enterprises balance adoption with data leak risks
stories.Summary:
Enterprises are facing a conflict between adopting generative and agentic AI for tasks such as debugging code, summarizing contracts and automating decision-making, and preventing proprietary data from leaking into unauthorized models. Security and compliance leaders are working at the same time to stop proprietary source code, financial projections and regulated customer records from leaking into unauthorized AI models. For most Chief Information Security Officers the question is no longer whether employees are using AI, because that use is now acknowledged. Their focus has shifted to understanding what employees are doing with AI and to securing that use rather than blocking it. Semantic DLP is presented as a way to secure enterprise generative AI data without hindering adoption.

The story requires enterprises to balance the adoption of generative and agentic AI against the risk of data leakage, and it changes the focus of security leaders from whether AI is used to how it is used. The tasks named in the articles are debugging code, summarizing contracts and automating decision-making, and the data at risk includes proprietary source code, financial projections and regulated customer records. The articles give no numbers, no dates beyond the publication date of November 20, 2026, and no named individuals. The only named technology is semantic DLP, which the articles say helps secure enterprise generative AI without hindering adoption. The articles do not describe how semantic DLP works or what it costs.

Chief Information Security Officers are the people responsible, and the articles say they acknowledge that employees use AI and have shifted their focus to securing it. Security and compliance leaders are also described as working to prevent proprietary data from leaking into unauthorized models. The articles paraphrase no individual by name and carry no direct statement from any officer or company. The context is a tug-of-war between adopting generative and agentic AI for everyday work and keeping sensitive data inside authorized systems. The articles do not say what happens next, beyond the stated aim of securing generative AI use without hindering adoption.

stories.Headline: NYPD plans to buy AI-powered stingrays despite outcry as 44 groups urge mayor to refuse
stories.Summary:
The New York Police Department moved last month toward a no-bid contract with the Israeli company Cognyte for highly advanced cellphone tracking devices, according to a New York Daily News report that brought the technology into public view. After the story broke and drew public outcry, the city scrapped plans to move forward with that Cognyte contract, a company the NYCLU links to human rights violations around the world. At the same time, the city announced that the NYPD still intends to buy an AI-powered version of the surveillance technology, known as cell-site simulators or stingrays, through an open bidding process in which Cognyte can take part. Last week 44 groups, including the NYCLU, the Justice Committee, the Center for Constitutional Rights, Desis Rising Up and Moving, the Drug Policy Alliance, Jews For Racial & Economic Justice, Jewish Voice for Peace, the Legal Aid Society and Make the Road New York, sent a letter to the Mamdani administration.

The letter detailed the problems with stingrays and urged the Mayor not to acquire these AI-powered devices, which mimic cell towers and suck up data from every nearby device, including phones of people not suspected of any crime. Cognyte's AI-equipped version, FalcoNet, has reportedly been used by Florida officials to spy on Haitian immigrants, and governments around the world have used it to persecute dissidents, journalists and LGBTQ people. Stingrays can be mounted on a drone or carried in a backpack, making them easy to deploy almost anywhere in New York City, and certain forms can even read texts and listen to conversations. FalcoNet's behavior analysis capabilities add another layer of concern because it is totally unclear what those capabilities are, what behaviors the technology is analyzing and how it does so.

The NYCLU, whose policy counsel Medha Raman and editorial manager Simon McCormack wrote the article, says the idea that the NYPD could abuse this technology is not hypothetical, because in 2016 the organization revealed the department used stingrays more than a thousand times between 2008 and May of 2015 without a written policy and almost always without a warrant. In 2017 a Brooklyn state court ruled that the NYPD's warrantless use of stingrays was unconstitutional, and department guidelines now say investigators must obtain a warrant in most cases. The NYCLU says there is very little transparency about how often the NYPD obtains warrants, how the department uses the devices and what discipline, if any, officers receive when they violate department policy. The group argues that stingrays are a dragnet surveillance technology that should require a warrant every time the NYPD uses them, and that even considering such technology, tied to scores of human rights violations across the globe, is reckless and puts New Yorkers' rights at risk.

stories.Headline: Snowflake's Vivek Raghunathan says skipping rollout stages causes uneven AI coding results
stories.Summary:
Many engineering organisations have deployed AI coding tools but frequently encounter uneven results, according to insights from industry leaders reported by TechGig on November 20, 2026. This outcome is often attributed to overlooking critical phases in the rollout, specifically the transition from initial experimentation to codified best practices. Vivek Raghunathan, senior vice president of engineering at Snowflake, outlined a five-stage progression for AI rollouts that draws inspiration from Intel's Andy Grove. The initial phase involves allowing chaos to reign, followed by discovering effective practices, codifying them into a shared language, scaling that language across the organisation, and finally reorganising around the new operational reality.

Organisations often bypass the second and third stages, which involve discovering and codifying what actually works, because of an eagerness to demonstrate a quick return on investment for new tool purchases. Skipped stages frequently lead to measuring inappropriate metrics too early, such as lines of code or merged pull requests, instead of focusing on tool adoption across diverse tasks. A lack of a shared vocabulary for effective practices also prevents individual successes from becoming organisational knowledge. Raghunathan's team at Snowflake identified approximately 14 named patterns, including plan in writing before you write code and fence agents into separate git worktrees, which provide a concrete framework for teaching and measuring AI-assisted work.

Scaling AI adoption through mechanisms like regular focus weeks, where dedicated time is allocated for learning or innovation, proved more effective than relying on mandates. Reorganising roles and responsibilities, the final stage, should only occur once a clear understanding of reliable AI-assisted work is established within the company. The article attributes the uneven results to skipped rollout stages rather than to problems with talent or the tools themselves. It does not say what happens next for organisations that follow the model or what further steps Snowflake plans.

stories.Headline: North Dakota poll finds 40 percent expect AI to cut more jobs than it creates
stories.Summary:
A new North Dakota Poll, conducted by Mason-Dixon Polling and Strategy from October 19 through October 21, 2026, with 625 adult residents interviewed statewide by telephone and a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points, found that 40 percent of respondents believe artificial intelligence will eliminate more jobs than it creates in the state over the next decade, while 22 percent say it will create more than it eliminates, 28 percent expect no impact and 10 percent are unsure. Young adults are the heaviest users of AI, with 42 percent of 18- to 34-year-olds reporting daily or weekly use, yet 49 percent of that group say they are very or somewhat concerned about AI taking their job or displacing jobs in their household, compared with 41 percent of 35- to 49-year-olds. Across all age groups, 17 percent report daily use of AI tools or chatbots, 17 percent report weekly use, 29 percent report occasional use and 37 percent report not using AI at all, and 51 percent say they are not too comfortable or not comfortable at all doing business with firms that use AI to provide products and services. Asked whether they were concerned about AI eventually threatening humanity, 33 percent say they are very concerned, 33 percent somewhat concerned, 20 percent not too concerned and only 14 percent not concerned at all.

Terry Effertz, executive director of TechND, said people are mostly worried about job elimination in the abstract but that youth concerns should be addressed, which makes workforce training and education a real priority. Andrea Pfennig, vice president of government affairs at the Greater North Dakota Chamber, said the immediate challenge for many employers is finding enough people to fill the jobs they already have, and that AI offers an opportunity to support existing employees and help businesses grow despite persistent workforce shortages, with employers reporting that AI could change the skill sets needed for many jobs without necessarily reducing the numbers in the labor force. State Representative Robin Weisz, R-Hurdsfield, said the demand for skilled workers is not going to end because of AI and that in the next 10 to 20 years demand will still outpace supply, though the state may face an issue getting younger generations to want to go into those fields. Cale Dunwoody, vice president of public policy at the Fargo-Moorhead-West Fargo Chamber of Commerce, said AI may displace or transform some existing jobs but also has the potential to improve productivity, help existing employees work more efficiently and create new jobs and industries, which matters in North Dakota because it faces one of the most severe workforce shortages in the nation.

John Bitzan, Menard Family Director of the Sheila and Robert Challey Institute for Global Innovation and Growth and a professor of management at North Dakota State University, said fears over job loss arise whenever there is technological change, and that AI will destroy certain types of jobs but free up resources to create even better jobs and more opportunities, though some routine jobs will disappear. State Representative Zachary Ista, D-Grand Forks, said it should give people some concern that about two-thirds of respondents are worried AI is a threat to human civilization, calling that incredibly concerning. The latest figures from the North Dakota Labor Market Information Center show over 13,500 full-time openings in the state, a 2.5 percent rise over September and 6.2 percent higher than this time last year, and those following the labor market note the statistics do not capture all job openings, so the number of workers needed is somewhat higher. Among respondents, 40 percent identify as Republican, 39 percent as Independent and 21 percent as Democrat, with even representation among age groups and genders, and geographically 25 percent are from Fargo and Cass County, 25 percent from other parts of eastern North Dakota, 19 percent from the Bismarck-Mandan region and 31 percent from western North Dakota.

The expansion reflects Intuit's continued investment in India as a significant innovation hub, according to the company.

Nearly 25 per cent of Intuit's global technology talent is based in Bengaluru, where teams have operated since 2005. Those teams develop platforms, products, and AI-driven experiences for consumers, businesses, and accountants worldwide. The new campus reinforces Intuit's commitment to driving global AI innovation from India, the company said. Alex Balazs, Chief Technology Officer at Intuit, emphasised that the Bengaluru teams are central to building AI-driven experiences that help customers prosper. stories.Headline: Anthropic researcher warns superhuman AI may arrive by late 2027
stories.Summary:
Anthropic AI researcher Tao Lin predicted on November 20, 2026, that broadly superhuman artificial intelligence could emerge within about 1.3 years, potentially by the end of 2027. Lin said this AI would rival or surpass human skills in fields such as programming, medicine, law, and filmmaking. He highlighted risks including major workforce displacement and permanent reliance on state welfare. Automation-driven job cuts are already affecting technology firms like Salesforce, Amazon, and Oracle, according to the report.

The forecast sets a timeline of roughly 1.3 years from the November 2026 report to a possible arrival by late 2027. Lin cautioned about losing control over autonomous systems as one of the risks of rapid progress. He urged AI developers to slow progress so that comprehensive safety testing can take place. The article names programming, medicine, law, and filmmaking as the fields where such a system could match or exceed human skills.

Lin, an AI researcher at Anthropic, is the person responsible for the prediction and the warnings that came with it. He said developers should slow down to allow for comprehensive safety testing before such systems arrive. He also pointed to workforce displacement and permanent reliance on state welfare as risks of the technology. The article does not say what Anthropic itself plans to do in response to his remarks.

The context is that automation-driven job cuts are already affecting technology firms including Salesforce, Amazon, and Oracle. Lin's warning comes as those cuts show the workforce effects that he says could grow much larger. The article does not say what happens next beyond his call for slower progress and safety testing. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Peter Kant employs neurodivergent talent to improve AI data labeling for federal agencies
stories.Summary:
Peter Kant founded Enabled Intelligence to employ neurodivergent talent for AI data labeling. He built this workforce to support AI applications for the intelligence community and defense. This effort focuses on creating the training data that AI models learn from. The company provides high reliability and accuracy for critical government technology. These workers perform the meticulous work required to prevent AI hallucinations.

The process requires technical proficiency, pattern recognition, and puzzle solving skills. It involves repetitive tasks and hyper focus to label data for federal agencies. The National Geospatial Agency is the largest customer and launched a neurodiversity hiring pilot. Enabled Intelligence worked with MITRE and Melwood to identify and staff these roles. The company uses skills based assessments and merit based recruiting for all applicants.

Peter Kant said that neurodiverse people are often underemployed but highly capable. He believes that agencies already have neurodiverse workers even if they do not know it. Kant stated that the goal is to avoid treating this as a special program. He explained that the company avoids the word accommodation to remove negative connectivity. He wants to provide whatever helps staff reach their best performance levels.

The National Geospatial Agency is affected because its pilot program was based on this work. Other federal agencies in defense and intelligence are now expanding their neurodiversity programs. Some employees are entry level workers who are holding their first professional job. These staff members benefit from full time job coaches to improve their communication. They also receive training to reach a professional analytical capability for their roles.

Kant researched innovation economies and learned about the Israeli military's approach to autism. Israel created battalion 9900 to use neurodiverse soldiers for cybersecurity and finding code vulnerabilities. Most domestic data labeling previously happened in China, Nepal, or the Philippines via internet cafes. This overseas labeling created significant security and privacy issues for critical and classified data. Kant saw a green field for a professional domestic market in the United States.

The company will continue using the Caitlin Clark rule to support individual worker needs. This includes providing headphones, specific lighting, or flexible start times for the staff. They will continue investing in bigger monitors and job coaches to ensure employee retention. The articles leave open how many other federal agencies will adopt these hiring practices. They do not state the specific number of employees currently working at Enabled Intelligence.

stories.Headline: Razorpay plans updated DRHP filing next week for February 2027 IPO
stories.Summary:
Razorpay plans to file its updated Draft Red Herring Prospectus next week, targeting a potential initial public offering by February 2027, according to a Bloomberg report cited by TechGig. The Bengaluru-based fintech firm had confidentially filed its draft IPO papers in June 2026, and the Securities and Exchange Board of India cleared that confidential filing on November 3. Investor roadshows are expected to begin immediately after the public filing of the updated prospectus. The public issue is reportedly planned at around $600 million, comprising fresh shares and an Offer For Sale component.

The IPO could value Razorpay at approximately $5 billion, or about ₹47,000 crore, which marks a markdown from its $7.5 billion valuation in 2021. Razorpay reported a 65 per cent year-on-year increase in operating revenue to ₹3,783 crore in FY25, but it recorded a loss due to ₹1,209 crore in ESOP expenses and one-time costs linked to its domicile shift from the US to India. The company is also exploring a 0.4 per cent merchant discount rate on eligible UPI transactions above ₹2,000 to boost monetisation, though its rollout might be delayed until after the 2027 state elections due to concerns over merchant backlash. Beyond payments, Razorpay is expanding into AI-led products, including its Agent Studio platform for deploying task-specific AI agents.

Razorpay was founded in 2014 by Shashank Kumar and Harshil Mathur, and it offers payment processing, business banking, payroll, and lending solutions. The company has raised over $800 million from investors including Tiger Global Management, Y Combinator, Ribbit Capital, and Lightspeed. India's IPO market has seen firms raise around $18.6 billion through initial share sales so far in 2026. The articles do not include direct statements from the founders or other company officials about the filing or the listing plans.

stories.Headline: OpenAI launches GPT-6.2 Astra, which builds working websites from written prompts
stories.Summary:
OpenAI introduced GPT-6.2 Astra, a new frontier model that can build functional, interactive websites from written descriptions, the company announced on Tuesday. TechGig published its report on the model on Nov 20, 2026 at 05:00 AM IST. OpenAI's own announcement of GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol is dated 2026-11-17. The model shows improved coding, visual design, and handling of complex projects that require multiple steps. A test used a single detailed prompt to build a family command center website.

The test site included a calendar, meal planner, grocery list, and chore tracker, and it was fully functional, interactive, mobile-friendly, and remembered changes. GPT-6.2 Astra is available through ChatGPT Work for eligible Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu users. Users can customise prompts to build simple web applications such as vacation planners or budget dashboards. OpenAI also introduced GPT-6.2 Sol, an efficient, versatile model for everyday work, and both models deliver better results with fewer output tokens. In the API, GPT-6.2 Astra's input and output token prices are 20% lower than GPT-6 Astra's, with a 60% discount on cached input at $8 for input, $0.40 for cached input, and $40 for output, all per million tokens, while GPT-6.2 Sol keeps GPT-6.1 Sol's API token prices.

OpenAI said GPT-6.2 Astra sets a new quality bar for AI in complex professional work, with slides, spreadsheets, and documents that read less like AI and follow the templates and conventions of a user's field. OpenAI said the model writes cleaner code and builds frontends that look and work better, particularly for websites, gaming, and 3D design. OpenAI said it believes GPT-6.2 Astra is the best model in the world for scientists. OpenAI said GPT-6.2 Sol is smarter and more efficient than GPT-6.1 Sol and lets users complete more tasks on the same paid plan. OpenAI said many of its employees use GPT-6.2 Sol as their default model for technical and non-technical tasks.

On Agents' Last Exam, GPT-6.2 Astra scored 5.2 points higher than GPT-6 Astra at less than a third of the cost and 5.5 points ahead of Claude Fable 5.2 at just 5% of the cost, with Fable 5.2's leaderboard results excluding nine tasks that used a fallback model. GPT-6.2 Astra scored 9 percentage points higher than GPT-6 Astra on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1 at less than one-third the cost and set a new high on the Vals Science Index. In Cognition's FrontierCode 2.0, GPT-6.2 Sol came within 0.5 points of GPT-6.2 Astra at about one-fifth the cost, both at max. On LifeVal, GPT-6.2 Sol outscores GPT-6 Astra at about one-seventh the cost. On Harvey LAB-AA v1.1, GPT-6.2 Astra more than doubled Claude Fable 5.2's pass rate at about one-sixth the cost, and Astra for Law scored even higher.

On the internal GDPval v2 benchmark, GPT-6.2 Astra was up 6.2 percentage points from GPT-6 Astra while using 22% fewer output tokens, and GPT-6.2 Sol improved 5.3 points from GPT-6.1 Sol. On Artificial Analysis's AA-AnalystAgent, GPT-6.2 Astra answered 62.5% of questions correctly on all five independent attempts. Marquis Wong, Principal AI Engineer at IMC, said Astra's documents were a significant step up from GPT-6 Astra. Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora, said Astra used 62% fewer tokens than GPT-6.1 Sol on complex legal-agent tasks and scored higher than alternative models on 8 of 10 research tasks across tax, M&A and litigation work. Niko Grupen, Head of Applied Research at Harvey, said Astra completed more than 3x as many Legal Agent Benchmark tasks with 34.5% fewer output tokens.

Jay Hack, Head of AI at ClickUp, said GPT-6.2 Astra edged out ClickUp's production model in blind testing with about 40% fewer tokens and 30% fewer review rounds. OpenAI said Astra's more precise computer use lets it work down to individual parts and connections in CAD and simulation tools. OpenAI asked GPT-6.2 Astra to visualize chassis dynamics of a car on a mountain road, and Astra created the 3D model, wrote a Python solver to simulate dynamics between the tires and suspension, and animated the results in Blender. OpenAI's team used GPT-6.2 Astra to turn the scalloped balconies of Chicago's Marina City towers into a paper lamp, and the site generated by the model can be used to create your own paper lamp. OpenAI said GPT-6.2 Astra brings stronger visual reasoning to web design, choosing layouts and imagery that give each site a distinctive look.

stories.Headline: Open-source BehaviorLock blocks unproven API behavior to counter AI-driven attacks
stories.Summary:
BehaviorLock, a new open-source library for ASP.NET Core, was released to block unproven API behavior as a defense against fast-moving, AI-driven exploitation of vulnerabilities, according to a TechGig report published on November 20, 2026. The library records SQL statements and outbound HTTP calls for each API endpoint into a behavior.lock.json file while running in a Learn mode. In an Enforce mode, it blocks any access not present in that recorded profile, returning a 403 error and raising an alert. The approach is meant to counter attacks that outpace traditional patching cycles, including SQL injection, mass assignment, forgotten debug switches, Server-Side Request Forgery and compromised dependencies, whenever those attacks produce new endpoint behaviors.

The articles give several numbers on how quickly exploitation now follows disclosure, and they show why the library's authors see patching alone as insufficient. Attackers needed 63 days on average to exploit a vulnerability after its patch release in 2018-2019, according to Google's Mandiant team, but that duration dropped to 5 days in 2023 and was negative for 2024 and 2025 estimates. In August 2025, DARPA's AI Cyber Challenge saw automatic systems find 54 of 63 planted vulnerabilities and patch 43 of them, while also discovering 18 real vulnerabilities at a cost of about $152 per task. Anthropic announced in April 2026 that its Mythos Preview model found thousands of zero-day vulnerabilities in major operating systems and web browsers, with the count exceeding 10,000 high or critical findings by May 2026.

BehaviorLock runs inside the application process and currently supports EF Core and IHttpClientFactory for .NET 11, with future plans to extend coverage to Dapper, raw ADO.NET, direct HttpClient, file access and background jobs. The library does not replace existing security practices such as parameters, authorization checks or patching, and instead serves as an additional defensive layer against rapid, unknown attacks. Its code is available on GitHub under the Apache-2.0 license. The report does not name the individuals behind the library or attribute any statements to them, so responsibility for the project rests with its open-source contributors as a whole.

stories.Headline: AI agents make Spec-Driven Development effective again by shortening feedback loops
stories.Summary:
AI agents are making Spec-Driven Development effective again by shortening the feedback loops that long challenged the Waterfall Model, according to a recent analysis reported by TechGig on November 20, 2026. The approach moves the main effort from writing code to the discovery and design phases of software development, which enables faster iteration. Better large language models over the past year fixed earlier problems where correcting generated code cost more time than it saved. The method closely mirrors the sequential phases of the Waterfall Model, including specification, requirement analysis, technical planning and system design. Both methodologies stress structured, detailed documentation and move to the next phase only after the current one is completed and approved.

The historical problem with the Waterfall Model was feedback loops lasting weeks or months, along with unclear upfront requirements. AI agents cut individual phase durations to minutes or hours, letting developers quickly rework specifications, turn intents into structured documents and check that requirements stay consistent. The faster cycles allow iterative work on smaller increments, so unsatisfactory outcomes can be easily reverted or discarded. Documentation such as specifications and decision logs is now cheap and central to the method, a benefit that often suffered in agile environments because of time constraints. The articles do not name who is responsible for the analysis or attribute any statements to a person.

The analysis says the improved quality of large language models over the past year addressed the earlier issue where fixing generated code outweighed the time savings. It also says AI helps quickly rework specifications and validate requirement consistency. No further context or next steps are given beyond these points. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Onlook lets designers build and edit real app code visually with AI
stories.Summary:
Onlook, an open-source AI-first design tool, was published on GitHub by the onlook-dev organisation, and TechGig reported on it on November 20, 2026. The tool lets designers and visual engineers build, style and edit code visually with AI on a canvas. It works directly with real app code running live from any Git repository on a user's machine. The GitHub repository, onlook-dev/onlook, had 1,644 commits, 27.3k stars, 121 watchers and 2.2k forks when the articles were written. TechGig published its report on November 20, 2026 at 04:51 AM IST, and the GitHub page was dated November 19, 2026.

Onlook is released under the Apache 2.0 License, and the license covers source code but not every asset in the repository. Artifacts can be exported as self-contained HTML, PNG, JPEG or PDF files, with PNG and JPEG captured through Electron capturePage and PDF through Electron printToPDF and pdf-lib. The macOS desktop application is available for download for Apple Silicon and Intel x64, while Windows and Linux versions are planned, with waitlists for both. The source build needs no Onlook account, cloud keys or .env file, and a build from source asks before collecting usage analytics, which can be turned off in Settings or with STUDIO_TELEMETRY=0. The desktop app is built with Electron, React 19, Astryx, React Flow, Zustand and CodeMirror, and uses Git, node-pty, Bun and Turborepo.

The GitHub page says Onlook is the developer tool for designers and describes it as a free, local-first editor where designers craft exceptional experiences in code. It states that Onlook does not ship its own model, and that users connect the Claude Code or ChatGPT/Codex account they already have so that agent does the work inside their project. It says Onlook opens any Git repository on a machine and runs the user's own dev server, so what is designed is the actual product, not a mockup someone has to rebuild later. It says the app runs on the user's computer, code stays there, and more tools can be plugged in through MCP connectors. The page also says the team is hiring engineers and designers in SF.

TechGig describes Onlook as an open-source alternative to Figma, V0, Replit Agent, Base 44 and Webflow, and the GitHub page lists the same alternatives. The GitHub page says users can design apps, websites, posters and graphics with local fonts and assets, work on multiple design tasks at once across repos and pages, and use mobile, tablet and desktop frames side by side. It says a safe worktree copy means the user's folder is never touched, and that projects run as parallel tabs. It says users can ask about any element on the canvas, have the agent arrange the canvas for variations, states and flows, reference images on the canvas, and sketch and share artifacts for quick HTML sketches outside the repo. It says users can import a GitHub repo, start entirely new codebases from scratch, and make one-press pull requests from checks to merge.

The GitHub page says Onlook works with all web frameworks or languages the user's dev server already supports, because it runs the project with its own tooling. It describes a workflow where a user starts a new empty project with the New Draft button in the upper left corner of the projects page and writes a request in the input box in the lower right corner. It says the user answers clarifying questions from the agent and waits for it to build, then clicks frames for context in follow-up prompts or double-clicks an element to use inline chat. It says the user selects a frame, asks the agent to convert it into an Artifact, exports it as HTML/CSS or PNG with the export button in the upper right corner of the frame, and pastes it into Slack, email or any messaging tool. It says changes show up on the canvas as the dev server reloads, and Git keeps track of everything that changed.

The GitHub page says the previous browser-based version of Onlook, v1, lives on the v1 branch of the repository, and the first desktop version is at onlook-dev/desktop. It says Onlook's icons come from Central Icons by Iconists and are licensed to Onlook for its own product, a license that does not extend to forks, and that brand marks, DMG art and sounds are not covered either. It points to ASSETS.md for what is covered and what to replace when forking, and to NOTICE for third-party notices. It says the official download has product usage analytics on by default, and points to the privacy policy for details. It lists contact channels including Discord, email, Twitter, LinkedIn, YouTube and Substack, and the website onlook.com.

The GitHub page invites users to fork the repo and create a pull request, browse open issues, and read CONTRIBUTING.md for instructions and a code of conduct. It says security issues should be reported by following SECURITY.md instead of opening a public issue. It says Windows and Linux users can join waitlists to be emailed when there are updates, and that the team is still gauging demand for Linux. It says SOURCE_BUILD.md covers building and running Onlook on a Mac. The articles do not say when Windows or Linux versions will be released, and they do not give a release date for the macOS app.

stories.Headline: AI bug hunting prompts rushed patches that overwhelm systems and cause outages
stories.Summary:
A series of recent technology outages affecting JPMorgan Chase transactions, Microsoft Outlook and a classified National Security Agency network may stem from a rapid effort to patch security vulnerabilities, according to officials who briefed members of Congress. Wall Street executives and the NSA told lawmakers that the disruptions were caused by attempts to fix flaws identified by artificial intelligence models, The Washington Sun reported. The outages do not appear to be cyberattacks, and officials said the sheer volume of fixes temporarily overwhelmed the systems they were designed to protect. A congressional official noted that AI models are identifying massive vulnerabilities, which increases the urgency for immediate patching.

Microsoft fixed a record 1,400 security flaws in a single monthly update recently, a significant jump from about 170 a year earlier, The Wall Street Journal reported. That increase is linked to AI bug-hunting models such as Anthropic's Mythos and similar models from OpenAI. The NSA's classified internal network, NSANet, went offline because of a software patch for major PHP vulnerabilities discovered last month, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton confirmed. PHP powers approximately 70 per cent of the world's websites, and Clayton stated that the incident was not a cyberattack or a coordinated nation-state action.

Not all the outages fit that explanation, since Microsoft's Outlook disruption, which affected over 450 million Microsoft 365 users, was traced to a latent bug on its networking gateway servers. The Federal Aviation Administration's nationwide ground stop resulted from a data flood hitting its network, possibly linked to a new router, and the FAA blamed legacy equipment. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin indicated that pushing new technology onto older systems seems to overwhelm them, suggesting more such incidents are likely. Companies and government agencies are using powerful AI models to find weak spots before hackers exploit them, and that pressure has led to faster rollout of fixes, according to The Washington Sun.

Articles.Title: AI-driven bug fixes overwhelm systems, causing major outages

The update enhances the Project Genie experience by enabling users to generate and explore interactive worlds with real-time editing and audio.

Google is the company responsible for the rollout, and it made Genie 4 available to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers as the article reports. stories.Headline: Calif researchers use GPT-6 Cyber to find a critical Java memory bug
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the cybersecurity startup Calif used OpenAI's GPT-6 Cyber to uncover a critical memory corruption bug in Java, a programming language widely used across banking, aviation and other critical sectors, according to TechGig. The vulnerability affects the memory safety of Java's base64 decoder, which is a common method for representing binary data as text. Calif stated that malformed input, specifically 64 "A" characters followed by one equal sign, can overwrite neighbouring memory. That corruption can reveal sensitive memory or lead to remote code execution, which grants unauthorised access to the underlying system. The discovery was published on November 20, 2026.

Oracle, Java's current steward, has issued patches for the flaw and urged customers to apply them without delay. The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team, known as CERT-In, has issued a high-severity advisory and urged Indian organisations across public sector, private banking, fintech and consumer internet verticals to apply the Oracle patch. Java powers 90 per cent of Fortune 500 companies and is used in critical sectors globally. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency also urged users to identify all Java installations and monitor for security patches.

Calif's researcher Quang Luong used AI to find and weaponise the Java vulnerability, and the startup coined the term "centaur hacker" for human-AI collaboration in security research. The company said the approach combines AI and human expertise to discover the flaw. This discovery follows Calif's AI-assisted research that exposed critical flaws in PHP a month prior. The articles do not say what further steps, beyond patching and monitoring, are planned.

stories.Headline: Trina Storage unveils Elementa Hybrid Genset for AI data centers at RE+ 2026
stories.Summary:
Trina Storage introduced a new hybrid power product on Nov. 18, 2026 at RE+ 2026 in Las Vegas, combining gas-fired generation with the company's battery storage platforms under a single hybrid plant controller. The Elementa Hybrid Genset is aimed at data center developers that need on-site power while grid interconnection is delayed, limited, or unavailable. The launch follows a preview of the solution at Data Center World Power in September. Trina Storage unveiled Elementa Hybrid Genset at RE+ 2026, according to a PR Newswire release dated Nov. 19, 2026 in Las Vegas. The solution combines gas-fired generation from qualified partners with Trina Storage's Elementa DC battery systems and Electra AC platform, coordinated by a hybrid plant controller.

The system consists of three main components, with gas generation providing sustained power using reciprocating engines rated up to 2.5 MW in modular configurations. Trina Storage acts as the system integrator, while qualified engine partners supply the generation equipment. The Elementa and Electra BESS solution provides rapid power response and grid-forming capabilities, with reference configurations based on 5 MW/10 MWh building blocks. A hybrid plant controller coordinates all power sources in real time, and its scalable control architecture is designed to support applications ranging from 5 MW to 1 GW. The solution supports four reference scenarios: grid-connected with backup generation, grid-constrained, bridge-to-grid, and off-grid, and solar PV can also be integrated where appropriate.

Load Transient Sensing uses the power plant controller to predict changes in power demand and coordinate a rapid BESS response, allowing the system to accommodate swift load fluctuations before slower-responding power sources can adjust. Hybrid Power Coordination dynamically coordinates power output between the BESS and gas generators, so when a sudden load increase occurs the BESS responds immediately while the gas generators gradually ramp up. Fault Isolation and Resilient Power Supply addresses failures, and when a fault occurs the control system identifies and isolates the affected equipment while the BESS and remaining available gas generators respond to support critical loads. Two system architectures are available, with Load Sensing prioritizing cost efficiency and system performance while Double Conversion provides full electrical isolation and enhanced power quality. The choice between the two depends on the IT load profile and grid conditions at a given site.

Eric Cao, Vice President of Trina North American PV and BESS Business, said AI data centers have demanding power requirements, particularly when grid capacity is constrained or workloads fluctuate rapidly. Cao said Elementa Hybrid Genset brings gas generation, battery storage, and hybrid controls together in one system architecture, designed to coordinate these resources according to project needs. Trina Storage describes itself as a global leader in energy storage solutions and enters the growing field of hybrid power solutions for data centers where grid access cannot keep pace with demand. The company framed the product as a response to a pairing of limitations, since AI workloads can cause rapid and substantial fluctuations in power demand that gas generators alone may struggle to follow. Battery storage responds quickly to those fluctuations but is not designed to supply energy through extended outages on its own, according to Trina Storage.

Trina Storage says it continues to develop and validate the product through simulation, hardware-in-the-loop testing, and an integrated validation platform incorporating real power generation, conversion, and storage equipment. Further testing of grid-forming functionality and hybrid control strategies is ongoing, alongside relevant certification activities. Final system configurations and performance specifications will be assessed based on individual project requirements. The company describes the product as designed to accommodate different power requirements and grid conditions, from grid-connected sites seeking additional power flexibility to projects operating with limited or no grid access. System architecture and equipment selection can be tailored to each project's load profile, site conditions, and operational requirements.

Trina Storage is currently engaging with data center developers and project partners to explore potential applications and develop project-specific configurations. The articles state that these capabilities help coordinate different power sources within one system, with the specific operating strategy depending on the project configuration and requirements. The articles leave open the final system configurations and performance specifications, which will be assessed based on individual project requirements. The articles also leave open the outcomes of the ongoing grid-forming functionality testing, hybrid control strategy testing, and relevant certification activities. The articles do not state when the Elementa Hybrid Genset will be commercially available or which specific projects will use it.
