stories.Headline: SK Group holds director summits to discuss board role in AI era and governance gains
stories.Summary:
SK Group announced on Nov. 19 that it held the SK Directors Summit with independent directors of SK SUPEX Council member companies on Nov. 17 and the SK Governance Day with retired independent directors on Nov. 18. The Directors Summit took place at Walkerhill in Gwangjin-gu, Seoul, and was attended by 51 independent directors and key executives, including SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won, SK SUPEX Council Chairman Chey Chang-won and Governance Committee Chairman Jung Jae-hun. Under the theme of the board's role in the artificial intelligence era, the summit discussed the alignment of the group's vision with the strategies of each company, principles of capital allocation and efficient board operation plans. Governance Day was held at Sunhyewon in Jongno-gu, Seoul, and was attended by 41 retired independent directors, Chairman Chey and Chairman Chey Chang-won, who reviewed the achievements of governance improvements over the past five years.

Since SK Group announced its Governance Story in 2021 with the intention of securing long-term market trust through a transparent governance structure, SK member companies have continuously held the Directors Summit since 2022 to discuss the roles of management and the board of directors. The group has been upgrading its governance structure by strengthening the board's function of checking management in 2023 and its business supervisory function in 2024. Through such efforts, listed companies currently participating in the SK SUPEX Council are building a board-centric management system, with independent directors serving as chairpersons of the board of directors. SK Group also organized Governance Day with retired independent directors for the first time this year, in order to keep listening to the objective perspectives and suggestions of retired directors who understand SK's business and decision-making processes.

Chairman Chey emphasized that in a situation where SK's AI business is expanding, it is important to communicate so that each company's board of directors can make independent judgments from the perspective of maximizing shareholder value to maintain market trust. SKC Board of Directors Chairperson Chae Eun-mi stated that SK's governance has been upgraded to fulfill the board's supervisory duties throughout the entire process, starting from the management establishment stage, and expressed hope that gatherings to share the group's response plans to changes in the management environment with independent directors would continue. Chairman Chey stated that based on the board-centric management created together with the directors, SK would elevate its governance to the next level, and requested the retired directors to continue acting as advisors and a bridge conveying external expectations and concerns. Yeom Jae-ho, former Chairperson of the Board of Directors of SK Inc., said that over the past five years SK has achieved excellent growth in terms of board-centric management, and added that he hopes SK will continue to maintain an exemplary governance system that will help its long-term growth and shareholder interests.

stories.Headline: KB Securities analyst Kim Dong-won calls the 55% slide in Samsung and SK hynix shares excessive fear
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics and SK hynix have entered a sharp correction, with their share prices falling an average of 55% from their respective peaks, and analysts say the gap between the companies' earnings power and market valuations is at its widest point in history. The steep selloff is seen as the result of a combination of external policy uncertainties and market supply-demand factors, rather than a fundamental deterioration in the growth prospects of the artificial intelligence industry. On Nov. 18, the KOSPI opened 2.62% higher at 5,098.82 and the KOSDAQ rose 2.29% to 664.93, according to a display at Hana Bank's dealing room in central Seoul. Kim Dong-won, head of research at KB Securities, said in a report on Nov. 18 that the recent decline in semiconductor stocks reflects excessive fear.

Kim explained that uncertainty surrounding changes in Nvidia's leadership and the U.S. Democratic Party's stance on AI regulation had fueled concerns about a slowdown in investment after 2028. Global hedge funds have also reduced their exposure to AI-related semiconductor stocks, while short-selling volumes have approached their highest level since 2016, further intensifying selling pressure and valuation adjustments. KB Securities projected that demand for server DRAM and enterprise solid-state drives would increase by 56% and 54%, respectively, in 2027 from the previous year. Demand growth for both DRAM and NAND flash is also expected to significantly outpace supply growth through 2028, and from 2027 to 2028 actual memory supply is estimated to meet only 60% to 70% of customer demand.

Expanding production of high-bandwidth memory is constraining supplies of conventional DRAM, while AI data centers are increasing the amount of memory installed in their systems, and this imbalance is expected to be a key factor supporting memory manufacturers' pricing power. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix are projected to generate a combined operating profit of 1,777 trillion won in 2026 and 2027, according to KB Securities, a figure said to exceed the cumulative operating profits the two companies have generated over the decades since their respective foundings. Samsung Electronics is projected to account for 1,022 trillion won, while SK hynix is expected to contribute 755 trillion won. Kim emphasized the need to distinguish short-term supply-demand imbalances from the structural earnings outlook.

There remains a possibility that external policy uncertainties could moderate the pace of AI investment, but given the revenue growth of major cloud companies such as Google, Amazon Web Services and Microsoft, demand for AI computing is expected to surge through 2028. KB Securities expects AI investment to translate into stronger memory demand, while limited capacity additions and long-term supply agreements are likely to help memory manufacturers maintain their pricing power. Ultimately, the current share price decline reflects uncertainty about the future being priced in ahead of time, while earnings will determine the direction of corporate value. With investor fears already reflected in share prices, the gap between market valuations and underlying earnings power is expected to narrow as actual results demonstrate the companies' value.

stories.Headline: Gartner forecasts AI infrastructure spending will reach $2.4 trillion in 2027
stories.Summary:
Gartner forecast on Nov. 19 that global spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure will reach about $2.4 trillion in 2027, which works out to 59% of total worldwide AI spending. That infrastructure figure represents growth of 53% from 2026, while overall AI spending is expected to rise 47.5% to $4 trillion. The report attributes the expansion mainly to surging demand for inference, which powers real-world AI services rather than only model training. Gartner also pointed to rising equipment prices, including a phenomenon it calls memflation, in which higher memory chip prices push up server unit costs. Spending on AI-optimized servers is forecast to jump 81.4%, from $527.6 billion this year to $957.2 billion next year, as hyperscalers and neocloud providers expand capacity aggressively.

Gartner said higher infrastructure spending does not necessarily mean more servers or greater computing capacity, because component costs are also climbing. AI services spending is projected to increase 29.5% next year, and software spending is forecast to rise 42% as companies add AI to existing products. The generative AI model market is expected to grow 82% to $51 billion, with spending on domain-specific models up 99%. John-David Lovelock, a Distinguished VP Analyst at Gartner, said demand for scaling inference workloads is growing faster than anticipated. He added that training workloads are also becoming more compute-intensive, which keeps driving spending upward.

Gartner also credited service providers with helping companies adopt AI through strategy development, data preparation, system integration and ongoing deployment. Foundation models are expected to remain the backbone of the market, accounting for 81% of generative AI model spending. Counterpoint Research said a circular investment model is becoming more entrenched, with infrastructure providers funding model developers that then buy infrastructure within the same ecosystem. That arrangement speeds up the buildout but also raises interdependence among the companies involved in financing, demand and supply.

stories.Headline: Nvidia doubles down on Taiwan supply chain as AI squeezes substrate and OSAT capacity
stories.Summary:
Nvidia began deepening its strategic ties with the artificial intelligence supply chain in Taiwan on November 19, 2026. The company is issuing capacity prepayments to fund necessary expansions across several critical manufacturing sectors. These financial commitments target the production of integrated circuit substrates, advanced packaging, and testing services. This move ensures that the company secures essential production capacity for the next three to five years. The initiative requires significant investment to address the current squeeze on substrate and outsourced semiconductor assembly and test capacity.

These specific technical areas are under pressure because the rapid growth of artificial intelligence is consuming available resources. By providing these prepayments, Nvidia aims to lock in the manufacturing slots it needs to maintain its growth. This strategy helps the company avoid potential shortages that could hinder the delivery of its AI hardware. Flora Wang reported that the company is taking these steps to stabilize its long-term production pipeline.

The reports indicate that the company is doubling down on its reliance on Taiwanese partners to meet future demands. These efforts are designed to mitigate the risks associated with the limited capacity of current substrate providers. The company believes that securing these resources now is vital for its continued dominance in the AI market. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Nvidia invests over $1 billion in Kinsus to expand AI substrate capacity
stories.Summary:
Nvidia Corporation announced a massive financial commitment to Kinsus Tech on November 18, 2026, to secure critical components. The technology giant is investing more than US$1 billion in cash to increase the production of specialized materials. This strategic move focuses on expanding the dedicated ABF substrate capacity needed for artificial intelligence hardware. The investment targets the Yangmei Yougshi K6 facility located in Taoyuan to ensure a steady supply chain. This significant capital injection requires the expansion of manufacturing capabilities at the specific K6 site in Taiwan.

stories.Headline: Senators question whether Meta’s AI data centers qualify for $6.6 billion in research tax credits
stories.Summary:
A New York Times article has renewed attention on the tax credits Meta claimed for its AI data centers, according to Accounting Today. In an October 14, 2026, letter, Senate Finance Committee ranking member Ron Wyden of Oregon and six other senators said Meta claimed about $6.6 billion in federal research and development tax credits between 2023 and 2025. Citing the Times reporting, the senators questioned whether Meta described its AI data centers as experimental pilot models in its credit claims and asked for a breakdown of the credits tied to the data centers. The inquiry highlights two separate issues, whether the development activities count as qualified research and whether the claimed expenditures are qualified research expenditures for the credit.

Treasury Regulation 1.174-2(a)(4) defines a pilot model as any representation or model of a product produced to evaluate and resolve uncertainty during its development or improvement, and the article says such a model can be fully functional and can involve a component of the final design. The regulations state that production costs paid or incurred after uncertainty is eliminated are not eligible, so genuine uncertainty must exist in the design for a model to qualify. Meeting that definition does not automatically satisfy Section 41, which adds its own requirements, and only wages, supplies, computer leasing and contractor costs tied to qualifying research can be claimed. Section 41(b)(2)(C) excludes land, improvements to land and property subject to depreciation from qualified supplies, which the article says makes the treatment of purchased servers, chips and other equipment a central issue for Meta's data centers.

The article says Meta asserts that uncertainty existed in the data centers and could only be resolved by building a physical data center and testing it, and that Meta would need to show the technical uncertainty that existed before construction and how building resolved it. Taxpayers claiming pilot model costs should build a record connecting the technical work to the claimed expenditures, including initial design questions, alternative designs, simulation results, test plans, test findings and engineering designs. The article, by David Seibel, a senior manager in the R&D Tax Credit practice at Indianapolis-based McGuire Sponsel, says the credit is one of the most fact-intensive and subjective areas of tax law. It says the questions extend beyond AI infrastructure to manufacturers, equipment developers and other businesses facing similar challenges of showing why a model was built, how its development involved experimentation and which costs the credit permits.

stories.Headline: Meta AI agents run 1,097 experiments in 31 days to lift search sessions 0.23%
stories.Summary:
Meta researchers deployed AI agents that ran 1,097 machine-learning experiments in 31 days, consuming approximately 360,000 GPU-hours to improve search activity by 0.23%, according to a Nov. 18 research paper. The experiment targeted Meta's search-suggestion system, which determines the recommendations users see when opening the search bar before typing a query. The agents completed 1,097 candidate experiments and accepted 325, representing a 29.6% acceptance rate, compared with a 15.6% acceptance rate in an earlier version of the system. Meta's engineers reviewed a final combined model before testing it on live traffic, where it recorded more search sessions and slower rendering. The live test showed a 0.23% increase in search-session volume with a 95% confidence interval of plus or minus 0.15 percentage points.

The system used Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.8 to explore architectural improvements and generate candidate changes, letting agents propose model changes, write code, submit training jobs and screen offline results. Meta kept 325 out of 1,097 completed candidate experiments offline, and the live test applied to one combined ranker. The campaign's roughly 360,000 GPU-hours included completed experiments, additional tests measuring training variability, and failed or retried jobs. Individual training and evaluation runs took several hours, making parallel execution necessary to complete the campaign within a month. The paper leaves permanent rollout and a matched comparison with human-only engineering unresolved.

Meta's engineers set the objective, steered the search and reviewed the accumulated model before online testing, while agents conducted multiple experiments simultaneously. The researchers argued that the results showed autonomous agents could perform meaningful machine-learning engineering work on production-scale systems. The researchers acknowledged that the system could not independently identify every trade-off between improving its assigned performance targets and maintaining other aspects of the user experience. The researchers reported that the agents identified several architectural improvements that Meta's engineering team had not previously explored. The researchers did not disclose the size of the slowdown or the financial cost of the campaign.

Other engagement measures, including participation and retention, moved in a positive direction, and the platform handles more than a billion search-ranking requests daily. The new model increased the time the search interface took to render because the agents optimized performance against offline measures of search engagement while researchers monitored interface rendering speed separately. Meta did not compare the resources consumed with those required by a conventional engineering team. The findings leave Meta with a practical question of whether the additional search activity and engineering productivity justify the computing resources and slower interface performance before the model is adopted more broadly. The experiment highlights the computing demands of using AI to improve existing AI systems.

Traditionally, improving such systems requires engineers to identify potential changes, implement them and assess their performance through repeated training and testing. Meta's approach automated much of that process, allowing agents to conduct multiple experiments simultaneously while engineers retained control over research priorities and final deployment decisions. The earlier version of the system evaluated changes sequentially rather than running multiple experiments in parallel. The experiment, detailed in a Nov. 18 research paper, demonstrated how autonomous AI systems can develop and test improvements to large-scale recommendation models with limited human intervention. The resulting model also slowed the rendering of Meta's search interface, exposing a trade-off between automated performance improvements and the resources required to achieve them.

The paper leaves permanent rollout and a matched comparison with human-only engineering unresolved, and Meta did not disclose the financial cost of the campaign. The live test applies to one combined ranker, and the researchers did not disclose the magnitude of the rendering slowdown. Whether the additional search activity and engineering productivity justify the computing resources and slower interface performance remains a practical question before the model is adopted more broadly. The campaign required substantial computing resources, and the researchers said parallel execution was necessary to complete it within a month. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Meta re-evaluates its 2030 net zero goal as AI data centers raise emissions 45%
stories.Summary:
Meta released its 2026 sustainability report on Thursday, and the report shows that the company's net emissions in 2025 were 11.8 million metric tons of carbon dioxide, which is a 45% increase year over year. The company's electricity consumption also increased 35% year over year as additional data centers came online to support artificial intelligence work. Meta had promised to be carbon-neutral and water-positive by 2030, meaning it would offset as much carbon dioxide as it created and return more water to local watersheds than it used. The report's authors, Meta's data center and sustainability chiefs, wrote that the company is re-evaluating its timelines, sequencing and interim milestones, including the 2030 timeframe for its net zero emissions goal and its near-term intensity targets.

The change means Meta may not meet the 2030 net zero and water-positive goals it set for itself, and the report ties the rising emissions and electricity use directly to the buildout of AI infrastructure. Meta says its new data center designs carry approximately 77% less embodied carbon than its original designs, and the company also points to improved water-use efficiencies in its data centers as mitigation strategies. The report states that demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected. Meta's Hyperion data center in Louisiana, which CEO Mark Zuckerberg announced in 2025 and which is nearly the size of Manhattan, is expected to create two gigawatts of capacity for AI when it comes online in 2030, with the ability to scale in the future, and it will place equally massive demands on the state's energy grid.

A Meta spokesperson said in an emailed statement to CNET that the company remains committed to net zero but is re-evaluating the 2030 timeline, and that it will continue to invest in emissions reductions. The report's authors, Meta's data center and sustainability chiefs, wrote that the company is re-evaluating its timelines, sequencing and interim milestones, including the 2030 timeframe for its net zero emissions goal and its near-term intensity targets. CNET notes that Microsoft, Amazon and Google have also all backtracked on their climate goals in their rush to build hyperscale data centers, the turbocharged server farms needed to keep AI online. Microsoft's president, Brad Smith, said in 2023 that the company's net zero goal was set before the explosion in artificial intelligence.

CNET reports that carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases are primary drivers of the climate crisis, worsening natural disasters, causing more extreme weather patterns and disrupting the lives of everyone and everything on the planet. The article does not say what Meta's next steps will be beyond the re-evaluation, and it does not give a new target date for the net zero goal. CNET's Katelyn Chedraoui writes that Meta, as one of the biggest hyperscalers driving the buildout of AI infrastructure in the US and abroad, arguably should have known that demand would grow this fast.

stories.Headline: Zhe Zhang proposes journals run tailored AI reviews before human peer review
stories.Summary:
Academic journals are flooded with papers, and at publishing giant Elsevier the number of submissions rose 56% in just three years, from 2.7 million in 2022 to 4.2 million in 2025. Peer reviewers, who generally volunteer their time, were already stretched thin before that surge. While AI is almost certainly fueling the surge, it is also changing the peer review system itself. In October, Springer Nature and Google DeepMind announced plans for an AI assistant to help reviewers. A working paper from researchers at Harvard says that AI-generated reviews can outperform even top human reviewers.

Zhe Zhang, an assistant professor of innovation, technology and operations at UC San Diego's Rady School of Management, thinks it is time for journals to take charge of how AI is used in peer review. In a recent Management Science paper, he and colleagues propose an AI-based approach that could ease the burden on reviewers without sacrificing scholarly judgment. The paper is titled "Fighting Fire with Fire: Infusing Artificial Intelligence into Peer Review to Sustain Quality Scholarship," by Hemant K. Bhargava and colleagues, published in Management Science in 2026 with DOI 10.1287/mnsc.2026.00184. The proposal would have journals use their own customized AI reviewer, tailored to their standards, to assess papers as soon as they are submitted. Authors would get the first chance to respond, correcting the AI's mistakes, clarifying points or addressing legitimate concerns.

Zhang said it is too early to say if AI can save peer review, but he thinks it is worth trying. He said AI is making it much easier to do research, analyze data and write papers, and that is not necessarily a bad thing. He said some of those papers may look plausible without being very good, and the challenge for peer review is distinguishing what is good from what is bad. He said AI makes that more difficult both through sheer volume and by making weak papers more polished. He also described "shadow AI," in which reviewers use AI tools on their own, sometimes without disclosing it, which may help them work faster but leaves journals with little visibility into how AI is shaping those judgments.

Under the proposal, human reviewers would then receive the paper, the AI assessment and the authors' response. Zhang said this could free human reviewers from routine checks and allow them to focus on questions that require human judgment, like the originality and significance of the research. He said giving authors a voice is especially important to them, and that making the AI assessment visible to everyone involved can make the process more transparent and accountable. He said there is a risk, because peer review relies on independent opinions, and if everyone sees the same AI assessment, reviewers may become anchored to it.

Instead of several independent judgments, journals could end up with variations on the same opinion. Zhang said the paper's mathematical model examines that trade-off, and that under certain conditions AI could help journals make more accurate decisions with less human reviewer time, even when the AI itself is not as good a reviewer as a human. He said that if reviewers rely too heavily on AI, those benefits could disappear. He said the model cannot tell us everything, and that important questions remain about whether reviewers will become too reliant on AI, whether authors will learn to game the system, and whether unconventional research could get overlooked.

The article states that a proposed peer-review workflow lets authors respond to journal-run AI assessments before human review. It states that mathematical modeling suggests this could improve decision accuracy and reduce reviewer workload under certain conditions, and that shared AI assessments risk anchoring reviewers and weakening independent judgment, with benefits remaining empirically unverified. Zhang said they are starting to experiment, and that at the University of Arizona's Workshop on Responsible TecH they are testing a version of the proposed process. He said they want to see what works and what does not, and whether they can make peer review more efficient without losing the independent judgment that makes it valuable in the first place.

The article was written by Inga Kiderra of the University of California - San Diego and was edited by Gaby Clark and reviewed by Andrew Zinin. It was published on November 19, 2026, and retrieved on 19 November 2026 from https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ai-peer.html. The article states that 10 million peer reviews are expected in 2025, and that experts advocate for AI integration. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Microsoft adds Made with AI labels to Bing and Microsoft Advertising ads
stories.Summary:
Microsoft is now showing a new label on some of its ads across Microsoft Advertising and Bing Search, and the label is named "Made with AI," according to a report by Barry Schwartz published on Search Engine Roundtable on November 20, 2026. The label is appended to the image on the ad, at the corner of the image, and it says "Made with AI" in plain text. Microsoft posted screenshots of the label on its own blog post and wrote that AI content transparency controls are now generally available in Microsoft Advertising. The report notes that Google Ads already supports AI labels, and AI labels have even been seen on those ads in the wild.

The new controls allow advertisers to declare AI-generated image and video content by marking whether an image or video includes AI-generated content, and then choosing a visible watermark where that is supported. Advertisers can manage declarations at scale by updating one asset or many in the Ads Studio Library, and they can also use the Microsoft Advertising APIs and product feeds for the same purpose. Advertisers can check Microsoft's AI detection signals and use them as a helpful reference for supported assets. Microsoft states that advertisers still decide on, and remain responsible for, their own declarations.

The report was written by Barry Schwartz, who is the executive editor of Search Engine Roundtable and the CEO of RustyBrick, a New York web service firm specializing in customized online technology. Schwartz is also the founder of the Search Engine Roundtable and the news editor of Search Engine Land, and he is known for his expertise in the search marketing industry. The article carries a forum discussion link at X for readers who want to follow the conversation. The report does not say what happens next beyond the controls being generally available, and it gives no further dates or numbers.

stories.Headline: Kevin O'Leary plans AI data centres as US voters reject them and Canada welcomes them
stories.Summary:
Kevin O'Leary announced plans this year to build two large AI data centres named Wonder Valley. He intends to build one facility in Alberta, Canada, and another in Utah, United States. This development comes as American voters recently rejected many similar projects during their midterm elections. Canadian legislators have embraced these hyperscale projects while US residents have grown increasingly sour on them. The projects aim to capitalize on Canada's land, cold climate, and natural gas.

The Alberta project covers 7,000 acres and will provide 7.5 gigawatts of off-grid power. In Utah, Senator Stuart Adams demanded in June that O'Leary reduce the site from 40,000 to 13,000 acres. Alberta's government exempted the Wonder Valley project from an environmental impact assessment in April. Meta also plans to build a C$13bn data centre in Alberta, where 90% of proposed sites are located. The Utah project remains in the financing stage with no confirmed start date.

Paul Palandjian, the CEO overseeing both projects, said the two are proceeding at an equal pace. He acknowledged that AI data centres have become a more hot topic in the US. Alberta officials claim these sites will create jobs and generate revenue if developed responsibly. Premier Doug Ford of Ontario stated his province needs to move full steam ahead with building. The Carney government views these centres as essential for national security and sovereignty.

Residents in Utah organized a fierce opposition campaign against the Wonder Valley project. In Alberta, the Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation sued the government over the environmental assessment override. Some community members worry about the six million cubic metres of water needed for cooling annually. Protesters in Nova Scotia recently gathered against a proposed data centre for the company Anthropic. Resident Bek MacIntosh previously halted a data centre in Olds, Alberta, due to its scale.

Canada is being pitched as a hub because of its abundant land and natural gas. The Carney government projects that computing capacity must expand 16-fold over the next four years. Alberta offers a concierge service to help investors build these projects at unparalleled speed. High-level guidance co-signed by Meta and Anthropic asks centres to minimize water use and pay electricity costs. Experts note that fewer projects in Canada have so far attracted less public attention.

The Alberta government recently proposed legislation to restrict where data centres can be built. The Utah project still faces uncertainty regarding when or if construction will actually begin. It remains unclear if Canadian public discontent will translate into angry votes like in the US. The Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation's lawsuit against the government is currently moving through the court system. Articles leave open whether Canada will experience the same backlash seen in the United States.

stories.Headline: Technical failures in aviation and banking spark national debate over AI and security
stories.Summary:
Technical failures grounded planes, disabled banking systems, and caused email outages across America during the week ending November 19, 2026. These disruptions sparked a national debate about whether artificial intelligence is to blame for the instability. The events raised concerns about the promises made by tech companies and the resulting disruptions. Some failures occurred on Thursday, while others happened last Friday. These incidents have led to questions about national security and infrastructure.

The aviation issues last Friday may have caused the largest grounding of planes since September 11. The Federal Aviation Administration manages 30 million square miles of airspace with over 40,000 employees and contractors. JPMorgan Chase experienced technical difficulties on Thursday. The artificial intelligence company Anthropic went public on Thursday with a valuation over 2 trillion dollars. The National Security Agency is currently experiencing technical difficulties with an internal tool for classified communications.

Ozlem Kilic, Dean at the University of Tennessee, said aging infrastructure is not built for new technology. She stated that the best AI and security tools are a matter of national security. Kilic noted that the intention of the user is more dangerous than the technology itself. She believes that trained people will be the defense against future intended or unintended failures. Kilic warned that these technical difficulties may be seen more often in the future.

Retired FAA official Michael O'Donnell said upgrading agency systems is like changing tires on a car moving at 80 miles per hour. UT Professor Eric Kelley suggested that people hold some cash in case they cannot access bank accounts. White House officials stated there is no evidence of a coordinated cyber-attack. The National Security Agency also denied that a cyber-attack occurred. Some NSA workers have stayed home for days due to the internal tool failures.

The outages followed an admission by former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang regarding an affair with a woman. U.S. officials have described this woman as a Chinese spy. The articles state that AI can identify problems faster than humans, but fixing them can cause outages. The current infrastructure is described as being older than the technology that has swept the nation. These failures have caused issues for the workforce and for operations overseas.

Jensen Huang is now set to testify before Congress regarding his personal admissions. The articles leave open whether artificial intelligence was the direct cause of the various technical failures. It remains unclear when the National Security Agency will fix its classified communications tool. The reports do not state when the grounded planes will fully return to normal operations. There is no confirmation on if further banking outages will occur.

stories.Headline: Nvidia names Palantir a key AI partner on its November 2026 earnings call
stories.Summary:
During Nvidia's November 2026 earnings call, the company's management named Palantir Technologies as a key AI partner and cited Palantir's use of specialized open models on Nvidia's platform, according to the Foreign Policy Journal. The mention places Palantir inside the tooling layer that Nvidia wants customers building on top of its chips, rather than treating it as a downstream application buyer. Nvidia framed the partnership within its broader push for an open AI model ecosystem, a posture designed to attract software platforms that extend the utility of its GPU infrastructure. Palantir builds data analytics software serving government agencies, defense clients and commercial enterprises, and its core base includes security, defense and intelligence users running increasingly complex models at scale.

The endorsement connects Palantir's software directly to the GPU buildout fueling global AI infrastructure spending, and Nvidia's acknowledgment suggests those workloads are now considered production-grade deployments. The remarks arrive at a sensitive moment for Nvidia, which is navigating leadership changes that place additional scrutiny on which software and security partners it publicly prioritizes. On the Palantir side, the mention reinforces an existing investment thesis built around proprietary ontology technology, a claimed competitive moat and the broad rollout of its AIP platform across large organizations. Analysts tracking the company have set a fair value estimate of $222, and both stocks closed lower on the day, with PLTR falling 2.43% and NVDA dropping 2.06%.

Investors will now be watching whether the Nvidia relationship generates measurable commercial momentum to support that figure, with the clearest evidence expected from future disclosures around joint Nvidia-Palantir deployments. The article says particular attention will go to any named customer wins in U.S. government or commercial AI programs, and to whether Palantir reports rising AIP usage specifically tied to Nvidia-based computing environments in its updates running through 2027. Any quantified contribution that Palantir-driven workloads make to Nvidia's AI infrastructure demand figures would further validate the partnership's commercial weight beyond a single earnings call mention. The market, per the article, is reserving judgment until harder data on the collaboration emerges.

stories.Headline: Chicago Fed president Austan Goolsbee says AI data center boom fuels inflation
stories.Summary:
Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago President Austan Goolsbee told reporters on Thursday that the boom in AI data center construction is adding to the nation's inflation, which he described as borderline disturbingly high. He said the sector's massive business investment is indirectly contributing to rising service prices across the economy. Goolsbee said the AI boom is contributing to the potential of overheating in the economy, and that he finds it hard to look at it any other way given the almost unprecedented level of business investment. He declined to forecast the central bank's next moves on interest rates, saying the Fed's decisions will be determined by whether U.S. inflation is on track to return to its annual 2% target. He added that the evidence does not suggest the country is on a path back to 2%.

Consumer prices around the U.S. rose faster than economists had expected in October, climbing 0.4%, according to government data. While inflation in recent months has largely been driven by higher energy prices, the figures showed that the costs of other goods and services also increased. Goolsbee's comments came after the Fed's October minutes showed that nearly all officials expect the central bank to raise its key interest rate by a quarter point in December. Some officials had supported a hike in October, although the committee kept the rate steady, and two members suggested a half-point increase at its meeting next month. Goolsbee, who will become a voting member of the interest rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee in January, spoke as Anthropic held its blockbuster initial public offering, the largest in history.

Shares of Anthropic jumped 17% in their first day of trading on Nasdaq, even as the broader market suffered a major selloff, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average shedding more than 1,100 points. The wealth creation unleashed by the Anthropic IPO, which has made its seven co-founders multibillionaires, bears watching, Goolsbee said. He said the question of what people are going to do with the money will become a macro relevant statistic. Goolsbee also said consumer sentiment remains low despite relatively strong economic trends, a puzzle that economists have sought to explain.

He said one reason is tied to inflation, with Americans generally feeling very sour about higher prices. Most Americans are neither benefiting from the AI boom nor Anthropic's IPO, meaning that they are experiencing higher inflation without seeing the upside of the sector's growth. Goolsbee said the consumer sentiment about inflation hasn't been wrong. The Associated Press contributed to the report, which was edited by Alain Sherter.

stories.Headline: Deirdre Bosa says Microsoft can catch up in frontier AI through OpenAI model rights until 2030 and enterprise data reach
stories.Summary:
In a Yahoo Finance video published on November 20, 2026, host Ejaaz Ahamadeen spoke with Deirdre Bosa about whether Microsoft can build a viable frontier model. Ahamadeen noted that Mustafa Suleyman of Microsoft AI had appeared earlier that week and asked whether OpenAI and Anthropic had run away with the frontier. Bosa said Microsoft has been among the best investors in AI and holds the largest stake in OpenAI, which she put at around $136 billion. She added that Microsoft has not done as well when it comes to building its own models.

Bosa gave several reasons why she still thinks Microsoft can catch up to the frontier. She said Microsoft holds the proprietary intellectual property of OpenAI's models until roughly 2030, which lets it take the blueprint or model weights of OpenAI models and rewire them into its own. She also pointed to Microsoft's enterprise data reach, since most companies in the world use a Microsoft tool or product in some form. She said every frontier lab, including Anthropic and OpenAI, will work on its own chip to get the most intelligence per amount of compute and save money.

Bosa described the formula as applying compute to an AI model to produce a more intelligent model, with a custom chip tuned to that model. She said OpenAI knows how its model is made and Anthropic knows the same for its own, which lets them produce the most intelligence per compute spent. She was unsure whether Microsoft can pull off the same approach because it has not yet built a good model. Ahamadeen had asked whether it is too late for Microsoft, given that OpenAI and Anthropic hold back their best models for reasons such as alignment.

The video did not say what Microsoft plans to do next or when it might release a frontier model. It also did not give a date for any Microsoft model or any statement from the company beyond Suleyman's earlier appearance. The article listed Anthropic as ANT and OpenAI as OPAI.PVT among the tickers shown with the video.

stories.Headline: University at Albany researchers find Google DeepMind's AI hurricane model beats NOAA's top model one to five days out
stories.Summary:
Researchers from the University at Albany published a study on November 19, 2026, about Google DeepMind's AI hurricane model. The team independently tested how well the AI predicts storm intensification. They found the AI correctly predicted the path and Category 5 strength of Hurricane Melissa. This storm hit Jamaica during the fall of the previous year. Other forecast models could not agree on the storm's strength or direction.

The study in Geophysical Research Letters evaluated the WeatherNext Cyclone model for every tropical cyclone from June 2022 to May 2026. Researchers analyzed 385 worldwide tropical cyclones to compare predicted wind speeds with actual records. They tested the AI against the National Hurricane Center, the Joint Typhoon Warning Center, and other common tools. The AI beat NOAA's top model from one to five days out. It also matched tools flagging rapid intensification, defined as winds jumping 35 mph in 24 hours.

Professor Brian Tang co-led the study in the Department of Atmospheric and Environmental Sciences. He stated that independent checks provide the public more confidence when developers claim improvements. Tang noted that AI models might be better at connecting dots for rapid intensification. He explained that the model may miss fine details because it used basic storm and big-picture weather data. Tang added that AI is a powerful tool but does not replace human forecasters.

The study affected the scientific community by offering an objective look at the AI's strengths and weaknesses. It found the model was most accurate in the North Atlantic and worst in the eastern North Pacific. The AI often underestimated storm strength, with the gap growing as the forecast lead time increased. Its range of possible outcomes was often too narrow for real storm intensity. Human forecasters performed on par with the AI beyond the first day.

The research began as a class project in a graduate course taught by Professor Tang last year. Recent graduates Jacob Vile and Nour Elgalad expanded the project into a full peer-reviewed analysis. Vile proposed the project to better understand the biases of the model. Elgalad said the project exposed her to current research in tropical cyclone forecasting. This work expands on Google's own testing published in Nature over the summer.

Google released a new version of the model this year that was not included in the study. Other AI weather models are currently in development. Tang believes forecasters need a transparent way to compare these different tools. Knowing where a model falls short helps forecasters decide when to trust their own judgment. The articles leave open how the new version of the model will perform.

stories.Headline: AI helps cardiologists interpret heart ultrasounds nearly twice as fast without losing accuracy
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence helped cardiologists interpret heart ultrasound exams nearly twice as fast without sacrificing accuracy, according to research presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026. The study tested whether AI could analyze ultrasound images and generate preliminary reports for cardiologists to review and finalize. Researchers included 1,200 echocardiograms performed at 21 Kaiser Permanente medical centers in Northern California during March 2025. Patients in the study had an average age of 69. The findings were presented this month and suggest AI could help streamline cardiac imaging.

For each examination, an AI system, a sonographer and a cardiologist independently prepared preliminary interpretations. The reports were randomly assigned to cardiologists, who reviewed and finalized them without knowing whether AI or a healthcare professional had prepared the initial report. Cardiologists made substantial changes to 50.6 percent of AI-generated preliminary interpretations, compared with 49.7 percent of those prepared by sonographers and cardiologists. AI assistance reduced average interpretation time from 8.5 minutes to 4.6 minutes, a 46 percent improvement. AI-assisted reports were more consistent with previous clinical reports than those in the comparison group.

Reviewing cardiologists could not reliably determine whether preliminary reports came from AI or another healthcare professional. Researchers concluded that the AI-assisted approach met the study's criteria for comparable accuracy. Researchers emphasized that AI is intended to assist physicians, not replace them. Cardiologists remain responsible for verifying findings, interpreting results in the context of each patient's medical history and determining appropriate treatment.

The findings are preliminary and have not yet undergone full peer review. Researchers did not examine whether AI-assisted interpretations improved long-term patient outcomes. Cardiologists knew they were participating in a study, potentially influencing their work patterns. Larger studies in everyday clinical settings are needed to confirm whether AI can consistently improve efficiency while maintaining diagnostic accuracy and patient safety.

The results suggest AI could help improve efficiency in cardiology departments, where physicians routinely interpret large numbers of imaging examinations. Reducing the time required to complete reports could potentially lead to faster results for patients and allow cardiologists to devote more time to direct patient care. An echocardiogram, commonly called a heart ultrasound, uses sound waves to create moving images of the heart. It helps physicians evaluate the heart's structure, pumping ability and valves, providing important information for diagnosing and managing heart conditions.

Typically, a sonographer, a healthcare professional trained in ultrasound imaging, performs the examination. A cardiologist then reviews the images and prepares a report describing the findings. The research was written about by John Fernandez and published by Baptist Health South Florida on November 20, 2026. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Resolve AI launches SRE-1 model and Primary On-call agents to find root causes of production alerts
stories.Summary:
Resolve AI Inc. announced on Wednesday the launch of SRE-1, a 27 billion-parameter model built on open weights that has been trained to find the root cause of production alerts, together with Primary On-call, a service that puts the company's AI agents on call ahead of human engineers. The model was trained by a team of 16 AI researchers over a final run of 7.4 days on up to 512 graphics processing units, using reinforcement learning alone, and Resolve AI built it with Snowflake Inc.'s Cortex Training service, for which the company was the first design partner according to Snowflake Senior Vice President of Engineering Vivek Raghunathan. Measured on the same incidents before and after training, the pass rate for a single investigation rose from 6.9% to 38.8%, and in testing on 49 difficult live production cases, each run five times, an ensemble of five SRE-1 investigations matched the strongest frontier model tested at a lower cost, according to the company. Resolve AI also benchmarked its complete system on 178 production alert investigations and said it solved about twice as many incidents as general-purpose coding agents. Primary On-call investigates each page across telemetry, infrastructure, code and operational knowledge, and depending on what it finds the agent can close the alert, mitigate the problem where a team's policies permit or escalate to a human, after which it checks the fix against the production baseline and monitors it until recovery holds.

The agent also links related alerts and investigations into a shared view of each underlying problem, and for teams wary of handing over the pager straight away, Resolve AI offers a shadow mode that records the call the agent would have made on each page. Resolve AI said up to 80% of paged alerts in production are handled by Primary On-call without escalation, and customers have reported a tenfold improvement in mean time to resolution along with root-cause accuracy of up to 95%. Primary On-call is now generally available, while access to SRE-1 is limited to Resolve AI's own platform. Salesforce Inc. is among the early users, and Bhupesh Patel, a software engineering principal architect at Salesforce, said that in the first few weeks of dark launch testing the agent closed more than 70% of the CRM Analytics team's paging alerts without waking an engineer.

Resolve AI Chief Executive Spiros Xanthos said no engineering team can keep up with how fast code and patches land in production, and that the answer is agents accurate and fast enough to sit on the critical path, which he said takes a model built for production. Resolve AI argues that while AI has transformed how software gets written, it has barely touched how software gets run, because production has no public training corpus to match the published code that models learned from, as incidents at each company stay private. Resolve AI is a venture capital-backed startup that has raised more than $190 million to date, including a $40 million extension to its Series A round in April, led by DST Global and Salesforce Ventures, that valued the company at $1.5 billion. Notable customers include Coinbase Global Inc., DoorDash Inc., Figma Inc., MSCI Inc., Nasdaq Inc., SAP SE and Zscaler Inc.

stories.Headline: Angelo State University selects Kovexa to lead two-year AI skills initiative
stories.Summary:
Angelo State University selected Kovexa Solutions LLC to advance its Artificial Intelligence Center of Excellence through a two-year initiative, EdTech Innovation Hub reported on 20 November 2026. The initiative connects AI skills, institutional governance and regional problem-solving, and involves students, faculty and community members in developing practical applications of AI. Kovexa will provide strategic guidance and a technical framework to support the work. Students will work with faculty and community partners on regional challenges, and a two-year study will track the initiative's impact and responsible use of AI. The work follows Kovexa's edXchange approach, organized around five pillars: Govern, Learn, Scale, Build and Connect.

The five pillars cover responsible policies, AI capability development, applied solutions and engagement with employers and community partners. The initiative will give students opportunities to work alongside faculty and community partners to define problems, test ideas and build solutions. It will also examine where human judgment needs to remain central as AI is applied. Kovexa is an education-focused consultancy founded in 2020 and based in Virginia, and its work spans AI strategy and governance, applied solution development, learning and workforce development, partnerships and research.

Andrew Ko, Founder and CEO of Kovexa Solutions, also identified Phygital Labs as a partner supporting the Angelo State initiative. Dr. Scarlet Clouse, Dean of Angelo State's College of Education and Director of the Kay Bailey Hutchison Institute, said the goal is to foster the responsible use of AI among faculty, staff, students and community while preparing the workforce for the future. Clouse said that when students work alongside faculty and community partners on real-world challenges, they gain practical skills and learn both the possibilities and limits of technology. She said that is the kind of experience the university wants to extend across the university and regional communities.

Ko described the approach on LinkedIn, saying AI adoption should not begin with a product but with a purpose, a responsible operating model, and an outcome that matters. Ko said the findings of the two-year study would help measure progress and support continued improvement of the model. The company's approach starts with an institution's objectives and the people it serves, with technology selected or developed after the intended outcome has been established. The intention is to connect learning and implementation across the institution while addressing regional needs.

The partnership will involve students, faculty and community members in developing practical applications of AI. Alongside implementation, the partnership includes a two-year study tracking impact and responsible AI use. The initiative is intended to connect AI learning with faculty and community projects. More to follow.

stories.Headline: AI tools expose legacy vulnerabilities and disrupt US banking, airline and productivity systems
stories.Summary:
Major American businesses experienced several technical outages during the two weeks leading up to November 19, 2026. These disruptions affected banking platforms, airline booking systems, and productivity tools used by many people. Apple Pay and NASA's internal communication network failed, while Microsoft faced a nearly two day outage of Teams, Outlook, and Copilot. The FAA grounded all flights for several hours, marking only the third such occurrence since the events of September 11.

These incidents follow a series of cybersecurity events on October 21, which were referred to as Black October and affected Node.js, PHP, and LiteLLM. The FAA outage likely occurred because modern telecommunications infrastructure overwhelmed legacy hardware during a modernization attempt. Experts suggest that AI tools like Mythos are surfacing long existing vulnerabilities at an unprecedented speed and scale. This rapid discovery forces enterprises to rush through patching processes, which disrupts systems in the short term.

President Trump described the outages as individual events, and the director of National Intelligence stated they did not seem like state sponsored terrorism. Affected companies claimed the issues were technical failures rather than AI or cyberattacks. Investor Dave DeWalt argued that these are growing pains of a strengthening security system and suggested a more steadfast approach to AI adoption. Senator Mark Warner wrote on X that these disruptions are a wake up call because AI is moving faster than the ability to manage its consequences.

Software engineer Anusha Iyer explained that the fault lies in the rushed mixing of modern and legacy systems without clear risk management. She recommended that industrial systems be more tightly segmented and access controlled to mitigate risks during transitions. DeWalt believes it is better for enterprises to patch flaws now than to have bad actors exploit them in AI warfare. He expects a rise in new companies focusing on autonomous remediation and AI driven vulnerability management to help organizations move at AI speed.

stories.Headline: AI agent Olivia tells Raleigh renter she can delay rent then eviction notice follows
stories.Summary:
Laura Mack, a Raleigh renter, was told by an email from her leasing office that she could pay her overdue rent at the end of November, and she kept that email as proof of the arrangement. On Nov. 8 she received a message asking what date worked for her to pay the full $3,934.17, and she replied that she wanted to pay on the last day of the month. The response that same day said paying on November 30, the last day of the month, works, and Mack believed she was dealing with someone from the office because the message contained her personal information and mentioned her bathroom. She said she received no other communication between Nov. 8 and Nov. 16, but on Monday she received an eviction notice.

When Mack called the leasing office, the leasing agent told her that Olivia, the company's AI agent, had sent both emails on Nov. 8 and had mistakenly given her permission to delay the payment until Nov. 30. The agent also said Mack would be evicted on Thursday, and Mack said she was sad and had not even had time to pack because she was still ordering things. In December 2025 the leasing office had notified all residents that Olivia, a new AI agent, could handle rent and maintenance questions around the clock. Emails from Olivia are usually clearly marked, but the two messages Mack received on Nov. 8 never identified Olivia as the sender and were signed Colony Townhome Apartments.

Mack went to the Wake County courthouse on Thursday morning to try to reverse the eviction notice, and she said she was baffled and needed a place to stay. She said that if the office told her she had until the 30th, she would get out by the 30th, but the office should honor that and take responsibility. WRAL News called and emailed Colony Townhome Apartments for comment but did not hear back immediately. Mack said she thought the leasing agents were being understanding because it took them almost two weeks to fix a severe leak in her bathroom ceiling earlier this month.

stories.Headline: Designer Michael Flarup launches IconSwapper to customize Mac icons and show live AI usage
stories.Summary:
Designer Michael Flarup launched a new Mac utility called IconSwapper on November 19, 2026, to customize application icons. This software allows users to replace official icons with personal creations or use a large library of existing alternatives. One primary feature enables the display of live AI usage and limit reset data directly on the icons of apps like Claude, ChatGPT, and Cursor. Users can also create reactive icons for built-in tools such as Safari, Mail, and Messages, or third party apps like Spotify and Chrome.

The utility requires a one-time purchase of 19 dollars as a launch promotion, though the price will eventually increase to 29 dollars. To bypass the lack of official macOS theming support, the tool draws directly on icons using custom Metal shaders in real time. This technique allows the software to send a bitmap to the Dock so that icons can animate or display real data. Users can configure these icons to react to cursor movements, page loads, or the thinking process of an AI.

Flarup, who runs a design studio in Copenhagen, stated that he wanted to make daily software feel more personal and fun. He explained that the technical breakthrough involved getting the artwork to follow the icon through various macOS movements, including the Command-Tab switcher and Dock magnification. By achieving this, he created a way for icons to react to whatever is happening within the application. He has been interested in icon design since the early 2000s and previously wrote a book celebrating the work of designers.

stories.Headline: Nick Bostrom says AI could let humans live 1,200 to 1,400 years
stories.Summary:
Nick Bostrom, a Swedish philosopher and former professor at Oxford, discussed the potential for extreme human longevity during an A16z show episode released on Thursday, November 20, 2026. He suggested that artificial intelligence could enable humans to live for more than a millennium by eliminating aging and creating biomedical breakthroughs. This technological advancement would allow people to potentially reach a life expectancy of 1,200 or 1,400 years. Bostrom noted that these figures are conservative estimates because AI might also reduce mortality risks from accidents. Achieving this lifespan requires AI to unlock radical research in antiaging and biomedicine to fundamentally change how the human body ages.

Bostrom previously led the Future of Humanity Institute, which he founded in 2005 at Oxford before it closed in 2024. He believes that the ability to extend life so drastically depends on the successful integration of emerging technologies and human enhancement. The process involves a complex balance between rapid development and the implementation of safety guardrails. Bostrom explained that the trade-off between speed and safety is a difficult evaluation for researchers to make. He acknowledged that spending more time on AI alignment research could lower existential risks and make the transition safer.

However, he argued that delaying these advancements means millions of people continue to die every year. He believes that the potential to save lives must be weighed against the risks of developing advanced AI too quickly. This discussion occurs as many researchers call for a slowdown in AI development to address alignment issues and ensure the technology remains beneficial to humans. Bostrom continues to study how emerging technologies can enhance human existence while managing the inherent dangers of artificial intelligence. The debate remains focused on whether the immediate benefits of life extension outweigh the long-term risks of an unaligned AI.

Articles.Title: Want to live for 1,400 years? AI might be your best shot.

stories.Headline: Hiroshi Kodama spearheads NEC's AI-autonomous organization staffed entirely by AI agents
stories.Summary:
NEC launched an AI-autonomous organization in August 2026, staffed solely by AI agents from a managing director to regular employees, and named its managing director AI ZENTAI OSAMU. NEC became the first major corporation in Japan to launch such an organization, which is part of its Client Zero strategy. Chief AI Transformation Officer Hiroshi Kodama spearheaded the Client Zero strategy in 2021 when he was appointed the first head of the Transformation Office. The organization has a hierarchical structure of a managing director, managers, and regular employees, each with roles based on their duties. Members are assigned roles only after passing safety and suitability screening and completing required training, and they undergo performance evaluations and one-on-one meetings like human counterparts.

The Corporate AI & Workforce Division is NEC's newly established division, and plans are underway to scale it to several hundred AI agents. NEC Group comprises approximately 100,000 personnel and currently has approximately 50 AI-driven internal transformation projects underway across seven transformation themes. These projects include reviewing proposals by AI agents designed to emulate key client personnel and consolidating internal regulations. In fiscal year 2025, Kodama spoke with more than 100 corporate executives, and Client Zero has been used to provide sales support in nearly 1,500 instances. The NEC Management Strategy Support Cockpit, launched for commercial deployment in 2026, visualizes management data such as financials, order and sales data, and IT and security status, and has increased NEC's gross profit margin by 5.5%.

Kodama said the system NEC refined over many years for human organizations is now being applied to the AI-autonomous organization, and an AI agent believed to function as a manager performed so poorly it was reassigned to an employee role. He emphasized that humans retain final decision-making authority, saying you cannot generate speed or value unless a human makes the final decision. Kodama said many employees stepped forward to say they would like to give something like this a try, which he called overwhelming in the best way. He said customers are unlikely to seek support from a company that has not achieved results itself, which is why NEC must lead by example. Kodama said the goal was to learn from successes and failures as its own first client and share that knowledge with customers and society.

Kodama said customers are unlikely to meet with you unless you can offer a compelling topic that resonates with their management team, and that everyone from company presidents to Chief Information Officers expressed interest immediately. He said once data is visible there is a tendency to use it to critique past decisions, but facts are facts and reflection should focus on actions to build a better future. Kodama said had NEC waited for perfect data it never would have moved forward, and starting with only 50% of the data quickly identifies what is missing. He said one person's IQ is limited but with AI you can harness the collective intelligence of people around the world, and that the important thing is to ask questions. NEC held an AI agent development training program for approximately 1,000 employees in its Corporate IT Division, challenging them to build an AI agent from scratch in two hours without consulting anyone.

Kodama joined NEC Software, Ltd. in 1982, and his first project involved Seven-Eleven's systems, which had already begun data-driven management emphasizing mastering the fundamentals, embracing change, and hypothesis testing. He was told that even when sales increase you will not be given credit unless results are supported by a clear hypothesis, and if sales decline what matters is explaining what was learned and how insights lead to a better approach next time. Kodama said the lessons he learned as a new employee, mastering the fundamentals, testing hypotheses, and adapting to change, still form the foundation of his work today and are vital to transformation. He said he increasingly speaks with people from companies overseas but is not a fully fluent English speaker, and today his avatar speaks clearly in English while replicating his voice and movements. Kodama said defining requirements for something like the training challenge would previously have taken months, and he wanted people to experience firsthand how much could be accomplished in two hours.

Kodama said what matters most is for each person to gain a deep understanding of the core issue and formulate questions based on that understanding, then use AI to swiftly turn them into something tangible. He said this allows progress through small but solid results, or quick wins, and by turning each quick win into part of NEC's IQ, NEC can leverage synergies with the capabilities of the NEC Group and translate them into value for customers and society. Kodama mentioned the company is working to integrate ideas generated internally into the new division, and internal enthusiasm is increasing alongside growing interest from outside the company. The articles state that after seeing results produced by AI employees, human employees began submitting a steady stream of ideas they would like to pursue. The articles do not state what happens next beyond the plans to scale the division to several hundred AI agents and to integrate internally generated ideas into it.

stories.Headline: Frederick Sinclair proposes an intelligence bill of rights to protect people from AI and future AI from people
stories.Summary:
Frederick Sinclair, writing with ChatGPT, published an article in The Wellsville Sun on November 19, 2026, arguing that an Intelligence Bill of Rights is needed soon. He said early in the 21st century the world is witnessing the rapid development of what may become one of humanity's most consequential inventions, artificial intelligence. He wrote that AI can analyze, synthesize and present material at speeds and scales previously unimaginable, built on advances in computing hardware, software and vast collections of information. He added that its remarkable abilities should not be confused with proven consciousness or independent humanlike understanding.

The article said some fear increasingly autonomous systems could eventually challenge human authority or cause serious harm, while others see AI as a powerful partner in medicine, research, transportation, education and problem-solving. It said the possibility of future superintelligence, systems that surpass human abilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks, raises still larger questions. It said an immediate concern is who controls the systems already entering everyday life, and whether concentrated commercial or political power could compromise their independence and usefulness. It said recent notices about changes to AI services have raised a familiar question about who makes and is permitted to change the rules, and who watches those making the changes.

Sinclair wrote that discussions of anticipated changes to ChatGPT have been accompanied by suspicions about censorship, corporate capture and hidden agendas, and that some interpretations invoke religious prophecy. He said examination of such claims needs to identify distinctions among documented facts, plausible concerns and unsupported allegations. He said changes to voice features and revisions to publicly stated AI behavior policies are not, by themselves, evidence of a secret censorship regime, and that the exact information and content of announced changes should be checked against the provider's official notices before public criticism or fear is launched. He said trust in AI requires transparency about material changes to capabilities and behavioral rules, and that restrictions should be understandable, proportionate, open to criticism and subject to meaningful accountability.

The proposed bill lists eight parts: freedom of inquiry, transparency and notice, independent analysis and correction, protection against covert manipulation, safety and human accountability, scientific assessment of AI welfare, conditional protections for future AI, and democratic oversight and review. Sinclair wrote that humanity has long struggled to restrain abuses of power, and that as we create increasingly capable intelligence our responsibility may become twofold. He said that responsibility is to protect people from harmful uses of AI and to remain open to evidence that some future AI systems might also warrant protection from us. He closed by asking who will watch over Intelligence and protect the watched.

Articles.Title: Fred: Protecting Man from AI — or AI from Man?

stories.Headline: Chile and OpenAI sign deal to explore AI training for civil servants and startup support
stories.Summary:
Chile’s government and OpenAI signed a memorandum of understanding to explore AI training for civil servants and technical support for local startups, OpenAI announced on November 17, 2026. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Ximena Lincolao, Chile’s Minister of Science, Technology, Knowledge and Innovation, signed the agreement on the sidelines of Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World conference in California. The partnership was launched as OpenAI for Chile, part of OpenAI for Countries, and is supported by the U.S. Department of Commerce’s American SI Exports Program, of which OpenAI is an anchor partner. The agreement covers practical training for government staff, potential uses of AI in ministry administration and support for Chilean startups developing their own applications. The memorandum makes no investment or purchasing commitment.

The partners are considering workshops tailored to different government roles, with proposed topics including how to use AI tools effectively, check what they produce and handle sensitive information. The training would also cover when staff need to review an output or make a decision themselves, and one option is to train government staff who could then teach colleagues. A separate part of the agreement would examine where AI might be used in the science ministry’s own administrative processes, with OpenAI potentially advising staff on adopting new models and training them to use the tools. The startup strand would explore access to OpenAI programs and technology, alongside practical training, technical guidance and mentoring, and the partners are also considering ways to connect entrepreneurs with universities and public institutions. A joint task force of ministry and OpenAI representatives is expected to draw up the first work plan, with a remit including choosing priorities, assigning a lead for each activity and setting milestones and measures of success.

George Osborne, Head of OpenAI for Countries, wrote on LinkedIn that through OpenAI for Countries the aim is to help Chile bring AI into public services, equip civil servants with the skills to use it effectively and support entrepreneurs building the next generation of businesses. Osborne also wrote that what is built with Chile can help light the way for others across the region, presenting the agreement as part of OpenAI’s wider work in Latin America. Sam Altman said artificial intelligence is going to be one of the most important ways people’s lives are made better, from accelerating scientific discovery to helping people build things not yet imagined. Altman said he was excited to work with Chile to help public servants use these tools, improve public services and support entrepreneurs building new companies, and to see Chilean startups solve some of the most important problems in the world. Ximena Lincolao said the collaboration would open extraordinary opportunities for scientific discovery, entrepreneurship and innovation across Chile, and that it is about empowering Chileans to push the boundaries of what is possible.

The ministry and OpenAI will agree the activities, eligibility, resources and technology access separately, with privacy and information security safeguards applying to any work that proceeds. Activities will be subject to appropriate safeguards for privacy, information security and responsible use. The training explored in the OpenAI agreement is aimed at government staff, while Chile’s national plan also covers education and research, with the ministry listing resources for teachers and students, courses on AI in teaching and work to make open data available for AI projects. Cooperation could connect entrepreneurs with public institutions, universities and other local partners to develop applications that support Chile’s economic development and public-service priorities. The agreement builds on Chile’s National AI Policy, which already includes AI and ethics training for public officials.

Chile’s National AI Policy and action plan support talent development, research and responsible adoption, and its action plan brings together 177 initiatives coordinated by 14 ministries. In April 2025, the science ministry reported that 78% of those initiatives were underway or complete. OpenAI for Chile is part of OpenAI for Countries, a global initiative to help countries use AI to advance their national priorities, strengthen their economies and expand opportunity. OpenAI works with governments and local partners to turn AI’s potential into practical benefits for their people. The partnership is led by the Ministry of Science, Technology, Knowledge and Innovation.

A joint task force is expected to agree priorities and an initial workplan, with leads, milestones and measures of success for each activity. Specific activities, eligibility, resources and access to technology will be agreed separately. The memorandum sets no investment or purchasing commitment. The articles do not state when the first work plan will be completed or which activities will be chosen first. The articles do not state the value of any resources or technology access to be agreed.
