stories.Headline: Universities are underused national security assets in the AI era
stories.Summary:
In an opinion piece published by Times Higher Education on 20 November 2026, Dan McCluskey, professor of aerosol biodetection technology and dean of the School of Physics, Engineering and Computer Science at the University of Hertfordshire, argued that UK universities are underused national security assets in the AI era. He pointed to recent warnings from MI5 director general Ken McCallum about AI’s potential to transform the biological threat landscape, and to Covid-19, officially responsible for more than seven million deaths worldwide, as evidence of how quickly biological threats can disrupt lives, economies and public services. McCluskey said the misuse of AI to create biological weapons has not yet materialised, but its potential to accelerate new threats concerns security agencies around the world, while technologies able to detect airborne biological agents in real time remain relatively underdeveloped. He noted that PCR and lateral flow tests proved invaluable during the pandemic but were mostly reactive, and that large-scale environmental surveillance systems able to identify pathogens before widespread infection occurs are needed. McCluskey described the Biodetection Technologies Hub, a £13.5 million consortium led by the University of Hertfordshire alongside Cranfield University and the universities of Leeds and Manchester, which has worked with the Ministry of Defence to develop advanced bioaerosol detection systems capable of identifying biological threats rapidly and accurately.

He said the benefits extend beyond defence, with technologies originally developed for security applications already helping agricultural industries detect wheat pathogens that threaten up to 20 per cent of yields annually, and similar approaches being adapted for healthcare, food production, transportation and public infrastructure. He compared this to GPS, satellite navigation and the internet, which emerged from defence-related challenges before transforming civilian life. He also cited the University of Oxford’s Pandemic Sciences Institute, more than 120 research groups at Imperial College London working on pandemic preparedness, and biosecurity and pandemic risk initiatives at the University of Cambridge. McCluskey argued that detection technology alone is not enough and that national preparedness requires expertise across biological sciences, engineering, data science, artificial intelligence and environmental monitoring, strengths that are often dispersed across institutions, funded through separate programmes and only intermittently connected to national priorities.

He said universities are among the few places where multidisciplinary capability already exists on single sites, and that what is missing is a more systematic way of connecting that capability to national priorities and emerging threats. He stressed that this does not mean turning universities into extensions of government, since their independence remains one of their greatest strengths, but that institutions possess long-term research capacity, specialist facilities, multidisciplinary expertise and the ability to develop the next generation of scientists, engineers and technologists. As a practical starting point, McCluskey proposed a standing national resilience partnership bringing together universities, security agencies, defence organisations, public health bodies and industry, which could identify emerging threats, map capabilities across the sector and rapidly assemble multidisciplinary teams around specific national priorities. He also said universities should be more routinely involved in technical scenario planning and resilience exercises, which would help identify capability gaps earlier, focus research effort more effectively and strengthen relationships before the next crisis occurs, whether it emerges from nature, human error or malicious intent.

Articles.Title: Universities are underused national security assets in the AI era

stories.Headline: South Korea's top tax exam scorer admits using AI to cheat, casting doubt on CPA exam fairness
stories.Summary:
In South Korea, people who passed the certified public accountant exam are facing a tighter job market and new doubts about exam fairness, after the top scorer in this year's certified tax accountant exam admitted using generative artificial intelligence and electronic devices to cheat, The Korea Times reported on Nov. 20, 2026. The same person confessed to using those methods during the CPA exam, though he did not pass it, and he appeared before reporters at the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency. A candidate who spent at least three years preparing and missed the passing score by less than a point said it felt deeply unfair that people who played by the rules were paying the price. He added that if the top scorer had not admitted to cheating, candidates might never have realized they had been denied a fair shot.

Passing the CPA exam does not by itself qualify a candidate to practice, because under the Certified Public Accountant Act each passer must first complete a year of practical training at an approved institution such as an accounting firm, a public corporation or a private company. As of September, 723 passers had yet to register with a training institution, according to the Korean Accounting Association. The annual quota has already been lowered twice, from 1,250 in 2024 to 1,200 in 2025 and 1,150 in 2026, and expectations are growing that it will be cut by another 50 places next year. The Financial Services Commission is expected to set the minimum number of candidates that can be selected from next year's exam by the end of November.

The Financial Supervisory Service, which administers the CPA exam, said it would work with experts and relevant institutions to develop measures to prevent cheating using sophisticated electronic devices. In a study released Nov. 4, researchers at the Korean Accounting Association estimated that AI adoption could reduce accounting firms' demand for audit staff by about 10 percent over the next three to five years, with the decline reaching 12 to 16 percent thereafter, and they proposed reducing the annual quota by as many as 300 over the next two to three years. A 30-year-old accountant at a major entertainment company said she was glad to have found a job before AI took off, though she doubts demand for junior staff will hold up over time. The scandal has unsettled people still studying for the exams as well as those who have already passed, raising questions about whether the exam's safeguards are keeping pace with advanced technology.

Articles.Title: Aspiring accountants face tougher odds as AI reshapes hiring, shakes confidence in CPA exam

stories.headline_source: Aspiring accountants face tougher odds as AI reshapes hiring, shakes confidence in CPA exam

stories.Headline: Amazon adds SageMaker inference recommendations to Studio and Python SDK in 2026
stories.Summary:
Amazon published a 2026 review of Amazon SageMaker Inference launches on November 19, 2026, on the AWS blog. The post covered HyperPod Inference routing strategies, broader model serving framework support, and expanded multi-Region networking. It said the Inference Gateway delivers the routing and that managed NVIDIA Dynamo is a new serving framework. It said managed endpoints would get deeper integration with the rest of the AWS AI landscape. It followed a hypothetical team that launched a customer support assistant on a 70B-parameter model in the spring.

The post said inference recommendations launched in April as an API and gained four updates. In July 2026, recommendations arrived in SageMaker AI Studio as a guided, low-code workflow under Jobs and Inference optimization. In August 2026, they arrived in the SageMaker Python SDK v3, version 3.17.0 and later. In September 2026, recommendations began accepting LoRA adapters as Model Package ARNs or S3 URIs. Also in September 2026, a search with search_recipe set to max-concurrency-under-sla reported feasible_max or infeasible_min.

The post said the aws-ai-ml skill, available through the Agent Toolkit for AWS, gives coding agents such as Kiro built-in SageMaker AI inference expertise. It said setup takes about 10 minutes and the skill works with any agent that supports the Model Context Protocol and in SageMaker AI Studio JupyterLab spaces. It said Inference Components became available in the SageMaker AI console in October 2026. It said GPU partitioning with NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU arrived in October 2026, dividing one physical GPU into as many as seven partitions. It said managed NVIDIA Dynamo on HyperPod Inference arrived in November 2026.

The post said the team added four LoRA adapters, one for each product line, and set a target of 500 milliseconds for time to first token at peak load. It said the team's April configuration was never tested against either change. It said the team's embedding model, reranker, and classifier each used a fraction of a GPU but each model copy held a whole accelerator. It said the team's next model is a reasoning model whose weights alone exceed the GPU memory of any single instance.

It said long, retrieval-heavy prompts slowed token generation for every other user on the endpoint. The post said the April launch automated instance, container, and optimization selection through APIs. It said Studio benchmarks candidate configurations on real GPU infrastructure using NVIDIA AIPerf and applies techniques such as speculative decoding for throughput or kernel tuning for latency. It said the SDK can run recommendation jobs in parallel to compare serving frameworks such as LMI and vLLM.

It said the concurrency search uses the same CreateAIWorkloadConfig and CreateAIBenchmarkJob APIs as concurrency sweeps. It said MIG isolates GPU compute and memory between partitions while models on the same instance still share host CPU, host memory, networking, storage, and endpoint routing. The post said the team would move the reasoning model workload to HyperPod Inference and keep the support assistant on managed endpoints. It said the team would run the embedding model, reranker, and classifier in separate partitions of one GPU on a single endpoint.

It said the team would manage every component, including the assistant and its adapters, from the console. It said you pay the standard rate for the full instance-hour, so the saving comes from placing more models on each instance. The post was cut off mid-sentence in its final section on managed NVIDIA Dynamo. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Amazon SageMaker Inference: 2026 launches in review, part 2

stories.Headline: Suneung was built for a world before AI
stories.Summary:
Han Won-seok recently admitted to using a smartphone, a miniature camera, and generative artificial intelligence to achieve the highest score on a national tax accountant exam. This admission occurred as over half a million students prepared to take the College Scholastic Ability Test, known as Suneung, on Thursday, November 19, 2026. The scandal has sparked wider concerns about AI-assisted cheating on other high-stakes tests, including the Legal Education Eligibility Test and civil service exams. Government officials have launched a broad investigation into various national qualification exams held throughout the current year.

The ruling Democratic Party is now pursuing legislation that would impose a ten-year ban on any test-taker caught cheating with artificial intelligence. Meanwhile, the Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education is pushing a December 2025 roadmap that suggests starting systemic changes in 2028. This specific plan proposes a shift toward essay-based assessments and the complete phaseout of the Suneung by the 2040 academic year. Such a transition would move the primary responsibility for assessing applicants away from a national exam and into the hands of individual universities.

Park Do-soon, the first director of the Korea Institute for Curriculum and Evaluation, stated that written exams only test about one-tenth of curricular goals. He argued that the current system is limited because it asks questions that artificial intelligence can easily answer. Similarly, Korea University professor Cho Byeok has called for the total abolition of the Suneung to reduce the knowledge burden on students. Cho predicted that the national education system will undergo major changes within the next five years.

The government has pledged zero tolerance for cheating, but critics argue that simply removing devices from rooms does not solve the underlying problem. The debate now focuses on whether traditional written exams can still accurately measure a student's actual abilities in an AI-driven world. While the Seoul education office has provided a concrete timetable for retirement, the national government has not yet adopted the proposal. Future efforts may focus on giving students more opportunities to demonstrate their reasoning through written work.

Articles.Title: Suneung was built for a world before AI

stories.Headline: South Korea detects 111 exam cheating cases as AI fears grow
stories.Summary:
The 2027 College Scholastic Ability Test took place on Thursday, November 20, 2026, amid high anxiety over AI assisted cheating. Many students and experts now question if traditional safeguards can keep exams fair against advancing technology. The Education Ministry reported that 111 cheating cases involving smartphones and other electronic devices were detected. Some examinees attempted to cheat despite advance warnings from the Interior Ministry and the Education Ministry. These violations occurred at various testing sites, including a high school in Yeongtong District, Suwon, Gyeonggi.

The government sent three highest level emergency alert messages, including one announced in advance and two unannounced, to identify phones. These alerts sound even when devices are set to silent, and they helped uncover 54 of the cheating cases. Five cases involved the use of smart devices during the exam, while 52 others were detected through Wi-Fi signal detection. Examinees had to roll up sleeves to expose wrists and place stickers over clothing buttons, measures credited to Han Seong-sook. Proctors checked these analog measures during each session, and bags were placed in hallways to prevent the use of devices.

Vice Education Minister Choi Eun-ok briefed reporters on AI cheating cases at the Government Complex Sejong on November 19. Park Joo-ho, president of Daelim University College, stated that maintaining traditional assessment methods will only place a greater burden on examinees. He argued that the weight of the CSAT in university admissions must be reduced to ensure fairness. Park suggested that universities should evaluate applicants through a wider range of methods beyond written exams. He noted that while these changes are necessary, they would be difficult to implement for the 2028 CSAT.

Parents like 48 year old Jung Mi-seo, waiting at Duksung Girls' High School in Jongno District, Seoul, expressed deep anxiety. Jung noted her daughter wore contact lenses instead of glasses and wondered if this would be required for every exam. Seventeen year old Lee Si-yeon questioned the point of exams if people can get high scores by using AI. A 29 year old teacher surnamed Kim in Seocho District, Seoul, said students made cynical remarks about powerful AI tools. One test taker in Suwon described the exam room atmosphere as unsettling after a student was caught with a smartphone.

The tech industry doubts that current methods can catch AI cheaters as hidden devices become smarter. This year's CSAT followed a pattern of increasing concerns over whether some AI violations went undetected by proctors. The government used emergency alerts because some students failed to surrender their phones before the exam began. Traditional analog inspection methods are now being questioned for use in upcoming professional licensing exams. These events highlight a growing conflict between advancing technology and the premise that the entire testing process is fair.

The government will continue to monitor cheating as the nation considers whether traditional exam methods can still ensure fairness. Experts believe serious discussions must begin regarding the reform of assessment methods to combat technological advances. It remains open whether analog checks, like stickers on buttons, will be applied to other national examinations. The industry continues to doubt the effectiveness of current security measures against smarter hidden devices. It is unclear if the admissions system will be reformed in time for the 2028 CSAT.

Articles.Title: Pencils down, worries up: CSAT may be over, but nation's anxiety over AI cheating continues

stories.Headline: South Korea's personnel minister says AI will shift civil servants toward judgment and problem-solving work
stories.Summary:
South Korea's Minister of Personnel Management, Tschoe Dong-seok, said in an interview with The Korea Herald published on Nov. 19, 2026, that artificial intelligence will take over routine administrative tasks and that civil servants will increasingly be expected to exercise independent judgment, solve complex problems and engage with the public. He said the next 10 years will be a period of fundamental change in the roles of public officials and the way the civil service operates, driven by the rapid advancement of AI and other technologies. As AI takes over simple and repetitive tasks, he said, public officials will be able to concentrate more on roles that only humans can perform, such as policy judgment, solving complex problems and communicating with the public. Those changes have prompted the government to rethink how it recruits, trains and evaluates its workforce.

The Ministry of Personnel Management plans to expand the Public Service Aptitude Test, currently used for Grade 5 and Grade 7 recruitment, to Grade 9 examinations by 2029, and the new assessment is designed to evaluate logical reasoning, data analysis and decision-making abilities rather than primarily testing memorized knowledge. The government also plans to introduce the assessment to local government Grade 7 recruitment in 2027 and firefighter officer candidate examinations in 2028, while encouraging broader adoption across public institutions. The ministry is pursuing additional pay increases for junior officials in Grades 7 through 9 and discussing further improvements with fiscal authorities, aiming to bring starting salaries for Grade 9 officials to approximately 3 million won, including allowances, in 2027. For specialized AI and information technology positions, the government already offers special salary arrangements that allow compensation comparable to private-sector levels, and the ministry is expanding AI-related hiring to include computer systems development and data. All civil servants are now required to complete at least two hours of AI training annually, supported by a government learning platform that integrates educational resources from public and private providers, and the ministry plans to expand practical training that enables officials to identify workplace problems and develop solutions using AI, alongside specialized programs for managers responsible for leading organizational transformation.

Tschoe said attracting young talent would also require improvements in compensation, and he emphasized that adapting to technological change would require more than simply introducing new tools. He said government workplace culture must also move away from hierarchical management toward greater autonomy, professionalism and collaboration. The ministry introduced a continuous performance management system across government ministries in October, allowing supervisors and employees to regularly review work progress and document individual contributions, and Tschoe said the changes would improve evaluation transparency and ensure civil servants in demanding fields, including disaster response and public safety, receive greater recognition for their contributions. He said the ultimate goal of reforming how the civil service works is not simply to improve efficiency but to enable public officials to focus on policy judgment and problem-solving for citizens and provide better public services.

Tschoe's remarks came as Korea hosted the fourth annual meeting of the Asia Public Service Network in Seoul on Wednesday, bringing together representatives from 14 countries and the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development to discuss the future of public administration. The conference was held under the theme "Leadership for Transformation" and focused on organizational reform, performance management and building a workforce capable of adapting to emerging technologies. Among the findings scheduled to be shared at the conference were those of a joint study South Korea and the OECD conducted from 2025 to 2026 on how participating countries use digital technologies to recruit civil servants, and further joint research and exchanges are planned.

Articles.Title: AI will put premium on human judgment in Korea’s civil service: personnel minister

stories.headline_source: AI will put premium on human judgment in Korea’s civil service: personnel minister

stories.Headline: Korea Consumer Agency finds over half of surveyed Koreans who changed medication on AI advice suffered side effects
stories.Summary:
The Korea Consumer Agency released a survey on Thursday, November 19, 2026, showing that many Koreans suffered health problems after following medical advice from generative AI chatbots. Out of 500 adults who used AI for medicine or supplements in the past year, 110 people changed or stopped their medication without professional help. More than half of those individuals, specifically 56 people, experienced negative health consequences including worsened conditions or adverse reactions. Other findings showed that 133 respondents skipped or delayed hospital visits because they trusted the information provided by the AI services.

The survey revealed that 27.3 percent of affected users had mild reactions like indigestion, while 19.1 percent suffered treatment setbacks and 14.5 percent required additional medical care. AI tools were used most often for over the counter drugs at 76.2 percent, health supplements at 63.8 percent, and prescription drugs at 15.6 percent. Testing of ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and Perplexity showed that some provided medicine advice without checking age or existing health conditions. Furthermore, ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Claude directed users to proxy purchase websites for drugs that are banned from online sales.

The Korea Consumer Agency urged AI companies to block illegal drug sites and make their medical warnings more prominent for users. OpenAI and Anthropic stated they would consider improving their warnings and information filtering, while Google said it would maintain its current system. Perplexity did not provide a response to the agency's recommendations regarding these safety concerns. The agency also warned consumers to use AI only for reference and to always consult a pharmacist or doctor before altering any medication.

Articles.Title: Half of Koreans who changed medication on AI advice suffered side effects, survey finds

stories.Headline: Anthropic raises 81.34 billion dollars in record Nasdaq IPO
stories.Summary:
Anthropic raised 81.34 billion dollars during a record Nasdaq initial public offering on Thursday, November 20, 2026. The company and its seven co-founders completed the largest IPO in history to take the artificial intelligence giant public. Shares opened at 111.50 dollars, which was 34 percent above the initial IPO price of 83 dollars. The stock later closed up 17 percent at 97.17 dollars per share. This debut gave the company a market capitalization of 1.3 trillion dollars.

The offering valued the company at 1.5 trillion dollars, though it briefly topped a 2 trillion dollar valuation. Including a separate 26 billion dollar private placement, the company raised a total of 107.34 billion dollars. Menlo invested over 1 billion dollars for a 1.5 percent stake, while Lightspeed invested over 3 billion dollars for 2 percent. The IPO could deliver 156 billion dollars to charity. The company is a public benefit corporation.

CEO Dario Amodei stated that he and his co-founders believe the most powerful technology should benefit humankind. He mentioned that AI will have a positive human impact on gene editing and CRISPR. Amodei said it will take everyone working together to ensure the technology goes well for future generations. He noted that he and Daniela Amodei lost their father to a disease. He described the mission as bigger than any one company or country.

Protesters rallied against the company in New York and San Francisco following the stock market debut. Some AI safety advocates challenged the safety branding used by the company. Over 400 employees are estimated to be worth more than 100 million dollars each. Some insiders claim these new millionaires are too science-obsessed to buy mansions. Others worry that these wealthy employees might leave the company.

The company launched the first version of Claude and was pre-revenue when it received 50 million dollars in March 2023. Investment firm Iconiq initially passed on the Series E round but changed its mind two months later. Yasmin Razavi of Spark Capital was the only venture capitalist listed in the S-1. The company rose from a startup to a global power in five years. It now ranks as the sixth most valuable public company.

The company will now trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT. Market analysts are watching to see if the success of this IPO will reshape the venture industry. Some investors are monitoring the stock's volatility after it pulled off its highest levels. The articles leave open whether the company can maintain its high valuation. They do not state the company's long-term financial projections.

stories.Headline: Check Point Research publishes a principle it calls gatekeeper asymmetry doom
stories.Summary:
Check Point Research published on November 19, 2026 an exposition of a principle it calls gatekeeper asymmetry doom, stating that if the system vetting adversarial input has strictly less power than the system processing that input, without leveraging some hard problem, this will inevitably lead to doom. The article lists examples of the principle in action, including the limits of static binary classification, the proliferation of sandbox evasions and Check Point's own PuzzleMask research for bypassing external AI guardrails. It also gives a short exposition of how the Time Hierarchy Theorem exemplifies the same principle. It concludes with a recommendation that doomed attack surfaces should be noticed and the gap narrowed as much as possible, by upgrading gatekeeper power or using its existing power more comprehensively. It notes that frontier LLMs, with scaffolding, extended reasoning and code execution in the chain of thought, have significant power in this sense and can meaningfully contribute to narrowing doom gaps, though they themselves are still subject to the principle.

The principle is offered in the same spirit as Moxie Marlinspike's Cryptographic Doom Principle, and the article says leveraging a hard problem excludes cases such as signature verification for binary files, which is many times simpler than executing the file but can still in a certain theoretical world determine whether the binary is malicious. The article phrases the principle more glibly as every quick sanity check involving either cryptography or a silent prayer, and shortens gatekeeper asymmetry doom to doom. Its warm-up example is hash comparison, which it says someone in the industry must have thought solved malware at some point during the 1990s, by collecting all hashes of malicious binaries in a large database for an antivirus to check each executed binary against. The gap there was truly huge, the article says, because the target is the full Turing-complete execution of a binary and the gatekeeper is a simple observation of whether the binary is in some set of known files. Threat actors' counter was infamous and trivial, randomizing the value of some non-load-bearing byte for each compiled binary.

The article says pattern matching and regular expressions underlie YARA rules and act as a backbone of binary classification still to this day, and that as of 2026 AI-augmented YARA rule generation has already improved the throughput of signature authorship considerably, though coverage and consistency are not close to a defender-optimistic utopia. It says regular expressions are not powerful enough to parse HTML and are also not powerful enough to capture the class of assembly subroutines that perform some action, or that perform some action using some specific algorithm, or that perform some action as implemented by some specific sequence of instructions subject to moderate mutation. It says the projected end state would be some malware generation process that takes care to inject this moderate mutation into every subroutine, a new kind of polymorphism. It says static reverse engineering, also known as reading the disassembly, is considered the apex form of static analysis, and that even frontier LLMs have historically struggled with dynamic-equivalent static analysis and in the worst case still do. It says the target victim machine can run the malicious binary but the gatekeeper, human or LLM, cannot natively, and through this capability gap came packers, opaque predicates, control flow flattening, the movfuscator and the Rust Programming Language.

The article says basic computability theory tells us the gap can't disappear outright, and that in the static reverse engineering utopia of a human-expert-level LLM analyzing every new binary in the wild, the new equilibrium lives in the gap, with binaries universally obfuscated to such a degree that a debugger is strongly required. It cites the SolarWinds compromised update, which it says unabashedly attempted to brainwash anyone reading its source code into compliance with the idea that they are looking at benign software. It says mitigations exist for this technique in both LLMs and humans, but it is representative of the general shape of the gatekeeper asymmetry that emerges there. It says malware has traditionally had the property of not wanting to be read, and we do not quite yet live in a world where selection pressures have pushed it to either adopt bleeding edge obfuscation or perish. It describes a possible post-equilibrium world where we miss the old days when we could unpack binaries to make code readable, where our favorite disassembler becomes the vessel of a futile hope, and where an LLM told to reverse engineer a binary ends up forced to reinvent the sandbox from first principles.

In an interlude on what gatekeeper asymmetry doom is not, the article cherry-picks disastrous phenomena in information security that it says have absolutely nothing to do with the principle. It says fuzzing being viable as a vulnerability discovery strategy involves typically no gatekeeper standing between adversarial input and the target application. It says the possibility of supply chain attacks is out of scope, because gatekeepers by definition exist to vet untrusted input, and facing trusted adversarial input is very bad but out of scope. It describes the lagging race for automatic detection of fast flux domains, with detection models advancing from an ineffectual shrug to calculating domain entropy to catch xrewrgfuvhnadfsajkaldsfj.biz, then n-gram frequency engines, then weird edit distance to the dictionary hacks to catch Kwyjibo. It says attackers evolved to use concatenations of randomly generated dictionary words, and the text of the article ends there, mid-sentence, with defenders could have re.

The article leaves open what defenders could have done next in the fast flux domain race, since its text stops at that point. It leaves open how the gap should be narrowed in each of the examples it lists, beyond the general recommendation to upgrade gatekeeper power or use existing power more comprehensively. It leaves open what the post-equilibrium world of obfuscated binaries will look like in practice, beyond the shape it says we can see and find little to like about. It leaves open how frontier LLMs will fare as contributors to narrowing doom gaps while remaining subject to the principle themselves. It gives no date for when the projected end states it describes might arrive, and no figures beyond the 1990s and 2026.

Articles.Title: 30 Years of Gatekeeper Asymmetry Doom: The Paradox that Makes Powerful LLMs More Vulnerable

stories.headline_source: 30 Years of Gatekeeper Asymmetry Doom: The Paradox that Makes Powerful LLMs More Vulnerable

stories.Headline: Sitespace co-CEO Lee Ju-yeon demonstrates smart glasses at Seoul education office training for CSAT staff
stories.Summary:
Lee Ju-yeon, co-CEO of the nonprofit startup Sitespace, is the woman shown wearing black smart glasses and looking at a test paper in recent articles about exam cheating using artificial intelligence glasses. The photo was taken on the 11th at the Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education in Yongsan-gu, Seoul, during a training session for dedicated smart-glasses headquarters staff for the College Scholastic Ability Test. Sitespace had first contacted the Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education to propose introducing the functions of smart glasses, which led to the event. At the training, they demonstrated functions such as taking photos with smart glasses, solving test questions, and communicating with a smartphone. Reporters flocked in to film the demonstration, and photos of Lee appeared in multiple outlets after suspicions emerged on the 12th about cheating with smart glasses by the top scorer in the tax accountant exam.

The session taught staff assigned to test sites in Seoul about the features of smart glasses and how to identify them. Co-CEO Jeong Jin-seorang said they first went to show the actual glasses to supervisors at the education office, and after they asked that teachers also be allowed to handle them directly, it turned into a training session. The other woman photographed with Lee was a practicum guide hired short-term for the day's training. Sitespace assisted with smart-glasses identification at test sites on the 19th, the day of the CSAT, identifying models by checking photos sent by the education authorities when a device suspected of being smart glasses was found. A smart-glasses identification aid app developed by Sitespace, which detects nearby Bluetooth and Wi-Fi signals and helps determine whether glasses are AI-enabled based on photos taken from multiple angles, was also used by CSAT proctors.

Lee said in a phone call with Kyunghyang Shinmun on the 19th that AI glasses can be used for public-interest purposes as well, but it seemed like public opinion was becoming too negative. She said they told the education office they wished to explain the functions of the glasses free of charge for the public good. Lee said she was there for work, so she wore comfortable clothes with no makeup, and she did not expect reporters to come. She said that because the proctor teachers have portrait rights issues, she told them it would be better to photograph us doing the demonstration instead. Lee said that at first she was flustered, but now she thinks she has come to enjoy it a bit, and that she is glad many people have learned that there are AI-glasses services like ours engaged in public-interest work.

Jeong recalled that she finished a lecture for teachers in the basement auditorium and came upstairs, and Lee was surrounded by cameras firing flashes like a movie scene. They said they had attended without knowing the event would be open to the press. After the articles ran, people with visual impairments and related institutions reportedly inquired about trying out the app. Jeong said they received many identification requests, but most turned out to be ordinary glasses. According to the Ministry of Education, one case of cheating using smart glasses during the exam was uncovered that day at a CSAT test site in South Chungcheong Province.

Sitespace launched after winning the top prize in April at the startup competition of Hongik University, the alma mater of the two co-founders. Jeong said they at first envisioned a docent service in museums based on smart glasses, but after meeting many people with visual impairments, they realized what was truly needed was technology that helps with mobility. Sitespace is developing an app that uses the cameras and speakers of commercially available smart glasses to provide audio guidance about the surrounding environment, recognizing objects in the user's line of sight with the camera and conveying them through sound. Instead of long sentences, it is designed to deliver only the necessary information quickly and concisely, such as sliding door, automatic door, and half open. They are currently improving functions through pilot use.

After CES 2027 in Las Vegas, USA, next January, they plan to officially release the app on the Apple App Store and Google Play Store. Lee said that AI glasses and ultra-miniature cameras are being used in negative ways, but technology continues to advance. She said they want to let people know that there are organizations that use technology for the public good. The articles do not say what became of the cheating case uncovered in South Chungcheong Province. The articles do not say how the identification requests were resolved beyond most turning out to be ordinary glasses. The articles do not give the outcome of the tax accountant exam cheating suspicions.

stories.Headline: Waswo X Waswo uses AI to expand photographs in Delhi exhibition
stories.Summary:
Waswo X Waswo’s solo exhibition Long Short Stories opened at Latitude 28 in Delhi and runs until November 20, 2026, bringing together photography, miniature painting, old engravings, a video installation and sculpture. The show is built around an imagined American traveller called Dandy, played by Waswo in Mughal robes, who arrives in a fantastical Indian city with a telescope, befriends a prince, survives battles of magic and finally flees with the prince on an old scooty with arrows flying behind them. The story is funny, absurd and in parts autobiographical, and the photographic works follow Dandy as he is welcomed into a royal court, grows too powerful, is exiled and escapes with the prince. The exhibition also includes a series called Other Stories, which begins with pages from an 1804 Belgian book, The Costume of Hindostan by Baltazard Solvyns, featuring 60 hand-coloured engravings of 18th century India.

The show takes forward the Udaipur-based artist’s long interest in India, the outsider’s gaze and the small personal stories that official history leaves out, which he says build up the larger narrative and give the exhibition its title. Waswo shoots black-and-white photographs that are then hand-coloured and worked on with miniature painting techniques, with flowers, birds and other details painted onto them by his collaborators, a process he says took a year and involves considerable handcraft. The biggest departure this time is the use of AI, which he used to expand his usual square-format photographs into panoramas, and he is wary of the assumption that AI does all the work, saying the craft is still there. He now works with a new team in Udaipur including Dalpat and Banti Jingar, Shankar Kumawat and Chirag Kumawat, with Bhavesh Jingar contributing to the video installation, and he makes sure their names appear alongside his in the gallery and catalogue.

Waswo says he certainly realises he is an outsider here, an American very far from his distant land, though he is now accepted in the Indian art world and treated almost like family in Udaipur, where he has lived for about 20 years. He is also conscious that being a white American has opened many doors for him, and he believes Indians can recognise themselves in this outsider because India is so diverse that people can feel foreign even when they move from one part of the country to another. On his team he says they are stronger together than apart, like a rope that is the sum of its individual strands. Of the Other Stories works, in which he and his collaborators add contemporary details and symbols to the Solvyns engravings to make them satirical and sometimes funny, he says viewers are invited to construct their own stories about those, with no single narrative and each work leaving room for the viewer to imagine one.

stories.Headline: TiE Bangalore and the Aerospace Industry Association of India call for integrated AI adoption in aerospace and defence
stories.Summary:
A report released at the Bengaluru Tech Summit on November 19, 2026, said India’s aerospace, defence and space industry needs to move beyond isolated artificial intelligence experiments toward integrated, production-ready applications. The report, titled “Intelligent by Design: AI Adoption in India’s Aerospace, Defence and Space Industry,” was brought out by TiE Bangalore and the Aerospace Industry Association of India. It identified AI as a significant opportunity to improve engineering productivity, manufacturing efficiency, maintenance and operational performance across the sector. The study also cautioned that adoption across the industry remains uneven, with significant differences in technological maturity, investment capacity and organisational readiness.

Drawing on practitioner perspectives gathered through interviews, working sessions and written contributions, the report identifies four major constraints: fragmented data access, inadequate integration with existing engineering systems, shortages of specialised talent and concerns around accountability in safety-critical applications. It pointed out that aerospace and defence manufacturing involves complex engineering processes, stringent certification requirements and long product lifecycles, so AI-generated outputs cannot be accepted without adequate validation, traceability and human oversight. Applications with potential include predictive maintenance, engineering design optimisation, quality inspection, supply-chain analytics, digital twins and automated documentation, and AI could also help analyse large volumes of engineering data, identify anomalies and improve decision-making. The report highlighted that access to reliable, structured and integrated data was fundamental to successful adoption, since fragmented records, inconsistent data formats and legacy systems often prevent organisations from deploying AI solutions at scale.

The report also underlines the importance of protecting sensitive technical information, intellectual property and operational data, and it flags the non-availability of skilled manpower as another major concern. It says the industry needs engineers who combine domain expertise with knowledge of AI, machine learning, data science and digital engineering tools, and it calls for stronger collaboration between industry, academic institutions and technology providers to develop these capabilities. It also stresses that smaller suppliers and MSMEs could face greater challenges because of limited resources, technology access and investment capacity, and it suggests shared infrastructure, collaborative platforms and targeted support could help them participate in the emerging AI ecosystem. The report was published on November 19, 2026, and the articles do not say what steps, if any, have been taken since its release.

stories.Headline: Sudhanshu Trivedi says AI can predict Rahul Gandhi's repeated remarks and suggests sending an AI version abroad
stories.Summary:
BJP spokesperson and Rajya Sabha MP Sudhanshu Trivedi held a press conference at the party headquarters in New Delhi on Thursday, November 19, 2026, and criticised Congress leader Rahul Gandhi over remarks he made during a two-day visit to the United States. During that trip, Gandhi interacted with students and faculty at Columbia University in New York on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, and at the University of Chicago on Wednesday, November 18, 2026. At the University of Chicago, Gandhi said Indian democracy is sacred and that the Congress is ready to face electoral defeats until people realise the system has been completely demolished. He also said that boycotting elections over alleged flaws in the system would bring an end to Indian democracy, which the Congress does not intend to do.

Trivedi said it was unfortunate that Gandhi was making remarks against India in Chicago, the city where Swami Vivekananda had once brought glory to the country, and that a leader of the opposition was lowering the prestige of Mother India at the same place. He was responding to Gandhi's remarks questioning the 2024 Lok Sabha elections and concerns over electoral irregularities, and to Gandhi's claim that a Brazilian model voted 23 times in India, asking whether anyone coming from abroad should not have an immigration record. Trivedi accused Gandhi of making what he called Hawai allegations about India's electoral process and of lowering the country's image on foreign soil. Taking a swipe at Gandhi's frequent foreign visits, Trivedi said the Congress should stop spending money on sending him abroad.

Trivedi said it is the age of AI and that the Congress should simply send an AI-generated version of Gandhi because he has to repeat the same sentences and words again and again. He suggested an AI model could be programmed with four options, namely making derogatory remarks against India, saying something against the prime minister, creating an uproar over democracy, and embarrassing his own party by raising something anti-India. He claimed artificial intelligence could do a better job than Gandhi's repeated remarks and that AI models were now capable of predicting what the Congress leader would say and the responses to his statements. The BJP also said the Congress should consider sending an AI-generated version of its leader abroad because he keeps repeating the same words.

stories.Headline: Education minister Choi Kyo-jin admits he cannot detect AI cheating as 550,000 students sit a chaotic exam
stories.Summary:
The 2027 College Scholastic Ability Test took place on Thursday amid a controversy over cheating using artificial intelligence. This exam was conducted at 1,312 testing centers nationwide during a period of unprecedented confusion and anxiety. The government failed to prepare and respond adequately to repeated warnings about AI assisted cheating before the test. Some 550,000 applicants took the exam while emergency disaster alerts sounded three times throughout the day. Administrative incompetence and irresponsibility turned this crucial national examination into a crisis and a textbook government failure.

The government required students to cover buttons with stickers and place their bags in hallways to prevent cheating. Prime Minister Han Seong-sook was reportedly behind these specific measures to combat the fears surrounding artificial intelligence. Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin attended a government ruling party meeting at the National Assembly on November 18. He appeared before the National Assembly Education Committee on Monday to discuss the measures against AI assisted cheating. These hastily devised and outdated countermeasures only deepened the confusion for the students and the exam supervisors.

Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin bears particular responsibility for the lack of preparation and crisis management expertise during the exam. Choi is a former middle school Korean language teacher and a regional leader of the Korean Teachers Union. He also served as a three term superintendent of education in South Chungcheong before becoming the minister. When asked if he could detect AI cheating, Choi replied that he could not, perhaps because of his age. This response provoked public outrage and highlighted the failure of the ministry to handle the technological risks.

Many students were likely unsettled by the unprecedented disruptions and the loud noise of the emergency disaster alerts. The tech industry expressed doubts about whether the government can actually catch those who cheated using artificial intelligence. Parents opened up about their frustration over the cheating fears and the chaotic environment of the testing day. The entire examination administration system has now been exposed to international ridicule due to the government's negligence. Students who spent years preparing for the test deserved a fair and orderly environment instead of this uncertainty.

The Anti Corruption and Civil Rights Commission had received 44 petitions calling for measures against AI assisted cheating. AI cheating had already surfaced in a national examination in May and a university essay examination last month. The CSAT was introduced more than three decades ago, but it has never been this chaotic before. Generative AI became widely available recently, which increased the risks of cheating in various high stakes national tests. These repeated failures raise questions about whether education officials understood the risks posed by rapidly advancing technology.

Authorities must now work with investigators and telecommunications companies to determine if AI assisted cheating occurred during the exam. They should also examine how extensively AI was used for cheating in previous CSAT examinations since generative AI appeared. The government must identify the officials responsible for failures in preparation, oversight, and the emergency communication system. The articles leave open whether Minister Choi will resign or if the administration will implement a fundamental overhaul. Systematic planning and effective coordination among agencies are required to prevent future cheating and restore public confidence.

stories.Headline: Riddhipratim Basu wins 2026 Infosys Prize in mathematical sciences
stories.Summary:
Riddhipratim Basu, an associate professor at the International Centre for Theoretical Sciences in Bengaluru, has been awarded the 2026 Infosys Prize in the mathematical sciences category. The ICTS is part of the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research, and before joining it Dr. Basu was an assistant professor at Stanford University. In his work he uses mathematics to understand how random events produce predictable patterns in physical systems. He corresponded with The Hindu by email after the Prize, and the newspaper presented the exchange after editing it for length.

The interview asked Dr. Basu whether there are important phenomena in nature or society for which we still lack the mathematical tools to understand them, and what it would take to develop those tools. He replied that nature has endless mysteries and that we have barely scratched the surface, adding that there are many phenomena we still lack a precise understanding of. He said the systems mathematicians study are more often than not highly simplified versions of the real-world phenomena they are trying to model. He added that mathematicians nevertheless believe these simplified systems capture the essential features of those phenomena.

The 2026 Infosys Prize in mathematical sciences is the award named in the headline, and Dr. Basu is the laureate it refers to. The article gives no further detail on the prize money, the citation or the award ceremony, and it does not say when or where the prize will be presented. It also does not say what Dr. Basu plans to do next with the award or how the recognition might change his research. The published material is limited to the announcement of the award and his edited email remarks on the limits of mathematical modelling.

The article does not report any statement from Dr. Basu on keeping humans at the centre of mathematics as we adapt to artificial intelligence, beyond what the headline indicates. It also carries no comment from the Infosys Prize organisers, from ICTS or from Stanford University on the award. No date is given for when the prize was announced beyond the publication date of November 19, 2026, and no other numbers appear in the text. The article says nothing further about what happens next, so the only follow-up it supports is the interview itself.

stories.Headline: Sociologist William Robinson says AI capital drives global crisis and links with fascism
stories.Summary:
The Cockroach movement in India and cost of living protests across France and Germany in recent weeks express a broader crisis of global capitalism, according to William I. Robinson, professor of sociology at University of California, Santa Barbara. Robinson said the crisis includes a social reproduction dimension that has catalysed movements from below through an explosion of critical consciousness and social solidarity. He said agents of the transnational elite have tried to divide working classes through propaganda, threats and mass psychology. He said the protests resist capitalism's bid to enhance the power of the transnational elite at the common man's expense. He said the system's trajectory, felt through intensified intra-capitalist competition and class wars, is undermining its capacity to reproduce itself and leading to a point of no return.

Robinson's latest book, Pax Silica: The New Ruling Class, explores the emergence of new lords of the world in the age of AI and how they reshape the world to consolidate power. He said AI turbocharges capital's centuries-old drive to deskill and cheapen labour and threatens to eliminate labour altogether. He said AI is extremely expensive, with data centre construction requiring hundreds of billions of dollars in investment, so constant capital grows enormously relative to variable capital. He said the tech sector extracts surplus value from labour and rents from other sectors of capital that do the exploitation. He said the newest and most important source of profits worldwide now, and the accumulation strategy of the new hegemonic block of capital, is repression, warfare, genocide, conflict and chaos.

Robinson said historical figures such as Modi and Trump generate political, social and cultural conditions that deflect from the epochal crisis of global capitalism and disorganise, atomise, divide and confuse the labouring masses. He said the hegemonic block of AI capital brings together tech capital, military-industry repression capital and transnational finance capital, all linked to the new ruling class in the US and worldwide. He said that block decided over the last four to five years to link up with fascism in the state, with Trumpism, with Modiism, with Javier Milei in Argentina and with Netanyahu in Israel. He said the fascist project allows capital to accumulate, including through repression of the working class, and capital in turn supports fascism's political project. He said capital no longer needs our social reproduction.

Robinson said masses of people do not need to read Capital or call themselves Marxists to understand what is going on, and people are in rebellion worldwide without having read Marx. He said the ruling class wages psychological warfare at every level, and AI lets them wage new age warfare through social media, the attention economy and intervention in electoral processes. He said capital has fragmented and atomised people and turned them against one another, so mass struggles need new ways to recompose the global working class. He said a crisis of social reproduction and social disintegration is taking place in India, the US and Africa, and billions of people cannot survive or reproduce themselves and their communities. He said the students' rebellion in France is a working-class struggle against AI and a restructuring of global capitalism driven by digitalisation.

Robinson said the more global capital does not need workers, the more workers become surplus humanity and surplus labour. He said the more AI, machinery and constant capital take over, the less transnational capital needs young people trained to read and think in the abstract. He said there is no need to educate people who become surplus labour, only to control them, lock them up in mass incarceration or even commit genocide against them. He said education is being savagely defunded in France. He said the transition from precariatisation of labour, the shift towards unprotected employment, to the elimination of labour could in theory end capital-labour relations and therefore capitalism as known.

Robinson said AI, like fossil fuel extraction, represents an ability to concentrate disparate sources of value under centralised control and extract rent. He said Harry Braverman, building on Karl Marx in Labour & Monopoly Capital, laid out how capital seeks to deskill labour, cheapen it and take control of the labour process. He said Yanis Varoufakis's Technofeudalism: What Killed Capitalism is really brilliant, but the problem is that it is not feudalism, which is very distinct. He said rents are not new to capitalism and were always there, and super-profits come from profit made in different sectors migrating to the super-profits sector. He said globalisation unleashed an unprecedented historical centralisation and concentration of capital on a world scale in transnational capital and the transnational capitalist class.

Robinson said these people appear as lords of the world because they are the lords of the world, but they are capitalist lords, not feudal lords. He said the construction of data centres means fixed capital is enormously expanding relative to living labour, and the decline in the rate of profit in the long run is new territory. He said AI capital is constructing AI to expand profits, continue to accumulate and control global labour, and it will backfire on capital in the long run. He said we are moving towards World War III and towards a dystopic future nightmare society that previously existed only in Hollywood films. He said the more the struggle pushes forward, the more counter-consciousness to fascist consciousness expands.

stories.Headline: South Korea plans unannounced alerts during exam to catch phone and AI cheaters
stories.Summary:
The government is considering sending unannounced disaster alert messages during this week's annual college entrance exam to catch cheaters using their phones and prevent cheating assisted by artificial intelligence, an interior ministry official said Wednesday. Authorities have been mulling measures to root out cheating during the College Scholastic Ability Test on Thursday following a recent cheating scandal in the certified tax accountant exam using AI. As part of anti-cheating measures unveiled Tuesday, the government said it would send an emergency alert message before the start of the exam to detect any unsubmitted devices. The official said the government is considering sending alerts unannounced in addition to the planned alert scheduled to be sent between 8:25 and 8:30 a.m. President Lee Jae Myung said Tuesday he had instructed authorities to review sending additional alerts, even during testing, to catch cheaters.

The government will send another disaster alert at an unspecified time during this week's annual college entrance exam, the interior ministry said Wednesday. While the first alert will be sent at 8:30 a.m., just before the start of the test, the ministry plans to send another message at an undisclosed time to find any test takers with unsubmitted phones. The ministry said the alerts will ring for 10.5 seconds at full volume, urging the public not to be alarmed. The education ministry notified schools nationwide Wednesday that it will allow test takers to only bring in pencils inside CSAT exam rooms, revising its list of permitted items. Authorities earlier notified test takers that they were allowed to bring black marker pens, correction tape, erasers, pencils and mechanical pencil lead for the exam, and under the revised rules, stationery items except for pencils will be provided at the test sites.

President Lee Jae Myung called on officials Tuesday to thoroughly prepare anti-cheating measures for the nationwide college entrance exam set to take place this week, describing cheating as a grave crime that undermines social trust. Lee made the remarks during an emergency meeting to inspect the country's readiness for the CSAT, also known in Korean as Suneung, scheduled for Thursday, following widespread concerns over cheating using AI. Lee said the Suneung is a symbol of fairness and a ladder of opportunity in our society during a video meeting held from Manila, as he wrapped up his visit to the city for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit. Lee added that officials must take strict action against those who engage in misconduct, adhering to a zero-tolerance policy, while asking them to come up with response measures against AI-assisted cheating. In a subsequent social media post, Lee said the government plans to offer a reward of over 100 million won, or US$74,805, per case to those who report instances of cheating involving advanced gadgets, should the case be confirmed.

Anti-cheating measures announced earlier Tuesday include physically checking all glasses worn by test takers, covering buttons on their clothes with stickers and blocking Wi-Fi networks inside and near the test sites. The government also warned that test takers caught cheating will be banned from the CSAT for the next 10 years, while facing criminal punishment. The move appears to reflect concerns of misconduct involving miniature cameras hidden inside personal items brought by test takers. South Korea has recently been rocked by the recent confession of the top scorer on this year's certified tax accountant exam that he had cheated with the help of AI and digital devices.

The incident has deepened worries of such cheating on the upcoming CSAT, widely seen as a major life event in South Korea, where the university one goes to can heavily influence career prospects. The anti-cheating measures were unveiled Tuesday, and the education ministry notified schools nationwide Wednesday of the revised permitted items list. The first alert will be sent at 8:30 a.m. just before the start of the test, while the planned alert was scheduled to be sent between 8:25 and 8:30 a.m.

The interior ministry official said that if the time is known, there would effectively be no point in additional alerts. President Lee made his remarks during a video meeting held from Manila, as he wrapped up his visit to the city for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit. The CSAT, also known in Korean as Suneung, is scheduled for Thursday. The government is considering sending alerts unannounced in addition to the planned alert, and the ministry plans to send another message at an undisclosed time to find any test takers with unsubmitted phones.

The ministry said the alerts will ring for 10.5 seconds at full volume, urging the public not to be alarmed. Under the revised rules, stationery items except for pencils will be provided at the test sites. The government plans to offer a reward of over 100 million won per case to those who report instances of cheating involving advanced gadgets, should the case be confirmed. Test takers caught cheating will be banned from the CSAT for the next 10 years, while facing criminal punishment.

stories.Headline: Krishna Rao steers Anthropic through its blockbuster initial public offering
stories.Summary:
Krishna Rao, the 43-year-old Indian-origin finance chief, is steering Anthropic through its initial public offering, which the livemint.com article published on 19 November 2026 says goes public today. Rao joined Anthropic in 2024 and is set to become one of Wall Street's closely watched executives as the AI company lists. The livemint.com article calls the listing a blockbuster initial public offering and says Rao has played a pivotal role in the company's growth and financing strategy. Earlier this year Anthropic found itself at odds with the US government over the safe use of artificial intelligence, and Rao stood firm during that dispute. The Pentagon wanted the company to loosen restrictions on how its tools could be used in combat and threatened to cancel a contract worth hundreds of millions of dollars.

The prospectus, signed by Rao and other executives, reported a revenue run rate of $81 billion as of October 31, up $10 billion from the end of September. When Rao joined in 2024, Anthropic had annualised revenue of about $250 million, and the company was aiming to scale that to $1 billion. Rao initially wondered how long it would take to reach that target, but the milestone was reached within months, he said on a podcast. At JPMorgan Chase's New York headquarters last Friday, a packed room of high-net-worth investors gathered to hear Anthropic's top executives. JPMorgan Asset and Wealth Management CEO Mary Erdoes singled out Rao, calling him the "CFO extraordinaire" and the person "who is helping us get through things".

Rao leads hundreds of finance staff and has five close deputies, and he has helped expand Anthropic's investor base globally, including in the Middle East. "We think the benefits of AI are not specific to one country or region," Rao said in a previous interview with Bloomberg News. "We really want the benefits of what we're building to be global in nature." Anthropic declined to make Rao available for the story, Bloomberg reported. Rao has said he has moved away from thinking about sales growth in linear terms, and he said on a podcast that "it's really hard to predict this business."

Gaurav Kapadia, who runs investment firm XN and holds a large stake in Anthropic, said Rao was a great firewall preventing investors from pushing the company into a decision that was culturally incompatible with their long-term objectives. Kapadia's account was reported by Bloomberg, which described Rao fielding calls from investors urging Anthropic to give in to the Pentagon's demands. Brad Gerstner, founder of Altimeter Capital, told Bloomberg that "Krishna is humble and purposely flies under the radar," and he described Rao as "an important voice in the AI discussion". Before joining Anthropic, Rao worked at Blackstone and Airbnb, where he played an important role in the company's IPO and interacted with top investors. Goldman Sachs bankers viewed Rao as the "killer in the room" who could answer every question about Airbnb's IPO, according to a person familiar with the matter cited by Bloomberg.

Rao was among the first executive hires outside Anthropic's close-knit group of seven co-founders. One of his early priorities was helping the company expand its enterprise business, which was still nascent and overshadowed by OpenAI. Anthropic's expensive AI roadmap, investments in chips and data centres, and commitment to responsible AI development will be under closer examination by shareholders once the company enters public markets. Rao's ability to balance commercial interests with Anthropic's principles is likely to face greater scrutiny once the company enters public markets. While CEO Dario Amodei has become a prominent voice in the AI debate, Rao's job will be to help investors understand the financial risks and rewards of the technology's rapid expansion.

The livemint.com article was published on 19 November 2026 at 12:46 PM IST and was written by Sanchari Ghosh. The Axios article, titled "Behind the Curtain: Anthropic contradictions," was published on 18 November 2026 and written by Jim VandeHei and Mike Allen. Anthropic declined to make Rao available for the story, Bloomberg reported. The articles leave open how Anthropic's shares will perform once the company enters public markets. The articles also leave open how Rao's balancing of commercial interests and Anthropic's principles will fare under shareholder scrutiny.

stories.Headline: UBS forecasts S&P 500 reaching 8,200 by end of 2027 while cutting US equities to neutral on AI uncertainty
stories.Summary:
UBS Global Wealth Management said on 19 November 2026 that it expects the S&P 500 to reach 8,200 by the end of 2027, an upside of around 12% from current levels, according to a Livemint report. The brokerage based that target on resilient economic growth and continued expansion in corporate earnings across the US equity market. At the same time, UBS shifted its rating on US equities to neutral, citing elevated valuations, high market concentration and growing uncertainty around the artificial intelligence investment cycle. The report said the year-end 2027 target is broadly in line with Wells Fargo's outlook but remains below the more bullish projections from Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley. UBS estimated that S&P 500 earnings will rise 29% in 2026 and then expand a further 15% in 2027, even as it anticipates a moderation in earnings growth.

It expects global AI-related investment to keep expanding, rising to $1.4 trillion in 2027 and reaching $1.5 trillion in 2028. Within the AI ecosystem, the brokerage favours well-capitalised hyperscalers and select semiconductor and chip-equipment companies with strong competitive positions and clear opportunities to generate revenue from AI adoption. UBS cautioned that the path to further market gains could be volatile, flagging rising risks around AI-related disruption, financing and execution alongside elevated investor expectations. UBS explained its move to a neutral stance by saying that cannibalization, financing and execution risks around AI have increased while expectations and index concentration remain high. The brokerage added that while it expects gains, the path could be volatile.

The report noted that the AI trade has come under pressure amid opposition to large data-centre projects and concerns over the returns generated by heavy investment in the technology. Regulatory uncertainty following the US midterm elections and developments surrounding Nvidia have also contributed to investor caution, according to the report. The sustainability of the AI investment cycle is emerging as a key consideration for equity investors as markets assess whether substantial spending on AI infrastructure can translate into lasting earnings growth beyond 2027. UBS said the ability of companies to convert heavy AI spending into sustainable revenue and profits will be crucial in determining whether the current market momentum can be maintained. The brokerage's outlook suggests that while AI investment and corporate earnings could continue supporting US equities, investors may need to be more selective as expectations remain elevated.

stories.Headline: Police in Seoul continue investigating alleged AI cheating by perfect LEET scorer Lee Jin-woo after his death
stories.Summary:
Lee Jin-woo was found dead in Seoul on Thursday, November 19, 2026. He was the first person to earn a perfect score on the Legal Education Eligibility Test. Police and fire authorities found the 32 year old man in Gangdong District. He died before a planned livestream to dispel allegations of AI assisted cheating. A short note was found, but it did not address the cheating claims.

The IDA admissions research institute planned a verification event at a Gangnam District studio. It required metal detectors and ear endoscopy checks to rule out any hidden devices. Lee would solve the Korean language section of the current College Scholastic Ability Test. The event would be livestreamed on YouTube and include a session with a language instructor. Lee had previously entered Korea University in 2024 and Seoul National University in 2026.

Police said they will continue the investigation to establish the substantive truth of the case. They assigned the matter to the financial crimes investigation team of the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency. Lawyer Park Eun-sun of 2yoo law firm said it is important to uncover cheating methods. Lawyer Kwak Joon-ho of Law Firm Chung said investigations can proceed to establish the facts. Police are now seeking a forensic examination and an autopsy to determine the cause.

Lawyer Jeong Joon-yeong of HMP Law said meaningful results are difficult without a statement from Lee. Some test takers say the state is failing to manage exams properly in the AI era. A 22 year old preparing for civil service exams said national exams have lost credibility. This person mentioned the tax accountant cheating case and the LEET case as examples. Others view the failure to appear at the verification as a tacit admission of guilt.

Lee once placed in the sixth to eighth tiers on the national college entrance exam. He later claimed to have developed his own study method to improve his scores. He faced allegations that his sharp improvement resulted from using artificial intelligence during his tests. Some claimed he received suspicious private tutoring in life science just before the CSAT exam. His LEET answer sheet showed signs that he had marked answers in the wrong rows.

Police applied for an order to preserve Lee's answer booklet at Younghoon High School in Gangbuk. They want to use the booklet from last year's CSAT as evidence in the probe. Investigators are looking for any accomplices who may have helped Lee cheat on the exams. The articles leave open whether the police will find evidence without a statement from Lee. It remains unknown if the forensic examination will reveal more about his death.

stories.Headline: LG Electronics promotes 44 executives and forms a CEO-led AI partnership team to speed AI and robotics growth
stories.Summary:
LG Electronics announced on November 19, 2026, that it promoted 44 executives and reshuffled its leadership to improve its competitive edge during the AI era. The company created a new AI partnership team that reports directly to CEO Lyu Jae-cheol to strengthen ties with global tech firms. These changes aim to accelerate growth in future businesses such as robotics, mobility, smart factories, and data center cooling. The organizational restructuring will take effect on December 1, while the executive promotions become official on January 1.

The reshuffle includes promoting Baek Seung-tae, the head of the home appliance business, and Lee Sang-woo, the head of management strategy at LG Corp, to presidents. Lee Sang-woo will now lead the TV and display business, while Baek Seung-tae continues to manage home appliances and robot actuator commercialization. LG Electronics is establishing a new applied business unit under its Eco Solution division to expand its data center cooling operations. Additionally, a new unit under the vehicle division will focus on advanced driver assistance systems and high-performance computing.

Company leadership stated that these moves are intended to speed up decision-making and respond more quickly to changing market conditions. To achieve this, regional heads for Asia, Europe, North America, Latin America, the Middle East, and Africa will now report directly to the CEO. The company is also leveraging a multibillion-dollar deal to supply chillers for data centers with a combined capacity of 5 gigawatts. LG Electronics aims to reach 1 trillion won in annual chiller sales as early as next year.

To support this growth, the company plans to establish a manufacturing subsidiary in Virginia next year to meet rising demand. This strategy builds on the creation of a robotics business center in July that also reports directly to the CEO. The electronics maker continues to streamline its global management structure by reducing layers between regional operations and headquarters. These efforts are part of a broader push to develop robotics and AI infrastructure into primary growth engines.

stories.Headline: JPMorgan co-president Doug Petno calls AI market swings expected as winners and losers emerge
stories.Summary:
JPMorgan Chase co-President Doug Petno discussed the current state of artificial intelligence and the Japanese market during a recent exclusive interview with Nikkei. He addressed the significant market swings currently affecting companies related to artificial intelligence on November 20, 2026. Petno explained that these fluctuations are a normal result of a sector that has expanded very rapidly. This growth has been driven by massive amounts of capital moving through the industry and substantial funds being raised.

The situation requires an understanding that volatility is expected when so much money enters a new technological space. While the bank is very keen to adopt these new technologies, Petno emphasized that the human element in banking is not going away. He believes that the emergence of clear winners and losers within the AI field will naturally cause these price swings. The bank continues to monitor how these shifts impact the broader financial landscape and the Japanese market.

Doug Petno is the person responsible for sharing these views on behalf of the leadership at JPMorgan Chase. He stated that the current instability is simply the expected volatility of a space that has grown dramatically. By highlighting the movement of capital, he suggested that the market is adjusting to the scale of AI investment. He maintained that the integration of technology will not replace the essential role of human professionals.
