stories.Headline: Van Hollen centers AI regulation in bid to lead Senate Democrats
stories.Summary:
Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland held a news conference in the Capitol Building in Washington, D.C., on Thursday, November 19, 2026, to make artificial intelligence regulation a central part of his campaign to lead Senate Democrats. Van Hollen argued that Congress must move more aggressively to confront the technology's growing risks. He said the party needs a leader willing to challenge the powerful companies seeking to shape the rules. The remarks offered one of the clearest policy distinctions yet in his challenge to Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the current Democratic leader. Schumer is seeking another term leading the caucus after helping engineer the party's sweeping victories in this month's midterm elections.

Van Hollen laid out a vision for a more assertive Senate that would impose mandatory safeguards on AI companies and hold them liable for harm caused by their products. He also proposed overhauling congressional procedures to prevent legislation opposed by powerful corporate interests from languishing indefinitely. His proposed safeguards include mandatory independent evaluations of AI systems, greater corporate liability for the harm they cause, and protections against threats to employment, privacy and cybersecurity. He has also raised the possibility of banning systems capable of recursively improving themselves, a development he fears could eventually exceed humanity's ability to control them. He endorsed a rules proposal advanced by Senator Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Senator Steve Daines, a Montana Republican, that would allow qualifying bipartisan legislation emerging from Senate committees to receive expedited consideration.

Van Hollen, 67, has sought to cast his candidacy as a response to voters demanding fundamental change, arguing that Democrats cannot return to the governing practices that preceded their election victories. He said the Senate moves like a glacier compared to the rushing stream of AI risks, and that the chamber needs to be equal to the AI age. He said there has been way too much centralization of power in the body, and that things coming out of Senate committees with big bipartisan votes never see the light of day. He said it is important to have someone who has clearly been leading in the fight against special interests, to get big money out of politics. He warned that proposals to regulate AI would encounter an army of lobbyists, and that you have to turn the page to get that done.

Schumer, 75, who has led Senate Democrats for a decade, has countered that his record of recruiting candidates, raising money, and building a majority demonstrates why he should remain in charge. In a Senate floor speech Wednesday, Schumer warned that insufficient federal action could expose the country to serious technological disruptions. He said the country needs to ensure the safe development and deployment of AI, or there will be more outages and, God forbid, even catastrophic events going forward. Schumer has also advocated stronger AI safeguards, making the contrast between the candidates more a question of legislative strategy and urgency than a disagreement over whether regulation is necessary. Critics of Schumer also note that one of his daughters recently joined OpenAI to oversee policy and partnerships in the Northeast, after previously working on public policy for Amazon, and another of his daughters has worked at Meta.

The contest is the first competitive race for Senate Democratic leader in more than three decades, and it will be decided in a secret ballot on Dec. 1. With 56 current and incoming senators eligible to participate, either candidate would need at least 29 votes to win if everyone votes. Schumer has said he has secured enough commitments to win, and he has the public backing of 15 senators and senators-elect, including Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, Tammy Baldwin of Wisconsin, Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada, John Fetterman of Pennsylvania, Ruben Gallego of Arizona, Kirsten Gillibrand of New York, Mazie Hirono of Hawaii, Mark Kelly of Arizona, Angus King of Maine, Jack Reed of Rhode Island, Jacky Rosen of Nevada, Brian Schatz of Hawaii, Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, and Sherrod Brown of Ohio. His supporters credit him with helping Democrats win a Senate majority that is expected to reach 56 seats next year. Van Hollen has said that approximately 15 colleagues support him, although most have not publicly declared their intentions, and his announced backers include Senators Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Senators-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota.

Van Hollen pointed Thursday to the American Innovation and Choice Online Act, bipartisan legislation sponsored by Senators Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota and Charles Grassley of Iowa that sought to restrict anticompetitive practices by dominant technology platforms. The measure advanced out of committee in 2022 but never received a floor vote after an intense lobbying campaign by technology companies. Schumer declined to bring that measure to the floor at the time, expressing doubts that it could secure the 60 votes needed to advance. Van Hollen said the episode exemplified a broader institutional failure. Concerns about AI's potential to displace workers, threaten cybersecurity, and drive up electricity costs due to the proliferation of energy-intensive data centers was a central topic on the campaign trail this year, Van Hollen said.

Several other Democrats, including Senator Elissa Slotkin of Michigan and newly elected senators who campaigned on changing the party's leadership, have said they will not support Schumer without committing to backing his challenger. An additional 30 Democrats have not said whom they plan to support. Asked Thursday whether special interests were influencing the leadership contest, Van Hollen did not directly accuse Schumer of a conflict of interest, but he emphasized his own record of challenging wealthy donors and corporate lobbyists. In a video posted on social media this week, Van Hollen said the country needs to make sure people aren't paying higher electric bills for data centers built by the biggest and richest corporations on the planet. The articles do not say what happens after the Dec. 1 secret ballot.

stories.Headline: Insurers and clinicians say a licensed human should make final medical-necessity decisions, not AI
stories.Summary:
Panelists at a recent HLTH discussion agreed that artificial intelligence should not make final medical-necessity decisions in prior authorization, and that a licensed human should make the call instead. Sean Robbins, executive vice president and chief operating officer of the Blue Cross Blue Shield Association, said on the panel that artificial intelligence should not deny an authorization for medical necessity. He said a licensed clinician should make the call rather than merely review it, and that artificial intelligence can help that clinician but the human should decide. Dr. Warris Bokhari, chief executive officer of Claimable, a company that helps patients appeal denied health insurance claims, agreed that a qualified human should make denial decisions. He argued that in oncology that human should be the treating physician rather than the insurance company.

Bokhari said he does not think an unnamed person at an insurance company who is effectively practicing medicine should make the decision, and that although it is called a coverage decision, to the patient it is absolutely a necessity decision. He described it as a clinical decision rendered by a human who has never met the patient, never looked at their tests, never met their family and has no context. He said he believes there should be a way to hold health plans accountable for making the wrong call, and he cited Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Illinois, alleging it had denied liver transplants for cancer patients using evidence that included case data from 1994. He urged Blues plans and other insurers not to stand in the way of treating physicians and patients when a patient's life may be at risk within a certain period of time.

Robbins responded that he does not want there to be an inappropriate denial in any situation ever, and he added that accountability and transparency are important. He said the industry needs to be getting the right answers to the right people quickly. Dr. Mandy Cohen, another panelist and a national advisor of Manatt Health, stressed that the whole model needs a revamp, and she said the question is not how to speed up the process but how to rethink the whole process. She said the rethink is important and is linked to underlying payment incentives, and that the reason insurance companies exist and have these guardrails is because providers do ask for low-value care.

stories.Headline: Independent mathematicians verify that Levent Alpöge used Claude to prove the Riemann hypothesis
stories.Summary:
On the morning of November 20, 2026, Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claimed that he had used the company's Claude AI model to solve the Riemann hypothesis, which Scientific American describes as perhaps the most important open problem in mathematics. The hypothesis was first posed in 1859 by mathematician Bernhard Riemann, and it suggests that a hidden pattern underlies the distribution of the prime numbers, which are divisible only by themselves and 1. Alpöge initially checked the work by writing out the proof in the programming language Lean, since a Lean-coded proof that compiles without error is usually taken as confirmation that the logic and math in each step is correct. Independent researchers, including Massachusetts Institute of Technology mathematician Andrew Sutherland, have now separately compiled Alpöge's result in Lean without issues.

Verifying the claim required answering more than whether the code compiles, because a proof can be correct while addressing a subtly different point or idea. Kevin Buzzard of Imperial College London explained in a blog post that the first question when judging a PDF that comes with Lean code is what the theorem statement in the code actually says and whether it corresponds to the real theorem statement. Sutherland said the Lean proof has been compiled and independently rechecked by the Lean kernel with only the three standard axioms, and he added that the chance of anything being fishy is approximately zero. Researchers are still making sure the proof contains no hack, dodge or shortcut that changed the meaning of the initial hypothesis or any other mathematical rules or truths.

That remaining check is called a comparator run, which typically takes a matter of hours, and Buzzard wrote on an online chat server for the Lean community that a successful run would confirm two things. It would check that the code does not do anything nefarious such as redefining the meaning of any of the symbols in the statement, and, assuming it is run in paranoid mode, that the code compiles with several independent kernels. The second point matters because it would show the code is not just exploiting an as yet unknown bug in Lean's official kernel. Scientific American's editor's note of November 20, 2026 states that this is a developing story and will be updated.

Articles.Title: The AI Riemann hypothesis proof is almost certainly true, independent mathematicians attest

stories.Headline: American Hospital Association hosts webinar on protecting patient care from AI-era cyberattacks
stories.Summary:
The American Hospital Association announced on Nov. 19 that it will host a webinar on Dec. 2 at 1 p.m. ET about protecting patient care as cyberattacks become more frequent in the age of artificial intelligence. The session will explore strategies for identifying the critical systems that must remain operable during an incident and for strengthening cyber resilience and readiness. Attendees will learn how to define and rehearse the minimum set of systems needed to continue care delivery during a cyber incident. The webinar will also cover steps organizations can take to strengthen their cyber resilience within 90 days, and registration is open now.

The announcement sits alongside several recent AHA items on cybersecurity risks facing hospitals. F5, a technology company specializing in multi-cloud application delivery, disclosed six critical vulnerabilities on Nov. 18 in its BIG-IP network traffic service, which is used in healthcare. An AHA Cybersecurity Advisory released Nov. 18 details a Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency alert about a critical Java vulnerability. An FBI report released Nov. 13 describes cyber actors weaponizing ARTEX, an open-source, large language model-driven agentic artificial intelligence platform, and other AI platforms to accelerate cyberattacks.

The AHA is responsible for the webinar, which is aimed at helping hospitals prepare for attacks that the association says are becoming more frequent with artificial intelligence. The articles do not name individual speakers or quote officials about the December session. The related items point to federal agencies and companies as the sources of the warnings, including CISA, the FBI and F5. The AHA also produces a podcast featuring Brian Kaiser, a supervisory special agent with the FBI's Cyber Division, and Chad Beebe, deputy executive director of the American Society for Health Care, discussing why hackers target hospital operational technology.

The context is a run of federal and industry warnings about vulnerabilities in hospital systems and tools that attackers can exploit. Operational technology, which includes network-connected devices that control physical systems like elevators and security systems, is often vulnerable, according to an AHA blog item. The articles do not say what will follow the webinar beyond the 90-day resilience steps it covers. Hospitals interested in attending can register through the AHA.

stories.Headline: Nvidia leadership upheaval and Anthropic IPO prompt investors to weigh AI sector health as stocks fall
stories.Summary:
Stocks tumbled to end the week on Friday, November 20, 2026, as worries about artificial intelligence rattled the market, and by the closing bell all three major averages were deeply in the red. The Dow Jones industrial average fell more than 900 points on the day, while the Nasdaq dropped more than 5 percent and erased all of its gains for the year. The S&P 500 is now down more than 10 percent from its recent high, which means it is in what investors call correction territory. Investors were weighing the health of the AI sector following Nvidia's leadership upheaval and Anthropic's record IPO, according to the PBS News report.

The market move came as a second federal judge blocked President Trump's Memorial Arch in Washington, D.C., and the judge in Virginia called the project a rush job that lacks a legal basis. She put construction there on hold indefinitely, pending the outcome of legal challenges to the arch, after a separate judge earlier in the week extended a previous block for two more weeks. President Trump is trying to build a 250-foot Memorial Arch near Arlington National Cemetery, which has led to criticism from veterans groups and local environmentalists. In Iowa, a federal appeals court is blocking the U.S. Army from detonating several tons of bomb-making chemicals amid concerns over environmental and health risks, and the controlled explosion had been scheduled for that day.

The explosion was expected to send lead dust as far as 60 miles around the area, and Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle had agreed to postpone the detonation until Monday. Telle warned that a coming drop in temperatures could further destabilize the material, and it is unclear whether the court will weigh in again before Monday. In Florida, heavy storms are moving north after drenching parts of the Atlantic coast, and torrential rains turned roads into waterways, with some areas already seeing their wettest November on record. The National Hurricane Center is warning of severe widespread flash flooding for parts of Eastern Florida and says the threat could carry into next week, while in California heavy flooding left some neighborhoods in Los Angeles underwater.

In Poland, authorities say two Russian missiles and a suspected drone landed in Polish territory overnight, and CCTV footage in Southeastern Poland showed a large explosion and a bright flash. The crash site was around 20 miles from where European troops from 11 countries were taking part in rare military exercises to prepare for a potential postwar Ukraine mission. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the incursions an intentional provocation and said Poland, which neighbors both Ukraine and Russia, must be involved in future peace talks. Russia carried out new strikes on Ukraine overnight and into the day as part of its response to Kyiv's recent attacks on a strategic bridge, and authorities in Western Ukraine said a Russian attack on a railway station killed at least two people.

stories.Headline: University of Chicago IT staff build AI prototypes at internal hackathon
stories.Summary:
At the University of Chicago, IT leaders noticed that AI implementation was not keeping up with the tools, policies and training rolling out across campus, Valerie Archambeau, director of communication technology services, said. Archambeau and a group of IT colleagues devised a hackathon for IT Services staff instead of producing another round of training. Ultimately, 81 staff members formed 17 teams, working in person and remotely, and built more than a dozen working prototypes with Claude Code at the event. The hackathon was held in March 2026 and started as a way to get developers comfortable with AI coding tools. The team soon realized the event needed to extend beyond those who already had coding experience.

UChicago’s AI rollout began in 2024 with tools including Zoom AI Companion, Microsoft Copilot and an in-house ChatGPT instance called Phoenix AI. Despite a dedicated website with resources and training opportunities, users were not adopting AI as readily as leaders hoped. Participation in the event was voluntary, and the ITS team offered information sessions ahead of the event so participants were prepared. Representatives from Amazon Web Services were onsite to answer questions, and attendees received a temporary AI enterprise license to use during the event. The organizers also held office hours where people could talk to them one on one.

Allison Kallo, manager of learning design, said leadership was looking for people to experiment and try using code in a safe, fun environment. Archambeau said the original thought was to show developers what they could do with the tool, but by the very next meeting the team asked why they were limiting it to developers. Archambeau said the focus was on the problems participants were seeing that the technology could address. Tom Kompare, manager of application development, said his team members already had some experience with the tool, so he created a short guide on the software development process and the AI tool itself. Fingerhut said office hours meant you were not going to show up and be the only one who did not understand it.

Staff submitted project ideas and signed up by self-reporting their skills and experience, from never having touched an AI tool to using it daily. Kompare said the hackathon team made sure groups had different levels of AI experience and professional skills, and hopefully the same interest in their team’s chosen idea. Kompare wrote a prompt for the AI tool to suggest team assignments, then reviewed the results himself. Mentors including Kompare, UChicago IT Manager Arjun Lagisetty and several AWS staff were on hand in case teams got stuck. On day two, teams had the morning to finish and test their projects and put together a three-slide presentation, which they delivered in the afternoon.

The HR team built a tool that classifies a role, matches it to the official job catalog and job code, and drafts job descriptions from standard templates and approved language. Kallo said the prototype became the base of a tool the department now uses. Another team built a synthetic data generator that produces deliberately messy data sets with edge cases included. A third project was a language-learning Chrome extension that swaps selected words on any web page into a foreign language. The university has also started a monthly AI user group, open to anyone on campus, where people demo what they have made.

Participants did not have access to production systems or test environments, and anyone working with structured data had to sanitize it first, with no student records, no health data and no personal information of any kind. Kompare said the directive was to bring your own data but fake it. Archambeau said university data is not allowed to leave the institution’s environment or be used to train the vendor’s tools, and she advises other institutions to meet with their security teams early. The organizers brought in the head of IT’s accessibility group and gave participants a prompt asking the tool to meet Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1 AA standards, with sufficient color contrast, alt text and keyboard navigation. The team plans to implement lessons in the event’s next iteration early next year, when the virtual option will be eliminated, teams will be smaller and participants will have more time to demonstrate their tools on the second day.

stories.Headline: Fear Erupts, AI Stocks Tank, but so Do Gold, Silver, Cryptos, Nearly Everything but Treasuries
stories.Summary:
Fear hit the markets on Friday, November 20, 2026, and during the week, and everything sold off, stocks, especially semiconductor stocks, gold, silver and crypto, everything except Treasury securities, which rallied. The Nasdaq fell 5.3% on Friday to 22,618, down 10.0% during the week, down 18.4% from its high on October 6, and down 2.7% since the beginning of 2026. The S&P 500 index fell 3.7% on Friday to 6,910, down 8.6% for the week and down 11.9% from its high in early October. Nvidia's stock plunged 14% on Friday to $125.53 at the close, down 47% from its high on October 6, and the seven-week plunge unwound all the gains since June 2024. The Cboe Volatility Index jumped to 40.03 intraday on Friday and ended the day at 35.89, after being below 20 a week earlier.

The Anthropic IPO seems to have sapped the last bit of energy out of the stock market, and its shares fell 8.5% during regular hours on Friday to $88.91, after falling through the IPO price of $85 a share during the day before recovering a bit. SanDisk fell 16.1% on Friday and was down 73% from its June high, Intel fell 8.0% and was down 64%, Micron fell 13.9% and was down 51%, Qualcomm fell 7.5% and was down 41%, Broadcom fell 12.2% and was down 37%, AMD fell 13.3% and was down 36% from its October high, and TSMC fell 9.5% and was down 35% from its October high. Silver plunged 7.4% on Friday to $41.08 per troy ounce, down 16% during the week and down 66% from its all-time high in late January, unwinding all the gains since July 2025. Gold dropped 4.0% on Friday to $3,539 per troy ounce, down 9% during the week and 37% from its all-time high, unwinding the gains since August 2025. Bitcoin dropped 14% this week to $58,761, where it had first been in March 2021, and since its peak in September 2025 it has dropped by over half.

Wolf Richter wrote in WOLF STREET that there was fear in the markets on Friday and also during the week, and that for months everyone has been talking about the end of the AI bubble. He wrote that the fear now is that it is not just idle talk anymore and that the pieces are starting to line up for all to see. He wrote that Nvidia was at the core of the AI trade and of all the circular financing, selling the shovels into the gold rush and charging more for them than its customers could afford. He wrote that to maintain its revenues, profits and stock price, Nvidia recycled these cash flows and added commitments to help fund its customers so they could afford its shovels at its sky-high prices. He wrote that this system already started unraveling a while ago and that the fear now is that it will unravel entirely.

Richter wrote that fears get exhausted after a while, the profit motive takes over, people jump back into the fray to pick up sold-off stuff, and then there is a bounce, and that there may have been enough fear on Friday to trigger that. He wrote that contrarians use a big jump in the VIX, which doubled this week, as a buy signal for at least a short-term bounce. He wrote that another indication was Friday's after-hours trading, with many beaten-down semiconductor stocks, including Nvidia, trading higher by 2% or 3% or more after hours. He wrote that even the 10-year Treasury yield, which had plunged during the day as Treasury prices jumped on the haven trade, reversed in late trading and headed higher. He wrote that "Nothing goes to heck in a straight line" is the old WOLF STREET dictum, and that we just might see a bounce in tech stocks next week along with some unwind of the massive Treasury rally.

Richter wrote that Nvidia's shares started tanking in early October even before everyone was crawling all over the company for the scandal of a lifetime that keeps spawning new scandals, and that the company is in the process of getting vivisected. He wrote that the x trillions in market value, portfolio value and 401(k) value that have evaporated during this selloff set everyone atwitter, and that on the way up those trillions appeared out of nothing and it was no big deal. He wrote that when a lot of it happens it impacts consumer spending and the economy overall. He wrote that other people have been waiting for this sell-off, cash in fist, to jump in and buy some beaten-up stuff, no matter how dubious, and that this is starting to line up. He wrote that the Nasdaq is still positive, if barely, year-over-year, and is not at the low of the year, which was in late March when it fell to 20,690 briefly before rallying massively again and setting a new high.

Richter wrote that the S&P 500 is still 1% in the green for the year and up 4.7% year-over-year. He wrote that the Nasdaq is down 2.7% since the beginning of 2026. He wrote that the semiconductor stocks had been plunging off their highs for months, interrupted by big bounces. He wrote that gold and silver had already gotten hammered for much of the year after the huge years-long rally topped off by a proper mania ended in late January. He wrote that bitcoin's drop to $58,761 marked six-and-a-half years of massive volatility to nowhere, with no interest and no dividends.

Richter wrote that we just might see that bounce in tech stocks next week, along with some unwind of the massive Treasury rally. He wrote that a dead-cat bounce allows the stock market to breathe. He wrote that fears get exhausted after a while and the profit motive takes over. He wrote that there may have been enough fear on Friday to trigger a bounce. The article leaves open where the selloff will end and whether any bounce would last.

stories.Headline: Accenture cuts token spend 40 to 85 percent on Amazon Bedrock across four client engagements
stories.Summary:
Accenture applied six levers for optimizing token spend in four client engagements across telecom, insurance, mining, and a large enterprise deployment, as described in an AWS blog post published on November 19, 2026. The post says Accenture applied these levers in production on Amazon Bedrock. Where savings were measured, token spend fell by about 40 to 85 percent, the post says. Accenture withheld the client names to protect client confidentiality. The post says results are specific to each client's workload and may vary.

The post describes cost allocation tags applied through Amazon Bedrock application inference profiles, one profile per application or workload, tagged by team, cost center, and environment. It names AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR 2.0) delivered through AWS Data Exports, Amazon CloudWatch, and Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging as the telemetry. It describes Accenture's Cost per Business Transaction framework, which aggregates model invocations, retries, tool calls, and agent handoffs into one fully loaded cost figure. It says Amazon Bedrock prompt caching is designed to reduce cached input token costs by up to 90 percent for supported models. It says Amazon Bedrock batch inference runs at 50 percent lower cost than on-demand pricing for select models and writes results to Amazon Simple Storage Service.

The post says Amazon Bedrock intelligent prompt routing can reduce costs by up to 30 percent without compromising accuracy, and it points readers to Amazon Bedrock Pricing for any routing charges. It says semantic caching can be implemented on AWS with a vector store such as Amazon ElastiCache in front of the model. It cites an AWS benchmark on 63,796 real chatbot queries where a 0.90 similarity threshold produced a 74.5 percent cache hit rate, 92.3 percent accuracy, and 72.5 percent cost savings. It says distilled models in Amazon Bedrock are up to 500 percent faster and up to 75 percent less expensive than original models, with less than 2 percent accuracy loss for use cases such as RAG. It says Amazon Bedrock Guardrails should stay on every route and semantic cache expiry should be set so users do not receive outdated answers.

The post says the first engagement was a large enterprise deployment where every request went to a frontier model with no caching, model tiering, or batching, and three changes together cut monthly token cost by 85 percent. It says about 15 percent of tasks still needed the top model for hard, open-ended reasoning and the rest ran on lighter models. It says the second engagement was a telecom operator with $12 million in annual token spend, where input tokens fell by 70 percent and annual token spend fell from $12 million to $3.8 million, a 68 percent reduction. It says Accenture validated output quality against the operator's pre-change performance benchmarks. It says the third and fourth engagements each applied a single cache layer, an insurer using model-layer prefix caching and a mining operator using an application-layer semantic cache, and token spend fell by about 40 percent combined without model routing changes or training investment.

The post says the Linux Foundation has launched the Tokenomics Foundation to develop open standards for AI cost economics. It says token spend often grows even as per-token prices fall, and that without cost allocation tags a cloud invoice shows AI spend as a single line item rather than by team, workload, agent, or model. It says cheaper tokens expand adoption and agentic workloads multiply invocations, so consumption can rise faster than unit prices drop. It says the economic question is whether business value grows faster than the cost of the intelligence required to produce it. It says the six levers are organized into three phases and that AWS and Accenture recommend working through the phases in order, and it says two of the engagements applied several changes at once so those results reflect the combined effect.

The post recommends connecting consumption to owners and outcomes, applying one lever at a time, measuring cost, quality, and business value, and building on what works. It lists four operating tenets: establish a quantitative baseline for cost and quality before applying any lever, validate output quality with held-out evaluation sets drawn from actual production traffic rather than synthetic benchmarks, apply one lever at a time per workload to attribute results and roll back cleanly, and document quality test results and rollback procedures in regulated industries such as financial services, insurance, and healthcare. It says Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is an environment to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model, and it mentions AgentCore Evaluations, a capability that provides batch e. The post does not give the outcome of the fourth engagement separately or name the clients.

stories.Headline: Uzbekistan cybersecurity official Bekzod Muminov urges UN, UNESCO and ITU to lead global AI dialogue
stories.Summary:
Bekzod Muminov spoke at the second International Conference on Cyber Diplomacy on 19 November 2026. He is the Head of the International Relations Department of Uzbekistan's Cybersecurity Center State Unitary Enterprise. Muminov discussed the role of artificial intelligence during panel discussions at the event. He addressed how this technology affects governments and international relations. The official highlighted both the benefits and the risks of these tools.

Muminov stated that the UN, UNESCO, and the International Telecommunication Union should lead the international dialogue. He noted that nations currently have different approaches to regulation, data protection, and technological standards. He also mentioned that countries differ in their access to computing resources. These differences could lead to isolated technological ecosystems if they are not addressed. Such isolation might restrict the exchange of innovation, knowledge, and technology.

Muminov said that artificial intelligence helps governments process large volumes of information and analyze international developments. He claimed it allows for better assessment of economic risks and political risks. He also stated that the technology can improve diplomatic communication. However, he warned that it creates challenges regarding disinformation and information reliability. He noted that it can lead to cyber threats and the manipulation of public opinion.

The official argued that diplomacy must go beyond discussing technological issues to shape international rules. He believes this approach can build trust and prevent new forms of geopolitical tension. Muminov wants the development of artificial intelligence to strengthen cooperation between nations. He believes it should not become a new instrument for technological competition. He views these processes as an opportunity to strengthen positions in the international system.

The articles explain that artificial intelligence enables faster analysis of global developments for various governments. This technology is being integrated into diplomatic efforts to manage risks and communication. The current landscape is marked by a lack of unified global standards for AI. Multilateral platforms are seen as necessary to represent the interests of the international community. These platforms would provide a balanced approach to global technological governance.

The articles do not state what specific actions the UN or ITU will take next. They leave open how nations will resolve their differences regarding data protection and standards. It remains unclear if the international community will successfully prevent the rise of isolated ecosystems. The text does not specify a timeline for creating these new international rules. No further details are provided on the outcomes of the conference.

stories.Headline: Researchers warn AI may entrench clinical evidence monopoly without data access reform
stories.Summary:
Researchers Shenwei Wan and Xiaoguang Lei published an opinion in PLOS Digital Health on November 19, 2026. They evaluated if artificial intelligence will dismantle the global concentration of medical evidence or establish a new monopoly. The authors examined how AI could reshape clinical evidence production systems. They focused on the resources required to generate authoritative clinical evidence. This evidence currently remains skewed toward high-income nations and well-funded institutions.

The authors cite 784,585 trial sites from 2006 to 2012, where 83 percent were in 25 OECD nations. Meanwhile, 91 low-income or lower-middle-income countries hosted only 5 percent of these sites. They note a median trial cost of 19 million US dollars for US drug approvals between 2015 and 2016. Wan and Lei propose an AI-enabled evidence commons to allow more institutions to produce and challenge evidence. This requires secure data access, documented methods, and local research capacity.

Wan and Lei state that an evidence monopoly is the structural concentration of funding, data, and expertise. They argue that this imbalance shapes global practice guidelines, regulatory approvals, procurement choices, and reimbursement policies. The authors suggest that academic journals require structured statements documenting software versions and validation protocols for AI synthesis. They advocate for design fitness, where methodological choices match the specific research question. They claim technical refinements alone cannot resolve the geographic concentration of clinical research.

The authors note that clinical AI models and triage algorithms are subject to software revisions and algorithmic drift. They mention that automated depression detection tools showed narrow linguistic and geographic coverage. Large language models shifted emotional category distributions when applied to online cancer-support posts. The authors warn that AI can produce fabricated claims, inconsistent data extractions, and search omissions. They state that AI cannot recover patient populations that were never recorded.

Evidence-based medicine was established to integrate research evidence with clinical expertise rather than professional authority alone. Randomized controlled trials are indispensable but demand substantial capital, personnel, ethics oversight, and infrastructure. A scoping review identified 388 AI tools across 137 studies for evidence synthesis. These tools may reduce workloads like searching literature, screening citations, translating text, and extracting data. However, this experimentation has not yet demonstrated reductions in overall synthesis costs.

Funders and international bodies must invest in local trial infrastructure, regulatory frameworks, and community partnerships. This should align with the World Health Organization 2025 action plan for sustainable clinical trial ecosystems. The authors suggest using quasi-experiments, implementation science, and target-trial emulations as complementary approaches. The articles leave open whether AI will actually reduce systemic global research inequality. They do not state if the proposed evidence commons has been implemented.

stories.Headline: GC Evans president Mark McNamer uses AI to help small manufacturers compete globally
stories.Summary:
GC Evans, an automated packaging manufacturer tucked into a wooded area just off Interstate 530 in Little Rock, has been building custom systems for the food and beverage industry since the 1950s, and it is now using artificial intelligence to reshape both what it builds and how it operates, according to a November 19, 2026 article by Jeremy Harper in Arkansas Money & Politics. Company president Mark McNamer said that with AI, GC Evans can offer the same resources and capabilities that previously only very large companies could offer, and that work a staff of 10 once did can now be done more efficiently by just one or two engineers. AI-assisted tools let the company's engineers create three-dimensional floor plans and visualize custom packaging solutions with considerably less time and effort, while tasks that once required hours of coding can increasingly be accomplished through simple prompts. Manuals, instructions and technical documentation can also be generated in a fraction of the time, which the article says leaves a smaller company capable of offering services, speed and pricing that can compete with much larger international manufacturers.

Artificial intelligence is also becoming part of the machinery itself, with GC Evans manufacturing inspection and rejection systems that identify flaws in packaging as products move through a production line. Those systems can increasingly incorporate AI cameras, meaning machine-vision cameras paired with artificial-intelligence software capable of analyzing products and packaging almost instantaneously, and rather than relying exclusively on traditional programming, the systems can be trained to recognize acceptable products and identify defects or inconsistencies. On a beverage line, that might include damaged cans, improper labels, faulty closures or other packaging problems, and McNamer said the AI cameras enable the systems to process 2,000 12-ounce standard aluminum cans per minute. He said the cameras are programmed through prompting rather than tedious coding, which means a person does not need to be a computer scientist to make an adjustment.

McNamer is the person responsible for the effort described in the article, and he said many food and beverage companies would very much like to work with USA-based manufacturers, but overseas conglomerates have acquired many of the companies providing automated packaging solutions. He said AI is one tool GC Evans uses to even the playing field and bring manufacturing to Arkansas, and he believes the effect on jobs could look very different for small and midsize companies than for large ones. While very large companies will likely reduce workforce, he said, smaller companies like GC Evans will increase hiring due to added productivity, and what is happening is a shift of workforce to where it is most needed. He added that like any technology, companies will adapt to it and be better for it.

The article places GC Evans in the context of a national conversation that has focused on the possibility that automation will eliminate jobs, and it says the combination of speed and accessibility shows why AI could prove especially consequential for smaller manufacturers. It is not simply automating individual tasks but giving smaller teams access to capabilities that once required significantly more personnel, specialized expertise and capital. For Arkansas manufacturers, the article says, that may ultimately be one of AI's greatest opportunities, because the technology can give smaller companies productivity, engineering capabilities and sophisticated tools once available primarily to multinational corporations. That allows Arkansas businesses not simply to compete globally but to bring more of that work home, according to the article.

stories.Headline: Google AI search answers push marketer Marshall Evans to cut search ad spending
stories.Summary:
Marshall Evans, a North Carolina marketer who has bought Google search ads for small businesses like home repair companies and fitness studios for more than a decade, has moved ad dollars away from those ads over the past six months because AI-written responses now often appear above the usual links and ads. For one trophy company he now allocates $500 a month to search ads, down from $2,000 a month about a year ago when Google introduced a feature called AI Mode, and he is shifting money toward streaming services such as Tubi, other search engines like Bing and social media sites like Reddit and Nextdoor. Last month Google reported for the first time that search advertising had fallen to less than 50% of its $128 billion in quarterly revenue, with search ad revenue rising 12% and falling short of the 15% Wall Street expected. Google CEO Sundar Pichai said during the earnings call that the company is focused on building the best search user experience, followed by monetization, and Google has said it wanted to make AI search features appealing to users and would think about advertising later.

Users now often see AI Overviews, an AI-written answer to their query, at the top of the search results page, and the bottom of the summary invites them to interact with a chatbot through AI Mode, but advertising in those AI answers and chatbots has not yet taken off. Advertisers can pay more for the chance to feature their ads in AI Mode, but there is no guarantee the promotion will show up, and Google does not offer advertisers a way to buy guaranteed placement in AI Overviews. Google spokesperson Thomas Schoenfelder said AI is driving an expansionary moment for Search, with AI features leading to increased usage and overall query growth including commercial queries, and that the company's ads experiments have shown promising results. Google also said users were flocking to its AI search tools and that the number of search queries was growing faster than it had in the past five years.

Thomas Monteiro, a senior analyst at Investing.com, said Google is trying to take a business that was the best in the world for 10 years and transform it into a different business without the same advantages, and that making the transition is a lot harder than management thought it would be. Valerie Schlosser, a marketing executive at the global creative agency VML in New York, said what is being seen is arguably the biggest change in searcher behavior, with people spending more time in conversation with chatbots and less time surfing the web. She added that advertisers are not abandoning Google search but are trying to figure out how to survive in the new system, and that clients want to test new things like ChatGPT and Perplexity without totally pulling back from Google. Max Anderson, CEO of OnlyFinder, a service that helps users find creators on the adult entertainment site OnlyFans, said his ads either will not show on the page at all or will show down the page below an AI Overview, and that his costs have probably tripled or quadrupled in the last three years.

Anderson said he is gradually and mathematically pulling back as costs rise and now devotes about half as much spending to Google ads as he did in the early days of the business, declining to discuss specific spending because the numbers were proprietary. He is not planning to abandon Google but is flummoxed by how to get his business mentioned in AI Overviews, saying he would love a way as a business to predictably play there but has not seen one yet. The article describes AI as a double-edged sword for even the biggest companies, with Google standing to benefit enormously from the technology including in its booming cloud computing business while AI takes a toll as the company adjusts. The articles do not say what happens next beyond Google's stated focus on the user experience first and its confidence about its trajectory.

stories.Headline: Samsung promotes three semiconductor executives to president and keeps its dual-CEO structure
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics announced on Nov. 20 its regular executive reshuffle for 2027, involving six appointments: three promotions to president and three changes in responsibilities, about a week earlier than the late-November timing the company had followed over the previous two years. The company retained its dual-CEO structure, with Vice Chairman Jun Young-hyun, head of the Device Solutions Division, and President Roh Tae-moon, head of the Device eXperience Division, remaining in their current roles. Both men will step down from their concurrent roles as heads of the Memory Business and the Mobile eXperience Business, respectively. Samsung reported consolidated operating profit of 107.4 trillion won in the third quarter, with the DS Division contributing 106.5 trillion won, or approximately $79.67 billion.

The centerpiece of the reshuffle is the promotion of three semiconductor executives who have helped strengthen the division's technological competitiveness. Hwang Sang-joon, who served as head of Memory Development and the DRAM Development Office, has been promoted to president and appointed head of the Memory Business, and he will continue to lead the DRAM Development Office alongside his new role. Cho Sang-yeon, previously a vice president overseeing Device Solutions America, has been promoted to president and appointed head of the System LSI Business, and he is expected to focus on securing new clients. Lee Jong-myeong, previously head of Process Development at the DS Division's Semiconductor Research Institute, has also been promoted to president and will serve as the DS Division's chief technology officer and head of the institute.

Jun will focus on strengthening the competitiveness of future semiconductor businesses, including foundry, in his capacity as head of the DS Division, while Roh will concentrate on developing new businesses, including robotics, while continuing as head of the DX Division and the RX Business Development Office. Choi Won-joon, previously head of the MX Business Development Office, has been appointed the new head of the MX Business, and he has served as the division's chief operating officer since March 2025 and led the development of the Galaxy S26 and Galaxy Z Fold8. Samsung said the appointments were intended to strengthen organizational dynamism and promote generational renewal by placing executives who had driven record semiconductor performance and improved development competitiveness in key leadership positions. The company also plans to finalize and announce regular executive appointments at the vice president level and below, along with an organizational restructuring, in the near future, and it will continue its policy of promoting outstanding employees through appointments throughout the year.

stories.Headline: Amazon says Connect Talent uses structured questions and evidence-based scoring to run AI-led job interviews at scale
stories.Summary:
Amazon published a blog post on November 19, 2026 describing Amazon Connect Talent, an AI-led structured interview service. The post says Connect Talent uses structured questions, adaptive follow-ups and evidence-based scoring to gather consistent, job-related information. Amazon built the service around three core design principles and evaluated it through internal research and independent expert review. The post says the service brings established hiring science to AI-led interviews at scale. The article appears on the AWS blog under the Artificial Intelligence topic.

Connect Talent builds each interview around the competencies required for the role, using job requirements and established occupational frameworks to create behaviorally anchored scorecards. The AI interviewer checks after every answer whether the candidate has provided enough evidence and asks targeted follow-up questions when details are missing. A separate evaluation process identifies demonstrated behaviors, cites supporting transcript passages and calculates each competency score from 1 to 5 using a fixed formula. When the transcript lacks sufficient evidence, Connect Talent flags the competency instead of producing a score, and missing evidence does not automatically count against the candidate. The service evaluates transcribed responses without video, voice tone or physical appearance, excludes candidate identity information from scoring and evaluates each competency separately.

An independent I-O psychology firm reviewed Connect Talent's baseline output before human editing and found it retained critical job information in 100% of the job descriptions reviewed. The firm found 91% of generated competencies were clearly traceable to the job description, 98% of interview questions targeted the intended competencies and 94% of rubric signals clearly measured the intended competency. Hiring teams can review, select and edit the competencies, scorecards and questions before using them. The post says this human oversight gives organizations control over the interview process while helping them apply structured hiring practices at scale.

A second independent review covered 36 interviews assessing specific strengths and concerns, creating 252 rubric signals, and Connect Talent aligned with expert scoring decisions in 89.3% of cases. Scoring alignment reached 97.6% when candidates provided clear evidence and 92.9% when only considering candidate concern signals. The evaluation produced a Cohen's kappa of 0.79, which the post calls substantial agreement and just under the 0.81 standard for almost perfect agreement. In a preliminary evaluation, scores based only on the first response were up to 1.14 points lower on a five-point scale than scores based on the full conversation. Connect Talent's structured scoring used all five points of the rating scale, while holistic LLM-as-judge scoring concentrated its ratings within the middle three points.

The post cites decades of research in industrial-organizational psychology, including Schmidt and Hunter, 1998, and Sackett et al., 2022, showing structured interviews help organizations evaluate candidates and predict job performance. It says delivering structured interviews at scale requires significant time and expertise to develop competencies, create questions, train interviewers and evaluate responses consistently. It cites Zhu et al., 2026, finding that some AI scoring approaches concentrate ratings within a narrow range, making differences harder to recognize. It also lists Booth et al., 2021, on bias and fairness in multimodal machine learning, as a reference. The post says a traditional one-way video interview gives a candidate a fixed question and only one opportunity to answer it.

Amazon will present BIZ332, "Every Candidate, Every Time: AI-Led Structured Interviews with Amazon Connect Talent," a Chalk Talk led by Sunitha Srivatsa and Gerald Friedland at AWS re:Invent 2026. Session 1 runs Monday, November 30, 2026, 10:00, 11:00 AM at Caesars Forum, Level 1, Academy 409, with a repeat Thursday, December 3, 2026, 3:00, 4:00 PM at MGM Grand, Premier 309. The post says the session will explore structured interviewing, adaptive follow-up questions and evidence-based scoring. The post does not give pricing, availability dates or customer names for Connect Talent. The post does not say how many candidates or organizations have used the service.

stories.Headline: SK hynix earns SIL 3 certification for its LPDDR5X memory and development processes
stories.Summary:
SK hynix said on Nov. 11 that its LPDDR5X product and its development processes had received Safety Integrity Level 3 certification under IEC 61508, an international standard written to reduce accident risks from failures in electrical and electronic systems. The certification, announced in a report dated Nov. 13 by The Elec, extends the low-power DRAM from vehicles into robots and smart factories. The company had already obtained automotive functional safety certification in January. IEC 61508 defines four safety integrity levels, running from SIL 1 up to SIL 4, and SK hynix's chip was designed and validated to hold safety conditions in real time without interrupting system operations.

The certification lets SK hynix answer functional safety requirements from customers building real-time robotic control platforms and systems-on-chip. Earlier, the company obtained Automotive Safety Integrity Level D, the highest rating under the ISO 26262 automotive functional safety standard, for the same LPDDR5X product. SK hynix also received certification under ISO/SAE 21434 for its cybersecurity management system, which covers threat analysis, security design and verification, and vulnerability management during development and mass production of automotive memory. The article says data security has grown more important as memory is deployed in physical AI systems, because autonomous vehicles and robots act on sensor data and AI results stored in memory.

Kim Jong-hwan, vice president and head of DRAM Development at SK hynix, said that as the physical AI market takes shape it is becoming increasingly important to establish safety and security systems that comply with international standards throughout the memory development process. He said the company will strengthen its memory leadership in the physical AI market by building on safety and security capabilities validated across the automotive and industrial sectors. The article states that if cyberattacks manipulate stored data, vehicles could fail to detect obstacles and brake, while robots could move in the wrong direction and potentially cause accidents. The report does not say what SK hynix plans to do next beyond using the certification to meet customer requirements.

stories.Headline: Texas regulator restarts data center permits before ERCOT audit finishes
stories.Summary:
Texas environmental regulators restarted data center permit reviews in November 2026. The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality resumed processing after the Governor's office gave notice on November 13. This action ended a pause that began with Governor Greg Abbott's September 21 directive. The agency issued an air permit for a data center and gas plant on November 16. This restart occurred before the grid operator ERCOT finished its full audit.

The pause required the agency to halt permits until ERCOT completed an audit of data centers. ERCOT plans to file two reports by December 10, including the Community Impact Review Report. The Batch Zero Eligibility Verification Report will decide which loads of 75 MW and above remain eligible. The Public Utility Commission of Texas is expected to discuss these reports on December 17. A new Democratic governor, Gina Hinojosa, takes office on January 19, 2027.

The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality is responsible for evaluating applications under state and federal laws. A spokesperson for the agency stated that they will follow all applicable laws during reviews. Governor Greg Abbott previously directed the agency to stop permits until the ERCOT audit was finished. The Governor's office later told the agency that ERCOT finished gathering information on community impacts. Gibson Dunn confirmed that the permit pause described in its alerts has ended.

Public Citizen and other watchdogs claim that the agency is issuing permits unilaterally and prematurely. Kathryn Guerra of Public Citizen said that agency leadership began issuing these permits on its own. These critics argue the restart is early because the final audit reports are not yet filed. Developers waiting on the grid are affected by the ERCOT study and the April 9, 2027, deadline. AI builders who depend on Texas capacity must track these changing regulatory and political conditions.

Governor Abbott directed the PUC and ERCOT to audit data centers in August 2026. The agency took its electronic filing system, STEERS, offline after some approvals were flagged in October. ERCOT reviewed responses from 257 developers and about 5,140 questions by November 5. Bipartisan proposals filed between November 9 and March 12, 2027, seek to repeal data center sales tax exemptions. These proposals also aim to require water-use disclosure and bar local tax incentives.

The 90th Texas Legislature convenes on January 12, 2027, and the regular session ends May 31, 2027. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa may rescind or replace the directives issued by Governor Greg Abbott. TCEQ chair Paup's term expires August 31, 2027, and two PUC terms expire September 1, 2027. It remains open whether the restart covers every permit type or only some specific ones. The articles leave open which specific projects will benefit from the resumed permit reviews.

Alton will also offer its manufacturing capacity to help XUP move its autonomous designs into full-scale production. XUP brings specialized technology including vision AI, lidar, inertial measurement units, and RTK-GNSS-based precision positioning. An official from Alton stated that their experience in sourcing and mass production for electric bicycles provides a core competitive strength. This expertise allows the company to extend its capabilities into various next-generation smart mobility fields, including AI robotics. The partnership will pair Alton's network integration and hardware skills with the precision perception and control technologies developed by XUP.

stories.Headline: Mike Diegel argues AI oversight must govern actions as he builds Pulpo in Arizona
stories.Summary:
A letter published on November 19, 2026 in The Gila Herald, written by Mike Diegel of Pima, Arizona, responded to a November 18 article about Senator Mark Kelly’s new framework to protect Americans from the most advanced AI models. Diegel wrote that Senator Kelly is right about the problem, saying companies should not grade their own homework and that self-regulation has failed. He added that oversight which only arrives after an incident is not oversight at all. The letter argued that Kelly’s proposed fix still misses the core issue because it governs the model rather than the action.

The framework described in the letter calls for a rulebook of hazard levels, independent examiners embedded at AI companies to review safeguards as models are built, and testing and liability before and after deployment. Diegel wrote that none of that stops a consequential action at the moment it happens, because a test can pass, an examiner can sign off, and a company can disclose a risk while the AI system still makes the transfer, deletes the file, or sends the data. He argued the danger is not only how smart a model is but what authority it has been given to act, since a safe model with write access is dangerous and a dangerous model with no authority does nothing. For that reason he said his team is building Pulpo in Arizona, with governance sitting before execution as a narrow, one-use permit for one specific action, with durable evidence afterward.

Diegel wrote that no permit should mean no governed effect, and that anything else is monitoring dressed up as prevention. He said he respects Senator Kelly’s intent and his service, but that protecting Americans requires governing what AI is allowed to do, not just how it is tested or watched. The letter was signed by Mike Diegel of Pima, Arizona. The articles give no further details on the framework, on Pulpo, or on what happens next.

stories.Headline: Apple builds its M5 Pro, Max and Ultra chips from three dies in a first true chiplet design
stories.Summary:
SemiAnalysis published a teardown on 20 November 2026 finding that Apple's M5 Pro, M5 Max and M5 Ultra are the company's first true chiplet design, built from three separate dies. The analysis rests on physical inspection rather than vendor briefings, because SemiAnalysis bought the chips and had them torn down. The speaker walks through die sizes, core counts, cache allocations and PHY structures measured from the silicon. The M5 Ultra fuses two M5 Max dual-die assemblies with a connection density Apple claims is more than 6x that of the M3 Ultra's UltraFusion. The lab had not yet obtained an M5 Ultra, so its layout is inferred from the M5 Max's second interconnect and Apple's own marketing claims.

Apple taped out three dies, one CPU die and two GPU dies, a small and a large one, all fabricated on TSMC's N3P process. The CPU chiplet is roughly 168 mm², the small GPU chiplet about 157 mm² and the large GPU chiplet about 300 mm². The M5 Pro pairs the CPU chiplet with the small GPU chiplet, the M5 Max pairs it with the large GPU chiplet, and the M5 Ultra uses two CPU chiplets and two large GPU chiplets. The CPU die carries 18 cores in three clusters, four Thunderbolt 5 PHYs and no E-cores, and the GPU chiplets scale cleanly at 2:1, the large one with 40 GPU cores, 48 MB of System Level Cache and a 512-bit memory interface.

The speaker draws a firm line between Apple's earlier multi-die chips and the M5 generation, saying the M1, M2 and M3 Ultra fused two of the largest dies of a generation in a classic multi-chip-module arrangement. He defines a true chiplet architecture by two design targets, optimizing the area of each individual die to improve yield and outsourcing different functions of the SoC onto different chiplets so the final product only works once at least two different chiplets are combined. He acknowledges the definition is contestable, saying everyone is entitled to their own chiplet based opinion, but states it as his position. He calls the GPU chiplets interesting and a bit boring at the same time, because the halving is so exact that the small die reads as a straightforward cut of the large one. He flags the four Thunderbolt 5 PHYs as the standout by area, saying it is crazy to see how big analogue SerDes are becoming and how much space the command-and-control area is taking up.

The speaker says the new interconnect uses TSMC's SoIC-mH, called SoIC-X F2F by TSMC, the same hybrid bonding technology behind AMD's 3D V-Cache but deployed side-by-side rather than stacked, with mH standing for molding horizontally. Standard advanced packaging attaches finished dies to an interposer through microbumps around 25 µm and perhaps down to 18 µm, while hybrid bonding aligns matching exposed copper interconnects surrounded by dielectric and heats them so the copper fuses directly. He describes the result as almost like fusing the metal layers, creating one large coherent chip, and says the pitch drops below 10 µm and approaches 3 µm in the most advanced processes. He says placing the chiplets side by side rather than stacked avoids the thermal problems of a vertical sandwich, citing the A20 Pro's move to WMCM packaging with DRAM moved to the side of the SoC. He says Apple had access to hybrid bonding for some time, as other TSMC customers did, but waited for the side-by-side implementation, and that it is not unlikely Apple worked on the solution with TSMC directly.

The speaker says the last UltraFusion chip, the M3 Ultra, used InFO-LSI packaging with a local silicon interconnect and solder-based microbumps, and that Apple never published the bump pitch but measurements show 25 µm. He says a 6x density increase implies a pitch of about 10 µm or less, squarely in hybrid bonding territory and impossible with solder. He says the left side of the CPU die holds the classic 16-core Neural Engine of eight dual-cores, which he notes has since been doubled on the M6, and that only the M5 Ultra gets double the NPU because it uses two CPU chiplets. He says the twelve new P-cores, internally called M-cores, are split into two mirrored six-core clusters each with 8 MB of shared cache and a dedicated AMX unit, and suggests the split may be for power management so an entire cluster can be shut off. He says the S-core cluster is slightly asymmetrical with two S-cores on top and four below a 16 MB shared cache, each S-core getting a 1 MB slice of L2 cache.

The speaker says the CPU die is larger than a base M5 and that the small GPU die is essentially a cut-in-half version of the large one, which he suggests helps with development time. He says the bottom shoreline of the CPU die is a large IO array running from left to right through an Apple proprietary high-speed PHY for cameras and other sensors, a 4-lane Display PHY and 16 lanes of PCI-Express, most likely Gen 5, arranged in four 2x2 clusters. He says the die also includes an on-die NAND controller and an AES engine in the secure enclave, and that four large Display Engines sit to the right of the M-cores. He says only some media acceleration logic near the die-to-die interface stays the same size across both GPU chiplets. He says the faint striped structure on the CPU die's upper shoreline is the physical layer of the new die-to-die interconnect and matches an identical PHY on the adjacent shoreline of either GPU die.

The speaker's verdict is that hybrid bonding materially improves the M5 series rather than serving as a label, and he closes with the aside, Can't innovate anymore my ass. The open item to track is the M5 Ultra itself, whose configuration is derived from the M5 Max's second interconnect and Apple's density claim, not from a teardown, so the first physical analysis of that part will either confirm the two-Max construction or complicate it. The other thread worth watching is whether side-by-side hybrid bonding spreads to other Apple products, given the company's apparent shift toward thermal-conscious packaging across the A20 Pro and M5 lines. The articles give no date for when the M5 chips shipped or when the M5 Ultra will be torn down. The articles give no statement from Apple beyond its marketing claim on connection density.

stories.Headline: Local authority teams learn to assess AI risks to human rights at Paris academy
stories.Summary:
Teams from 20 local and regional authorities took part in the first HUDERIA Academy for Local Authorities, held in Paris from 17 to 19 November 2026, where they learned to assess the risks that artificial intelligence poses to human rights, democracy and the rule of law. The event was organised by the Centre of Expertise for Multilevel Governance at the Congress of Local and Regional Authorities, working closely with the Council of Europe's Steering Committee for New and Emerging Digital Technologies. Over the three days, participants from 18 member states applied HUDERIA, the Council of Europe's methodology for assessing the impact of AI systems, to a fictional AI-supported public consultation. They identified risks, mapped stakeholders and designed measures to mitigate those risks. The authorities represented included Camden from the United Kingdom, Fingal County from Ireland, Amaroussion from Greece, Bergen from Norway, Valongo from Portugal, Lviv and Rivne from Ukraine, Arezzo from Italy and Harghita County from Romania.

The list also included Ventspils from Latvia, Vigo from Spain, Diyarbakır from Türkiye, Bitola and Resen from North Macedonia, Bălți from the Republic of Moldova, Shkodër from Albania, Kutaisi from Georgia, Szentendre from Hungary, Turnišče from Slovenia, Nõo from Estonia and the Association of Netherlands Municipalities. Participants described HUDERIA as practical and relevant, and several began applying it to their own projects while obtaining feedback from their peers. They committed to maintaining an alumni network and called for follow-up and continued opportunities to engage with HUDERIA. The Academy is an official event on the Road to Geneva AI Summit 2027 and a contribution to the Council of Europe's New Democratic Pact for Europe, and it supports implementation of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence.

Annika Vaikla, the Congress co-rapporteur on AI and Deputy Mayor of Viimsi in Estonia, urged authorities to use AI to give public servants more time for people while keeping people in control. She called for AI literacy among political leaders, staff and citizens, and for smaller municipalities to have access to shared expertise. The articles say several themes ran through the Academy, including that local AI should be human-centred, socially anchored and community-led, and that public trust has to be earned through openness and clear accountability by keeping humans in the loop. The articles do not say what specific follow-up measures were agreed beyond the alumni network and the calls for continued engagement.

stories.Headline: SemiAnalysis finds Apple builds M5 Pro, Max and Ultra as three-die chiplets on TSMC hybrid bonding
stories.Summary:
SemiAnalysis published a die-level teardown finding that Apple's M5 Pro, M5 Max and M5 Ultra are the company's first true chiplet design, splitting the system-on-chip across three separately built dies. The teardown, published on 2026-11-20, reports that the dies are joined with TSMC's SoIC-mH hybrid-bonding packaging instead of solder. SemiAnalysis bought the chips, pulled them apart and measured them rather than relying on a vendor briefing. The CPU chiplet measures roughly 168 mm² and carries 18 cores, four large Thunderbolt 5 PHYs and no efficiency cores. The GPU chiplets are a precise 2:1 scaling of one another at about 300 mm² and 157 mm².

Apple taped out three dies, one CPU die and two GPU dies, a small one and a large one, all on TSMC's N3P process. The M5 Pro pairs the 168 mm² CPU chiplet with the small GPU chiplet of about 157 mm², and the M5 Max pairs the CPU chiplet with the large GPU chiplet of about 300 mm². The M5 Ultra uses two CPU chiplets and two large GPU chiplets and was not measured because the lab had no unit. The large GPU die has 40 GPU cores, 48 MB of System Level Cache and a 512-bit memory interface, while the small die has 20 cores, 24 MB of cache and a 256-bit interface. The CPU chiplet holds 18 CPU cores in three clusters, a 16-core Neural Engine of eight dual-cores, four Display Engines, a 4-lane Display PHY and 16 lanes of PCI-Express, most likely Gen 5, in four 2x2 clusters.

SemiAnalysis said the M5 Ultra's UltraFusion link reaches more than 6x the connection density of the M3 Ultra, which implies hybrid bonding and rules out solder. It said the teardown was inferred, not measured, for the Ultra, reconstructed from a second, larger interconnect on the large GPU die plus Apple's own density claim. It said copper-to-copper bonding can be pitched below 10 µm, versus microbumps stuck at 25 µm, and approaches 3 µm in the most advanced processes. It said the result is the highest quality interconnect you can think of, almost like fusing the metal layers, creating one large coherent chip. It said it is not unlikely that Apple worked on the solution directly with TSMC, and closed with the aside, Can't innovate anymore my ass.

SemiAnalysis said the M1, M2 and M3 Ultra simply took two of the largest dies of a generation and fused them in a classic multi-chip-module arrangement. It said the M3 Ultra used InFO-LSI packaging with a local silicon interconnect and solder-based microbumps, and that measurements show a 25 µm bump pitch. It said the SoIC-mH is the same hybrid bonding behind AMD's 3D V-Cache, but deployed side by side rather than stacked, and that the mH stands for molding horizontally. It said placing the chips side by side avoids the heat trapping of a vertical sandwich, citing the A20 Pro's move to WMCM packaging with memory moved beside the chip. It said the twelve new P-cores, internally called M-cores, are split into two mirrored six-core clusters, each with 8 MB of shared cache and a dedicated matrix engine, and that the S-core cluster is slightly asymmetrical with two S-cores above and four below a shared 16 MB cache.

SemiAnalysis said the CPU die, at roughly 168 mm², is actually larger than a base M5, and that the small GPU die is essentially the large one cut in half, which it suggests shortens development time. It said the four Thunderbolt 5 PHYs outclass the M-cores in size and are not far behind an S-core, and flagged how big analogue SerDes are becoming and how much space the command-and-control area is taking up. It said the 16-core Neural Engine has since been doubled on the M6, and that only the M5 Ultra gets twice the AI hardware because it uses two CPU chiplets. It said it speculates the two-cluster split may be for power management, letting an entire cluster shut off when idle. It said hybrid bonding raises bandwidth and cuts the energy cost of moving data, making it a packaging moat as much as a process one, and puts TSMC's advanced packaging roadmap at the center of Apple's silicon story the way N3P once was.

SemiAnalysis said the first physical analysis of the M5 Ultra will either confirm the two-Max construction or complicate it. It said the other thread worth watching is whether side-by-side hybrid bonding spreads to other Apple products, given the company's apparent shift toward heat-conscious packaging across the A20 Pro and M5 lines. It said the signal for investors is that advanced packaging is becoming a competitive battleground in its own right. It said to watch whether AMD, NVIDIA and the hyperscalers' in-house silicon follow Apple into side-by-side hybrid bonding, and whether TSMC's packaging capacity, not its wafer capacity, becomes the binding constraint on the next generation of high-end processors. It said Apple had access to hybrid bonding for some time, as other TSMC customers did, but waited for the side-by-side implementation.

stories.Headline: Keysight launches Chiplet 3D Interconnect Designer for multi-die 3D IC routing and simulation
stories.Summary:
Keysight Technologies has introduced a tool called Chiplet 3D Interconnect Designer, which is meant to streamline the design of chiplet and multi-die 3D IC systems, according to an Electronic Design article published on November 20, 2026. The article, written by William G. Wong, says the tool provides pre-layout workflows for defining, routing, and simulating chiplet interconnects. Wong spoke with Hee Soo Lee, the High Speed Digital Segment Lead at Keysight, about the product in a video that accompanies the article. The tool supports interconnect standards such as UCIe and Bunch of Wires, which is also known as BOW.

According to the article, the designer is used to define silicon and organic interposer systems for chiplet interconnects and to simulate and test those designs. Its electromagnetic-based simulation is described as delivering precise electrical analysis of 3D package interconnects as well as printed-circuit-board designs. The tool can also create microbump maps, vias, and bus interconnects for chiplet and multi-die work. In addition, automated autorouting support for via structures is said to reduce manual operations in the design workflow.

Hee Soo Lee, identified as the High Speed Digital Segment Lead, discussed the tool with Wong, and the conversation is available in the video embedded in the article. The article does not include direct remarks from Lee beyond that discussion, and it presents the tool's features as described above. Wong is the author of the piece and serves as Senior Content Director for Electronic Design and Microwaves & RF. The article lists Marie Darty among its contributors.

The article places the tool in the context of chiplet and multi-die 3D IC design, which it says can be streamlined using Keysight's product. It does not state pricing, availability dates, or performance benchmarks for the designer. The piece also does not say what happens next with the tool or how customers can obtain it. More to follow.
