stories.Headline: KPMG runs an AI-assisted audit alongside a conventional one for a FTSE 250 company
stories.Summary:
KPMG deployed more than 100 AI agents alongside its conventional audit of an unnamed FTSE 250 company, according to the Financial Times. The agents gathered and analysed information, documented their work and produced draft conclusions. They also suggested next steps. The experiment was reported on 19 November 2026 by Claudine Cassar. KPMG ran two audits alongside each other: its conventional audit and an experimental AI-assisted audit called Project Exponential.

An audit partner signed off the experimental work, but KPMG based its statutory audit opinion on the conventional audit. KPMG did not rely on the AI-assisted exercise when issuing its audit report. KPMG built the agents in four months. Two partners and a director worked with senior managers and junior staff to build and run them, although the firm declined to disclose the team's exact size. Humans set the agents' objectives, supplied information about the business and previous audits, reviewed their work and challenged their conclusions.

KPMG's UK head of audit, Cath Burnet, said that in some situations the technology asked better questions than the human team. Burnet described instances in which the agents investigated issues more deeply, saying "the AI was able to go so much deeper". In one area, a person intervened after an agent failed to match regulations to company documents. KPMG's pilot does not establish better audit quality overall. Deeper questioning still needs to produce reliable evidence.

PwC argued in its 5 August submission to the PCAOB that the use of AI by companies and auditors should become the board's foremost priority. PwC sought guidance on automation bias, explainability, traceability and the ability to reconstruct AI-generated work. PwC identified the need to assess the relevance and reliability of audit evidence and to maintain professional scepticism even when an AI output appears plausible. PwC also identified the need to ensure that agentic workflows allow adequate human oversight and intervention. Wayne Banks has warned about automation deference, the weakening of scepticism when reviewers become accustomed to plausible, professionally presented AI output.

KPMG US has redesigned its audit internship training around fraud scenarios, incomplete information and critical thinking. PwC is introducing critical-thinking and judgement certification for more than 85,000 professionals, including simulations that require employees to challenge AI-generated conclusions. In his examination of Arthur Andersen's training model, William Englehaupt argues that firms must reconsider staffing, promotion and incentives alongside formal instruction. The traditional audit pyramid distributes work across different levels of experience and provides a route through which recruits become managers, directors and partners. That structure also supports the economics of the partnership, with a relatively small group of senior professionals directing and reviewing work carried out by a much larger workforce.

If agents reduce production work, firms could operate with smaller teams. If reviewing their conclusions requires a greater proportion of experienced staff, those teams may also become more senior. The effect on costs and partner leverage would depend on how much production work disappears and how much review remains. The commercial risk is that firms reduce their staffing pipeline before they understand the sustained demand for human expertise. Firms may need fewer people to produce the work, but they will still need people capable of challenging it.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Cloud host reports AI API key exposure as PHP fixes critical flaws
stories.Summary:
A cloud hosting platform disclosed in October that an unauthorized third party may have accessed encrypted environment variables and, for some of them, obtained the decrypted contents. The platform said those variables may contain secrets such as API keys or database and registry credentials. It advised customers to immediately roll all environment variables. The platform said the impact may be limited to a subset of users. It said it believes the incident is part of a series of attacks on platform companies aimed at compromising AI inference providers.

The platform said it has since invalidated all of its API tokens. In a preliminary report, it said the attack was attempting to obtain AI provider API keys. It said at most 1.85% of workspaces had some environment variables potentially compromised. It said it is not yet able to share the specific details and scale of the exploits. The same day, the PHP project released fixes for two critical flaws that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution.

Both PHP flaws are rated 9.2 under CVSS v4.0 and affect all PHP installations serving web requests. The PHP project says there are no complete mitigations and updating is the only safe choice. Versions 8.1 and older are past end of life and get no new official release. For 7.4 through 8.1, the project posted only minimal source patches. Steven de la Fe wrote the Accounting Today article published November 20, 2026, at 9:00 a.m. EST.

De la Fe said an API key is a password that software uses, and an agent often uses one to pull a trial balance or read a client file. He said that if a key leaks from a breached host or an unpatched server, whoever holds it can get whatever the agent could get. He said that makes it a Safeguards Rule issue. In July, the IRS Office of Professional Responsibility said firms in the business of completing income tax returns are defined as covered financial institutions under the FTC Safeguards Rule. IRS Publication 5708 adds that this holds regardless of size and that a written information security plan is required.

De la Fe said the rule requires each authorized user to get only the customer information they need, and customer information to be encrypted at rest and in transit. He said the rule also requires multifactor authentication, monitoring and logging of user activity, and contract oversight of service providers with periodic checks. He said firms that do not qualify for the small-institution exception (314.6) must also run continuous monitoring or periodic penetration testing and vulnerability assessments. He said none of that mentions AI agents, and he would treat an agent's key like an authorized user. He said the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications names excessive functionality, excessive permissions and excessive autonomy as typical root causes when agents overreach.

De la Fe cited a January 2025 technical blog in which NIST's AI safety team, now its Center for AI Standards and Innovation, wrote that many AI agents are vulnerable to agent hijacking. He said the finding came from lab tests in simulated environments, not field data. He said an attacker hides instructions in data the agent reads, which in a firm includes client emails and uploads. He proposed a one-page AI key and patch policy for a partner to sign, with seven of 10 lines tied to the rule or IRS guidance. He said line 7 follows CISA's advice and lines 4 and 5 are his recommendations.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: AI literacy: The next core CPA competency?
stories.Summary:
Akhila Chandrashekar, chief learning officer and a qualified CPA, CMA, CIA and CFE, published an opinion article on November 20, 2026, in Accounting Today arguing that AI literacy should become a core competency for certified public accountants. She opened with a hypothetical in which a CPA asks an AI tool to research a complex tax issue and receives a polished report with regulatory citations and a confident recommendation, only for the CPA to discover the regulation does not exist because the AI fabricated it. She wrote that when something goes wrong the client will not sue the AI company but the CPA, because the accountant remains accountable. The article asks whether AI literacy should become a core CPA competency and notes that the profession's exam already acknowledges AI.

The article states that the AICPA's 2026 CPA Exam Blueprints explicitly added artificial intelligence to the Auditing and Attestation section, where students are expected to understand confidentiality risks in using AI tools, recognize how AI adoption could affect the risk of material misstatement, and evaluate the accuracy, completeness, authenticity and potential bias of AI-prepared information. The 2027 CPA Exam Blueprints, effective January 2027, make what the article calls a nuanced but meaningful change, shifting terminology in AUD17 from information prepared using technologies including AI to information generated using those technologies, and AUD18 explicitly identifies AI-generated information among potential sources of audit evidence. The article stresses that the 2027 blueprint did not introduce AI verification for the first time, since those responsibilities were already reflected in 2026, and it does not create a separate AI examination. Chandrashekar describes the change as a step forward but not a leap, and she argues that foundational AI literacy should be assessed across the CPA exam's Core sections, with more advanced competencies addressed through specialization.

Chandrashekar illustrates AI literacy by contrasting two accountants using the same tool, one who copies results into a report and sends it to management and another who checks the underlying data, questions unusual assumptions, verifies calculations, investigates inconsistencies and documents the review. She defines AI literacy not as writing clever prompts or knowing which tool is trending but as understanding AI's limitations, detecting fabricated information, protecting confidential data, recognizing bias and knowing when human judgment must override a machine's recommendation. She gives sample exam scenarios, including an AI-recommended tax deduction supported by three authoritative-looking citations where one is fabricated, one is outdated and one does not apply, and an AI system that finds no significant revenue anomalies in a dataset that excludes the final month of the financial year. She also raises the case of a CPA who passed the exam 15 years ago and may never have studied generative AI, hallucinations or algorithmic bias yet could now be approving AI-assisted tax advice, supervising automated audits or signing off on AI-prepared financial reports, and she asks whether continuing professional education should evolve to teach identifying errors, challenging outputs, protecting client information and remaining accountable.

The article credits the AICPA for recognizing AI-related risks in the 2026 blueprints and for making AI-generated evidence more explicit in 2027, and it concludes that there is a burning need for AI literacy to become a core competency for every CPA. Chandrashekar writes that in a profession built on skepticism, evidence and trust, the greatest risk is not what AI does not know but that accountants may not know what AI does not know. The article does not say what action, if any, the AICPA or state boards plan to take on making AI literacy a core competency or on changing continuing professional education requirements.

stories.Headline: Justice department launches Super Intelligence Task Force to coordinate AI enforcement
stories.Summary:
The Department of Justice has launched a Super Intelligence Task Force, known as DOJ-SITF, to promote American artificial intelligence and to coordinate criminal and civil enforcement against actors who misuse AI, according to a November 19, 2026 article by McCarter & English attorneys Lindsey R. Harteis, Zachary Myers and Erin Prest. The Attorney General’s press release announcing the Task Force signals that enforcement will be forthcoming for those who use AI to engage in fraud or other criminal conduct. The new body merges the Artificial Intelligence Task Force that the former Attorney General announced in January 2026. Under Executive Order 14434, the executive branch uses the terms Super Intelligence and SI instead of Artificial Intelligence or AI.

The Task Force is charged with organizing the Department’s criminal and civil enforcement efforts involving AI and with deconflicting investigations, cases and other matters among Department components and United States Attorneys’ Offices. It will recommend enforcement priorities meant to promote public safety and prevent misuse of AI, serve as the Department’s point of contact with the President’s separate AI Task Force and other federal agencies, and coordinate the Department’s affirmative civil litigation involving AI. It will also develop guidance on prosecuting AI-related unlawful conduct and on evaluating compliance measures, and advise on legislative or regulatory proposals that promote AI innovation without burdensome regulation. The announcement does not establish a new regulatory or legislative framework for AI, so potential enforcement would proceed under existing laws.

The Task Force will be led by the Attorney General or his designees, with the Associate Attorney General and Associate Deputy Attorney General serving as co-chairs. Additional members will include representatives of the Antitrust Division, the Attorney General’s Advisory Committee, Civil Division, Criminal Division, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the National Fraud Enforcement Division, the National Security Division and the Office of the Solicitor General. The DOJ release says the Task Force will ensure a comprehensive approach across the Department and will ensure that America’s leadership in AI is not compromised by misuse by foreign state and state-sponsored actors, transnational criminal organizations, and individual or corporate actors engaged in fraud or other unlawful conduct. The Task Force will work in partnership with the separate AI Task Force established by President Trump.

The article says the DOJ does not explain what constitutes misuse of AI or establish the precise scope of conduct that could result in civil or criminal liability. It says companies’ use of AI in connection with government payment claims, cybersecurity controls, and representations made while negotiating and performing government contracts could present potential exposure under existing federal statutes. Using AI to present false claims for payment from the government, failing to maintain necessary cybersecurity controls while using AI resources, and making material misrepresentations about AI use in government contracts might conceivably result in liability, according to the article. The authors write that companies should understand the Task Force’s objectives and composition and should consider steps to mitigate potential civil or criminal exposure from their use of AI technologies and platforms.

stories.Headline: Mid-cap Indian IT firms buy AI skills as acquisitions outpace organic growth
stories.Summary:
During Coforge's Q2 earnings call, an analyst asked Chief Financial Officer Saurabh Goel to explain the gap between consolidated and organic growth. Revenue grew 10.9% sequentially in constant currency, against organic growth of 3.8%, indicating how much acquisitions are supplementing the company's growth. Goel attributed the difference partly to the consolidation of a full quarter of Encora's revenue in Q2, compared to only two months in Q1. Encora, the digital engineering firm Coforge acquired for ₹22,090 crore, contributed ₹1,382, 1,391 crore in revenue. It contributed about ₹940 crore during the two months included in Q1.

Q2 was busy not just for Coforge, but also for Cyient and Mphasis, which acquired data engineering and decision intelligence firms. Meanwhile, Persistent is expected to complete its acquisition of Nagarro in the first quarter of 2027. Coforge said its AI-led engineering, data integration, and cloud businesses contributed 86% of consolidated revenue. Mphasis said AI-led deals accounted for 66% of its ₹4,380 crore in net new total contract value. Zensar reported that AI-influenced deals made up 36% of its order book, while Sonata Software put AI-led order bookings at 25%.

Gartner's Distinguished Vice President Analyst Milind Govekar tells AIM that most mid-tier companies are acquiring to get new skills and new technology. Coforge has already integrated Encora into its business, and the company no longer distinguishes between the two entities. Coforge's consolidated EBIT margin stood at 16%, against 17% for its standalone business. Integration costs reached about ₹160 crore, exceeding the company's guidance of ₹141 crore to ₹150 crore. Cyient acquired AI-native data engineering firm TAO Digital for ₹2,049 crore, and TAO contributed ₹90 crore in its first month.

Excluding the acquisition, organic revenue grew 1.6% sequentially and 0.4% year-on-year in constant currency. CFO Shrinivas Kulkarni said TAO's annual revenue run rate had risen from about $80 million (₹752 crore) at acquisition to nearly $100 million (₹940 crore). He expects it to reach ₹1,034 crore over the next 12 months, while cautioning against extrapolating from one month's revenue. Cyient now plans to take TAO's AI data engineering capabilities to existing customers. The company's technology order intake rose 39.7% during the quarter.

Persistent secured approximately 94.04% of Nagarro's share capital and voting rights, excluding treasury shares and including its existing holding. The deal awaits RBI approval and foreign investment clearances in Austria and Spain. The acquisition would expand Persistent's European presence through Nagarro's delivery centres in Romania, Portugal, Hungary, and Poland. Persistent's European revenue fell 8.5% year-on-year in Q2 in US dollar terms, which it attributed to two client-specific events. North American revenue grew 22.5%.

Persistent booked ₹185 crore in Nagarro-related transaction costs in Q2, including advisory, financing, and legal expenses. Its PAT margin was 7.5% and operating PAT margin 10.6%. It expects another ₹235, 282 crore in costs over the next two quarters, taking cumulative one-time expenses to approximately ₹420, 467 crore. Mphasis acquired Canadian decision-intelligence firm Theory and Practice Business Intelligence (TAP) in April and expects to complete its acquisition of IT staffing firm Red Oak Tech's customer contracts, worth up to ₹265 crore, in November. CFO Aravind Viswanathan cited TAP-related amortisation as a pressure on margins during the earnings call.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Brazil's Senate approves an AI regulation bill while Peru enacts a general AI law
stories.Summary:
Brazil’s Senate approved a bill on December 10, 2024 regulating the use, development, and deployment of AI, and that general framework remains before a special committee in the Chamber of Deputies with no vote date confirmed. On February 25, 2026, another law turned Brazil’s National Data Protection Authority into a full regulatory agency with greater technical, administrative, and financial authority. Peru passed legislation in 2023 establishing principles including data privacy, the development of national AI talent, and cooperation on AI development at home and abroad. In 2025, a supreme decree approved regulations implementing Peru’s law, setting out financing provisions, accountability mechanisms, and implementation periods. The Atlantic Council published the analysis on November 19, 2026, written by Olivia Torres, a project assistant at its GeoTech Center, and Angel Ortega, a Panamanian attorney and policy researcher.

An attached proposal in Brazil would expand the role of the National Data Protection Authority, making it the default AI regulator alongside sectoral regulators. Peru’s 2023 law designates regulatory authority to the existing Secretariat of Government and Digital Transformation. Peru’s 2025 decree clarifies how responsibilities are divided among government institutions and enforcement authorities, and provides that when the Secretariat encounters a regulatory breach it has authority to consult the competent authorities. In Peru, the National Data Protection Agency handles AI-related personal data breaches, the National Institute for the Defense of Competition and Protection of Intellectual Property handles industry competitiveness and consumer protection, and the National Police specializes in cybercrimes. The Organization of American States launched the Inter-American Framework on Data Governance and Artificial Intelligence, known as MIGDIA, a regional initiative developed by multisector stakeholders and governments.

Ahead of the 2026 Brazilian elections, Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court issued fourteen resolutions governing the electoral process, including restrictions on AI use. The resolutions barred AI systems from recommending candidates or signaling voting preferences and required disclosure of AI-generated or digitally manipulated campaign content. The court was able to enforce the resolutions through the suspension of profiles. Dilmar Villena, director of Hiperderecho, one of Peru’s leading digital safety organizations, warned the authors in an interview that without additional resources institutions will have limited bandwidth to oversee all emerging AI technology concerns. Villena noted that oversight of most emerging technologies, including cloud computing and platform regulation, falls under the Secretariat of Government and Digital Transformation, which faces concerns around its budgetary capacity due to its reliance on funding from the Presidency of the Council of Ministers.

Brazil’s first AI proposal was criticized for insufficient inclusion of Indigenous voices in the legislative debate and failure to consider structural racism in public security. São Paulo’s Smart Sampa city surveillance pilot project was heavily scrutinized by civil society since its presentation in 2022, as it was found to disproportionately profile black individuals. Brazil’s legislative debates incorporated concerns about racial discrimination and other contextual issues. Peru has launched digital government indicators that track the implementation of digital government initiatives and institutional capabilities and show where administrative capacity is thin. The indicators do not yet measure whether AI implementation itself is working, but are described as an important building block for future institutional readiness assessments.

Countries in Latin America are developing AI regulatory frameworks, many drawing on European regulatory traditions, from data protection to emerging risk-based AI rules. Brazil and Peru have become regional leaders in regulation while still at an early stage of AI governance, pioneering different approaches. Brazil has begun strengthening its institutions while its general AI framework remains in development, and Peru has become one of the first Latin American countries to pass a general AI law coupled with implementation mechanisms. One MIGDIA recommendation is to clearly define the processes, roles, and responsibilities of actors involved across the data lifecycle. Brazil has already taken steps in this direction by assigning a role of AI regulator to the National Data Protection Authority.

Brazil is developing authority before its regulatory framework is concretized into law, while Peru has a more clearly assigned authority now that AI legislation has been approved and is beginning to be applied. The articles leave open whether Brazil’s Chamber of Deputies will vote on the general AI framework and when. They leave open whether the attached proposal making the National Data Protection Authority the default AI regulator will be adopted. They leave open whether Peru will scale up institutional resources as regulatory responsibilities expand. They leave open whether Peru’s digital government indicators will later measure whether AI implementation itself is working.

stories.Headline: Bajaj Finserv and Pennant Technologies invest $4 million in Soket AI as it launches EKA-1 model
stories.Summary:
Bajaj Finserv's applied research initiative Finserv Intelligence invested about $2 million in AI research company Soket AI, and its investee firm Pennant Technologies put in a further $2 million in the same round, for a total of $4 million. Soket AI, which is backed by the IndiaAI Mission, also launched EKA-1, a 26-billion-parameter foundation model under Project EKA, its flagship sovereign AI initiative focused on math, code and reasoning. The model is being built to support over 100 languages, including Indian and Global South languages, alongside programming languages. The investment supports Soket AI's work on indigenous AI solutions for applications where data security, reliability and technological sovereignty are critical.

Sanjiv Bajaj, Chairman and Managing Director of Bajaj Finserv, said in a statement that demand is for AI systems that are not only intelligent but also reliable, secure, auditable and able to operate within trusted environments. He said the group is investing in indigenous research that meets these requirements. Rajeev Jain, Vice Chairman and Managing Director of Bajaj Finance, said the next phase of AI will be defined by outcomes delivered at sustainable cost. He said Soket AI's efficient reasoning-led models can make advanced AI economically viable for financial services while allowing the firm to deploy it securely within its own infrastructure, with full control over data. He added that the startup's depth in Indian languages can help the firm serve customers in the language they are comfortable with.

Abhishek Upperwal, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Soket AI, asserted that the backing of Bajaj Finance and Pennant Technologies reinforces the company's belief that India has the talent and capabilities to develop foundational AI technologies at a global scale. Pradeep Verma, Founder and Managing Director of Pennant Technologies, said the firm is building agentic AI into its lending platform so banks can use AI across their operations while retaining control over their data and decisions. He said there is a clear need for locally built large language models that regulated institutions can run on their own infrastructure and govern under their own policies. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the launch and the funding.

stories.Headline: Texas senator Sarah Eckhardt urges statewide AI safeguards for schools as lawmakers convene
stories.Summary:
Last year, Texas lawmakers required public schools to restrict students' use of cell phones throughout the school day, including between classes, according to a Nov 19, 2026 Houston Chronicle opinion piece by Kris Perry. Artificial intelligence is now moving into classrooms, homework assignments, school-issued computers and the software teachers use every day, Perry wrote. When the Legislature convenes in January, Texas has an opportunity to lead the country again, she wrote. A 2026 Stanford University review examined a research repository containing over 1,600 papers on AI in K-12 education, Perry wrote. Only 52 studies met its standards for strong causal evidence, few examined long-term learning outcomes, and only five of the high-quality studies of student AI use took place in American K-12 classrooms, she wrote.

Perry called for statewide standards for AI products used by students, with providers required to demonstrate evidence of educational effectiveness and safeguards for student privacy, data security and developmental well-being before schools adopt a tool. Schools should know what information is collected, how it is used and whether students' interactions are retained or used to train AI systems, she wrote. A law should require meaningful human oversight, with teachers remaining responsible for instruction, assessment and decisions affecting students, and AI should never independently determine a child's academic progress, disciplinary consequences or access to educational opportunities, she wrote. Students should not be required to engage in unrestricted, emotionally responsive conversations with AI systems as part of their education, she wrote. The Texas Education Agency could establish an independent review process, publish approved-use guidance and maintain a transparent list of evaluated products, and schools should have the right to disable unnecessary AI features without losing access to essential educational services, she wrote.

Perry, executive director of Children and Screens: Institute of Digital Media and Child Development, wrote that Google has made access to search on school-managed devices contingent on accepting AI features built into the search engine. That puts schools in the position of accepting AI features they may not want simply to preserve access to a basic educational resource, she wrote. She asked who should determine how children learn: their teachers and communities, or the companies supplying their software. She wrote that a small rural district and a large urban district may have different educational needs, but children in both deserve the same basic safeguards and access to high-quality resources. She wrote that none of this requires banning every use of AI.

Perry wrote that some early studies suggest students can perform better on assignments when AI is available, but when the technology is removed, evidence of lasting learning is mixed. She wrote that evidence shows general-purpose chatbots do not support learning as well as tools designed to align with core pedagogical theory and practice, supporting learning through guided reasoning rather than supplying answers. She wrote that early research suggests AI may help teachers reduce preparation time, but schools should evaluate whether those savings preserve instructional quality. She wrote that carefully designed tutoring systems that guide students through problems rather than simply supplying answers may also prove useful, with educators directing their use and evidence determining whether they belong in classrooms.

She wrote that AI cannot solve budget shortfalls, academic struggles and shortages of individual attention, and that effective education depends on relationships with teachers, meaningful interaction with classmates and opportunities to work through difficult material with support. Perry wrote that a 2026 letter to Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick from State Sen. and Comptroller-elect Sarah Eckhardt calls for examining AI literacy, student safety and statewide guidance. She wrote that the work should become enforceable protections, not simply another set of recommendations schools are left to interpret on their own.

She wrote that parents should ask their state representatives and senators to support legislation establishing independent AI product review, strong student-data protections, meaningful teacher oversight and the ability for schools to reject unwanted AI features. She wrote that local school boards should be required to disclose which AI tools students encounter and how those tools are evaluated. She wrote that with its school phone law, Texas showed that protecting children can be a bipartisan priority. Perry wrote that the question is not whether children should learn about artificial intelligence, because they should.

She wrote that the question is whether we will allow companies to determine how children experience it before parents, teachers and researchers have established what is safe and educationally sound. She wrote that Texas still has time to make that choice. She wrote that Texas faces a harder version of the same question it answered with its phone law. She wrote that the goal should be to establish clear statewide guardrails for the use of AI in schools before a piecemeal approach becomes so widespread that meaningful oversight is difficult.

Articles.Title: Texas got cell phones out of classrooms. Now it’s time to confront AI. | Opinion - Houston Chronicle

stories.Headline: MIT and Mecalux find 57% of firms expect AI to make over a quarter of warehouse decisions autonomously by 2028
stories.Summary:
A study by the MIT Centre for Transportation & Logistics and Mecalux found that 57% of organisations expect AI to make or execute more than a quarter of warehouse operational decisions autonomously by 2028, based on a survey of nearly 2,000 supply chain and warehousing professionals across 21 countries. The report, published on 20 November 2026, examined generative and agentic AI in warehouse operations and found that 61% of organisations reported using generative AI at large-scale deployment or full integration, compared with 56% for agentic AI. About three in four deployments had been at their current stage for less than a year, yet 87% of generative AI applications and 81% of agentic AI applications showed at least moderate improvement in their target metrics. Only 39% of generative AI use cases and 36% of agentic AI use cases had significant gains that were both quantified and documented, and where respondents could estimate the scale, the typical gain was about 20% on the main target metric.

Companies are giving AI systems authority in selected areas while keeping tighter controls elsewhere, with inventory movements the area where agents were most often allowed to decide without human approval at 51% of agentic AI use cases, followed by data corrections at 42%. Only 22% of these systems were allowed to make customer-facing commitments and 12% were permitted to make financial decisions, and the most common oversight model was human-on-the-loop, in which AI operates within defined limits while employees monitor and can intervene. Organisations with comprehensive, actively enforced AI governance were about twice as likely to report significant, documented improvements, at 51% versus 26% for generative AI and 46% versus 23% for agentic AI, a pattern that held after accounting for deployment status, region, industry and budget, though the study noted association rather than proof of causation. Legacy system integration was the biggest constraint on scaling generative AI for 40% of respondents, while 54% said better integration with warehouse management and ERP systems would have the greatest effect on adoption.

Matthias Winkenbach, Director of the Intelligent Logistics Systems Lab, said the objective was to move beyond general sentiment and provide practical guidance on where these technologies deliver operational value today and where they remain experimental. Javier Carrillo, Chief Executive Officer of Mecalux, said warehouse decision-makers need AI they can measure and that the research gives clients a clear map of where the technology is working and what it takes to prove it. On employment, 56% of organisations said the technology had mainly shifted staff towards higher-value tasks, while 11% reported reduced headcount and 9% reported increased headcount, and 73% said they were upskilling warehouse-floor staff while 61% were creating new technical roles. Ninety per cent anticipated an increase in AI investment over the next two to three years, with 29% expecting that rise to exceed 25%, broadly in line with the previous year's study, and among companies that had fully integrated the technologies, 70% expected agentic AI to make or execute more than a quarter of warehouse operational decisions autonomously by 2028.

Articles.Title: Study finds AI will run more warehouse decisions by 2028 - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Lenexa Medical wins three VIC AI Awards including Best in Australia
stories.Summary:
Lenexa Medical, a Victorian health technology startup, won three prizes at the VIC AI Awards 2026 in Melbourne, where it was named Best Use of AI in Healthcare, AI Startup of the Year and Best in Australia, the awards recognising projects across technical and creative artificial intelligence categories with winners drawn from Victoria, elsewhere in Australia and overseas. The company was the biggest winner on the technical side of the program through its LenexaCARE product, and it has also been recognised by TIME Magazine as one of the world's top Health Technology companies. Other technical winners included Rostrum AI, which took the Best Enterprise AI Tool award for RostrumLink with Orato, and SPQR Technologies, which won Best AI for Safety for Aegis Runtime Control: Independent Execution Authority for AI Agents. The creative awards covered art, film, music and advertising made with AI tools, with Annelise (Wink.) Clark winning Best in AI Art for Cul-de-Sac Couture and the Best AI Campaign/Commercial prize going to Chapel Street Precinct Film, created by Toby Goodman and the team at CoastGen.

In the film categories, Glamourexia by John Paul DeFazio won Best in AI Short Films, while Edmond Yang took Best in AI Animation for When You Run From Your Mom, and the Best AI Music / Music Videos award went to Is This Not real? by Jason Joseph Dainter. A special Rising Star award went to Peek-a-Boo! A Bunny's Halloween Night, directed by Guillaume Descamps. Matt Kirby, Director of the VIC AI Awards and VIC AI Boom, said the quality of entries stood out before judging began, noting that submissions came from local Victorian individuals and companies alongside international ones and that startups without a profile yet sometimes blew the judges away. He also pointed to the commercial focus of the technical category winners, saying they are all driven by a real-world need and that it is easy to fall in love with the power of AI but there must be a worthwhile outcome for it to stack up commercially.

Kirby said two of the winning filmmakers showed how AI-assisted work could still rely on traditional storytelling strengths, saying both know how to tell a story and that AI is supporting their ideas but it is still driven by human emotion and creativity. The winners reflected a mix of Victorian startups, Australian creatives and international entrants, and the awards were intended to recognise achievements in AI innovation, creativity, consumer work and large-scale business applications. For Victoria's startup scene, Lenexa Medical's result is likely to draw the most attention because of the breadth of its wins, taking category honours in healthcare and the startup competition and then securing the overall Best in Australia award, which placed the company at the centre of this year's judging. Rostrum AI's award underlined the presence of local business software developers in the field, while SPQR Technologies' win highlighted the attention being paid to AI safety tools as the use of autonomous systems expands.

The results come as Australian AI activity continues to spread beyond large technology companies to specialist startups, creative studios and individual artists, and the list of winners suggests judges weighed both commercial application and creative execution across a wide range of work. Kirby said the event left him encouraged by what he had seen from participants, saying VIC AI Boom and the VIC AI Awards came along at the right time and that when everyone else is feeling tired at the end of the year he is feeling inspired by what he is seeing. He added that he cannot wait for the next event.

stories.Headline: Prompt engineering won’t make enterprise AI trustworthy. Data engineering will.
stories.Summary:
Arjun Danda Sureshbabu, a Staff Software Engineer at Snowflake, wrote in SD Times on 2026-11-20 that a few months into building an AI assistant for finance teams, someone asked it what bookings looked like for one region last quarter. The assistant answered in a few minutes with a table and a summary explaining how it got there, and the number was inaccurate. His first instinct was to blame the prompt, into which the team had put role instructions, worked examples and a long description of the schema. When he analyzed the query, the model had done exactly what was asked, finding a table with an AMOUNT column, a REGION_CD column and a date, and summing it up. The model could not know that the amounts included reversals, that region codes had been remapped after a reorg, and that bookings there means something narrower than every row in that table.

The article says most enterprise data was designed for applications and reports, not for a language model reading it cold, and that a finance table is mostly surrogate keys, status codes, amounts and timestamps. It says what those things mean is written down somewhere else, if at all, in a reporting team's SQL, a spreadsheet of code mappings, or the memory of an analyst who has been around for six years. It says a STATUS column with values 1 through 7 will lead the model to decide for itself what they mean, and it won't ask. It says describing the data in the prompt holds up in a demo with five tables and gets shaky at enterprise scale, because definitions and mappings change every quarter and nobody updates the prompt with each mapping change. It says a rule in the ninth paragraph can stop being honoured after a model upgrade, and you find out when a user does.

The article says the teams that get this right stop trying to explain the business to the model in prose and put that knowledge in the data layer, where developers already have tools to build, review and version it. It says that starts with a semantic layer instead of raw tables: named business entities, ontologies, metric definitions, plain-language descriptions of columns and their allowed values, their synonyms and accurate joins. It says bookings gets defined once, in code, and any change to that definition goes through review like everything else, and the model picks from definitions business teams have agreed on rather than creating on its own. It says access control stays in the database, enforced by the same row- and column-level policies that apply to every other query, so the data the model can reach has already been filtered. It says the third piece is making answers checkable, with verified queries reviewed by the owners of those numbers, and when the model writes something new it shows the query, definitions and filters it used.

The article says a prompt tends to belong to whoever wrote it, often one person tweaking it until the demo works, while definitions, policies and verified queries belong to an engineering team with code review, monitoring and someone on call when an answer goes wrong. It says the developers who do this well understand both the data model and the business it describes, sitting with a finance analyst to find out why a code was remapped two years ago and turning that into a definition the system enforces using patterns such as a verified query repository. It says data engineers and domain experts, who often sit at the edge of AI projects, end up doing some of the most important work. It says a better bar than a good demo is whether known or frequently asked questions return the same report the finance team consistently produces, which a human verifies, and whether each answer can be traced back to its definitions and source data. It says prompts still matter, setting the context surrounding the data and how the model asks a follow-up when it is unsure, but they sit on top of everything else.

The article says the author has seen versions of that failure many times since, and the usual response is to tune the prompt, which he thinks is the wrong place to look. It says you can tell the model not to show compensation data to the wrong person, but that is a request, not a permission check. It says moving to a bigger model does not help much, because it writes a more convincing guess and still has no idea when your fiscal year starts. It says you cannot really test a prompt the way you test code. It says most of this is ordinary engineering, schema design, contracts, authorisation and testing, and the unusual part is the consumer, which won't tell you when it's confused or fails silently.

The article says that when an enterprise AI system gives a confident wrong answer, the prompt is usually the last thing the author would change, and he would look first at what the data tells the model, the context layer and grounding factors, and at what it leaves the model to guess. It says the teams keep test sets of real questions with known answers, which is how they tell whether a change actually made things better or just felt like it did. It says the author designs and runs production AI systems that answer questions over enterprise finance data for finance teams and thousands of employees. It says a good answer in a demo tells you very little. It does not say what the finance teams did after the inaccurate answer, or when any of the changes it describes were made.

Articles.Title: Prompt engineering won’t make enterprise AI trustworthy. Data engineering will. - SD Times

stories.Headline: Digital.ai launches Release 26.3 to bring governed AI agents into enterprise delivery pipelines
stories.Summary:
Digital.ai unveiled Release 26.3 today, November 20, 2026, according to SD Times, elevating AI agents to first-class citizens alongside human developers and automated pipelines. The upgrade addresses risks from AI agents inserting themselves into production environments and taking ungoverned actions on code and workflows. It embeds agentic workflows directly into established compliance and governance frameworks, so organizations no longer choose between velocity and security. The release lets probabilistic AI agents operate in harmony with deterministic automations such as security scans and testing. Humans stay in the loop whenever policy demands it, the company announcement said.

Release 26.3 includes DevOps Agent Orchestration, which integrates context-aware AI agents into existing delivery flows and keeps every dynamic action fully auditable and compliant. It adds a Release MCP Server that lets developers and coding agents initiate, analyze, and optimize release pipelines from AI environments like Cursor, Claude Code, and Codex. A Release Assistant is a native AI companion helping release managers diagnose pipeline failures, optimize release velocity, and streamline troubleshooting. The release is available starting today, and existing users can immediately upgrade current templates to integrate AI across legacy infrastructure and modern cloud platforms. A flexible bring your own model approach lets enterprises use Digital.ai's hosted infrastructure or connect their own internally approved AI models.

Derek Holt, CEO of Digital.ai, said enterprise software delivery in the AI era combines AI agents, people and automation as companies accelerate their agentic journey from coding to delivery. He said customers need those three to work seamlessly together across all delivery pipelines. He said Release 26.3 brings the power of agents and AI into harmony with traditional DevOps automation and human judgement. He said this spans all delivery targets from mainframe and data centers to cloud and containers. The announcement frames the release as solving the tension between innovation and control.

The article says AI is shifting software development into hyperdrive while enterprise delivery pipelines face potential risks from ungoverned agent actions. It says the release allows probabilistic agents to work alongside deterministic automations while humans stay in the loop when policy demands. The article describes the upgrade as embedding agentic workflows into compliance and governance frameworks. It says organizations no longer have to choose between velocity and security. The affected parties are enterprises running delivery pipelines and release managers using the new assistant.

The article's background is that AI agents are inserting themselves into production environments and taking ungoverned actions on code and workflows. It says this creates tension between innovation and control for enterprise delivery pipelines. It says Digital.ai Release 26.3 addresses that tension by elevating agents to first-class citizens. It says the release embeds agentic workflows in established compliance and governance frameworks. It says the result lets probabilistic agents operate in harmony with deterministic automations.

Digital.ai Release 26.3 is available starting today, and existing users can immediately upgrade their current templates. Enterprises can choose Digital.ai's hosted infrastructure or connect their own internally approved AI models under the bring your own model approach. The article directs readers to learn more about Digital.ai Release 26.3. The article does not give pricing, a list of supported legacy systems, or details of how policy keeps humans in the loop. The article does not say how the Release MCP Server connects to Cursor, Claude Code, and Codex.

stories.Headline: E2E Networks falls for a fourth day as AI financing worries hit Indian tech stocks
stories.Summary:
E2E Networks shares fell to the lower circuit limit for a second straight session on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, extending the stock's slide to four consecutive days since October 15. The shares dropped 5 percent to Rs 627.15 on the NSE, the lowest level permitted for the day. The weakness spread to other AI-related stocks in India as global AI shares came under selling pressure. Moneycontrol reported the story on the same day, with its report published at 12:53 pm.

Among the other Indian names, Black Box shares slipped 1.55 percent to Rs 880.75 on the NSE. Netweb Technologies India declined 0.36 percent to Rs 4,683 per share at around 12.50 pm. A related headline from the site said Netweb and Black Box had fallen by as much as 9 percent during the broader slide. The article itself gave the smaller figures for the two companies at the time of writing.

The selloff was tied to worries about how the rising costs of AI development and infrastructure will be financed around the world. Concerns about the debt burden carried by CoreWeave added to the pressure on global AI stocks. Fears that higher interest rates could curb spending on AI infrastructure also weighed on technology shares, particularly chipmakers and data centre operators. The article did not name any company or official as having announced a specific decision behind the moves, and it attributed the decline to investor sentiment.

The pattern appears to have built up over several sessions rather than a single day, since E2E Networks has now fallen every day since October 15. An earlier Moneycontrol piece from October 13 carried a headline saying that E2E Networks, Hitachi Energy India and other AI-related stocks had fallen by up to 5 percent amid global jitters over AI. The articles did not say what would happen next for these stocks. The reports left open whether the concerns over financing costs and interest rates would ease or continue to weigh on the sector.

stories.Headline: Together AI launches hosted API for Qwen3 TTS to support live assistants
stories.Summary:
Together AI added hosted Qwen3 TTS on November 20, 2026, to provide a managed API layer for the open weights model. The company launched this service to help builders create live assistants rather than focusing on batch narration alone. This release follows the open sourcing of the Qwen3-TTS weights by the Alibaba team earlier in the year 2026. The service is available through serverless inference and dedicated endpoints for users who need steady isolation. Together AI aims to pitch a full stack of services including agent eval work and a Storage Accelerator.

The Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B model costs 20 dollars per 1 million characters, which is more than Kokoro at 4 dollars. It offers nine preset voices including vivian, serena, ryan, aiden, uncle_fu, dylan, eric, ono_anna, and sohee. These voices support ten languages including zh, en, ja, ko, de, fr, ru, pt, es, and it. Users can provide plain language delivery instructions up to 500 characters in the extra_params.instructions field to control the style. The system supports wav, mp3, raw, and mulaw formats with sample rates of 24000 Hz or 8000 Hz.

Together AI claims that its inference team tuned serving so first audio can start in as little as 97ms. Authors Anthony Ji, Charles Duong, Sebastien Beurnier, Sahil Yadav, and Sonny Khan credited the launch post on the company blog. They stated that the model separates who speaks from how they speak by using fixed voices with flexible instructions. The company suggests that this allows one branded voice to work across different European and Asian locales. Together AI notes that the 97ms figure is a hosted claim on their own specific serving stack.

Hacker News commenters noted that the time to first audio does not cap the total end to end conversational delay. Product owners are affected by the pricing, with a call center prototype of 50 million characters costing 1,000 dollars. Builders comparing open TTS options may look at Nari Labs, Hugging Face speech to speech defaults, or Zyphra's ZONOS3-Mini. Some teams may prefer self-hosting to avoid the per character meter or to keep audio on premises for compliance. Others might choose HeyGen on OpenRouter or DeepL Voice Aure when emotional range and translation are more important.

Alibaba's Qwen team released the weights earlier in 2026, leading to various local CPU stacks and serving optimizations. Nari Labs previously reported sub 50ms p95 time to first audio using one H100 with a custom stack. Together AI now provides a single invoice for speech alongside Llama or DeepSeek calls for teams using their platform. The model is positioned as a mid tier option, being cheaper than Cartesia Sonic 2 at 65 dollars. This managed layer removes the need for users to operate their own GPUs for Qwen's instruction steered presets.

Users must now benchmark the latency in their own regions rather than trusting the single blog number provided by Together. The documentation leaves open whether instructions work identically across every language, though demos show aiden reading English and others. There is currently no support for word level alignment or opus, aac, and flac output formats on this model. Seed reproducibility is listed as best effort only when the input, voice, and seed match. The articles do not state if custom voice cloning will be added to the Qwen3 hosted offering.

stories.Headline: Nebius shares drop as investors pull back from AI stocks
stories.Summary:
Nebius Group N.V. shares traded lower during the premarket session on Friday, November 20, 2026, as investors pulled back from artificial intelligence stocks. This decline followed a recent rally sparked by the initial public offering of Anthropic PBC and strong quarterly earnings from NVIDIA Corp. The stock fell nearly 5 percent to approximately 92.19 dollars while S&P 500 futures dropped 0.9 percent.

The market shift follows Anthropic pricing its IPO at 83 dollars per share, which exceeded the expected range of 70 to 78 dollars. Investors are now questioning if neocloud providers can secure the capital and capacity needed to sustain their growth. Evercore ISI noted that NVIDIA has provided roughly 32 billion dollars in neocloud financing to support an extraordinarily strong demand environment. CoreWeave Inc. has discussed revenues of 11 million dollars per megawatt, though long-term and short-term contracts can reach 20 million and 40 million dollars respectively.

Amit Daryanani, a senior managing director at Evercore ISI, stated that financing and capacity are greater constraints than customer demand. He explained that the long-term success of the sector depends on how durable the current demand for AI infrastructure proves to be. Daryanani also suggested that tighter GPU restrictions on Chinese companies might increase available capacity within the Western ecosystem. He described this potential shift as a secondary benefit rather than the primary driver for these stocks.

Nebius currently holds a Buy consensus rating from 24 analysts with an average price forecast of 240.64 dollars. Recent target adjustments include Citigroup lowering its target to 215 dollars on November 16, while Baird lowered its target to 200 dollars on November 13. DA Davidson also cut its target to 125 dollars on November 13 while maintaining a Neutral rating. The company continues to face intermediate pressure as its current price remains well below its 20-day and 200-day simple moving averages.

stories.Headline: Michael Burry claims he warned investors about AI companies following a market rout
stories.Summary:
Former Scion Asset Management fund manager Michael Burry claimed on X on November 19, 2026, that he had previously warned investors about several artificial intelligence companies. His comments followed a market rout on Thursday that saw shares of Nvidia, CoreWeave, and Nebius all decline. Nebius holders experienced a 9.4 percent loss, while CoreWeave and Nvidia holders lost 6.1 percent and 3.3 percent respectively. These losses occurred as Nvidia shares fell 19 percent since November 8, following the resignation of co-founder Jensen Huang.

The current market situation involves several specific financial positions and corporate changes for the mentioned firms. Michael Burry holds Nvidia puts with a 140 dollar strike price expiring in February 2027, and he doubled his put options on the Nasdaq-100 index on November 12. He also rebuilt a put position in the VanEck Semiconductor ETF, which includes Nvidia as a top holding. Meanwhile, Nvidia reported that revenue jumped 103 percent to 115.8 billion dollars in its first earnings report after Jensen Huang left the company.

Michael Burry stated that while he never explicitly told anyone to short these stocks, he provided the necessary information for investors to sell. ET TechGig will hold a free live online masterclass titled "Turn Conversations into Completion with AI Agents" on 30 November 2026 at 4:00 PM IST, as announced in its article published on 19 November 2026. The session features Mehar Ullipalem, Head of Solutions Engineering for India and SAARC at Zoom, and it includes a live walkthrough of how conversations can become completed work. The article says every meeting, call and chat generates information such as decisions, tasks and next steps, yet after the conversation ends the work often remains scattered across applications and documents. Teams then spend hours organising notes, tracking responsibilities and following up manually, and the session examines how connected information can bridge the gap between a conversation and completed work.

The masterclass has six modules, starting with the context gap, which explores why work slows when teams must reconstruct discussions, retrieve notes and track follow-ups after meetings or customer interactions. The second module covers making conversations actionable by bringing conversation intelligence from meetings, calls, chats and contact centre interactions together with company knowledge and connected third-party systems. The third module is a live walkthrough showing conversations becoming answers, meetings triggering workflows and projects moving towards deliverables, including natural-language interfaces that let teams describe an automation and create it without a traditional workflow builder. The fourth module explains how Model Context Protocol servers and APIs make scheduling, transcription, search, administration and contact centre actions available across AI environments, and the fifth explores AI agents that act on context, respond to external events and coordinate specialised agents, with a team lead agent consolidating their outputs into one deliverable.

The sixth module covers keeping humans in the loop, including access controls, visibility, business-specific rules and human review when agents work with enterprise information or prepare client-facing content. Ullipalem leads Solutions Engineering for India and SAARC at Zoom, with more than 20 years of experience across Unified Communications, Contact Centre and Digital Workplace domains, and the article says he translates complex business requirements into scalable enterprise solutions. The session explores Zoom's Unified Context Layer, which connects conversation history with relevant documents and business data to give people and AI agents a fuller picture of ongoing work. The article says AI needs to understand what happened, why it matters and what should happen next, because context is spread across meeting notes, calls, chats, company documents and enterprise applications.

It adds that decisions can get buried, employees manually transfer information between tools, AI assistants may lack context to answer usefully or act appropriately, and customers may repeat details when service teams cannot access previous interactions. The masterclass is designed for developers, application builders, software and platform engineers, solution and enterprise architects, AI and automation professionals, technology leaders, engineering managers, students and early-career technologists interested in enterprise integrations and AI-powered workflows. stories.Headline: Anthropic lists shares on Nasdaq as Congress stalls on AI safeguards
stories.Summary:
Anthropic began trading its shares on the Nasdaq Global Select Market on Thursday, 19 November 2026, as the first frontier AI developer. The company priced its initial public offering at 83 dollars per share on 18 November, raising a record 81.3 billion dollars. This debut follows a public registration statement on Form S-1 that the company filed with the SEC on 26 October 2026. The listing marks a watershed moment for a technology that may revolutionize American life while highlighting how Washington has fallen behind. This event coincides with a period of heightened scrutiny regarding the risks and rewards associated with the pioneers of artificial intelligence.

The company lists under the symbol ANT, having set an initial roadshow price range of 70 to 78 dollars on 10 November. A Long-Term Benefit Trust holds Class T stock and generally elects four of the seven directors on the company board. Anthropic must now file annual and quarterly reports with the SEC and is liable for any material misstatements in those filings. California's SB 53 law, effective 1 January 2026, requires developers with 500 million dollars in revenue to publish catastrophic risk frameworks. This law allows the Attorney General to impose civil penalties of up to 1 million dollars for each reported violation.

Anthropic stated its mission is the responsible development of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity in its official company prospectus. The company warned that its inventions are rife with catastrophic or existential danger to life and every area of human endeavor. It noted that a single catastrophic AI incident could exceed the capacity of the insurance industry if systems are misused or weaponized. President Donald Trump told reporters that the technology is almost completely good but that the bad elements must be managed carefully. Kevin Hassett, director of the National Economic Council, rejected warnings that the AI sector could face a wider financial sell-off.

Senator Elizabeth Warren wrote to chief executive Dario Amodei on 27 October 2026, arguing that the listing could bring volatility to retirement accounts. She asked how the company can meet fiduciary duties under Delaware law without reducing existential risks and requested answers by 3 November. Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the American AI Sovereign Wealth Fund Act on 18 June 2026, proposing a one-time 50 percent stock tax. Senator Ted Cruz blocked the Artificial Intelligence Risk Management and Security Act, which would require government safety reviews before any model release. Displaced workers and businesses are affected by a lack of federal measures to address mass job losses and the safety net.

The Trump administration and Republican majority in Congress have done little over two years to mitigate hazards like mass job losses. The Brennan Center tracker, updated 9 November 2026, shows only one of 56 bills from the 119th Congress became law. A Stanford Digital Economy Lab paper from 12 August 2026 found employment for young workers in AI-exposed jobs fell 19 percent. In Europe, the EU AI Act has allowed the AI Office to request documentation and impose fines since 2 August 2026. Anthropic published its Frontier Compliance Framework on 19 December 2025 to meet the requirements of the California Transparency in AI Act.

Governor Gavin Newsom recommended on 18 November 2026 that California extend its framework to include mandatory independent oversight and emergency shutdown authority. This proposal would require new legislation to limit recursive self-improvement and ensure that the AI developers are held to higher standards. Many federal bills intended to contain security threats or address the energy grid and tax code remain stuck in the Congress. The articles leave open whether Anthropic or Senator Warren's office will ever publish a response to the letter sent in October. It remains unclear if public shareholders can influence company changes because Anthropic is designated as a controlled company under its governance.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave and Humatica release a study on scaling proprietary enterprise AI
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave and Humatica released a joint study on November 20, 2026, regarding the scaling of proprietary enterprise artificial intelligence. This research examines how large organisations turn technological ambition into durable competitive value through resilient data architectures and internal governance. The study drew on insights from 252 enterprises across 14 industries and more than 30 interviews with senior executives.

The report finds that 66 percent of surveyed organisations operate models or processes that would fail if their systems were switched off. Only 35 percent of enterprises have a formal operating model, while executives cite organisational barriers 2.4 times more than technological limits. Seventy-three percent move critical workloads to self-controlled infrastructure for proprietary intellectual property, followed by data security at 55 percent and control at 45 percent. Cost and predictability motivate 36 percent of these moves, while 42 percent of production use cases started in business units. Finally, 24 percent of these AI projects were launched independently by employees or small teams.

Chen Goldberg, the CoreWeave Executive Vice President of Product and Engineering, stated that businesses are becoming dependent on AI faster than they can run it. She explained that bringing managed PostgreSQL into Kubernetes clusters reduces latency by keeping data calls local and handles replication, patching, and backups. Goldberg also noted that the connections between compute and data require the same engineering attention as the components themselves. She highlighted that CoreWeave achieved target quality on DeepSeek-V3 2.7 times faster than its GB200 run in MLPerf results.

Andy Knobloch, a Partner at Humatica, said that winning leaders are those who decide who owns each AI system and how it improves. He noted that almost half of production AI started in business units without a formal budget or an executive sponsor. The study affects enterprises that rely on AI for core functions but lack the governance to secure and monitor production systems. These organisations face vulnerability as initial pilots transition into mission-critical applications that require scalable deployment and strict security.

The articles state that CoreWeave is the first cloud to publish multi-rack Vera Rubin results in MLPerf and holds Platinum rankings in SemiAnalysis ClusterMAX. CoreWeave also holds first-place inference speed and price-performance rankings from Artificial Analysis for Moonshot AI's Kimi K2.6 and Kimi K2.7 Code. The company partners with CrowdStrike for security, VAST Data for storage, and ClickHouse for real-time analytics. Other partners include Wayve for autonomous driving and PhysicsX for industrial physics AI, while Humatica works with GloCoach for leadership development.

Next, enterprises can use CoreWeave Forge for scalable deployment and the ARIA tool to transform institutional knowledge into proprietary assets. The CoreWeave Zero Trust AI Framework provides security, while Mission Control offers real-time infrastructure visibility across the entire lifecycle. Companies may also use CoreWeave Direct-to-Expert support to pair internal domain knowledge with external engineering expertise. The articles leave open how many more enterprises will establish formal operating models to bridge the gap in organisational readiness.

stories.Headline: IAM Union president Brian Bryant urges collective bargaining as the guardrail for AI at work

The panel was convened by the College of Employment and Labor Lawyers to discuss the future of work, and Bryant used the appearance to speak out about the biggest tool workers have to make sure AI enhances their jobs rather than replaces them, which he said is their union. He explained that the IAM Union is not opposed to AI that improves vital safety protections at work or otherwise improves jobs, such as the use of AI in simulation safety trainings. At the same time, he called for increased protections against AI that would replace human work, and he said one of the best protections is a union collective bargaining agreement that lets members negotiate over how and when AI is used at work.

Bryant said that everyone is going to be impacted by AI, with some people adversely impacted and some positively impacted, and he noted that the union is already seeing the impact of AI. He said artificial intelligence was on the ballot and that what the country does with it really needs to take focus, adding that the people who voted are in fear of where this is taking the country and society and are asking whether guardrails will be up that protect workers. He said the union does see advantages of AI and looks at employers that share its perspective, so that if AI can enhance a person's job and let them produce more product quicker, safer and more efficiently, then the union is in favor of it being used. Bryant said the union has taken on the initiative to get the strongest language it can that addresses the need for an employer to sit down with the union when bringing in a new technology such as AI and to negotiate over the terms and conditions of how it impacts members. If jobs are going to transform because of AI, he said, the union wants to make sure members have a say in how that impacts their workplace.

Bryant pointed out that although corporations were present at a recent AI Summit convened by the White House, workers and their unions were conspicuously uninvited. He also cautioned that in some cases automation and AI bring neither safety nor public benefits, and in those instances he was clear that sometimes it is okay to just say no, citing Waymo as an example.
